Example: t=tiledlayout(1,2);ax=nexttile(t);isgraphics(ax)   % true
Differences from MATLAB: Tile index is 1 to 256.

## nnz
Count nonzero elements.
Syntax: nnz(A)
Returns the number of nonzero elements; for a sparse array, the number of stored entries.
Example: nnz([1 0 2])   % 2
Example: nnz(speye(4))   % 4
Differences from MATLAB: none known, also for complex input.

## norm
Vector 2-norm.
Syntax: norm(v)
Returns the Euclidean length of a vector.
Example: norm([3 4])   % 5
Differences from MATLAB: Vectors only, no p argument. Matrices are rejected.

## not
Logical negation.
Syntax: not(A)
Same as ~A.
Example: not([1 0])   % [false true]
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## num2cell
Put each array element in its own cell.
Syntax: c = num2cell(A)
Returns a cell array of the same size as A. Numeric and logical input only, at most 65536 elements.
Example: c = num2cell([1 2]); c{2}   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: Character input is not supported yet.

## num2str
Convert numbers to text.
Syntax: s = num2str(x)
Syntax: s = num2str(x, precision)
Syntax: s = num2str(x, format)
Integers print in full. Otherwise every element gets floor(log10(m)) + 5 significant digits, where m is the largest finite abs(x), kept between 5 and 16; so pi gives '3.1416'. A matrix gives one text row per matrix row. precision is the number of significant digits. format is a sprintf format such as '%8.3f'. Character input is returned unchanged. Complex and logical input is accepted.
Example: num2str(pi, 8)   % '3.1415927'
Differences from MATLAB: Complex input with a format is not supported yet.

## numel
Number of elements.
Syntax: numel(A)
Returns rows times columns.
Example: numel([1 2; 3 4])   % 4
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## numfields
Count a struct's fields.
Syntax: numfields(S)
Returns a double scalar counting the field names, independently of the number of struct elements. Empty structs can still have fields. Exactly one struct input is required.
Example: numfields(struct('a',1,'b','x'))   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet.

## nuttallwin
Nuttall minimum 4-term window.
Syntax: nuttallwin(n)
Syntax: nuttallwin(n, 'periodic')
Returns an n-by-1 column vector. The default is symmetric.
Example: w = nuttallwin(64);   % 64-by-1 column
Differences from MATLAB: Double output only.

## ones
Array of ones.
Syntax: ones(n)
Syntax: ones(r, c)
Syntax: ones([r c])
ones(n) is n-by-n. A size vector such as size(A) is accepted.
Syntax: ones(..., 'single')
Syntax: ones(..., 'like', single(1))
Example: ones(2, 'single')
Example: ones(2, 3)   % 2-by-3 array of ones
Class names 'single' and int8 through uint64 are accepted, as are typed integer/single 'like' prototypes.
Differences from MATLAB: Two-dimensional output only.

## openfig
Open a saved figure.
Syntax: f = openfig('plot.mrfig')
Syntax: openfig('plot.fig', 'new')
Loads .fig, .mrfig or .mfig files from the Current Folder into a new figure and returns its handle.
Example: plot(1:3); savefig('plot.mrfig'); f = openfig('plot.mrfig')   % figure opens, f is its handle
Differences from MATLAB: Only the filename and the 'new' option. At most 16 figures can be open.

## or
Element-wise logical OR.
Syntax: or(A, B)
Same as A | B. Inputs are converted to logical.
Example: or([1 0], [0 0])   % [true false]
Differences from MATLAB: Exactly two arguments.

## patch
Draw filled polygons.
Syntax: p = patch(x, y, c)
Syntax: p = patch(x, y, c, Name, Value, ...)
Syntax: p = patch(x, y, z, c, ...)
Syntax: p = patch('XData', x, 'YData', y, 'FaceColor', color, 'EdgeColor', edge)
Syntax: p = patch(ax, ...)
Syntax: p = patch(s)
Syntax: p = patch('Faces', f, 'Vertices', v, 'FaceVertexCData', c)
Draws triangles or axis-aligned quadrilaterals with corners (x, y) in the given axes or current axes. Supports color letters/names/RGB or 'none', plus FaceAlpha, EdgeColor, EdgeAlpha, LineStyle, LineWidth, DisplayName and Visible.
An isosurface or isocaps struct defines indexed 3-D triangles. Faces contain one-based vertex indices and FaceVertexCData, when supplied, contains a scalar per vertex. Indexed faces and edges default to black. Use FaceColor 'flat' or 'interp' to map FaceVertexCData through the axes colormap and color limits.
Example: a = gca; p = patch(a, 'XData', [0;1;0], 'YData', [0;0;1], 'FaceColor', [1 0 0], 'EdgeColor', 'none'); get(p, 'Type')   % 'patch'
Example: p = patch('Faces',[1 2 3],'Vertices',[0 0 1;1 0 1;0 1 2],'FaceVertexCData',[0;.5;1],'FaceColor','interp'); view(3);
Example: p = patch([0 1 1], [0 0 1], 'g', 'FaceAlpha', 0.3); p.FaceAlpha   % 0.3
Differences from MATLAB: patch(x,y,c) supports triangles and axis-aligned quadrilaterals. The XData/YData name-value form requires explicit FaceColor and EdgeColor. Indexed faces must be triangles, Vertices must have three columns, and FaceVertexCData supports one scalar per vertex. Interpolated faces use one averaged color per triangle.

## phasez
Unwrapped phase response of a digital filter, in radians.
Syntax: [phi, w] = phasez(b, a, n)
Syntax: [phi, f] = phasez(b, a, n, fs)
Syntax: [phi, w] = phasez(b, a, n, 'whole')
Syntax: phi = phasez(b, a, w)
Syntax: phi = phasez(sos, n)
Syntax: phi = phasez(d, n)
Same frequency forms as freqz (default 512 points, at most 65536). A zero response gives NaN and restarts the unwrapping. A bare call plots it.
Example: p = phasez([1 1], 1, 8);   % 8-by-1 column
Example: [phi, w] = phasez([0 1], 1, 4, 'whole');   % phi = -w
Differences from MATLAB: a zero response is NaN.

## pi
The number pi.
Syntax: pi
A constant, 3.14159265358979.
Example: 2*pi   % 6.2832
Differences from MATLAB: Written without parentheses.

## plot
2-D line plot.
Syntax: plot(y)
Syntax: plot(x, y)
Syntax: plot(x, y, style)
Syntax: plot(x1, y1, style1, x2, y2, style2)
Syntax: plot(x, y, 'LineWidth', 2, 'Color', 'red')
Draws y against x in the current figure. With one input, x is 1, 2, 3, ...
style is a short text such as 'r--o' (color, line style, marker).
Name-value pairs at the end apply to the new lines.
Use hold on to add lines instead of replacing them.
Complex Z in plot(Z) draws real(Z) against imag(Z).
Supports datetime, duration, and categorical coordinate arrays (also in line, scatter, bar, area, stairs, and stem).
Example: x = 0:0.1:10; plot(x, sin(x), 'r--')
Differences from MATLAB: up to 16 figures and 64 lines per figure; many line
properties are not supported yet.

## plot3
3-D line plot.
Syntax: plot3(x, y, z)
Syntax: plot3(x, y, z, style)
Syntax: plot3(x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2, ...)
Syntax: plot3(x, y, z, 'LineWidth', 2)
Syntax: plot3(ax, ...)
Syntax: h = plot3(...)
Draws lines through the points (x, y, z). x, y and z are vectors of one length, or matrices of one size (one line per column), or vectors next to a matrix as plot allows. style and name-value pairs are those of plot. NaN in any coordinate breaks the line. Lines are clipped at the axes box: a segment outside XLim, YLim or ZLim is not drawn, and a segment crossing the box ends at the box face.
With hold off the axes switches to the 3-D view, view(3) = (-37.5, 30); with hold on the current view is kept. ZData of each line holds z.
Errors: "plot3: not enough input arguments; X, Y and Z are required", "plot3: X, Y and Z must be vectors of the same length", "plot3: X, Y and Z matrices must be the same size", "plot3: vector lengths must match the rows or columns of the X, Y and Z matrices", "plot3: data must be given as X, Y, Z triplets of real numeric arrays".
Example: t = 0:0.1:10; plot3(sin(t), cos(t), t)   % a helix
Example: h = plot3([1 2 3], [3 1 2], [0 1 0], 'r-o'); h.ZData   % [0 1 0]
Differences from MATLAB: Real coordinates only. The axes box is drawn as with box on (outline of the three back planes, plus the axis lines; box off keeps the axis lines only); no hidden-line removal for lines. zticks, zticklabels and camera properties are not supported yet; surfaces are drawn by surf and mesh.

## polyfit
Fit a polynomial to data by least squares.
Syntax: p = polyfit(x, y, degree); [p,S] = polyfit(x,y,degree); [p,S,mu] = polyfit(x,y,degree)
Returns a row of coefficients in descending powers. x and y must be finite real vectors of equal length; logical inputs convert to double. Degree must be an integer from 0 to 4096, and the fitting matrix must fit the statement limit. Underdetermined and rank-deficient systems use a basic solution with dependent coefficients set to zero.
Example: round(polyfit(1:5,[1 4 9 16 25],2))   % [1 -0 0]
Differences from MATLAB: Ill-conditioned and rank-deficient coefficients can differ, and MATLAB's conditioning warnings are not printed. Underdetermined fits (fewer points than coefficients) work. For real inputs, S contains R (the unpivoted QR factor), df and normr. Three outputs center x by its mean and scale it by its sample standard deviation, returned in mu. Statistics require at least degree+1 points; normalization needs a positive finite scale. Complex multiple outputs are unsupported. Complex x or y is fitted by Householder QR of the Vandermonde matrix; the last digits can differ from MATLAB's MKL QR.

## polyval
Evaluate a polynomial.
Syntax: y = polyval(p, x); y = polyval(p,x,[],mu)
p holds coefficients from the highest power down (1 to 4096 values). Uses Horner's method.
Example: polyval([1 2 3], 2)   % 11
Differences from MATLAB: Finite inputs, one output. For real double inputs, mu=[center scale] evaluates at (x-center)/scale; the scale must be finite and positive. Error estimates are unsupported. Complex p or x is evaluated by the same recurrence; a result with zero imaginary parts is real.

## pow2
Power of two.
Syntax: pow2(X)
Syntax: pow2(F, E)
pow2(X) gives 2.^X. pow2(F,E) gives F.*2.^E, with E truncated toward zero.
Example: pow2(3)   % 8
Differences from MATLAB: Real double 2-D arrays, one output. F and E must have equal shapes or one must be a scalar.

## prod
Product along an array dimension.
Syntax: prod(A)
Syntax: prod(A, dim)
Multiplies along the first nonsingleton dimension by default: across a row vector, or down matrix columns. Dim 1 works down rows; dim 2 works across columns; dim above 2 leaves the values unchanged. Empty products are 1. Real, complex and logical inputs are accepted; logical inputs convert to double.
Example: prod([1 2;3 4],2)   % [2; 12]
Differences from MATLAB: Output-class and NaN-handling options are not supported for 2-D input. A complex product with zero imaginary parts is real. N-D arrays (part 2): dim, vecdim, 'all', 'omitnan'/'includenan' and 'double'/'native'/'default'; an integer product is double unless 'native', which saturates.

## rand
Uniform random numbers between zero and one.
Syntax: rand()
Syntax: rand(n)
Syntax: rand(m, n)
Syntax: rand([m n])
No size gives a scalar; one scalar size gives a square matrix. Values lie strictly between 0 and 1 and fill columns first. rand, randn and randi share one generator per engine session. Use rng to set the seed. An optional 'double' or 'single' class is accepted. Sizes must fit the matrix and statement limits; higher dimensions must be singleton.
Syntax: rand(..., 'single')
Syntax: rand(..., 'like', single(1))
Example: rand(2, 'single')
Example: rng(0); rand(1,3)   % [0.814724 0.905792 0.126987]
Differences from MATLAB: Legacy generator-state forms are not supported.

## randi
Uniform random integers in an inclusive range.
Syntax: randi(imax)
Syntax: randi(imax, m, n)
Syntax: randi([imin imax], [m n])
The scalar limit means 1 through imax. A pair gives inclusive lower and upper limits. Limits must be finite integers with absolute value below 2^53 and imin <= imax; a scalar imax must be at least 1. Sizes follow rand: no size gives a scalar and one scalar size gives a square matrix. Output is double, with optional 'double' accepted; higher dimensions must be singleton.
Example: rng(0); randi(10,1,4)   % [9 10 2 10]
Differences from MATLAB: Other output classes are not supported.

## randn
Normally distributed random numbers.
Syntax: randn()
Syntax: randn(n)
Syntax: randn(m, n)
Syntax: randn([m n])
Returns double values from a standard normal distribution. Sizes follow rand: no size gives a scalar and one scalar size gives a square matrix. Values fill columns first and share the session generator with rand and randi. Use rng to set the seed. An optional 'double' class is accepted; higher dimensions must be singleton, and sizes must fit the matrix and statement limits.
Example: rng(0); randn(1,3)   % [0.537667 1.833885 -2.258847]
Differences from MATLAB: Seeded normal values differ; do not expect identical MATLAB sequences. Other output classes and legacy generator-state forms are not supported.

## rank
Numerical rank from singular values.
Syntax: rank(A)
Syntax: rank(A, tolerance)
Counts singular values strictly greater than tolerance. The default is max(size(A))*eps(s), where s is the largest singular value. Empty input has rank zero. A must be finite and may be complex; logical input converts to double. An explicit tolerance must be a real numeric or logical scalar.
Example: rank([1 2 3;4 5 6;7 8 9])   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: Very small tolerances can give a different rank because the computed singular values differ.

## readmatrix
Read a numeric matrix from a text file.
Syntax: A = readmatrix('data.csv')
Syntax: A = readmatrix('data.csv', 'Delimiter', ';')
Syntax: A = readmatrix('data.xlsx', 'Sheet', 'Results', 'Range', 'B2:D20')
Syntax: A = readmatrix(filename, opts)
Syntax: A = readmatrix(filename, opts, 'OutputType', type)
With import options from detectImportOptions, every selected variable is read as a number (text that does not convert is an import error, NaN by default) and MissingRule, ImportErrorRule, DataLines or DataRange apply; 'OutputType' may be any numeric type or 'logical'.
Reads .csv, .txt or .dat files with numbers separated by comma, semicolon, tab or whitespace. 'FileType', 'text' allows other extensions. Spreadsheets (.xlsx, .xlsm, .xlsb, .xls, or 'FileType', 'spreadsheet') are read too: Sheet picks a sheet by name or 1-based index (default the first), Range picks a rectangle such as 'A1:C10' or a start cell such as 'B2'. Spreadsheet numbers and logical cells become doubles, every other cell NaN; without a Range, leading rows that hold no number (headers) are skipped.
Example: writematrix([1 2;3 4],'data.csv'); A = readmatrix('data.csv')   % 2-by-2 numeric matrix
Differences from MATLAB: Text files detect leading text headers; retained fields must be numeric. No ranges or missing-data options there. Spreadsheet header detection only skips leading rows without numbers; dates read as their Excel serial numbers; no named ranges. An .xls workbook is read whole and is limited to 16777216 cells over all its sheets.

## real
Real part.
Syntax: real(Z)
Returns the real part as a real array. Real input is returned unchanged.
Example: real(3+4i)   % 3
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## rectangle
Draw a 2-D rectangle or ellipse.
Syntax: r = rectangle('Position', [x y w h])
Syntax: r = rectangle(ax, 'Position', [x y w h], Name, Value, ...)
Draws a rectangle at [x y w h] in data coordinates. Supports Curvature (scalar or [cx cy] in 0..1; [1 1] draws an ellipse), FaceColor, EdgeColor, LineWidth, LineStyle and Visible.
Example: r = rectangle('Position', [1 1 2 3], 'Curvature', 1); r.Curvature   % [1 1]
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet.

## rectwin
Rectangular window.
Syntax: rectwin(n)
Returns an n-by-1 column of ones.
Example: rectwin(4)'   % [1 1 1 1]
Differences from MATLAB: No sampling option; double output only.

## rem
Remainder using division rounded toward zero.
Syntax: rem(A, B)
For finite inputs and nonzero B, a nonzero remainder has the sign of A. A zero divisor or a nonfinite input gives NaN. Inputs expand implicitly when their sizes match or one size is 1 in each dimension. Real numeric and logical inputs are accepted; complex input is rejected.
Example: rem([-7 7],3)   % [-1 1]
Example: rem([-5;-7],[2 3])   % [-1 -2;-1 -1]
Differences from MATLAB: none known, also for infinite divisors.

## repmat
Repeat an array.
Syntax: repmat(A, n)
Syntax: repmat(A, r, c)
Syntax: repmat(A, [r c])
repmat(A, n) tiles A n-by-n times.
Example: repmat([1 2], 2, 2)   % [1 2 1 2; 1 2 1 2]
Differences from MATLAB: Two-dimensional arrays only, including cell and struct arrays. Container results are limited to 65536 slots.

## reshape
Change the shape of an array.
Syntax: reshape(A, r, c)
Syntax: reshape(A, [r c])
One size may be [] and is computed. Elements are taken in column order.
Example: reshape(1:6, 2, 3)   % [1 3 5; 2 4 6]
Differences from MATLAB: Two-dimensional results only; trailing ones are accepted.

## rethrow
Raise a caught error again.
Syntax: rethrow(err)
Takes one scalar struct with a character message and optional character identifier. Raises that message and identifier for an enclosing catch block. The stack field is not restored, and an empty message still raises an error.
Example: try; try; error('r:q','rq 3'); catch e; rethrow(e); end; catch outer; disp(outer.message); end   % rq 3
Differences from MATLAB: MatRust uses structs with an empty stack, not MException objects.

## return
Stop the running function or script.
Syntax: return
In a function it returns to the caller. In a script it ends the run.
Example: for k = 1:3, if k == 2, return, end, disp(k), end   % prints: 1, then stops
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet.

## rmfield
Remove fields from a struct.
Syntax: T = rmfield(S, name)
Syntax: T = rmfield(S, names)
Accepts a character name or a cell array of names. Removes those fields from every element, preserving the struct shape and remaining field order. S is unchanged unless the result is assigned back to S. A missing field raises an error.
Example: s=struct('a',1,'b','x'); t=rmfield(s,'a'); t.b   % 'x'
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## rng
Seed or query the session's random number generator.
Syntax: rng(seed)
Syntax: rng(seed, generator)
Syntax: rng(generator)
Syntax: rng('default')
Syntax: rng('shuffle')
Syntax: s = rng
Syntax: s = rng(...)
Syntax: rng(s)
Controls the shared rand, randn, randi and randperm stream. Supported generators are 'twister' (default, MT19937), 'philox' (Philox4x32-10) and 'combRecursive' (MRG32k3a). Seed must be an integer from 0 to 2^32-1. 'default' selects 'twister' with seed 0; 'shuffle' derives a seed from the current time. s = rng returns a struct with Type, Seed and State (625x1 uint32 for 'twister'); s = rng(...) returns the previous settings; rng(s) restores the saved state.
Example: s=rng; a=rand(1,2); rng(s); b=rand(1,2); isequal(a,b)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: 'simdTwister', 'v4', 'v5uniform' and 'v5normal' are not supported. No claim that doubles match MATLAB bit-for-bit for 'philox', 'combRecursive', or randn.

## round
Round values to the nearest integer or to a specified precision.
Syntax: round(X)
Syntax: round(X,n) or round(X,n,'decimals')
Syntax: round(X,n,'significant')
Halves round away from zero. A finite integer n sets the number of decimal places, with negative n rounding to the left of the decimal point. In 'significant' mode, n is a positive count of significant digits. For complex input, each part is rounded separately.
Example: round(2.5)   % 3
Example: round(2.567,2)   % 2.57
Example: round(123.456,2,'significant')   % 120
Differences from MATLAB: Complex results with all imaginary parts zero are returned as real arrays.

## save
Save workspace variables to a MAT file or ASCII text.
Syntax: save('data.mat')
Syntax: save('data.mat', 'A', 'B', '-v7.3')
Syntax: save data.mat A
Syntax: save data.txt A -ascii -double -tabs
Without names it saves all variables. -ascii writes 2-D double arrays as text (complex arrays use their real parts); other types are skipped with a warning. An explicit ASCII filename is used as given. ASCII uses 8 significant digits by default and 17 with -double, spells special values Inf, -Inf and NaN, and separates columns with tabs when given -tabs. The default file is matlab.mat. Versions: -v6, -v7 (default), -v7.3; -nocompression needs -v7.
Example: A=5; save('data.mat','A')   % A is saved
Plain structs preserve field order, shape and supported field types. The -struct option takes a scalar struct variable name and optionally field names; each selected field is saved as a separate variable. Sparse fields are supported in -v6 and -v7; v7.3 sparse persistence remains unsupported. Nonempty nonscalar structs without fields are also rejected in -v7.3 because the group has no field-reference shape.
Differences from MATLAB: Statement only; no output assignment. No -append or wildcards. Objects and function handles cannot be saved.

## saveas
Save a figure in a chosen format.
Syntax: saveas(gcf, 'plot.svg')
Syntax: saveas(gcf, 'plot', 'svg')
Formats: fig, png, jpg, svg, pdf, bmp, tif, and 'epsc' when given explicitly. Call it as a statement.
Example: saveas(gcf, 'plot.svg')   % writes plot.svg
Differences from MATLAB: PNG, PDF and EPS export need the desktop build; SVG works everywhere. No monochrome or Level-2 EPS, EMF or M-file output.

## savefig
Save a figure to a file.
Syntax: savefig('plot.mrfig')
Syntax: savefig(n, 'plot.mrfig')
Saves the current figure, or figure n. Extensions are .fig, .mrfig (MatRust native) or .mfig.
Example: plot(1:3); savefig('plot.mrfig')   % figure saved
Differences from MATLAB: Statement only. No figure arrays, version or visibility options.

## sawtooth
Sawtooth wave.
Syntax: sawtooth(t)
Syntax: sawtooth(t, width)
Period is 2*pi. width is a scalar from 0 to 1 and sets where the peak occurs (default 1).
Example: sawtooth(pi/2)   % -0.5
Differences from MATLAB: Real double 2-D arrays only.

## gscatter
Scatter plot by group.
Syntax: gscatter(x, y, g)
Syntax: gscatter(x, y, g, clr, sym, siz)
Syntax: gscatter(..., 'doleg', 'off')
Syntax: h = gscatter(...)
Draws one marker-only Line per unique group in g (numeric, cellstr, categorical, or string) and adds a legend with the group names unless 'doleg' is 'off'.
Example: h = gscatter([1 2 3 4], [2 4 1 3], [1 1 2 2]);   % two grouped marker lines
Differences from MATLAB: Supports 2-D vector coordinates and 'doleg' option.

## scatter
Scatter plot.
Syntax: scatter(x, y)
Syntax: scatter(x, y, sz)
Syntax: scatter(x, y, sz, c)
Syntax: scatter(..., 'filled')
Syntax: scatter(..., marker)
Syntax: scatter(ax, ...)
Syntax: h = scatter(...)
Draws a marker at each point (x, y). sz is a scalar or per-point vector of marker areas in points^2 ([] keeps the default). c is a color name or RGB triplet, an n-by-3 matrix of RGB triplets, or an n-element vector mapped through the axes colormap and CLim. 'filled' sets MarkerFaceColor to 'flat'; marker is a symbol such as 'o', 's', 'd', or '^'. Name-value pairs and object properties include XData, YData, SizeData, CData, Marker, MarkerFaceColor ('none', 'flat', 'auto', or RGB), MarkerEdgeColor ('none', 'flat', or RGB), MarkerFaceAlpha, MarkerEdgeAlpha, and LineWidth.
Example: scatter([1 2 3], [2 4 3], [20 40 60], [1; 2; 3], 'filled')   % three markers with per-point size and color
Differences from MATLAB: Real coordinates only; no extra datasets in one call.

## scatter3
3-D scatter plot.
Syntax: scatter3(x, y, z)
Syntax: scatter3(x, y, z, sz)
Syntax: scatter3(x, y, z, sz, c)
Syntax: scatter3(..., 'filled')
Syntax: scatter3(..., marker)
Syntax: scatter3(ax, ...)
Syntax: h = scatter3(...)
Draws a marker at each point (x, y, z). sz is a scalar or per-point vector of marker areas in points^2 ([] keeps the default); c is a color name, RGB triplet, n-by-3 RGB matrix, or n-element vector mapped through the axes colormap and CLim, as for scatter. 'filled' fills the markers; marker is a symbol such as 'd' or '^'. Name-value pairs such as 'MarkerEdgeColor' and 'MarkerFaceAlpha' follow. Markers outside XLim, YLim or ZLim are not drawn.
With hold off the axes switches to view(3); with hold on the current view is kept.
Errors: "scatter3: not enough input arguments; X, Y and Z are required"; x, y and z follow the plot3 size rules and texts (with scatter3: in front). A line style such as 'r-o' is rejected with "scatter/bar support a single color letter; full line specs require plot"; give a color letter, a marker and 'filled' separately.
Example: scatter3([1 2 3], [3 1 2], [0 1 2], 36, 'r', 'filled')   % three red markers
Differences from MATLAB: Real coordinates only.

## semilogx
Plot with a logarithmic x axis.
Syntax: semilogx(x, y)
Syntax: semilogx(Z)
The y axis stays linear. A single complex array plots real(Z) against imag(Z).
Example: semilogx([1 10 100], [1 2 3])   % x on log scale
Differences from MATLAB: Properties are trailing name/value pairs such as 'LineWidth', 2.

## semilogy
Plot with a logarithmic y axis.
Syntax: semilogy(x, y)
Syntax: semilogy(Z)
The x axis stays linear. A single complex array plots real(Z) against imag(Z).
Example: semilogy([1 2 3], [1 10 100])   % y on log scale
Differences from MATLAB: Properties are trailing name/value pairs such as 'LineWidth', 2.

## set
Change properties of graphics and audio objects.
Syntax: set(h, 'PropertyName', value)
Syntax: set(h, 'Name1', value1, 'Name2', value2)
Audio players and recorders accept SampleRate while stopped, as well as Tag and UserData.
Up to 16 property and value pairs. Root defaults: set(0, 'Default<Type><Prop>', value) or set(groot, ...) sets session-wide defaults for newly created Figure, Axes, Line, Text, Patch, Surface, and Image objects (case-insensitive); pass 'remove' to restore the factory default or 'factory' to set the factory value. Figure-level defaults set(gcf, 'Default<Type><Prop>', value) apply to children created in that figure. Axes: XLim, YLim, XScale, YScale, XGrid, YGrid, NextPlot, FontSize, ColorOrder, Colormap, CLim and others. Figure: Name, Theme, ThemeMode, Color, Colormap, Visible. Lines: LineWidth, Visible, XData, YData. Titles and labels: String, Color. h.Prop = value is the same as set(h, 'Prop', value).
Example: plot(1:3); set(gca, 'XLim', [0 5]); get(gca, 'XLim')   % [0 5]
Example: set(0, 'DefaultAxesFontSize', 14); get(0, 'DefaultAxesFontSize')   % 14
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet. Unknown properties or values are rejected with an error. Call it as a statement.

## reset
Reset graphics object properties to their defaults.
Syntax: reset(groot)
Syntax: reset(0)
Clears all user-defined root default property values (Default<Type><Prop>) and restores root properties (Tag, UserData, ShowHiddenHandles) to their initial values.
Example: set(0, 'DefaultAxesFontSize', 14); reset(groot); get(0, 'DefaultAxesFontSize')   % 10
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet. Currently supports groot / 0.

## setdiff
Values in A that are not in B.
Syntax: C = setdiff(A, B)
Syntax: [C, ia] = setdiff(A, B, 'stable')
Syntax: [C, ia] = setdiff(A, B, 'rows')
Result is sorted by default; 'stable' keeps the order of A. ia holds first indices in A.
Example: setdiff([1 2 3 4], [2 4])   % [1 3]
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric/logical inputs support 2-D arrays with 'rows', 'sorted', or 'stable' (not 'legacy'). Character/cellstr forms also support 'legacy'; 'rows' warns and is ignored for cell inputs.

## setfield
Set a field in a scalar struct.
Syntax: T = setfield(S, field, value)
Syntax: T = setfield(S, field1, field2, ..., value)
Returns an updated struct without changing S unless assigned back to S. Follows nested scalar fields and creates missing struct fields along the path. Field names must be valid character names. Paths and resulting containers are limited to 16 nesting levels.
Example: s=struct('a',1,'b','x'); t=setfield(s,'a',7); t.a   % 7
Differences from MATLAB: Cell index arguments and nonscalar structs are not supported.

## setxor
Values in exactly one of two sets.
Syntax: C = setxor(A, B)
Syntax: [C, ia, ib] = setxor(A, B, 'stable')
Syntax: [C, ia, ib] = setxor(A, B, 'rows')
Result is sorted by default; 'stable' keeps input order.
Example: setxor([1 2 3], [3 4])   % [1 2 4]
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric/logical inputs support 2-D arrays with 'rows', 'sorted', or 'stable' (not 'legacy'). Character/cellstr forms also support 'legacy'; 'rows' warns and is ignored for cell inputs.

## sgtitle
Title for a whole figure.
Syntax: sgtitle('Title')
Syntax: sgtitle(fig, 'Title', 'Interpreter', 'none')
Sets one shared title above all axes of the figure. fig is an optional figure handle.
Example: sgtitle('Results')   % shared title
Interpreter defaults to tex; none and latex draw source text literally. The function returns a text handle.
Differences from MATLAB: Only a subset of text properties and TeX markup is supported.

## sign
Sign of real values or direction of complex values.
Syntax: sign(X)
Real elements give -1, 0 or 1; NaN stays NaN. A nonzero complex value gives X/abs(X), and complex zero gives zero. Logical inputs convert to double.
Example: sign([-2 0 3 NaN])   % [-1 0 1 NaN]
Differences from MATLAB: Only 2-D arrays are supported.

## sin
Sine of argument in radians.
Syntax: y = sin(x)
Elementwise sine; complex input is supported.
Example: sin(pi/2)   % 1
Example: sin(1+2i)   % 3.1658 + 1.9596i
Differences from MATLAB: logical input is not supported yet.

## sinc
Normalized sinc function.
Syntax: sinc(x)
Returns sin(pi*x)/(pi*x), with 1 at x = 0.
Example: sinc(0)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Real 2-D arrays only.

## single
Convert to single precision.
Syntax: single(X)
Each element takes 4 bytes. Arithmetic with double, logical or char values gives single, computed in single precision.
Example: x = single(pi)
Example: y = single(16777216) + 1   % stays 16777216
Differences from MATLAB: complex single is not supported yet; functions compute in double and round the result to single.

## size
Size of an array.
Syntax: size(A)
Syntax: size(A, dim)
Syntax: [r, c] = size(A)
size(A) returns [rows columns]. size(A, 1) is rows, size(A, 2) is columns, larger dim gives 1.
For an LTI model, rows count outputs and columns count inputs.
Example: [r, c] = size(ones(2, 3))   % r = 2, c = 3
Example: size(zeros(2,3,4),[1 3])   % [2 4]
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D input has no size(A, [d1 d2]) form. N-D arrays (part 2): size(A,dim), size(A,vecdim), size(A,d1,d2,...) and [d1,...,dn] = size(A,...); without dimension arguments the last output folds the remaining dimensions.

## sort
Sort array elements.
Syntax: B = sort(A)
Syntax: B = sort(A, dim)
Syntax: B = sort(A, dim, 'descend')
Syntax: [B, I] = sort(A, ..., 'MissingPlacement', value)
Sorts each column of A in ascending order, or along dimension dim.
I holds the original positions, so B equals A(I) for a vector.
Equal values keep their original order. NaN values go last when ascending.
Example: [B, I] = sort([3 1 2])   % B = [1 2 3], I = [2 3 1]
Example: sort(reshape([3 1 2 4],1,2,2),3,'descend')
Differences from MATLAB: Real, logical, complex, character and cellstr 2-D arrays are supported. Complex values order by abs, then angle in (-pi, pi], NaN last, stable in both directions; complex input accepts dim and 'ascend'/'descend' only. Cellstr input accepts no sorting options. N-D arrays (part 2): [B,I] = sort(A,dim,'ascend'|'descend') along any dimension for numeric, logical, char and complex input.

## sortrows
Sort rows of a matrix.
Syntax: B = sortrows(A)
Syntax: [B, I] = sortrows(A, cols, 'descend', 'MissingPlacement', 'last')
cols is a vector of signed column numbers; a negative number sorts that column in descending order. 'ascend' or 'descend' applies to all columns. NaN placement is auto, first or last.
Example: sortrows([3 1; 1 2; 2 0])   % [1 2; 2 0; 3 1]
Differences from MATLAB: Real, logical, character and cellstr 2-D arrays and tables are supported (see help table for sortrows(T, vars, direction)). No per-column direction arrays for arrays. Cellstr input accepts numeric column selectors, including negative columns, but no text options. Complex input sorts by abs, then angle, with numeric column selectors only.

## sosfilt
Filter with second-order sections.
Syntax: y = sosfilt(sos, x)
sos is an N-by-6 matrix, for example from butter_sos or cheby1_sos.
Example: y = sosfilt(butter_sos(2, 0.3), ones(1, 20))   % low-pass step response
Differences from MATLAB: No gain argument and no initial state; two inputs only.

## sosfreqz
Plot the magnitude response of SOS filters.
Syntax: sosfreqz(sos)
Syntax: sosfreqz(sos, n)
Plots dB magnitude at n points (default 512, at most 65536). It returns no values; use sosfreqzmag for numbers.
Example: sosfreqz(butter_sos(2, 0.3), 256)   % plots magnitude in dB
Differences from MATLAB: Plot only. No outputs, no sampling-rate argument.

## sosfreqzmag
Magnitude response of SOS filters.
Syntax: m = sosfreqzmag(sos)
Syntax: m = sosfreqzmag(sos, n)
Returns n linear magnitude values as a column (default 512).
Example: m = sosfreqzmag(butter_sos(2, 0.3), 128);   % 128-by-1 column
Differences from MATLAB: MATLAB has no sosfreqzmag.

## sosgrpdelay
Group delay of SOS filters.
Syntax: d = sosgrpdelay(sos)
Syntax: d = sosgrpdelay(sos, n)
Returns n values in samples as a column (default 512). Undefined points are NaN. A bare call plots it.
Example: d = sosgrpdelay(butter_sos(2, 0.3), 128);   % 128-by-1 column
Differences from MATLAB: MATLAB has no sosgrpdelay.

## sosimpz
Impulse response of SOS filters.
Syntax: h = sosimpz(sos, n)
Returns the first n samples as a column. n is required. A bare call plots it.
Example: h = sosimpz(butter_sos(2, 0.3), 32);   % 32-by-1 column
Differences from MATLAB: MATLAB has no sosimpz. n is required.

## sosphasez
Phase response of SOS filters.
Syntax: p = sosphasez(sos)
Syntax: p = sosphasez(sos, n)
Returns n phase values in radians as a column (default 512). A bare call plots it.
Example: p = sosphasez(butter_sos(2, 0.3), 128);   % 128-by-1 column
Differences from MATLAB: MATLAB has no sosphasez.

## sosstepz
Step response of SOS filters.
Syntax: s = sosstepz(sos, n)
Returns the first n samples as a column. n is required. A bare call plots it.
Example: s = sosstepz(butter_sos(2, 0.3), 32);   % 32-by-1 column
Differences from MATLAB: MATLAB has no sosstepz. n is required.

## sprintf
Format data into text.
Syntax: s = sprintf(format)
Syntax: s = sprintf(format, A, ...)
Returns a character row. format holds plain text and conversions such as %d, %i, %f, %e, %g, %s, %c, %x, %o and %%. Escapes such as \n and \t are converted. All values of all arguments are used in column order. If there are more values than conversions, the format is used again. Text arguments are used as one value for %s and as character codes for %d.
Example: sprintf('%d items, %.2f total', 3, 4.5)   % '3 items, 4.50 total'
A scalar string format returns a string scalar.
Example: sprintf("value=%d", 3)
Differences from MATLAB: cell array arguments and file ids are not supported; use compose for element-wise formatting of string arrays.

## sqrt
Square root.
Syntax: sqrt(X)
Applies the square root to each element.
Negative real input and complex input give the principal complex root.
Example: sqrt(16)   % 4
Example: sqrt(-4)   % 0 + 2i
Differences from MATLAB: double, logical and char 2-D arrays only.

## square
Square wave.
Syntax: square(t)
Syntax: square(t, duty)
Period is 2*pi. duty is the percent of the period that is +1 (default 50).
Example: square(pi/2)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Real double 2-D arrays only.

## stairs
Stairstep plot.
Syntax: stairs(x, y)
Syntax: stairs(y, 'r--')
Draws steps through the points. A line spec or name/value pairs such as 'LineWidth', 2 can follow.
Example: stairs(1:4, [2 4 1 3])   % four steps
Differences from MATLAB: Real coordinates only.

## std
Standard deviation.
Syntax: std(A)
Syntax: std(A, w, dim)
Syntax: std(A, 0, 'all', 'omitnan')
w is 0 (divide by n-1, default) or 1 (divide by n). dim is a positive integer or 'all'. 'omitnan' or 'includenan' may follow.
Example: std([1 2 3 4])   % 1.2910
Differences from MATLAB: Real and complex double arrays, one output. Vector weights and vecdim are not supported. Complex input gives a real result from abs(x - mean).^2.

## stem
Stem plot.
Syntax: stem(x, y)
Syntax: stem(y, 'filled')
Draws a vertical line and marker for each point. 'filled' fills the markers; BaseValue sets the baseline.
Example: stem([1 3 2])   % three stems
Differences from MATLAB: Real coordinates only.

## stepz
Step response of a digital filter.
Syntax: [s, t] = stepz(b, a)
Syntax: [s, t] = stepz(b, a, n)
Syntax: [s, t] = stepz(b, a, n, fs)
Syntax: [s, t] = stepz(sos, n)
Syntax: [s, t] = stepz(d)
The cumulative sum of the impulse response, with the same lengths and times as impz. A bare call plots it.
Example: s = stepz([1 1], 1, 6)   % [1; 2; 2; 2; 2; 2]
Example: [s, t] = stepz(1, [1 -0.5], 4, 100);   % t = [0; 0.01; 0.02; 0.03]
Differences from MATLAB: n must be a count, not a vector of sample indices.

## strcat
Join text horizontally.
Syntax: s = strcat(s1, s2, ...)
Syntax: c = strcat(c1, s2, ...)
For character arguments, trailing spaces of each argument are removed and the pieces are joined. If any argument is a cell array, the result is a cell array and cell elements keep their spaces. Cell arrays need the same size, or be 1-by-1.
Example: strcat('ab', 'cd', 'e')   % 'abcde'
String inputs concatenate element-wise with singleton expansion, preserving spaces and string shape.
Example: strcat(["a " "b"],"!")
Differences from MATLAB: string storage is two-dimensional and bounded.

## strvcat
Stack text vertically, padding shorter rows with spaces.
Syntax: s = strvcat(s1, s2, ...)
Syntax: s = strvcat(C)
Character arrays and exact integer UTF-16 codes are stacked into a character matrix. A cell array of character rows is read in column-major order. Empty inputs are omitted.
Example: strvcat('a', 'bcd')   % rows 'a  ' and 'bcd'
Differences from MATLAB: Two-dimensional arrays only, at most 65536 UTF-16 units. Numeric inputs must be exact integers from 0 to 65535; rounding and out-of-range conversion are unsupported.

## strcmp
Compare text, case-sensitive.
Syntax: tf = strcmp(a, b)
Returns true if a and b are the same text. If one input is a cell array, the result is a logical array of the same size. Two cell arrays compare element by element. Other input types give false.
Example: strcmp({'a','b'}, 'a')   % [true false]
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## strcmpi
Compare text, ignoring case.
Syntax: tf = strcmpi(a, b)
Same as strcmp, but upper and lower case letters are equal.
Example: strcmpi('ABC', 'abc')   % true
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## strfind
Find text inside text.
Syntax: k = strfind(s, pattern)
Syntax: c = strfind(c, pattern)
Returns the start positions of pattern in s as a row, or [] if there is none. Matches may overlap. A cell array input gives a cell array of positions.
Example: strfind('abcabc', 'bc')   % [2 5]
Differences from MATLAB: The ForceCellOutput option is not supported yet.

## strjoin
Join the text pieces of a cell array.
Syntax: s = strjoin(c)
Syntax: s = strjoin(c, delimiter)
Puts delimiter between the pieces. The default delimiter is one space. Escapes such as \n in the delimiter are converted.
Example: strjoin({'a','b','c'}, '-')   % 'a-b-c'
Differences from MATLAB: A cell array of delimiters is not supported yet.
String inputs are supported with bounded two-dimensional storage.
Example: strjoin(["a" "b"],",")

## strncmp
Compare the first n characters of text, case-sensitive.
Syntax: tf = strncmp(a, b, n)
Same as strcmp, but only the first n characters count. A text shorter than n is equal only to identical text. n = 0 gives true.
Example: strncmp('hello', 'help', 3)   % true
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## strncmpi
Compare the first n characters of text, ignoring case.
Syntax: tf = strncmpi(a, b, n)
Same as strncmp, but upper and lower case letters are equal.
Example: strncmpi({'ABx','aby'}, 'abz', 2)   % [true true]
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## strrep
Replace text.
Syntax: s = strrep(s, old, new)
Syntax: c = strrep(c, old, new)
Replaces every occurrence of old by new. A cell array input gives a cell array. An empty old leaves the text unchanged.
Example: strrep('hello world', 'o', '0')   % 'hell0 w0rld'
Differences from MATLAB: none known.
String inputs are supported with bounded two-dimensional storage.
Example: strrep(["ab" "ac"],"a","z")

## strsplit
Split text at delimiters.
Syntax: c = strsplit(s)
Syntax: c = strsplit(s, delimiter)
Syntax: c = strsplit(s, delimiter, 'CollapseDelimiters', tf)
Returns a 1-by-n cell array of character rows. The default delimiter is any white space (space, \f, \n, \r, \t, \v). delimiter can be text or a cell array of text. Repeated delimiters count as one unless CollapseDelimiters is false. At most 65536 pieces.
Example: c = strsplit('a,b,c', ',')   % c = {'a', 'b', 'c'}
Differences from MATLAB: The DelimiterType option is not supported yet.

## strtrim
Remove spaces at both ends of text.
Syntax: s = strtrim(s)
Syntax: c = strtrim(c)
Removes leading and trailing Unicode whitespace. Significant whitespace is kept: char(133), char(160), char(8199) and char(8239). A cell array of text gives a cell array.
Example: strtrim('  ab c  ')   % 'ab c'
Differences from MATLAB: Character matrices are not supported yet.
String inputs are supported with bounded two-dimensional storage.
Example: strtrim([" a " " b "])

## struct
Create a structure with named fields.
Syntax: struct()
Syntax: struct(field, value, ...)
With no arguments, creates a scalar struct with no fields. Field names must be unique ASCII identifiers of at most 63 characters; up to 1024 fields are allowed. Non-cell values repeat across the struct array; nonscalar cell values set its shape and distribute their contents by element. All nonscalar cell shapes must match. A scalar cell contributes its content to every element; use a nested cell to keep a cell as a field value. Dot access and dynamic access such as S.(name) are supported.
Example: s=struct('a',{1,2,3}); s(2).a   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: Some struct display spacing differs. Only 2-D structs are supported (s(i,j,k) assignment reports that N-D struct arrays are not supported yet); containers are limited to 65536 slots and 16 nesting levels. Object conversion forms are not supported.

## subplot
Select a grid cell for plotting and return its axes handle.
Syntax: subplot(rows, cols, index)
Syntax: h = subplot(rows, cols, index)
Syntax: subplot('Position', [left bottom width height])
index may be a vector to span cells. Rows and columns are 1 to 16. Add 'replace' or 'align' as the fourth argument.
Example: h=subplot(2,1,1);get(h,'Type')   % 'axes'
Differences from MATLAB: Returns the axes handle; supports command syntax subplot 211.

## sum
Sum of elements.
Syntax: sum(A)
Returns the sum of each column, or one value for a row vector. Logical input is allowed.
Example: sum([1 2 3])   % 6
Differences from MATLAB: No 'all', type or NaN options. The sum of [] is 0. Complex input sums the real and imaginary parts with the real kernel and gives a real result when every imaginary part is zero.

## svd
Singular values and singular vectors.
Syntax: s = svd(A)
Syntax: [U,S,V] = svd(A)
Syntax: [U,S,V] = svd(A, 'econ')
Syntax: [U,S,V] = svd(A, 0)
One output returns singular values in descending order as a column. Three outputs satisfy A approximately equal to U*S*V'. For m-by-n input and k=min(m,n), full output sizes are m-by-m, m-by-n and n-by-n. 'econ' gives m-by-k, k-by-k and n-by-k; option 0 uses economy only when m>n. Inputs must be finite and may be complex (S stays real); logical input converts to double.
Example: svd([1 2;3 4;5 6])   % [9.525518; 0.514301]
Differences from MATLAB: Singular vector signs (complex phases) and small singular values can differ; complex singular values can differ in the last digit, and a singular complex matrix can give an exact 0 where MATLAB gives about 1e-16. Two outputs are not supported.

## system
Run an operating system command.
Syntax: status = system(command)
Syntax: [status, output] = system(command)
Syntax: [status, output] = system(command, '-echo')
Runs command through sh -c (Linux and macOS) or cmd /C (Windows) and returns its exit status; output holds what it wrote to standard output and standard error, as text. With fewer than two outputs, or with '-echo', the output is also printed. Stop ends the command.
Example: [status, out] = system('echo hi')   % status 0, out 'hi' and a newline
Differences from MATLAB: Standard input of the command is empty; no environment-variable arguments; output is limited to 4 MiB. Not available in the browser console.

## exit
End a command-line run with an exit status.
Syntax: exit
Syntax: exit(status)
Stops at once: later statements do not run and no catch handles it. Output already printed stays. The matrust process exits with status (0 when omitted), an integer from 0 to 255; any other status is an error, which exits with 1. Works in scripts, --eval, -batch and the console. Same as quit.
Differences from MATLAB: no 'force' or 'cancel' options and no finish.m. The desktop app and the browser console report that exit is not supported in this host instead of closing.

## quit
End a command-line run with an exit status.
Syntax: quit
Syntax: quit(status)
Same as exit: stops at once and the matrust process exits with status (0 when omitted), an integer from 0 to 255; any other status is an error, which exits with 1.
Differences from MATLAB: no 'force' or 'cancel' options and no finish.m. The desktop app and the browser console report that quit is not supported in this host instead of closing.


## tan
Tangent of an angle in radians.
Syntax: tan(X)
Applies tangent to each element; complex input is supported.
Example: tan(0)   % 0
Differences from MATLAB: double 2-D arrays only.

## tic
Start a timer or return an independent timer identifier.
Syntax: tic
Syntax: id = tic
Syntax: id = tic()
Without an output, starts or replaces the session timer used by toc. With an output, returns an independent timer identifier and leaves the session timer unchanged. Pass that identifier to toc(id).
Example: id=tic; elapsed=toc(id); elapsed>=0   % true
Differences from MATLAB: Identifiers are positive double values in MatRust; do not depend on their exact value.

## tiledlayout
Create a tiled layout and return a TiledChartLayout handle.
Syntax: tiledlayout(rows, cols)
Syntax: t = tiledlayout(rows, cols)
Syntax: tiledlayout('flow')
'vertical' and 'horizontal' are also accepted. Select tiles afterward with nexttile. Supports GridSize, TileSpacing, Padding, Children, Parent, Title, Subtitle, XLabel, and YLabel properties.
Example: t=tiledlayout(2,2);t.GridSize   % [2 2]
Differences from MATLAB: Spacing options are set via handle properties rather than name-value constructor arguments.

## subtitle
Set a subtitle below the axes title and return its Text handle.
Syntax: subtitle(txt)
Syntax: s = subtitle(ax, txt)
Syntax: s = subtitle(t, txt)
An explicit target can be an axes or tiled layout. Its Subtitle property exposes String, FontWeight, FontSize, Color, and Interpreter.
Example: plot(1:3);s=subtitle('Measured data');s.String   % Measured data
Differences from MATLAB: Supports a subset of text properties and LaTeX markup.

## title
Set the plot title.
Syntax: title('My plot')
Syntax: [t, s] = title(txt, subtxt)
Syntax: [t, s] = title(ax, txt, subtxt)
Syntax: title('My plot', 'Interpreter', 'none', 'Color', [1 0 0])
Text accepts character text and bounded multiline cell or string arrays. Interpreter defaults to tex. Use none for literal text or latex for the supported LaTeX subset. RGB Color is also accepted on axes.
Example: title('Signal')   % title shown above the axes
Differences from MATLAB: Only a subset of text properties and TeX markup is supported.

## toc
Read elapsed time in seconds.
Syntax: toc
Syntax: elapsed = toc
Syntax: toc(id)
Syntax: elapsed = toc(id)
Without an id, reads the timer started by tic without an output; it errors if none was started. An id comes from id=tic. With an output, returns a nonnegative double scalar. Without an output, prints 'Elapsed time is ... seconds.' Reading a timer does not reset it.
Example: tic; elapsed=toc; elapsed>=0   % true
Differences from MATLAB: Measured times vary; error wording differs.

## trace
Sum of a square matrix's diagonal.
Syntax: trace(A)
Returns one scalar. Real, complex and logical square arrays are accepted; logical values convert to double. A nonsquare input raises an error.
Example: trace([1 2;3 4])   % 5
Differences from MATLAB: none known; a complex sum with zero imaginary part is real.

## transpose
Matrix transpose.
Syntax: transpose(A)
Same as A.'. Swaps rows and columns without conjugation for complex input.
Example: transpose([1 2 3])   % [1; 2; 3]
Differences from MATLAB: none known. N-D input gives MATLAB's error: Transpose on ND array is not defined. Use PERMUTE instead.

## trapz
Trapezoidal integral.
Syntax: trapz(Y)
Syntax: trapz(X, Y)
Syntax: trapz(Y, dim) or trapz(X, Y, dim)
X is a vector of sample points; without X the spacing is 1.
Example: trapz([1 2 3])   % 4
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D data; scalar spacing or a vector X. Complex Y works with a real vector X, where a scalar X is an error as in MATLAB; complex X is not supported.

## triang
Triangular window.
Syntax: triang(n)
Returns an n-by-1 column vector with no zero end points.
Example: triang(5)'   % [0.3333 0.6667 1 0.6667 0.3333]
Differences from MATLAB: No sampling option; double output only.

## tril
Lower triangular part.
Syntax: tril(A)
Syntax: tril(A, k)
Keeps entries on and below diagonal k (default 0) and zeros the rest.
Example: tril([1 2; 3 4])   % [1 0; 3 4]
Differences from MATLAB: Real 2-D arrays only.

## triu
Upper triangular part.
Syntax: triu(A)
Syntax: triu(A, k)
Keeps entries on and above diagonal k (default 0) and zeros the rest.
Example: triu([1 2; 3 4])   % [1 2; 0 4]
Differences from MATLAB: Real 2-D arrays only.

## true
Logical ones.
Syntax: true
Syntax: true(n)
Syntax: true(r, c) or true([r c])
true alone is a logical scalar; true(n) is n-by-n.
Example: true(1, 3)   % [true true true]
Differences from MATLAB: Two-dimensional output only.

## try
Run statements with optional error handling.
Syntax: try; statements; catch err; handler; end
Syntax: try; statements; catch; handler; end
Syntax: try; statements; end
On success, skips the catch block. A catchable runtime error skips the remaining try statements and runs the handler. Without a catch block, a catchable error is suppressed. Blocks may be nested; assignments completed before an error remain available. Parse errors are rejected before execution.
Example: try; error('stop'); catch; disp('caught'); end   % caught
Differences from MATLAB: The catch value is a struct with an empty stack. Cancellation and execution limits cannot be caught.

## typecast
Reinterpret the bytes of a numeric vector as another class.
Syntax: typecast(X, CLASSNAME)
X is a real integer, single or double vector; the byte count must be a multiple of the new element size. A row stays a row, a column stays a column.
Example: x = typecast(single(1), 'uint32')
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## uint16
Convert to unsigned 16-bit integers.
Syntax: uint16(X)
Rounds half away from zero and saturates at intmin('uint16')..intmax('uint16'); NaN becomes 0. Each element takes 2 bytes.
Arithmetic with the same class or a scalar double stays uint16; other mixes are errors.
Example: x = uint16([2.5 -3.5 1000])
Differences from MATLAB: complex input and the 'like' form are not supported yet.

## uint32
Convert to unsigned 32-bit integers.
Syntax: uint32(X)
Rounds half away from zero and saturates at intmin('uint32')..intmax('uint32'); NaN becomes 0. Each element takes 4 bytes.
Arithmetic with the same class or a scalar double stays uint32; other mixes are errors.
Example: x = uint32([2.5 -3.5 1000])
Differences from MATLAB: complex input and the 'like' form are not supported yet.

## uint64
Convert to unsigned 64-bit integers.
Syntax: uint64(X)
Rounds half away from zero and saturates at intmin('uint64')..intmax('uint64'); NaN becomes 0. Each element takes 8 bytes.
Arithmetic with the same class or a scalar double stays uint64; other mixes are errors.
Example: x = uint64([2.5 -3.5 1000])
uint64 values stay exact 64-bit integers.
Differences from MATLAB: complex input and the 'like' form are not supported yet.

## uint8
Convert to unsigned 8-bit integers.
Syntax: uint8(X)
Rounds half away from zero and saturates at intmin('uint8')..intmax('uint8'); NaN becomes 0. Each element takes 1 byte.
Arithmetic with the same class or a scalar double stays uint8; other mixes are errors.
Example: x = uint8([2.5 -3.5 1000])
Differences from MATLAB: complex input and the 'like' form are not supported yet.

## union
Combine two sets.
Syntax: C = union(A, B)
Syntax: [C, ia, ib] = union(A, B, 'stable')
Syntax: [C, ia, ib] = union(A, B, 'rows')
Result is sorted by default; 'stable' keeps input order.
Example: union([1 2], [2 3])   % [1 2 3]
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric/logical inputs support 2-D arrays with 'rows', 'sorted', or 'stable' (not 'legacy'). Character/cellstr forms also support 'legacy'; 'rows' warns and is ignored for cell inputs.

## unique
Unique values.
Syntax: C = unique(A)
Syntax: [C, ia, ic] = unique(A, 'stable')
Syntax: [C, ia, ic] = unique(A, 'rows')
Sorted by default; 'stable' keeps first-occurrence order. ia gives first occurrences (or last with 'last'). Each NaN counts as distinct.
Example: unique([3 1 3 2])   % [1 2 3]
Differences from MATLAB: Real/logical 2-D arrays and character/cellstr inputs are supported. Real/logical inputs support 'rows', 'stable', 'sorted', 'first' and 'last' (not 'legacy'). Character/cellstr forms also support 'legacy'; for cellstr, 'rows' warns and is ignored. Complex input supports 'rows', 'stable', 'sorted', 'first' and 'last' (not 'legacy'), in the order of sort; NaNs stay distinct.

## upfirdn
Upsample, filter, then downsample.
Syntax: upfirdn(x, h)
Syntax: upfirdn(x, h, p, q)
h is the FIR filter. p is the upsampling factor and q the downsampling factor (default 1).
Example: upfirdn([1 2 3], [1 1])   % [1 3 5 3]
Differences from MATLAB: Real numeric 2-D arrays; filter values must be finite.

## upper
Convert text to upper case.
Syntax: s = upper(s)
Syntax: c = upper(c)
A cell array of text gives a cell array. Numeric input is returned unchanged.
Example: upper('abc')   % 'ABC'
Differences from MATLAB: Character matrices are not supported yet.
String inputs are supported with bounded two-dimensional storage.
Example: upper(["a" "b"])

## upsample
Insert zeros between samples.
Syntax: upsample(x, n)
Syntax: upsample(x, n, phase)
Inserts n-1 zeros after each sample. phase is an integer from 0 to n-1.
Example: upsample([1 2 3], 2)   % [1 0 2 0 3 0]
Differences from MATLAB: Real numeric 2-D arrays only.

## var
Variance.
Syntax: var(A)
Syntax: var(A, w, dim)
Syntax: var(A, 0, 'all', 'omitnan')
w is 0 (divide by n-1, default) or 1 (divide by n). dim is a positive integer or 'all'. 'omitnan' or 'includenan' may follow.
Example: var([1 2 3 4])   % 1.6667
Differences from MATLAB: Real and complex double arrays, one output. Vector weights and vecdim are not supported. Complex input gives a real result from abs(x - mean).^2.

## vec2ind
Return the first largest element index of each column.
Syntax: indices = vec2ind(v)
Example: vec2ind([1 0;0 1])

## view
Viewpoint of the axes.
Syntax: view(az, el)
Syntax: view([az el])
Syntax: view(2)
Syntax: view(3)
Syntax: v = view
Syntax: [az, el] = view
Syntax: view(ax, ...)
az is the azimuth in degrees, measured from the negative y axis, counter-clockwise seen from above; el is the elevation in degrees up from the x-y plane. view(2) is (0, 90), the 2-D view; view(3) is (-37.5, 30). An axes is 3-D whenever its view is not (0, 90). With two outputs every form returns the angles now in effect: [az, el] = view(3) gives -37.5 and 30.
The projection is orthographic (the matrix of viewmtx); each axis is first scaled to its limits, so the axes box is a cube stretched to fill the axes. In the desktop, dragging a 3-D axes with the left mouse button rotates it (half a degree per point; elevation stays within -90 to 90) and View follows.
Example: plot3([0 1], [0 1], [0 1]); view(45, 20); v = view   % [45 20]
Differences from MATLAB: The camera properties (CameraPosition, CameraTarget, CameraViewAngle), view([x y z]), perspective projection and rotate3d are not supported yet.

## parfor
Parallel for-loop; runs serially in MatRust.
Syntax: parfor k = start:stop, statements, end
Syntax: parfor (k = start:stop, M), statements, end
MatRust has one worker, the client, so parfor runs exactly like for, in loop order. M (the most workers to use) is evaluated and ignored. Results equal those of the same for loop.
Example: s = 0; parfor k = 1:4, s = s + k; end   % s = 10
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust. Iterations run in order and the classification of loop variables (sliced, reduction, broadcast) is not checked.

## spmd
Single program, multiple data block; runs serially in MatRust.
Syntax: spmd, statements, end
Syntax: spmd (n), statements, end
The body runs once, on the client, with spmdIndex and spmdSize both 1. Worker counts in parentheses are evaluated and ignored. Variables set in the body are ordinary variables after the block.
Example: spmd, r = spmdIndex * 10; end   % r = 10
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust. Variables are not Composite objects, so r{1} indexing does not work on them.

## parpool
Start a parallel pool; MatRust's pool has one worker and runs serially.
Syntax: p = parpool
Syntax: p = parpool(n)
Syntax: p = parpool('Processes', n)
Syntax: p = parpool('Threads')
Returns a parallel.ProcessPool (parallel.ThreadPool for 'Threads') with NumWorkers 1, Connected true, Busy false and IdleTimeout 30. The requested size is accepted and ignored. A second parpool while one is open is an error; close it with delete(gcp('nocreate')).
Example: p = parpool(2); n = p.NumWorkers; delete(p)   % n = 1
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust: one worker, no cluster profiles, no idle shutdown.

## gcp
Current parallel pool.
Syntax: p = gcp
Syntax: p = gcp('nocreate')
Returns the open pool, starting one (NumWorkers 1) if there is none. With 'nocreate' it returns [] when no pool is open.
Example: p = gcp('nocreate');   % [] before any parpool
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust; the pool has one worker.

## parfeval
Run a function on the pool; runs at once in MatRust.
Syntax: F = parfeval(fcn, n, x1, ..., xm)
Syntax: F = parfeval(pool, fcn, n, x1, ..., xm)
Calls fcn with the inputs and n outputs immediately and returns a parallel.FevalFuture whose State is 'finished'. An error in fcn is kept in F.Error and raised by fetchOutputs. Futures concatenate with [F1 F2] for fetchNext.
Example: F = parfeval(@(x) 2*x, 1, 21); y = fetchOutputs(F);   % y = 42
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust, at the call. Indexed assignment F(k) = parfeval(...) is not supported yet; build arrays with [F1 F2]. Multiple outputs of builtins need a user function or anonymous wrapper.

## batch
Run a script or function as a batch job; runs at once in MatRust.
Syntax: j = batch('script')
Syntax: j = batch(fcn, n, {x1, ..., xm})
The script runs immediately in the client workspace, so load(j) has nothing to copy. The function form calls fcn with n outputs; fetchOutputs(j) returns them in a 1-by-n cell array. wait(j) returns at once.
Example: j = batch(@plus, 1, {2, 3}); r = fetchOutputs(j);   % r = {5}
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust, at the call; scripts share the client workspace. Name-value options are ignored.

## fetchOutputs
Outputs of finished futures or a batch job.
Syntax: [y1, ..., yn] = fetchOutputs(F)
Syntax: Y = fetchOutputs(F, 'UniformOutput', false)
For one future, returns its outputs. For an array of futures, each output is the vertical concatenation over the futures (or a cell column with 'UniformOutput' false). For a batch job, returns a cell array. A future that failed raises "One or more futures resulted in an error." with the cause.
Example: y = fetchOutputs(parfeval(@sqrt, 1, 16));   % y = 4
Differences from MATLAB: Futures are always finished in MatRust.

## fetchNext
Next unread future of an array.
Syntax: [idx, y1, ..., yn] = fetchNext(F)
Returns the index of the first future not yet read and its outputs, and marks it read. Since futures finish at once in MatRust, they come back in order.
Example: [k, y] = fetchNext(parfeval(@(x) x + 1, 1, 1));   % k = 1, y = 2
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust; the timeout argument is ignored.

## gpuArray
Array on the GPU; MatRust returns the input unchanged.
Syntax: G = gpuArray(X)
MatRust computes on the CPU, so gpuArray is the identity: the result keeps the class of X and works with every function. gather turns it back.
Example: g = gpuArray([1 2 3]); y = gather(g) * 2;   % [2 4 6]
Differences from MATLAB: Runs on the CPU in MatRust; class(G) is the class of X, not 'gpuArray'.

## gpuDeviceCount
Count GPU devices available to MatRust.
Syntax: n = gpuDeviceCount
Syntax: n = gpuDeviceCount("available")
Returns zero. MatRust computes on the CPU.
Example: n = gpuDeviceCount("available")   % 0

## gpuDevice
Query the current GPU device.
Syntax: gpuDevice
MatRust raises "No supported GPU device was found." with identifier parallel:gpu:device:NoDevicesAvailable.
Example: try; gpuDevice; catch err; id = err.identifier; end;

## canUseGPU
Check whether GPU computation is available.
Syntax: tf = canUseGPU
Returns logical false in MatRust.
Example: tf = canUseGPU   % false

## gather
Bring data back from a GPU or a pool; identity in MatRust.
Syntax: X = gather(G)
Syntax: [X1, ..., Xn] = gather(G1, ..., Gn)
Returns each input unchanged, since MatRust keeps every array on the CPU.
Example: x = gather(5);   % 5
Differences from MATLAB: Identity in MatRust; tall arrays are not supported.

## spmdIndex
Index of this worker in an spmd block; always 1 in MatRust.
Syntax: k = spmdIndex
MatRust runs spmd bodies once on the client, so the index is 1 inside and outside spmd.
Example: k = spmdIndex;   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust.

## spmdSize
Number of workers in an spmd block; always 1 in MatRust.
Syntax: n = spmdSize
Example: n = spmdSize;   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust.

## labindex
Older name for spmdIndex; always 1 in MatRust.
Syntax: k = labindex
Example: k = labindex;   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust.

## numlabs
Older name for spmdSize; always 1 in MatRust.
Syntax: n = numlabs
Example: n = numlabs;   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Runs serially in MatRust.

## while
Repeat statements while a condition is true.
Syntax: while condition, statements, end
The condition is tested before each pass, as for if. The browser allows 1,000,000 execution steps per run. Desktop/CLI runs have no step limit; use Stop / Ctrl+C to end a run. Use break to leave early.
Example: n = 0; while n < 3, n = n + 1; end, n   % n = 3
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet. The browser limit of 1,000,000 execution steps per run is a MatRust limit. Desktop/CLI runs have no step limit; use Stop / Ctrl+C.

## whos
List workspace variables.
Syntax: whos
Syntax: whos name1 name2 ...
Syntax: whos('-file', filename)
Prints name, size, bytes and class for each variable. Workspace filters accept names and wildcard patterns. With -file and a MAT filename, lists catalog rows without loading values. Optional explicit names select rows.
Example: whos   % one line per variable
Differences from MATLAB: Structure output is unavailable.

## writematrix
Write a numeric matrix to a text file.
Syntax: writematrix(A, 'out.csv')
Syntax: writematrix(A, 'out.csv', 'Delimiter', ';')
Delimiter is comma (default), semicolon, tab or space (also named 'space' or 'whitespace'). Use a .csv, .txt or .dat name, or add 'FileType', 'text'. Call it as a statement.
Example: writematrix([1 2; 3 4], 'out.csv')   % writes two lines: 1,2 and 3,4
Differences from MATLAB: Statement only; no output assignment. Overwrites the file; no append. Writing spreadsheets (.xlsx, .xls) is not supported yet and gives an error.

## xlabel
Set the x axis label.
Syntax: xlabel('Time (s)')
Syntax: xlabel('Time (s)', 'Interpreter', 'none', 'Color', [1 0 0])
Text accepts character text and bounded multiline cell or string arrays. Interpreter defaults to tex. Use none for literal text or latex for the supported LaTeX subset. RGB Color is also accepted on axes.
Example: xlabel('Time (s)')   % label below the x axis
Differences from MATLAB: Only a subset of text properties and TeX markup is supported.

## xlim
Set x axis limits.
Syntax: xlim([a b])
Syntax: xlim('auto')
Sets the visible x range, or returns it to automatic.
Example: xlim([0 5])   % x from 0 to 5
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric two-element limits or 'auto' only.

## xline
Draw vertical constant line(s) at x.
Syntax: h = xline(x)
Syntax: h = xline(x, linespec)
Syntax: h = xline(x, linespec, label)
Syntax: h = xline(ax, ..., Name, Value)
Draws one ConstantLine per value in x, spanning the axes from bottom to top. Supports Color, LineStyle, LineWidth, Alpha, Label, LabelHorizontalAlignment and LabelVerticalAlignment.
Example: h = xline(2); h.Value   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet.

## xor
Element-wise exclusive OR.
Syntax: xor(A, B)
True where exactly one of A and B is nonzero.
Example: xor([1 0], [1 1])   % [false true]
Differences from MATLAB: Exactly two arguments.

## xscale
Set the x axis scale.
Syntax: xscale('linear')
Syntax: xscale('log')
Switches the x axis between linear and log scale.
Example: xscale('log')   % x axis uses log scale
Differences from MATLAB: Only 'linear' and 'log'.

## ylabel
Set the y axis label.
Syntax: ylabel('Amplitude')
Syntax: ylabel('Amplitude', 'Interpreter', 'none', 'Color', [1 0 0])
The text must be quoted, up to 4096 bytes. Only Interpreter none and an RGB Color are accepted.
Example: ylabel('Amplitude')   % label beside the y axis
Differences from MATLAB: No other text properties; no handle output.

## ylim
Set y axis limits.
Syntax: ylim([a b])
Syntax: ylim('auto')
Sets the visible y range, or returns it to automatic.
Example: ylim([-1 1])   % y from -1 to 1
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric two-element limits or 'auto' only.

## yline
Draw horizontal constant line(s) at y.
Syntax: h = yline(y)
Syntax: h = yline(y, linespec)
Syntax: h = yline(y, linespec, label)
Syntax: h = yline(ax, ..., Name, Value)
Draws one ConstantLine per value in y, spanning the axes from left to right. Supports Color, LineStyle, LineWidth, Alpha, Label, LabelHorizontalAlignment and LabelVerticalAlignment.
Example: h = yline([1 3], '--r', 'lim'); h(1).Label   % 'lim'
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet.

## yscale
Set the y axis scale.
Syntax: yscale('linear')
Syntax: yscale('log')
Switches the y axis between linear and log scale.
Example: yscale('log')   % y axis uses log scale
Differences from MATLAB: Only 'linear' and 'log'.

## zeros
Create an array of all zeros.
Syntax: Z = zeros(n)
Syntax: Z = zeros(rows, cols)
Syntax: Z = zeros([rows cols])
zeros(n) is n-by-n. A size vector such as size(A) also works.
Negative sizes count as zero.
Syntax: zeros(..., 'single')
Syntax: zeros(..., 'like', single(1))
Example: zeros(2, 'single')
Example: zeros(2, 3)
Class names 'single' and int8 through uint64 are accepted, as are typed integer/single 'like' prototypes.
Differences from MATLAB: two-dimensional output only; zeros with no size is not supported.

## zlabel
Label the z axis.
Syntax: zlabel('text')
Syntax: zlabel(ax, 'text')
The label is drawn centred beside the z axis of a 3-D axes. The axes ZLabel property is its text object.
Example: plot3([0 1], [0 1], [0 1]); zlabel('Height')   % z axis label
Differences from MATLAB: Literal text only; Color and font properties of the z label are not supported yet.

## zlim
Set or query z axis limits.
Syntax: zlim([a b])
Syntax: zlim('auto')
Syntax: zlim('manual')
Syntax: L = zlim
Syntax: zlim(ax, ...)
Automatic limits span the z data of the axes (2-D lines count as z = 0) by the same rule as x and y. zlim('manual') freezes the current limits. axis([x1 x2 y1 y2 z1 z2]) sets all three; axis on a 3-D axes returns six values.
Example: plot3([0 1], [0 1], [2 5]); L = zlim   % [2 5]
Differences from MATLAB: Infinite ends such as [0 inf] are supported for auto-scaling one side.

## xticks
Set or query x axis tick values.
Syntax: xticks(ticks)
Syntax: xticks('auto')
Syntax: xticks('manual')
Syntax: t = xticks
Syntax: xticks(ax, ...)
Sets the x-axis tick positions (strictly increasing finite vector), restores automatic ticks with 'auto', or freezes current ticks with 'manual'. With no arguments, returns the current tick values.
Example: plot(1:5); xticks([1 3 5]); t = xticks   % [1 3 5]
Differences from MATLAB: Categorical or datetime tick values are not supported yet.

## yticks
Set or query y axis tick values.
Syntax: yticks(ticks)
Syntax: yticks('auto')
Syntax: yticks('manual')
Syntax: t = yticks
Syntax: yticks(ax, ...)
Sets the y-axis tick positions (strictly increasing finite vector), restores automatic ticks with 'auto', or freezes current ticks with 'manual'. With no arguments, returns the current tick values.
Example: plot(1:5); yticks([1 3 5]); t = yticks   % [1 3 5]
Differences from MATLAB: Categorical or datetime tick values are not supported yet.

## zticks
Set or query z axis tick values.
Syntax: zticks(ticks)
Syntax: zticks('auto')
Syntax: zticks('manual')
Syntax: t = zticks
Syntax: zticks(ax, ...)
Sets the z-axis tick positions (strictly increasing finite vector), restores automatic ticks with 'auto', or freezes current ticks with 'manual'. With no arguments, returns the current tick values.
Example: plot3([0 1], [0 1], [0 2]); zticks([0 1 2]); t = zticks   % [0 1 2]
Differences from MATLAB: Categorical or datetime tick values are not supported yet.

## xticklabels
Set or query x axis tick labels.
Syntax: xticklabels(labels)
Syntax: xticklabels('auto')
Syntax: L = xticklabels
Syntax: xticklabels(ax, ...)
Sets the x-axis tick labels from a cell array of character vectors, string array, or character matrix, or restores automatic labels with 'auto'. Labels pair with ticks in order; missing trailing labels are blanked.
Example: plot(1:3); xticks(1:3); xticklabels({'a', 'b', 'c'}); L = xticklabels; numel(L)   % 3
Differences from MATLAB: TeX markup in tick labels is drawn literally.

## yticklabels
Set or query y axis tick labels.
Syntax: yticklabels(labels)
Syntax: yticklabels('auto')
Syntax: L = yticklabels
Syntax: yticklabels(ax, ...)
Sets the y-axis tick labels from a cell array of character vectors, string array, or character matrix, or restores automatic labels with 'auto'.
Example: plot(1:3); yticks(1:3); yticklabels({'a', 'b', 'c'}); L = yticklabels; numel(L)   % 3
Differences from MATLAB: TeX markup in tick labels is drawn literally.

## zticklabels
Set or query z axis tick labels.
Syntax: zticklabels(labels)
Syntax: zticklabels('auto')
Syntax: L = zticklabels
Syntax: zticklabels(ax, ...)
Sets the z-axis tick labels from a cell array of character vectors, string array, or character matrix, or restores automatic labels with 'auto'.
Example: plot3([0 1], [0 1], [1 3]); zticks(1:3); zticklabels({'low', 'mid', 'high'}); L = zticklabels; numel(L)   % 3
Differences from MATLAB: TeX markup in tick labels is drawn literally.

## xtickangle
Set or query x axis tick label rotation angle in degrees.
Syntax: xtickangle(angle)
Syntax: a = xtickangle
Syntax: xtickangle(ax, ...)
Rotates the x-axis tick labels counter-clockwise by angle degrees.
Example: plot(1:5); xtickangle(45); a = xtickangle   % 45
Differences from MATLAB: Simple rotation about the label anchor.

## ytickangle
Set or query y axis tick label rotation angle in degrees.
Syntax: ytickangle(angle)
Syntax: a = ytickangle
Syntax: ytickangle(ax, ...)
Rotates the y-axis tick labels counter-clockwise by angle degrees.
Example: plot(1:5); ytickangle(30); a = ytickangle   % 30
Differences from MATLAB: Simple rotation about the label anchor.

## ztickangle
Set or query z axis tick label rotation angle in degrees.
Syntax: ztickangle(angle)
Syntax: a = ztickangle
Syntax: ztickangle(ax, ...)
Rotates the z-axis tick labels counter-clockwise by angle degrees.
Example: plot3([0 1], [0 1], [0 1]); ztickangle(15); a = ztickangle   % 15
Differences from MATLAB: Simple rotation about the label anchor.

## xtickformat
Set or query x axis tick label format.
Syntax: xtickformat(fmt)
Syntax: f = xtickformat
Syntax: xtickformat(ax, ...)
Sets TickLabelFormat on the x-axis ruler (datetime, duration, or numeric format string, or 'auto').
Example: plot(datetime(2024,1,1:3), 1:3); xtickformat('dd-MMM'); f = xtickformat   % dd-MMM
Differences from MATLAB: Categorical rulers do not support TickLabelFormat.

## ytickformat
Set or query y axis tick label format.
Syntax: ytickformat(fmt)
Syntax: f = ytickformat
Syntax: ytickformat(ax, ...)
Sets TickLabelFormat on the y-axis ruler (datetime, duration, or numeric format string, or 'auto').
Example: plot(1:3, hours(1:3)); ytickformat('hh:mm'); f = ytickformat   % hh:mm
Differences from MATLAB: Categorical rulers do not support TickLabelFormat.

## ztickformat
Set or query z axis tick label format.
Syntax: ztickformat(fmt)
Syntax: f = ztickformat
Syntax: ztickformat(ax, ...)
Sets TickLabelFormat on the z-axis ruler (datetime, duration, or numeric format string, or 'auto').
Example: plot3([0 1], [0 1], [0 1]); ztickformat('%.1f'); f = ztickformat   % %.1f
Differences from MATLAB: Categorical rulers do not support TickLabelFormat.

## run
Run a script file.
Syntax: run(name)
Syntax: run('name.m')
Syntax: run('folder/name.m')
Runs the .mr or .m script name in your workspace, as typing name does.
When both name.mr and name.m exist, name.mr runs.
With a folder part (relative to the Current Folder, or absolute), the script
finds other files and saves and loads data in that folder while it runs;
afterwards the old folder is used again.
A function file runs with no inputs, as typing its name does.
Example: run('setup.m')
Differences from MATLAB: at most 16 other folders per run, and scripts and
functions share a call depth of 32 (MATLAB allows 500).

## switch
Choose a block of statements by value.
Syntax: switch expr; case value; statements; otherwise; statements; end
Compares expr with each case value in turn and runs the first block that matches; at most one block runs. Numbers match by value, character rows match exactly, and a cell array of values matches when any element does. A single character compared with a number compares by character code. Use otherwise for the block that runs when nothing matches.
Example: x = 2; switch x; case 1; disp('one'); case {2, 3}; disp('two or three'); otherwise; disp('other'); end   % two or three
Differences from MATLAB: Multi-character text never matches a number.

## case
Give one branch of a switch block.
Syntax: case value
Syntax: case {value1, value2}
Runs the statements up to the next case, otherwise or end when the switch expression matches value. A cell array of values matches when any element matches. Only valid inside switch.
Example: s = 'b'; switch s; case 'a'; disp(1); case {'b','c'}; disp(2); end   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## otherwise
Give the default branch of a switch block.
Syntax: otherwise
Runs its statements when no case of the enclosing switch matched. Must come after every case. Only valid inside switch.
Example: switch 5; case 1; disp('one'); otherwise; disp('not one'); end   % not one
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## feval
Call a function by handle or by name.
Syntax: [y1, ..., yN] = feval(f, x1, ..., xM)
Syntax: feval('name', x1, ..., xM)
f may be a function handle or a character row naming a built-in or user function. The remaining arguments are passed through, and the outputs are returned.
Example: feval(@max, [3 9 4])   % 9
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## func2str
Return the text of a function handle.
Syntax: s = func2str(f)
For a named handle the result is the function name; for an anonymous function it is the full text starting with @.
Example: func2str(@(x) x.^2 + 1)   % '@(x)x.^2+1'
Differences from MATLAB: Anonymous function text is rebuilt from the parsed tokens, so spacing can differ from what was typed.

## str2func
Make a function handle from text.
Syntax: f = str2func('name')
Syntax: f = str2func('@(x) expression')
A name gives a handle to that function; text starting with @ gives an anonymous function. Variables in the text are not captured from the workspace.
Example: f = str2func('@(x) x + 1'); f(2)   % 3
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## arrayfun
Apply a function to each element of an array.
Syntax: A = arrayfun(f, X)
Syntax: [A, B] = arrayfun(f, X, Y)
Syntax: C = arrayfun(f, X, 'UniformOutput', false)
Calls f once per element (all inputs must have the same size) and collects the results in an array of that size. Each call must return scalars of one class unless UniformOutput is false, which collects the results in cell arrays.
Example: arrayfun(@(x) x^2, [1 2 3])   % [1 4 9]
Differences from MATLAB: ErrorHandler is not supported.

## cellfun
Apply a function to each cell of a cell array.
Syntax: A = cellfun(f, C)
Syntax: A = cellfun('isempty', C)
Syntax: C2 = cellfun(f, C, 'UniformOutput', false)
Calls f once per cell (all cell inputs must have the same size) and collects scalar results in an array, or in cell arrays when UniformOutput is false. The legacy names 'isempty', 'length', 'isreal' and similar are accepted as text.
Example: cellfun(@length, {'ab', 'cde', ''})   % [2 3 0]
Differences from MATLAB: ErrorHandler is not supported.

## isequal
Test whether arrays are equal.
Syntax: tf = isequal(A, B)
Syntax: tf = isequal(A, B, C, ...)
True when every input has the same size and the same values. Numeric, logical and character inputs compare by value regardless of class. NaN is never equal to NaN.
Example: isequal([1 2 3], [1 2 3])   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## lu
LU factorization with partial pivoting.
Syntax: [L, U, P] = lu(A)
Syntax: [L, U] = lu(A)
Syntax: Y = lu(A)
Syntax: [L, U, p] = lu(A, 'vector')
Syntax: [L, U, P] = lu(A, 'matrix')
P*A = L*U with L unit lower triangular. With two outputs L is the
permuted lower factor, so A = L*U. With one output Y holds U on and above
the diagonal and the multipliers of L below it. 'vector' returns the row
permutation as a row vector p, so A(p,:) = L*U. A may be rectangular.
Example: [L, U, P] = lu([1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 10])   % U(1,:) = 7 8 10
Differences from MATLAB: sparse input and other options are not
supported. Complex double input pivots by |re|+|im| as LAPACK does.
MatRust also accepts logical input.

## qr
QR factorization by Householder reflections.
Syntax: [Q, R] = qr(A)
Syntax: [Q, R] = qr(A, 0)
Syntax: [Q, R, E] = qr(A)
Syntax: [Q, R, p] = qr(A, 0)
Syntax: [Q, R, p] = qr(A, 'vector')
Syntax: [Q, R, E] = qr(A, 'matrix')
Syntax: H = qr(A)
Syntax: H = qr(A, 0)
A = Q*R with orthogonal Q. qr(A, 0) is the economy size when A has more
rows than columns. With three outputs columns are pivoted by their
remaining norm: A*E = Q*R, or A(:,p) = Q*R with the economy or 'vector' form.
With one output, qr(A) and qr(A, 0) both return the packed m-by-n factorization:
R on and above the diagonal and Householder vectors below it.
Example: [Q, R] = qr([1 2; 3 4])   % R = [-3.1623 -4.4272; 0 -0.6325]
Differences from MATLAB: sparse input is not supported. Complex input uses
the same unblocked Householder steps as LAPACK (column pivoting by remaining
norm for three outputs); results whose imaginary parts are all zero are real.

## chol
Cholesky factorization of a symmetric positive definite matrix.
Syntax: R = chol(A)
