Same as the family function, e.g. cdf('Gamma', X, A, B) is gamcdf(X, A, B); 'upper' gives the upper tail. Names as in pdf.
Example: cdf('Normal', 1.96)
Example: cdf('Exponential', 5, 1, 'upper')
Distribution objects from makedist or fitdist are accepted as the first argument; object parameters are supplied by the object.
Differences from MATLAB: parameter confidence intervals and truncated distributions are unsupported.

## icdf
Inverse cumulative distribution function of a named distribution.
Syntax: X = icdf(name, P, A, B, ...)
Same as the family function, e.g. icdf('T', P, NU) is tinv(P, NU). Names as in pdf.
Example: icdf('Normal', 0.975)
Example: icdf('Binomial', 0.5, 10, 0.3)
Distribution objects from makedist or fitdist are accepted as the first argument; object parameters are supplied by the object.
Differences from MATLAB: parameter confidence intervals and truncated distributions are unsupported.

## random
Random numbers from a named distribution.
Syntax: R = random(name, A, B, ...)
Syntax: R = random(name, A, B, ..., m, n, ...)
Syntax: R = random(name, A, B, ..., [m n ...])
Same as the family function, e.g. random('Normal', MU, SIGMA, 2, 3) is normrnd(MU, SIGMA, 2, 3): the first arguments after the name are the parameters, the rest the size. Names as in pdf.
Example: rng(1); random('Exponential', 2, 1, 4)
Distribution objects also support random(pd,m,n) or random(pd,[m n]).
Differences from MATLAB: draws use the session's Mersenne Twister stream, so rng(seed) makes them reproducible; for a given seed the numbers follow the same distribution as MATLAB's but are not the same numbers.

## normfit
Normal parameter estimates and confidence intervals.
Syntax: [muhat, sigmahat, muci, sigmaci] = normfit(X)
Syntax: [...] = normfit(X, alpha)
muhat is the sample mean and sigmahat the sample standard deviation (divided by N-1). muci and sigmaci are 100(1-alpha)% intervals (alpha default 0.05) from the t and chi-square distributions, one column per interval [lower; upper]. A vector is one sample; a matrix gives one estimate per column.
Example: [mu, sigma, muci] = normfit([4.1 5.3 2.2 6.0 4.8])
Differences from MATLAB: censoring and frequency arguments are not supported yet.

## expfit
Exponential mean estimate and confidence interval.
Syntax: [muhat, muci] = expfit(X)
Syntax: [muhat, muci] = expfit(X, alpha)
muhat is the sample mean; muci is the 100(1-alpha)% interval [lower; upper] (alpha default 0.05) 2*N*muhat./chi2inv([1-alpha/2, alpha/2], 2*N). A vector is one sample; a matrix gives one estimate per column.
Example: [mu, muci] = expfit([0.3 1.7 0.9 2.4 0.1])
Differences from MATLAB: censoring and frequency arguments are not supported yet.

## paramci
Confidence intervals for the parameters of a fitted distribution object.
Syntax: ci = paramci(pd)
Syntax: ci = paramci(pd, 'Alpha', alpha)
Syntax: ci = paramci(pd, 'Parameter', name)
ci is 2-by-k: row 1 holds the lower and row 2 the upper limits of the 100(1-alpha)% intervals (alpha default 0.05). Normal and Lognormal use the exact t and chi-square intervals of normfit, Exponential the exact chi-square interval with 2r degrees of freedom (r uncensored observations), Poisson the exact Garwood interval, Binomial the Clopper-Pearson interval and Rayleigh the exact chi-square interval. Other parameters get Wald intervals from ParameterCovariance: on the log scale for positive parameters, the logit scale for probabilities and the natural scale for locations and the GEV/GP shape k. Fixed parameters give a zero-width interval. 'Parameter' takes a name, a cell array of names or indices. pd.paramci(...) also works.
Example: pd = fitdist([4.1 5.3 2.2 6.0 4.8 5.1]', 'Normal'); ci = paramci(pd)
Example: pd = fitdist([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1]', 'Gamma'); paramci(pd, 'Alpha', 0.1, 'Parameter', 'a')
Differences from MATLAB: objects from makedist return zero-width intervals; Kernel objects have no parameters and raise an error. Interval methods are as listed (censored Normal, Lognormal and Rayleigh fits use Wald intervals).

## negloglik
Negative log-likelihood of a fitted distribution object.
Syntax: nll = negloglik(pd)
Returns the negative log-likelihood of the data the object was fitted to (with its censoring and frequencies), at the object's parameters; the same value as pd.NLogL. Objects from makedist return [].
Example: pd = fitdist([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1]', 'Weibull'); nll = negloglik(pd)
Differences from MATLAB: truncated distributions are not supported.

## mle
Maximum likelihood estimates for a named or custom distribution.
Syntax: phat = mle(data)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = mle(data, 'Distribution', name, Name, Value)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = mle(data, 'pdf', pdf, 'Start', start, Name, Value)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = mle(data, 'logpdf', logpdf, 'Start', start, Name, Value)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = mle(data, 'nloglf', nloglf, 'Start', start, Name, Value)
With no distribution the data are fitted as Normal. Names are the fitdist families except Kernel. Unlike fitdist and normfit, the Normal and Lognormal sigma is the maximum likelihood (biased) estimate; pci holds the paramci intervals (row 1 lower, row 2 upper). phat lists the free parameters only (Binomial p with 'NTrials', GeneralizedPareto k and sigma with 'Theta'). Options: 'Censoring' (1 = right-censored), 'Frequency', 'Alpha', 'NTrials', 'Theta', 'Options' (statset: MaxIter, MaxFunEvals, TolX, TolFun). Custom distributions: pdf(x, p1, p2, ...) or logpdf(x, p1, ...) returns one value per observation, with 'cdf' or 'logsf' for censored data; nloglf(params, data, cens, freq) returns the negative log-likelihood. They are minimised by Nelder-Mead from 'Start' within 'LowerBound'/'UpperBound', then refined by Newton steps; pci are Wald intervals from the numerical Hessian.
Example: phat = mle([4.1 5.3 2.2 6.0 4.8 5.1])
Example: [phat, pci] = mle([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1], 'Distribution', 'Exponential')
Example: phat = mle([4.1 5.3 2.2 6.0 4.8 5.1], 'pdf', @(x,m,s) normpdf(x,m,s), 'Start', [4 1])
Differences from MATLAB: left censoring (-1), 'OptimFun','fmincon', truncation, 'TruncationBounds' and gradient options are not supported; nloglf is always called with four inputs.

## statset
Options structure for the statistics fitting functions.
Syntax: options = statset()
Syntax: options = statset(Name, Value, ...)
Syntax: options = statset(oldopts, Name, Value, ...)
Returns a structure with the fields Display, MaxFunEvals, MaxIter, TolBnd, TolFun, TolX, DerivStep, FunValCheck, GradObj, Jacobian, OutputFcn, Robust, Tune and UseParallel; unset fields are []. Names are case-insensitive. fitdist, mle and the <family>fit functions read MaxIter, MaxFunEvals, TolX and TolFun.
Example: opts = statset('MaxIter', 500, 'TolX', 1e-8)
Differences from MATLAB: statset('fitfunction') default sets are not supported; only the listed fields are known.

## normlike
Normal negative log-likelihood and the asymptotic covariance of the parameters.
Syntax: nlogL = normlike(params, x)
Syntax: [nlogL, aVar] = normlike(params, x, censoring, freq)
params is [mu sigma]. aVar is the inverse of the observed Fisher information (the Hessian of nlogL) at params. censoring marks right-censored observations, freq gives frequencies.
Example: [nlogL, aVar] = normlike([5 1], [4.1 5.3 4.4 6.0 4.8 5.1])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## explike
Exponential negative log-likelihood and the asymptotic variance of mu.
Syntax: nlogL = explike(mu, x)
Syntax: [nlogL, aVar] = explike(mu, x, censoring, freq)
aVar is the inverse of the observed information at mu.
Example: [nlogL, aVar] = explike(2, [1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## gamlike
Gamma negative log-likelihood and the asymptotic covariance of [a b].
Syntax: nlogL = gamlike(params, x)
Syntax: [nlogL, aVar] = gamlike(params, x, censoring, freq)
params is [a b] (shape, scale); aVar is the inverse of the observed information at params.
Example: [nlogL, aVar] = gamlike([2 1], [1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## wbllike
Weibull negative log-likelihood and the asymptotic covariance of [A B].
Syntax: nlogL = wbllike(params, x)
Syntax: [nlogL, aVar] = wbllike(params, x, censoring, freq)
params is [A B] (scale, shape); aVar is the inverse of the observed information at params.
Example: [nlogL, aVar] = wbllike([2 1.5], [1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## lognlike
Lognormal negative log-likelihood and the asymptotic covariance of [mu sigma].
Syntax: nlogL = lognlike(params, x)
Syntax: [nlogL, aVar] = lognlike(params, x, censoring, freq)
params is [mu sigma] of log(x); aVar is the inverse of the observed information at params.
Example: [nlogL, aVar] = lognlike([0.3 0.6], [1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## evlike
Extreme value (minimum) negative log-likelihood and the asymptotic covariance.
Syntax: nlogL = evlike(params, x)
Syntax: [nlogL, aVar] = evlike(params, x, censoring, freq)
params is [mu sigma] of the type 1 extreme value distribution for minima.
Example: [nlogL, aVar] = evlike([5 1], [4.1 5.3 4.4 6.0 4.8 5.1])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## betalike
Beta negative log-likelihood and the asymptotic covariance of [a b].
Syntax: nlogL = betalike(params, x)
Syntax: [nlogL, aVar] = betalike(params, x)
Data must lie in (0, 1); aVar is the inverse of the observed information at params.
Example: [nlogL, aVar] = betalike([2 3], [0.2 0.45 0.31 0.6 0.12])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## gamfit
Gamma parameter estimates and confidence intervals.
Syntax: phat = gamfit(x)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = gamfit(x, alpha, censoring, freq, options)
phat = [a b] (shape, scale) maximises the likelihood; pci is 2-by-2 (Wald, log scale). censoring marks right-censored values; options is a statset structure.
Example: [phat, pci] = gamfit([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1 1.7])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## wblfit
Weibull parameter estimates and confidence intervals.
Syntax: phat = wblfit(x)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = wblfit(x, alpha, censoring, freq, options)
phat = [A B] (scale, shape); pci is 2-by-2 (Wald, log scale). With censoring the profile likelihood of the shape is solved directly.
Example: [phat, pci] = wblfit([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1 1.7])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## lognfit
Lognormal parameter estimates and confidence intervals.
Syntax: phat = lognfit(x)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = lognfit(x, alpha, censoring, freq, options)
phat = [mu sigma] of log(x), sigma unbiased (divided by n-1) for uncensored data and the maximum likelihood estimate with censoring; pci uses the exact t and chi-square intervals (Wald with censoring).
Example: [phat, pci] = lognfit([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1 1.7])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## betafit
Beta parameter estimates and confidence intervals.
Syntax: phat = betafit(x)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = betafit(x, alpha)
phat = [a b] maximises the likelihood of data in (0, 1); pci is 2-by-2 (Wald, log scale).
Example: [phat, pci] = betafit([0.2 0.45 0.31 0.6 0.12 0.38])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## raylfit
Rayleigh parameter estimate and confidence interval.
Syntax: b = raylfit(x)
Syntax: [b, bci] = raylfit(x, alpha, censoring, freq)
b = sqrt(sum(x.^2)/(2n)) (n uncensored observations); bci is the exact chi-square interval for uncensored data, Wald (log scale) with censoring.
Example: [b, bci] = raylfit([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1 1.7])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## evfit
Extreme value (minimum) parameter estimates and confidence intervals.
Syntax: phat = evfit(x)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = evfit(x, alpha, censoring, freq, options)
phat = [mu sigma] of the type 1 extreme value distribution for minima, from the profile likelihood of sigma; pci is Wald (mu natural, sigma log scale).
Example: [phat, pci] = evfit([4.1 5.3 4.4 6.0 4.8 5.1])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## poissfit
Poisson parameter estimate and exact confidence interval.
Syntax: lambdahat = poissfit(x)
Syntax: [lambdahat, lambdaci] = poissfit(x, alpha)
lambdahat is the sample mean of nonnegative integer counts; lambdaci is the exact (Garwood) chi-square interval [chi2inv(alpha/2, 2S); chi2inv(1-alpha/2, 2S+2)]/(2n) with S = sum(x). A vector is one sample; a matrix gives one estimate per column.
Example: [lambdahat, lambdaci] = poissfit([2 0 3 1 4 2])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## binofit
Binomial probability estimate and Clopper-Pearson confidence interval.
Syntax: phat = binofit(x, n)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = binofit(x, n, alpha)
phat = x./n for each element of x (n scalar or the same size); pci has one row [lower upper] per element, from the beta inverse (exact Clopper-Pearson interval).
Example: [phat, pci] = binofit(7, 20)
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## nbinfit
Negative binomial parameter estimates and confidence intervals.
Syntax: phat = nbinfit(x)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = nbinfit(x, alpha, options)
phat = [R P] maximises the likelihood of overdispersed counts (sample variance above the mean); pci is Wald (R on the log scale, P on the logit scale).
Example: [phat, pci] = nbinfit([0 2 5 1 0 7 3 1 0 9])
Differences from MATLAB: data that are not overdispersed raise an error.

## gevfit
Generalized extreme value parameter estimates and confidence intervals.
Syntax: phat = gevfit(x)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = gevfit(x, alpha, options)
phat = [k sigma mu] (shape, scale, location; k > 0 is the heavy-tailed type II case); pci is Wald (sigma on the log scale).
Example: [phat, pci] = gevfit([4.1 5.3 4.4 6.0 4.8 5.1 7.9 4.6])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## gpfit
Generalized Pareto parameter estimates and confidence intervals.
Syntax: phat = gpfit(x)
Syntax: [phat, pci] = gpfit(x, alpha, options)
phat = [k sigma] for exceedances x >= 0 over the threshold 0; pci is Wald (sigma on the log scale).
Example: [phat, pci] = gpfit([0.3 1.7 0.9 2.4 0.1 4.2 0.6])
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## probplot
Probability plot of data against a distribution.
Syntax: probplot(y)
Syntax: probplot(dist, y)
Syntax: probplot(dist, y, cens, freq)
Syntax: probplot(..., 'noref')
Syntax: probplot(ax, pd)
Syntax: h = probplot(...)
dist is 'normal' (default), 'exponential', 'extreme value', 'half normal', 'lognormal', 'logistic', 'loglogistic', 'rayleigh', 'weibull' or a probability distribution object. Each sorted value is plotted at plotting position (i-0.5)/n (Kaplan-Meier step midpoints with censoring or frequencies) on the distribution's quantile scale; the x axis is logarithmic for weibull, lognormal and loglogistic. The dashed reference line passes through the first and third quartiles (the minimum and median for half normal), or follows the fitted cdf of a distribution object. probplot(ax, pd) adds the fitted line of pd to an existing probability plot. h holds the data line and reference line of each column.
Example: probplot('weibull', [1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1 1.7]);
Example: h = probplot([4.1 5.3 4.4 6.0 4.8 5.1]);
Differences from MATLAB: probability labels are text objects beside dotted grid lines inside the axes, and the axis ticks keep the transformed scale; probplot(ax, fun, params) is not supported.

## normplot
Normal probability plot.
Syntax: normplot(x)
Syntax: h = normplot(x)
Same as probplot('normal', x) with the title Normal Probability Plot.
Example: h = normplot([4.1 5.3 4.4 6.0 4.8 5.1]);
Differences from MATLAB: the reference line is one dashed line through the quartiles; probability labels as in probplot.

## wblplot
Weibull probability plot.
Syntax: wblplot(x)
Syntax: h = wblplot(x)
Same as probplot('weibull', x) with the title Weibull Probability Plot; data must be positive.
Example: h = wblplot([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1 1.7]);
Differences from MATLAB: probability labels as in probplot.

## qqplot
Quantile-quantile plot.
Syntax: qqplot(x)
Syntax: qqplot(x, pd)
Syntax: qqplot(x, y)
Syntax: h = qqplot(...)
qqplot(x) plots the sorted x against standard normal quantiles at (i-0.5)/n; qqplot(x, pd) against the quantiles of a distribution object; qqplot(x, y) the quantiles of two samples, interpolating the larger sample at the plotting positions of the smaller. A solid line joins the first and third quartiles and a dashed line extends it. h holds the data, solid and dashed lines.
Example: h = qqplot([4.1 5.3 4.4 6.0 4.8 5.1]);
Example: qqplot([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1], makedist('Exponential', 'mu', 1.5));
Differences from MATLAB: x and y must be vectors (matrix columns are not plotted separately).

## ecdf
Empirical cumulative distribution function (Kaplan-Meier).
Syntax: [f, x] = ecdf(y)
Syntax: [f, x, flo, fup] = ecdf(y, Name, Value)
Syntax: ecdf(y, Name, Value)
x is [min(y); the distinct uncensored values] and f the estimate at them, starting with 0. Options: 'Censoring' (1 = right-censored), 'Frequency', 'Alpha' (0.05), 'Function' ('cdf', 'survivor' or 'cumulative hazard') and 'Bounds' ('on' draws the bounds in the plot form). flo and fup are Greenwood confidence bounds (NaN at the first point and where the variance is undefined). Without outputs it draws a stairstep plot.
Example: [f, x] = ecdf([3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6])
Example: [f, x, flo, fup] = ecdf([3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6], 'Censoring', [0 0 0 1 0 1 0 0]);
Differences from MATLAB: left and interval censoring and the fifth output D are not supported.

## cdfplot
Plot of the empirical cumulative distribution function.
Syntax: cdfplot(x)
Syntax: h = cdfplot(x)
Syntax: [h, stats] = cdfplot(x)
Draws the empirical cdf of x (NaN ignored) as a stairstep line with a grid. stats has the fields min, max, mean, median and std.
Example: [h, stats] = cdfplot([3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6]);
Differences from MATLAB: the stairs start at the smallest value rather than at -Inf.

## wfilters
Decomposition and reconstruction filters of a wavelet.
Syntax: [LoD, HiD, LoR, HiR] = wfilters(wname)
Syntax: [F1, F2] = wfilters(wname, type)
wname is 'haar', 'db1'..'db20', 'sym2'..'sym20', 'coif1'..'coif5', 'biorNr.Nd' or 'rbioNr.Nd' (1.1 1.3 1.5 2.2 2.4 2.6 2.8 3.1 3.3 3.5 3.7 3.9 4.4 5.5 6.8). type 'd' gives the decomposition pair, 'r' the reconstruction pair, 'l' the two lowpass and 'h' the two highpass filters. Filters are row vectors; the lowpass filters sum to sqrt(2).
Example: [LoD, HiD, LoR, HiR] = wfilters('db2')
Example: [LoD, LoR] = wfilters('bior2.2', 'l')
Differences from MATLAB: db21..db45, dmey and the non-discrete families are not available; wavemngr is not supported.

## dwt
Single-level 1-D discrete wavelet transform.
Syntax: [cA, cD] = dwt(x, wname)
Syntax: [cA, cD] = dwt(x, LoD, HiD)
Syntax: [cA, cD] = dwt(..., 'mode', extmode)
Extends x by the current dwtmode (or 'mode'), convolves with the decomposition filters and keeps every second sample: floor((n+lf-1)/2) coefficients, ceil(n/2) for 'per'. A column x gives column outputs.
Example: [cA, cD] = dwt([1 2 3 4 5 6], 'haar')
Example: [cA, cD] = dwt(sin(1:10), 'db2', 'mode', 'per')
Differences from MATLAB: real vectors only.

## idwt
Single-level inverse 1-D discrete wavelet transform.
Syntax: x = idwt(cA, cD, wname)
Syntax: x = idwt(cA, cD, LoR, HiR)
Syntax: x = idwt(cA, cD, wname, L)
Syntax: x = idwt(..., 'mode', extmode)
Upsamples, convolves with the reconstruction filters and returns the central part: 2n-lf+2 samples (2n for 'per') or L samples. Either cA or cD may be [] (a zero branch). idwt(dwt(x)) returns x.
Example: [cA, cD] = dwt([4 2 7 1 8], 'db2'); x = idwt(cA, cD, 'db2', 5)
Differences from MATLAB: real vectors only.

## dwtmode
Global signal extension mode of the discrete wavelet transform.
Syntax: dwtmode
Syntax: st = dwtmode('status')
Syntax: dwtmode(mode)
Syntax: dwtmode(mode, 'nodisp')
Modes: 'sym' (half-point symmetric, the default), 'symw', 'asym', 'asymw', 'zpd' (zeros), 'sp0', 'sp1', 'ppd' (periodic) and 'per' (periodization, ceil(n/2) coefficients). dwt, idwt, wavedec, waverec, appcoef, wrcoef, wden and wdenoise use it. 'nodisp' suppresses the message.
Example: dwtmode('per', 'nodisp'); st = dwtmode('status', 'nodisp')
Differences from MATLAB: dwtmode('save', ...) is not supported; the mode lasts for the session.

## wavedec
Multilevel 1-D wavelet decomposition.
Syntax: [C, L] = wavedec(x, n, wname)
Syntax: [C, L] = wavedec(x, n, LoD, HiD)
C = [cA_n cD_n ... cD_1] and the bookkeeping vector L = [length(cA_n) length(cD_n) ... length(cD_1) length(x)]. A column x gives column C and L. Uses the current dwtmode.
Example: [C, L] = wavedec(cos((1:40)/3), 3, 'db3')
Differences from MATLAB: real vectors only; n is at most 64.

## waverec
Multilevel 1-D wavelet reconstruction.
Syntax: x = waverec(C, L, wname)
Syntax: x = waverec(C, L, LoR, HiR)
Inverse of wavedec: waverec(wavedec(x, n, w), ..., w) returns x.
Example: [C, L] = wavedec(1:16, 2, 'sym4'); x = waverec(C, L, 'sym4')
Differences from MATLAB: real vectors only.

## appcoef
Approximation coefficients of a 1-D wavelet decomposition.
Syntax: A = appcoef(C, L, wname)
Syntax: A = appcoef(C, L, wname, N)
Syntax: A = appcoef(C, L, LoR, HiR, N)
Returns cA at level N (default the deepest level), reconstructing from the coarser levels; N = 0 gives the signal.
Example: [C, L] = wavedec(cos((1:40)/3), 3, 'db3'); A2 = appcoef(C, L, 'db3', 2)
Differences from MATLAB: real vectors only.

## detcoef
Detail coefficients of a 1-D wavelet decomposition.
Syntax: D = detcoef(C, L, N)
Syntax: D = detcoef(C, L, N, 'cells')
Syntax: D = detcoef(C, L, 'cells')
Syntax: [D1, ..., Dp] = detcoef(C, L, [N1 ... Np])
Returns cD at level N (default 1). A vector N or 'cells' gives a 1-by-p cell array; several outputs give one level each.
Example: [C, L] = wavedec(cos((1:40)/3), 3, 'db3'); [D1, D3] = detcoef(C, L, [1 3])
Differences from MATLAB: 'dcells' is not supported.

## wrcoef
Reconstruct a single branch of a 1-D wavelet decomposition.
Syntax: X = wrcoef(type, C, L, wname)
Syntax: X = wrcoef(type, C, L, wname, N)
Syntax: X = wrcoef(type, C, L, LoR, HiR, N)
type 'a' reconstructs the approximation at level N (0 allowed), 'd' the details at level N (default: the deepest level), with all other coefficients zero; the result has the length of the signal and wrcoef('a', ..., n) plus the details of levels 1..n gives the signal.
Example: [C, L] = wavedec(cos((1:40)/3), 3, 'db3'); D2 = wrcoef('d', C, L, 'db3', 2)
Differences from MATLAB: real vectors only.

## wmaxlev
Maximum useful wavelet decomposition level.
Syntax: lev = wmaxlev(sizeX, wname)
lev = fix(log2(n/(lf-1))) with lf the filter length (0 when that is below 1); n is the signal length (for a size vector of a 2-D array its smallest side).
Example: lev = wmaxlev(1024, 'sym4')   % 7
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## wthresh
Soft or hard thresholding.
Syntax: Y = wthresh(X, sorh, T)
's' gives sign(X).*max(abs(X)-T, 0), 'h' gives X.*(abs(X) > T).
Example: y = wthresh([-3 -1 0.5 2 4], 's', 1)
Differences from MATLAB: real arrays only.

## thselect
Threshold selection for wavelet denoising (unit noise level).
Syntax: thr = thselect(X, tptr)
tptr 'sqtwolog' gives sqrt(2*log(n)), 'rigrsure' the Stein unbiased risk estimate minimiser, 'heursure' a choice between the two from the signal energy and 'minimaxi' the minimax threshold 0.3936+0.1829*log2(n) (0 for n <= 32); n = numel(X).
Example: thr = thselect([0.3 -2.1 0.8 4.2 -0.4 0.1 1.7 -0.9], 'rigrsure')
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## wden
Automatic 1-D wavelet denoising.
Syntax: [xd, cxd, lxd, thr] = wden(x, tptr, sorh, scal, n, wname)
Syntax: [xd, cxd, lxd, thr] = wden(C, L, tptr, sorh, scal, n, wname)
Thresholds the details of levels 1..n with the thselect rule tptr ('sqtwolog' and 'minimaxi' use numel(C)), 's' or 'h' thresholding, and noise rescaling scal: 'one' (none), 'sln' (one estimate from level 1) or 'mln' (one per level), estimates median(abs(d))/0.6745. thr holds the threshold of each level.
Example: [xd, cxd, lxd] = wden(cos((1:64)/5) + 0.1*sin((1:64).^2), 'heursure', 's', 'mln', 3, 'db4');
Differences from MATLAB: 'modwtsqtwolog' (MODWT denoising) is not supported.

## wdenoise
Wavelet signal denoising.
Syntax: xden = wdenoise(x)
Syntax: xden = wdenoise(x, level)
Syntax: [xden, denoisedcfs, origcfs] = wdenoise(..., Name, Value)
Options: 'Wavelet' (default 'sym4'), 'DenoisingMethod' 'Bayes' (default, empirical Bayes with a Laplace prior), 'SURE', 'UniversalThreshold', 'Minimax', 'BlockJS' (block James-Stein) or 'FDR' / {'FDR', Q} (Q default 0.05), 'ThresholdRule' ('Median' (default), 'Mean', 'Soft' or 'Hard' for Bayes; 'Soft' (default) or 'Hard' for SURE, UniversalThreshold and Minimax; 'Hard' for FDR; 'James-Stein' for BlockJS) and 'NoiseEstimate' ('LevelIndependent' from level 1, the default, or 'LevelDependent'). level defaults to min(floor(log2(N)), wmaxlev(N, wavelet)). A matrix x is denoised column by column. The coefficient cell arrays hold the details of levels 1..level, then the approximation.
Example: xden = wdenoise(sin((1:256)/10) + 0.2*cos((1:256).^2))
Example: xden = wdenoise(sin((1:256)/10) + 0.2*cos((1:256).^2), 4, 'DenoisingMethod', 'SURE', 'ThresholdRule', 'Hard');
Differences from MATLAB: timetable input is not supported; the decomposition uses the current dwtmode.

## modwt
Maximal overlap discrete wavelet transform.
Syntax: w = modwt(x)
Syntax: w = modwt(x, wname)
Syntax: w = modwt(x, Lo, Hi)
Syntax: w = modwt(..., lev)
Syntax: w = modwt(..., 'reflection')
Undecimated transform (Percival and Walden) with the orthogonal filters of wfilters(wname) divided by sqrt(2); wname defaults to 'sym4' and lev to floor(log2(N)). w is (lev+1)-by-N: the wavelet coefficients of levels 1..lev, then the scaling coefficients. Boundaries are periodic; 'reflection' transforms [x flip(x)] and gives 2N columns. sum(w(:).^2) equals sum(x.^2) for periodic boundaries.
Example: w = modwt(cos((1:64)/4) + 0.1*(1:64)/64, 'db2', 3)
Differences from MATLAB: x must be a real vector; TimeAlign=true is not supported.

## imodwt
Inverse maximal overlap discrete wavelet transform.
Syntax: xrec = imodwt(w)
Syntax: xrec = imodwt(w, wname)
Syntax: xrec = imodwt(w, Lo, Hi)
Syntax: xrec = imodwt(..., lev)
Syntax: xrec = imodwt(..., 'reflection')
Inverts modwt (same wavelet, default 'sym4'); xrec is a row vector. lev (0 to size(w,1)-2, default 0) stops at that level and returns the projection onto its scaling space. 'reflection' keeps the first half.
Example: x = cos((1:32)/3); xrec = imodwt(modwt(x, 'db4', 3), 'db4')
Differences from MATLAB: real coefficients only.

## modwtmra
Multiresolution analysis from MODWT coefficients.
Syntax: mra = modwtmra(w)
Syntax: mra = modwtmra(w, wname)
Syntax: mra = modwtmra(w, Lo, Hi)
Syntax: mra = modwtmra(..., 'reflection')
Each row is the part of the signal from one row of w: details D1..Dlev, then the smooth Slev; sum(mra, 1) reproduces the signal. 'reflection' keeps the first half of the columns.
Example: mra = modwtmra(modwt(cos((1:64)/4) + 0.5*cos((1:64)*1.3), 'sym4', 3), 'sym4')
Differences from MATLAB: real coefficients only.

## emd
Empirical mode decomposition.
Syntax: [imf, residual, info] = emd(x)
Syntax: [imf, residual, info] = emd(x, Name, Value)
Sifts intrinsic mode functions (Huang 1998): the mean of the envelopes through the local maxima and minima is subtracted until ||h_prev - h||^2/||h_prev||^2 < 'SiftRelativeTolerance' (0.2) or 'SiftMaxIterations' (100) sifts. Stops after 'MaxNumIMF' (10) IMFs, when the residual has fewer than 'MaxNumExtrema' (1) extrema or 10*log10 of the signal-to-residual energy exceeds 'MaxEnergyRatio' (20). 'Interpolation' 'spline' (default) or 'pchip' builds the envelopes; the two extrema nearest each end are mirrored about the end sample. imf has one column per IMF and sum(imf, 2) + residual equals x(:). info holds NumIMF, NumExtrema, NumZerocrossing, NumSifting, MeanEnvelopeEnergy and RelativeTolerance.
Example: t = (0:299)'; [imf, r] = emd(cos(2*pi*0.12*t) + cos(2*pi*0.02*t));
Example: [imf, r, info] = emd(sin((1:200)/5) + 0.3*sin((1:200)*1.1), 'Interpolation', 'pchip', 'MaxNumIMF', 3);
Differences from MATLAB: timetable input, plotting and Display are not supported; the end treatment of the envelopes may differ.

## vmd
Variational mode decomposition.
Syntax: [imf, residual, info] = vmd(x)
Syntax: [imf, residual, info] = vmd(x, Name, Value)
ADMM of Dragomiretskiy and Zosso (2014) on the signal mirrored by half its length at each end. Options: 'NumIMFs' (5), 'PenaltyFactor' (1000), 'LMUpdateRate' (0.01), 'MaxIterations' (500), 'AbsoluteTolerance' (5e-6, mean squared change per sample of the modes), 'RelativeTolerance' (1e3*AbsoluteTolerance), 'InitializeMethod' 'peaks' (largest spectral peaks, the rest random), 'random' (uniform in [0, 0.5], from the rand stream so rng(seed) repeats it) or 'grid' ((0:K-1)/(2K)), and 'CentralFrequencies'. imf has one column per mode, ordered by ascending central frequency; residual = x(:) - sum(imf, 2). info holds ExitFlag, CentralFrequencies, NumIterations, AbsoluteImprovement, RelativeImprovement and LagrangeMultiplier.
Example: t = (0:255)'; [imf, r] = vmd(cos(2*pi*0.05*t) + 0.5*cos(2*pi*0.2*t), 'NumIMFs', 2);
Differences from MATLAB: timetable input, plotting, Display, InitialIMFs and InitialLM are not supported.

## ewt
Empirical wavelet transform.
Syntax: [mra, cfs] = ewt(x)
Syntax: [mra, cfs] = ewt(x, Name, Value)
Splits the spectrum (Gilles 2013) at boundaries between the peaks of a sine multitaper spectrum and filters with Meyer-type empirical wavelets that form a tight frame, so sum(mra, 2) equals x(:). Peaks: those above 'PeakThresholdPercent' (70) % of the largest, or the 'MaxNumPeaks' largest. 'SegmentMethod' 'geomean' (default, geometric mean of adjacent peak frequencies) or 'localmin' (first spectral minimum between them). 'FrequencyResolution' (at most 0.25, default 6/(M+1)) sets round(FrequencyResolution*(M+1))-1 tapers, M = max(N, 64). 'LogSpectrum' finds peaks on the log spectrum. Columns go from the highest band down to the lowpass part.
Example: t = (0:255)'; [mra, cfs] = ewt(cos(2*pi*0.05*t) + 0.5*cos(2*pi*0.2*t), 'MaxNumPeaks', 2);
Differences from MATLAB: the wfb and info outputs, timetable and complex input and plotting are not supported; the default frequency resolution and boundaries may differ.

## cwt
Continuous 1-D wavelet transform.
Syntax: wt = cwt(x)
Syntax: wt = cwt(x, wname)
Syntax: [wt, f, coi] = cwt(x, fs)
Syntax: [wt, f, coi] = cwt(x, wname, fs)
Syntax: [wt, f, coi, fb] = cwt(..., Name, Value)
Transform of the vector x with an analytic wavelet: 'morse' (default, symmetry gamma = 3 and time-bandwidth product P^2 = 60), 'amor' (analytic Morlet) or 'bump'. wt has one row per scale and one column per sample, rows ordered from high to low frequency; f holds the wavelet centre frequencies (cycles/sample, or hertz with a sampling frequency fs) and coi the cone of influence, one frequency per sample: coefficients below it are affected by the signal edges. fb is the cwtfilterbank that was used. The wavelets are L1-normalised (peak 2 in frequency), so a sinusoid of amplitude A has |wt| = A at its frequency. The scales are s0*2^(k/NV): the smallest puts the wavelet at 50 % (Morse) or 10 % (amor, bump) of its peak at the Nyquist frequency, the largest fits two wavelet time widths in the signal. A complex x gives a 3-D wt: page 1 is the analytic part (positive frequencies, counterclockwise rotation), page 2 the anti-analytic part (negative frequencies, clockwise).
Options: 'VoicesPerOctave' (NV, 1 to 48, default 10), 'FrequencyLimits' [fmin fmax] (clipped to the valid range), 'TimeBandwidth' (Morse P^2, 3 to 120), 'WaveletParameters' [gamma P^2] (Morse), 'ExtendSignal' (reflect the signal at both ends, default true; false treats it as periodic), 'FilterBank' (a cwtfilterbank object).
Example: [wt, f, coi] = cwt(cos(2*pi*0.05*(0:255)));
Example: x = cos(2*pi*100*(0:999)/1000); [wt, f] = cwt(x, 'amor', 1000, 'VoicesPerOctave', 12, 'FrequencyLimits', [20 300]); [~, k] = max(abs(wt(:, 500))); f(k)   % near 100
Differences from MATLAB: no scalogram plot without outputs; duration sampling periods, 'PeriodLimits', timetables, single precision and the scaling-coefficient output are not supported. The signal is reflected by floor(N/2) samples at each end for every length.

## icwt
Inverse continuous 1-D wavelet transform.
Syntax: xrec = icwt(wt)
Syntax: xrec = icwt(wt, wname)
Syntax: xrec = icwt(wt, f, freqrange)
Syntax: xrec = icwt(..., Name, Value)
Approximate inverse of cwt by the single-integral formula: xrec = 2*real(sum of the rows of wt)*log(2)/(NV*C), C the admissibility constant of the wavelet, returned as a row vector. The wavelet and 'VoicesPerOctave' must match the cwt call. With f and freqrange = [fmin fmax] only the rows with frequencies inside the range are used. A 3-D wt (from a complex signal) gives a complex xrec. Content outside the analysed frequency band, and the signal mean, are not recovered. The bump wavelet at the default 10 voices per octave reconstructs an in-band signal to about 4e-2.
Options: 'SignalMean' (added to xrec, default 0), 'VoicesPerOctave' (default 10), 'TimeBandwidth', 'WaveletParameters', 'AnalysisFilterBank' (a cwtfilterbank object).
Example: t = (0:1023)/1024; x = cos(2*pi*40*t).*exp(-((t - 0.5)/0.15).^2); xrec = icwt(cwt(x)); max(abs(xrec - x))   % about 2e-7
Example: x = cos(2*pi*0.05*(0:255)); [wt, f] = cwt(x, 'amor'); xrec = icwt(wt, 'amor', f, [0.03 0.08], 'SignalMean', mean(x));
Differences from MATLAB: 'ScalingCoefficients' and duration periods are not supported.

## cwtfilterbank
Continuous wavelet transform filter bank.
Syntax: fb = cwtfilterbank
Syntax: fb = cwtfilterbank(Name, Value, ...)
Syntax: [wt, f, coi] = wt(fb, x)
Syntax: [psidft, f] = freqz(fb)
Syntax: [psi, t] = wavelets(fb)
Syntax: s = scales(fb)
The requested rows-by-SignalLength filter matrix must fit the engine's element and memory limits before the object is created.
Object with the read-only properties SignalLength (default 1024), Wavelet ('Morse', 'amor' or 'bump'), VoicesPerOctave (10), SamplingFrequency (1), FrequencyLimits, TimeBandwidth (60), WaveletParameters and Boundary ('reflection' or 'periodic'). wt(fb, x) is the transform of a signal of SignalLength samples, the same as cwt. freqz returns the frequency responses of the wavelet filters, one row per scale, on the DFT grid the transform uses (one-sided; 'FrequencyRange', 'twosided' gives the full grid in DFT order); wavelets returns the time-domain wavelets, one row per scale, with the sample times t; scales returns the scales in samples; centerFrequencies(fb) and centerPeriods(fb) return the wavelet centre frequencies and their reciprocals.
Example: fb = cwtfilterbank('SignalLength', 256, 'Wavelet', 'bump', 'VoicesPerOctave', 12); [wt, f, coi] = wt(fb, cos(2*pi*0.1*(0:255)));
Example: fb = cwtfilterbank('SignalLength', 128, 'SamplingFrequency', 100); [psidft, f] = freqz(fb); [psi, t] = wavelets(fb); s = scales(fb);
Differences from MATLAB: wt, freqz, wavelets and scales are called as functions (wt(fb, x)), not with dot syntax; 'SamplingPeriod' and 'PeriodLimits', the lowpass (scaling) filter, the plots and the other methods (powerbw, qfactor, BPfrequencies, ...) are not supported.

## wsst
Wavelet synchrosqueezed transform.
Syntax: sst = wsst(x)
Syntax: [sst, f] = wsst(x, fs)
Syntax: [sst, f] = wsst(x, fs, wav)
Syntax: [sst, f] = wsst(..., Name, Value)
Sharpens the continuous wavelet transform of the real vector x along frequency: each coefficient moves to the bin of its instantaneous frequency, the phase transform imag(dW/dt ./ W)/(2*pi). sst has NV*(floor(log2(N)) - 1) rows and N columns; f (a row vector) holds the bin frequencies, log-spaced from fs/N to fs/2 and increasing. wav is 'amor' (default) or 'bump'. The transform keeps every coefficient above 1e-8 of the largest centred sample, weighted by log(2)/NV, so iwsst inverts it.
Options: 'VoicesPerOctave' (NV, even, 10 to 48, default 32), 'ExtendSignal' (reflect the signal at both ends, default false).
Example: t = (0:1023)/1024; [sst, f] = wsst(cos(2*pi*40*t), 1024); [~, k] = max(abs(sst(:, 512))); f(k)   % near 40
Differences from MATLAB: no plot without outputs; duration sampling periods are not supported; instantaneous frequencies outside the bins are assigned to the first or last bin instead of being dropped.

## iwsst
Inverse wavelet synchrosqueezed transform.
Syntax: xrec = iwsst(sst)
Syntax: xrec = iwsst(sst, f, freqrange)
Syntax: xrec = iwsst(sst, iridge)
Syntax: xrec = iwsst(..., wav)
Syntax: xrec = iwsst(sst, iridge, 'NumFrequencyBins', nbins)
Reconstructs the signal as 2*real(sum of the rows of sst)/C, C the admissibility constant of the wavelet wav ('amor' by default; it must match wsst), as a column vector. With f and freqrange = [fmin fmax] only the bins inside the range are summed. With ridge row indices iridge (one column per ridge, one row per sample) each ridge is reconstructed from nbins bins (default 16) on either side of it and xrec has one column per ridge.
Example: t = (0:1023)/1024; x = cos(2*pi*40*t) + 0.5*sin(2*pi*90*t); xrec = iwsst(wsst(x)); max(abs(xrec' - x))   % about 4e-7
Example: t = (0:1023)/1024; x = cos(2*pi*40*t) + 0.5*sin(2*pi*90*t); [sst, f] = wsst(x, 1024); x90 = iwsst(sst, f, [60 130]);
Differences from MATLAB: the analytic Morlet wavelet inverts to within 1e-6, and the bump wavelet to about 1e-3 at 32 voices per octave and about 2e-4 at 48 (its compact support is sampled by few scales).

## cell2mat
Convert a cell array of matrices to one matrix.
Syntax: M = cell2mat(C)
Concatenates the contents of C: each row of cells side by side, then the rows
on top of each other. All contents must have the same class (double, logical,
char or struct), and the pieces must fit together. An empty cell gives [].
Example: cell2mat({[1 2], 3; [4 5], 6})   % [1 2 3; 4 5 6]
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D cell arrays only. Error messages match MATLAB's.

## cellstr
Convert a character array to a cell array of character vectors.
Syntax: C = cellstr(S)
Each row of the char matrix S becomes one cell, with trailing whitespace
removed; the result is a column. A cell array of character vectors is returned
unchanged. cellstr('') is {''}.
Example: cellstr(vertcat('ab ', 'cd '))   % {'ab'; 'cd'}
String input produces character cells of the same shape, preserving spaces.
Example: cellstr(["a " "b"])
Differences from MATLAB: string storage is two-dimensional and bounded.

## deal
Copy inputs to outputs.
Syntax: [A, B, ...] = deal(X)
Syntax: [A, B, ...] = deal(X1, X2, ...)
With one input every output gets a copy of it; otherwise the number of inputs
must equal the number of outputs and each output gets its input.
Example: [a, b] = deal(1, 2); [a b]   % [1 2]
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## structfun
Apply a function to each field of a scalar struct.
Syntax: A = structfun(f, S)
Syntax: A = structfun(f, S, 'UniformOutput', false)
Syntax: A = structfun(f, S, 'ErrorHandler', g)
Calls f on each field value in field order. By default every call must
return a scalar of one class and the results form a column with one row per
field. With 'UniformOutput', false the results are returned as a struct with
the same field names. With 'ErrorHandler', g(err, value) supplies the result
for a field whose call fails; err has the fields message, identifier and
index. Several outputs are supported.
Example: s.a = 1; s.b = 2; structfun(@(v) v * 2, s)   % [2; 4]
Differences from MATLAB: uniform results must be numeric, logical or char
scalars.

## strtok
First token of a character vector.
Syntax: token = strtok(str)
Syntax: [token, remainder] = strtok(str, delimiters)
Skips leading delimiters and returns the text up to the next delimiter; the
remainder starts at that delimiter. The default delimiters are whitespace
(space, tab, newline, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return). For a cell
array of character vectors both outputs are cell arrays of the same size.
Example: [t, r] = strtok('a,b,c', ',')   % t = 'a', r = ',b,c'
Differences from MATLAB: string arrays are not supported.

## assert
Throw an error when a condition is false.
Syntax: assert(cond)
Syntax: assert(cond, msg, A1, ...)
Syntax: assert(cond, id, msg, A1, ...)
cond must be a logical or numeric scalar. When it is false, assert raises
"Assertion failed." or the message, formatted like error() with the extra
arguments; an identifier is kept for catch.
Example: x = 3; assert(x > 0, 'x must be positive')   % no output
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## warning
Display a warning and continue.
Syntax: warning(msg)
Syntax: warning(msg, A1, ...)
Syntax: warning(id, msg, A1, ...)
Syntax: warning('off', id)
Syntax: warning('on', 'all')
Syntax: s = warning('off', id)
Syntax: s = warning('query', id)
Syntax: s = warning
Syntax: warning(s)
Prints "Warning: " and the message (formatted like error() when there are
extra arguments) and continues. warning('off', id) silences that identifier
for the session, warning('off', 'all') silences all warnings, and 'on' turns
them back on. Assigning the result of 'on' or 'off' saves the previous state.
Query an identifier with warning('query', id), or query all states with
warning. Queries print the state or return it when assigned. Pass a saved
state to warning(s) to restore it.
Example: warning('Value %d is large', 7)   % Warning: Value 7 is large
Differences from MATLAB: the warning is one line without the "> In" location
lines. The 'backtrace' and 'verbose' options are unavailable.

## eval
Run MATLAB code held in text.
Syntax: eval(expression)
Syntax: eval(expression, catchExpression)
Syntax: x = eval(expression)
Runs the text in the current workspace, so variables it assigns stay. When
an output is requested, a text that is one expression returns its value and
the outer statement controls display. Otherwise, statements inside the text
control display, including their semicolons. With catchExpression, that text
runs instead when the first one fails.
Example: eval('y = 2 + 3;'); y   % 5
Differences from MATLAB: function definitions are rejected.
Syntax errors other than an incomplete statement
keep MatRust's parser wording after "Error: ".

## rat
Rational approximation.
Syntax: S = rat(X)
Syntax: [N, D] = rat(X)
Syntax: [N, D] = rat(X, tol)
With two outputs, N./D approximates X to within tol, by default
1e-6*norm(X(:),1). With one output, the continued fraction as text, one row
per element (for example 3 + 1/(7 + 1/(16)) for pi).
Example: [n, d] = rat(0.75)   % n = 3, d = 4
Differences from MATLAB: real input only.

## rats
Rational approximation as fixed-width text.
Syntax: S = rats(X)
Syntax: S = rats(X, strlen)
Each element becomes N/D (or N when D is 1), centred in a field of strlen+1
characters (strlen is 13 by default); a row of X is one row of text. The
tolerance is 1e-6*norm(X(:),1). An element that does not fit prints as *.
Example: rats(0.75)   % '      3/4     '
Differences from MATLAB: real input only. Widths other than the default and the * rule
are not checked yet.

## integral
Numerical integration of a function of one variable.
Syntax: q = integral(fun, a, b)
Syntax: q = integral(fun, a, b, 'Name', value, ...)
fun is a function handle called with a row of points; it must return a row of the same size. a and b are real scalars and may be -Inf or Inf. Options: 'AbsTol' (default 1e-10), 'RelTol' (default 1e-6), 'Waypoints' (real points where fun has kinks or jumps) and 'ArrayValued' (true calls fun with one point at a time and integrates every element of the array it returns). Complex integrands give a complex result. Adaptive Gauss-Kronrod (7,15) quadrature with the endpoint and infinite-interval transformations of Shampine (2008).
Example: integral(@(x) x.^2, 0, 1)   % 0.3333
Example: integral(@(x) exp(-x), 0, Inf)   % 1
Example: integral(@(x) [x; x.^2], 0, 1, 'ArrayValued', true)   % [0.5000; 0.3333]
Example: integral(@(x) abs(x - 1), 0, 3, 'Waypoints', 1)   % 2.5000
Differences from MATLAB: Complex limits and complex waypoints (contour integration) are not supported yet. Warnings use MATLAB's wording.

## integral2
Numerical integration over a planar region.
Syntax: q = integral2(fun, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
Syntax: q = integral2(fun, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, 'AbsTol', tol, 'RelTol', tol)
fun(x, y) is called with arrays of the same size and must return an array of that size. xmin and xmax are real scalars; ymin and ymax are real scalars or function handles of x. Any limit may be infinite. Defaults: 'AbsTol' 1e-10, 'RelTol' 1e-6.
Example: integral2(@(x, y) x .* y, 0, 1, 0, 2)   % 1.0000
Example: integral2(@(x, y) x.^2 + y.^2, 0, 1, 0, @(x) x)   % 0.3333
Differences from MATLAB: Always computes iterated one-dimensional integrals; 'Method' is accepted but has no effect. Uses tighter internal tolerances, scales inner absolute tolerances by the outer integration measure, and propagates inner error estimates. The last digits and warnings can differ from MATLAB's tiled method.

## integral3
Numerical integration over a three-dimensional region.
Syntax: q = integral3(fun, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax)
Syntax: q = integral3(fun, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax, 'AbsTol', tol, 'RelTol', tol)
fun(x, y, z) is called with arrays of the same size and must return an array of that size. ymin and ymax may be function handles of x; zmin and zmax may be function handles of (x, y). Limits may be infinite. Defaults: 'AbsTol' 1e-10, 'RelTol' 1e-6.
Example: integral3(@(x, y, z) x + y + z, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1)   % 1.5000
Differences from MATLAB: Iterated one-dimensional integrals with tighter internal tolerances, scaling of inner absolute tolerances by the outer integration measure, and propagation of inner error estimates; 'Method' is accepted but has no effect. The last digits can differ from MATLAB.

## quad
Numerical integration by adaptive Simpson quadrature.
Syntax: q = quad(fun, a, b)
Syntax: q = quad(fun, a, b, tol)
Syntax: q = quad(fun, a, b, tol, [], p1, p2, ...)
Syntax: [q, fcnt] = quad(...)
fun is a function handle or a function name called with a row of points (and p1, p2, ... after it). The default absolute tolerance is 1e-6. fcnt is the number of integrand values used. Limits must be finite scalars.
Example: quad(@(x) exp(x), 0, 1)   % 1.7183
Differences from MATLAB: A nonzero trace argument is not supported yet.

## quadgk
Numerical integration by adaptive Gauss-Kronrod quadrature.
Syntax: q = quadgk(fun, a, b)
Syntax: q = quadgk(fun, a, b, 'Name', value, ...)
Syntax: [q, errbnd] = quadgk(...)
fun is a function handle called with a row of points; it must return a row of the same size. a and b may be infinite, and fun may have integrable singularities at the ends. Options: 'AbsTol' (default 1e-10), 'RelTol' (default 1e-6), 'Waypoints' and 'MaxIntervalCount' (default 650). errbnd is an approximate bound on the absolute error.
Example: quadgk(@(x) exp(-x.^2), -Inf, Inf)   % 1.7725
Example: [q, err] = quadgk(@(x) 1 ./ sqrt(x), 0, 1)   % q = 2.0000, err = 2.5601e-13
Differences from MATLAB: Complex limits and waypoints (contour integration) are not supported yet.

## dblquad
Double integral over a rectangle by nested quad.
Syntax: q = dblquad(fun, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
Syntax: q = dblquad(fun, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, tol)
fun(x, y) is called with a row x and a scalar y and must return a row the size of x. The default tolerance is 1e-6.
Example: dblquad(@(x, y) x .* y, 0, 1, 0, 2)   % 1.0000
Differences from MATLAB: Only the default method @quad is supported.

## triplequad
Triple integral over a box by nested quad.
Syntax: q = triplequad(fun, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax)
Syntax: q = triplequad(fun, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax, tol)
fun(x, y, z) is called with a row x and scalars y and z and must return a row the size of x. The default tolerance is 1e-6.
Example: triplequad(@(x, y, z) x .* y .* z, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1)   % 0.1250
Differences from MATLAB: Only the default method @quad is supported.

## acos
Inverse cosine in radians.
Syntax: Y = acos(X)
Real input in [-1, 1] gives values in [0, pi]. Real input outside [-1, 1]
and complex input give the principal complex value.
Example: acos(0.5)   % 1.0472
Example: acos(2)   % 0 + 1.3170i
Differences from MATLAB: double, logical and char 2-D arrays only.

## asin
Inverse sine in radians.
Syntax: Y = asin(X)
Real input in [-1, 1] gives values in [-pi/2, pi/2]. Real input outside
[-1, 1] and complex input give the principal complex value.
Example: asin(1)   % 1.5708
Example: asin(2)   % 1.5708 - 1.3170i
Differences from MATLAB: double, logical and char 2-D arrays only.

## atan
Inverse tangent in radians.
Syntax: Y = atan(X)
Real input gives values in [-pi/2, pi/2]; complex input gives the principal
value. See atan2 for the four-quadrant form.
Example: atan(1)   % 0.7854
Example: atan(1+1i)   % 1.0172 + 0.4024i
Differences from MATLAB: double, logical and char 2-D arrays only.

## realsqrt
Square root of nonnegative real input.
Syntax: Y = realsqrt(X)
Stops with an error when an element is negative instead of returning a
complex result.
Example: realsqrt(16)   % 4
Differences from MATLAB: complex input gives an error.

## reallog
Natural logarithm of nonnegative real input.
Syntax: Y = reallog(X)
Stops with an error when an element is negative instead of returning a
complex result.
Example: reallog(1)   % 0
Differences from MATLAB: complex input gives an error.

## realpow
Array power with real output.
Syntax: Z = realpow(X, Y)
Same as X.^Y, but stops with an error when an element of the result would be
complex (a negative base with a non-integer exponent).
Example: realpow(2, 3)   % 8
Differences from MATLAB: complex input gives an error.

## plus
Addition, the function form of a + b.
Syntax: C = plus(A, B)
Evaluates a + b with the operator's own rules.
Example: plus(1, [2 3])   % [3 4]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the + operator.

## minus
Subtraction, the function form of a - b.
Syntax: C = minus(A, B)
Evaluates a - b with the operator's own rules.
Example: minus([5 6], 1)   % [4 5]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the - operator.

## times
Elementwise multiplication, the function form of a .* b.
Syntax: C = times(A, B)
Evaluates a .* b with the operator's own rules.
Example: times([1 2], [3 4])   % [3 8]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the .* operator.

## rdivide
Elementwise right division, the function form of a ./ b.
Syntax: C = rdivide(A, B)
Evaluates a ./ b with the operator's own rules.
Example: rdivide(1, [2 4])   % [0.5 0.25]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the ./ operator.

## ldivide
Elementwise left division, the function form of a .\ b.
Syntax: C = ldivide(A, B)
Evaluates b ./ a, which is what a .\ b means.
Example: ldivide(2, [4 8])   % [2 4]
Differences from MATLAB: the .\ operator itself is not parsed yet.

## mtimes
Matrix multiplication, the function form of a * b.
Syntax: C = mtimes(A, B)
Evaluates a * b with the operator's own rules.
Example: mtimes([1 2], [3; 4])   % 11
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the * operator. An N-D operand needs a scalar other operand (elementwise product); otherwise MATLAB's 2-D argument error is given.

## power
Elementwise power, the function form of a .^ b.
Syntax: C = power(A, B)
Evaluates a .^ b; a negative base with a non-integer exponent gives a
complex result.
Example: power([1 2 3], 2)   % [1 4 9]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the .^ operator.

## mpower
Matrix power, the function form of a ^ b.
Syntax: C = mpower(A, B)
Evaluates a ^ b: repeated squaring for an integer exponent, eigendecomposition
for a non-integer exponent or a scalar base with a matrix exponent. An
ill-conditioned eigenvector basis produces a warning; results may be inaccurate.
Example: mpower([1 1; 0 1], 3)   % [1 3; 0 1]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the ^ operator. An N-D operand gives MATLAB's error (use .^).

## uminus
Unary minus, the function form of -a.
Syntax: B = uminus(A)
Evaluates -a with the operator's own rules.
Example: uminus([1 -2])   % [-1 2]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the unary - operator.

## uplus
Unary plus, the function form of +a.
Syntax: B = uplus(A)
Evaluates +a with the operator's own rules.
Example: uplus(5)   % 5
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the unary + operator.

## eq
Equality test, the function form of a == b.
Syntax: TF = eq(A, B)
Returns a logical array, as the == operator does.
For handle objects of classdef classes it compares identity: true for copies of one object.
Example: eq([1 2 3], 2)   % [0 1 0]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the == operator.

## ne
Inequality test, the function form of a ~= b.
Syntax: TF = ne(A, B)
Returns a logical array, as the ~= operator does. For handle objects of classdef classes it is true unless both are copies of one object.
Example: ne([1 2 3], 2)   % [1 0 1]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the ~= operator.

## lt
Less-than test, the function form of a < b.
Syntax: TF = lt(A, B)
Returns a logical array, as the < operator does.
Example: lt([1 2 3], 2)   % [1 0 0]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the < operator.

## gt
Greater-than test, the function form of a > b.
Syntax: TF = gt(A, B)
Returns a logical array, as the > operator does.
Example: gt([1 2 3], 2)   % [0 0 1]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the > operator.

## le
Less-or-equal test, the function form of a <= b.
Syntax: TF = le(A, B)
Returns a logical array, as the <= operator does.
Example: le([1 2 3], 2)   % [1 1 0]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the <= operator.

## ge
Greater-or-equal test, the function form of a >= b.
Syntax: TF = ge(A, B)
Returns a logical array, as the >= operator does.
Example: ge([1 2 3], 2)   % [0 1 1]
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as the >= operator.

## nonzeros
Nonzero elements as a column.
Syntax: v = nonzeros(A)
Returns the nonzero elements of A in column order as a column vector,
0-by-1 when there are none. For a sparse array these are its stored values, as a full column.
Example: nonzeros([1 0 2; 0 3 0])   % [1; 3; 2]
Example: nonzeros(sparse([0 4; 5 0]))   % [5; 4]
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## perms
All permutations.
Syntax: P = perms(v)
Returns every permutation of the elements of v, one per row, in reverse
lexicographic order of their positions. Char input gives char rows.
Example: perms([1 2 3])   % 6-by-3, first row [3 2 1]
Differences from MATLAB: the table is limited to 8388608 elements.

## gradient
Numerical gradient.
Syntax: FX = gradient(F)
Syntax: FX = gradient(F, h)
Syntax: [FX, FY] = gradient(F, hx, hy)
Central differences inside, one-sided differences at the edges. For a vector
F the derivative is along its length; for a matrix FX is along the rows
(across columns) and FY along the columns.
Example: gradient([1 4 9 16])   % [3 4 6 7]
Differences from MATLAB: scalar spacings only (no coordinate vectors); two
outputs at most.

## del2
Discrete Laplacian.
Syntax: L = del2(U)
Syntax: L = del2(U, h)
Syntax: L = del2(U, hx, hy)
Returns (d2U/dx2 + d2U/dy2)/4 with second differences inside and linear
extrapolation at the edges; a dimension with fewer than three points adds 0.
Example: del2([1 4 9 16 25])   % [0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5 0.5]
Differences from MATLAB: scalar spacings only; 2-D arrays only.

## unwrap
Correct phase angle jumps.
Syntax: Q = unwrap(P)
Syntax: Q = unwrap(P, tol)
Syntax: Q = unwrap(P, tol, dim)
Adds multiples of 2*pi where consecutive elements differ by at least tol
(default pi). Works along a row vector, otherwise down each column.
Example: unwrap([0 3 6.5 -3])   % [0 3 0.2168 3.2832]
Differences from MATLAB: real 2-D arrays only.

## hankel
Hankel matrix.
Syntax: H = hankel(c)
Syntax: H = hankel(c, r)
hankel(c) is square with c as its first column and zeros below the first
anti-diagonal. hankel(c, r) has first column c and last row r; when the last
element of c and the first of r differ, the column wins.
Example: hankel([1 2 3], [3 4 5])   % [1 2 3; 2 3 4; 3 4 5]
Differences from MATLAB: real input only; no warning is printed for the
anti-diagonal conflict.

## cplxpair
Sort complex numbers into conjugate pairs.
Syntax: Z = cplxpair(A)
Syntax: Z = cplxpair(A, tol)
Pairs complex conjugates in order of increasing real part, negative
imaginary part first, then the real elements in increasing order. Elements
with abs(imag(z)) <= tol*abs(z) (default tol = 100*eps) count as real.
Example: cplxpair([1+1i 2 1-1i])   % [1-1i 1+1i 2]
Differences from MATLAB: vectors only; no dim argument.

## orderfields
Order structure fields by name.
Syntax: S = orderfields(S1)
Returns S1 with its fields in ASCII order of their names.
Example: s.b = 1; s.a = 2; fieldnames(orderfields(s))   % {'a'; 'b'}
Differences from MATLAB: one input and one output only.

## narginchk
Check the number of input arguments.
Syntax: narginchk(minArgs, maxArgs)
Inside a function, stops with "Not enough input arguments." or "Too many
input arguments." when nargin is outside [minArgs, maxArgs].
Example: narginchk(1, 2)
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## optimset
Create an optimization options structure.
Syntax: options = optimset('Name', value, ...)
Syntax: options = optimset(oldopts, 'Name', value, ...)
Returns a structure with one field per given option; a name given again
(case does not matter) replaces the earlier value. Used by fzero, fminbnd,
fminsearch, and nonlinear solvers.
Example: opts = optimset('TolX', 1e-8); opts.TolX   % 1.0000e-08
Differences from MATLAB: the structure holds only the options that were set,
not MATLAB's full list of optimization options, and names are not checked.

## optimplotx
Plot current point as a bar chart during optimization.
Syntax: stop = optimplotx(x, optimValues, state)
PlotFcns helper for fzero, fminbnd, and fminsearch.
Example: fminsearch(@(x) sum(x.^2), [1 2], optimset('PlotFcns', @optimplotx));
Differences from MATLAB: plots a bar chart of x on the current figure without
custom axis labels.

## optimplotfval
Plot objective function value vs iteration during optimization.
Syntax: stop = optimplotfval(x, optimValues, state)
PlotFcns helper for fzero, fminbnd, and fminsearch.
Example: fminsearch(@(x) (x - 2)^2, 0, optimset('PlotFcns', @optimplotfval));
Differences from MATLAB: plots fval vs iteration on the current figure without
custom axis labels.

## getenv
Read an environment variable.
Syntax: value = getenv(name)
An unset variable returns an empty character array. Reads engine overrides first, then the inherited host environment.
Example: setenv('MATRUST_HELP_ENV', 'abc'); getenv('MATRUST_HELP_ENV')   % abc
Differences from MATLAB: setenv changes are local to an engine; they do not modify the host process environment.

## setenv
Set an environment variable for this engine.
Syntax: setenv(name, value)
Syntax: setenv(name)
One argument, or an empty value, sets the variable to empty. At most 1024 overrides and 1 MiB of names and values are retained.
Example: setenv('MATRUST_HELP_ENV', 'abc'); getenv('MATRUST_HELP_ENV')   % abc
Differences from MATLAB: Changes are local to the engine and its clones; other engines and the host process environment are unchanged.

## ispc
True on Windows.
Syntax: tf = ispc
Returns a logical scalar describing the host operating system.
Example: isscalar(ispc)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: none known for this form.

## isunix
True on Unix systems, including macOS.
Syntax: tf = isunix
Returns a logical scalar describing the host operating system.
Example: isscalar(isunix)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: none known for this form.

## ismac
True on macOS.
Syntax: tf = ismac
Returns a logical scalar describing the host operating system.
Example: isscalar(ismac)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: none known for this form.

## computer
Identify the host computer architecture.
Syntax: c = computer
Syntax: arch = computer('arch')
Syntax: [c, maxsize, endian] = computer
The architecture names describe the supported 64-bit Windows, Linux and Intel macOS hosts. Endian is L or B. maxsize is the MATLAB-compatible theoretical limit; actual allocations retain MatRust limits.
Example: [c, n, e] = computer; ischar(c)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: The reported theoretical maximum does not raise the engine allocation limit.

## version
Return release text scripts can parse. This is not the MatRust product name.
Syntax: v = version
Syntax: r = version('-release')
Syntax: d = version('-date')
Syntax: s = version('-description')
With no arguments, returns the character vector '24.2.0.0 (R2024b)'. Scripts read the release name inside the parentheses. That text is the claimed R2024b compatibility target. It does not name an installed MATLAB product, and it is not the MatRust package version. -release returns '2024b'. -date returns 'September 12, 2024'. -description returns an empty character vector, the documented result for a general release that has no update.
Example: version   % 24.2.0.0 (R2024b)
Example: isempty(version('-description'))   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: The build field is zero rather than a MathWorks build number, and there is no update text. Product identity stays on ver and on matrust --version / -V. Unknown options still error.

## ver
Return MatRust product information.
Syntax: v = ver
Syntax: v = ver('matlab')
Syntax: v = ver('matrust')
Returns Name, Version, Release and Date fields. The matlab alias identifies MatRust, not an installed MATLAB product. Unknown products return an empty struct array with these fields. With no output, prints the information.
Example: v=ver('matlab'); v.Name   % MatRust
Differences from MATLAB: Reports MatRust package information; the Date field is empty because a build date is not recorded.

## verLessThan
Compare a product version numerically.
Syntax: tf = verLessThan(product, version)
Accepts one to three dot-separated unsigned version components. matlab compares the claimed R2024b version (24.2); matrust compares the package version. Unknown products report an error.
Example: verLessThan('matlab','25.1')   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: matlab denotes the claimed R2024b compatibility target (24.2), not a MATLAB installation; matrust denotes this application.

## isMATLABReleaseOlderThan
Compare claimed MATLAB release against a specified release.
Syntax: tf = isMATLABReleaseOlderThan(release)
Syntax: tf = isMATLABReleaseOlderThan(release, stage)
Syntax: tf = isMATLABReleaseOlderThan(release, stage, update)
Compares the claimed R2024b release against release (such as "R2025a"), optional stage ('release' or 'prerelease'), and optional nonnegative integer update.
Example: isMATLABReleaseOlderThan("R2025a")   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Compares against MatRust's claimed R2024b release rather than an installed MATLAB.

## beep
Produce a system beep or query/set beep state.
Syntax: beep
Syntax: beep on
Syntax: beep off
Syntax: s = beep
Rings a short system bell in the desktop app when enabled (no-op in CLI / -batch). beep('on') or beep('off') enables or disables the bell; s = beep returns 'on' or 'off'.
Example: beep('off'); s=beep; beep('on'); s   % off
Differences from MATLAB: No-op in CLI and -batch; desktop app uses the host bell if available.

## matlabroot
Return the MatRust installation folder.
Syntax: folder = matlabroot
Returns the folder containing the running executable.
Example: ischar(matlabroot)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Returns the MatRust executable folder rather than a MATLAB installation folder.

## filesep
Return the host file separator.
Syntax: s = filesep
Returns a backslash on Windows and a forward slash on Unix.
Example: numel(filesep)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: none known for this form.

## pathsep
Return the host search-path separator.
Syntax: s = pathsep
Returns a semicolon on Windows and a colon on Unix.
Example: numel(pathsep)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: none known for this form.

## pwd
Return the current folder.
Syntax: folder = pwd
The folder belongs to this engine. File I/O, cd and desktop job submission use it. With no output, prints the folder.
Example: isdir(pwd)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: The host process current directory is unchanged by engine folder changes.

## cd
Change the current folder.
Syntax: old = cd(folder)
Syntax: cd folder
Syntax: cd
Returns the previous folder when assigned. Sets file I/O and function lookup together; the desktop Files panel adopts changes after the job. With no argument, reports the current folder.
Example: old=cd(pwd); strcmp(old,pwd)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Changes the engine folder, not the host process current directory.

## path
View or change the user search path.
Syntax: p = path
Syntax: path
Syntax: oldpath = path(newpath)
Syntax: oldpath = path(path1, path2)
Returns the user folders joined by pathsep ('' when none); with no output, prints one folder per line. path(newpath) replaces the folders; path(path1,path2) sets path1 followed by path2. Arguments are pathsep-separated folder lists; empty entries are dropped and a missing folder warns and is skipped. Function lookup searches the current folder first, then these folders in order, then builtins.
Example: old=path; path(tempdir); n=numel(strsplit(path,pathsep)); path(old); n   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: The path holds only user folders, no toolbox folders. Folders are stored as absolute canonical paths.

## addpath
Add folders to the user search path.
Syntax: addpath(folder1, ..., folderN)
Syntax: addpath(..., '-begin')
Syntax: addpath(..., '-end')
Syntax: oldpath = addpath(...)
Each argument may be a pathsep-separated list such as genpath output. Folders go to the top in the given order (default -begin) or the bottom (-end); a folder already on the path moves. Relative names resolve against pwd. A missing folder warns "Name is nonexistent or not a directory" and is skipped. A .m/.mr file in a path folder shadows a builtin of the same name; the current folder still wins.
Private functions: a .m/.mr file in a subfolder named private is visible only to the files of the folder that contains it, and to the other files of that private folder. There it is found after local functions and before the current folder, the path and builtins; at the Command Window and from other folders it is not found. A handle made inside the folder keeps working elsewhere. Private folders do not go on the path; genpath leaves them out.
Example: old=addpath(tempdir); n=numel(strsplit(path,pathsep)); path(old); n   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: -frozen is accepted and ignored. No toolbox folders.

## rmpath
Remove folders from the user search path.
Syntax: rmpath(folder1, ..., folderN)
Syntax: oldpath = rmpath(...)
Each argument may be a pathsep-separated list. A folder not on the path warns "<name>" not found in path.
Example: addpath(tempdir); rmpath(tempdir); isempty(path)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: The path holds only user folders.

## genpath
List a folder and its subfolders as a path string.
Syntax: p = genpath(folder)
Depth first in sorted name order; each folder is followed by pathsep. Leaves out folders whose names start with @, + or ., and folders named private or resources. A missing folder gives ''. Walks at most 10000 folders; symbolic links to folders are followed once.
Example: d=tempname(tempdir); mkdir(d); p=genpath(d); rmdir(d); strcmp(p, [d pathsep])   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: A relative folder is returned joined to pwd. Subfolder order is sorted by name.

## restoredefaultpath
Remove all user folders from the search path.
Syntax: restoredefaultpath
Function lookup then searches only the current folder and builtins.
Example: addpath(tempdir); restoredefaultpath; isempty(path)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: The default path has no toolbox folders. This command neither reads nor changes pathdef.m; the next savepath overwrites it.

## prefdir
Return and create the per-user MatRust settings folder.
Syntax: d = prefdir
MATRUST_PREFDIR overrides the location. Otherwise reuse the desktop settings folder: the parent of MATRUST_SESSION_PATH when set, or LOCALAPPDATA/MatRust. Without those settings, use XDG_CONFIG_HOME/matrust (or ~/.config/matrust) on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/MatRust on macOS, or APPDATA/MatRust on Windows.
Example: d=tempname(tempdir); setenv('MATRUST_PREFDIR',d); p=prefdir; ok=exist(p,'dir')==7; rmdir(d); ok   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: MatRust uses the folder locations above, creates the folder on every query if needed, and does not accept prefdir(1). In the browser it returns ''.

## userpath
View or change the persistent user work folder.
Syntax: p = userpath
Syntax: userpath(newpath)
Syntax: userpath('reset')
Syntax: userpath('clear')
The default is ~/Documents/MatRust (USERPROFILE/Documents/MatRust on Windows). A new folder must exist. Changes are saved in prefdir and immediately remove the old folder from the live path and put the new folder at the top when it exists. clear removes the folder; reset selects the default. CLI and desktop startup add this folder before saved path folders. Engine::default() does not load settings.
Example: d=tempname(tempdir); setenv('MATRUST_PREFDIR',d); setenv('HOME',d); setenv('USERPROFILE',d); userpath('clear'); p=userpath; delete(fullfile(d,'userpath.txt')); rmdir(d); isempty(p)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: The default folder is not created automatically. Folder names containing pathsep or line breaks are unsupported. In the browser userpath returns '' and changes have no effect.

## savepath
Save the current ordered user search path.
Syntax: savepath
Syntax: savepath(file)
Syntax: status = savepath(...)
Writes a MATLAB-readable function p = pathdef with one quoted folder per line, joined by pathsep. Quotes in folder names are escaped. The default file is fullfile(prefdir,'pathdef.m'); an explicit filename resolves against pwd. Status is 0 on success and 1 on failure; failure warns when no output is requested. restoredefaultpath leaves the saved file alone. CLI and desktop load it once at startup, skipping missing folders with a warning.
Example: f=tempname(tempdir); status=savepath(f); delete(f); status   % 0
Differences from MATLAB: The default destination is always prefdir/pathdef.m. At startup pathdef is parsed as data in exactly the format written by savepath; it is never run. Invalid files warn and contribute no folders. Files are limited to 8 MiB and 10000 folders. In the browser savepath warns that files are unavailable and returns 1.

## dir
List file and directory information.
Syntax: entries = dir
Syntax: entries = dir(folderOrPattern)
Returns a column struct array with name, date, bytes, isdir and datenum fields. Directory listings include dot and dot-dot. Supports * and ? in the final path component; an unmatched pattern returns a 0-by-1 struct. With no output, prints names.
Example: d=tempname(pwd); mkdir(d); q=dir(d); n=numel(q); rmdir(d); n   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: Local paths only; parent-directory wildcards are rejected. Scans are limited to 10000 entries.

## ls
List file names.
Syntax: names = ls
Syntax: names = ls(folderOrPattern)
Returns a padded character matrix, one sorted name per row. With no output, prints the names. Uses the same wildcard and scan bounds as dir.
Example: d=tempname(pwd); mkdir(d); names=ls(d); rmdir(d); size(names)   % [2 2]
Differences from MATLAB: Always returns the Windows-style character matrix, including dot and dot-dot for directories.

## mkdir
Create a directory and any missing parents.
Syntax: status = mkdir(folder)
Syntax: [status, message, id] = mkdir(parent, child)
Returns logical success. An existing directory succeeds with message Directory already exists. Without outputs, failures raise errors and an existing directory emits a warning.
Example: d=tempname(pwd); ok=mkdir(d); rmdir(d); ok   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Network paths are not supported. Host operating-system failure messages can differ.

## rmdir
Remove an empty directory or a directory tree.
Syntax: status = rmdir(folder)
Syntax: [status, message, id] = rmdir(folder, 's')
The s option removes contents recursively. Without outputs, failures raise errors. Recursive removal checks cancellation and is bounded to 64 levels and 10000 entries; cancellation or failure may leave a partly removed tree.
Example: d=tempname(pwd); mkdir(d); rmdir(d)   % no output
Differences from MATLAB: Local paths only; recursive operations have explicit bounds and cooperative cancellation.

## visdiff
Compare two files or two folders.
Syntax: visdiff(file1,file2), visdiff(file1,file2,comparisonType)
The desktop opens the results in the Comparison Tool app. In batch mode, visdiff prints a comparison report. The default compares MAT variables for .mat files and UTF-8 lines for other files. Specify 'text' or 'binary' to select a comparison. Folder comparisons list immediate regular files.
Example: d=tempname(tempdir); mkdir(d); f=fullfile(d,'a.txt'); fid=fopen(f,'w'); fprintf(fid,'abc'); fclose(fid); visdiff(f,f); rmdir(d,'s');
Differences from MATLAB: visdiff takes no output arguments. Folder comparisons are non-recursive and skip symlinks. Text input is bounded to 16 MiB and must be UTF-8. MAT types follow load support, including recursive plain struct fields.

## fileread
Read a UTF-8 text file into a character row.
Syntax: text = fileread(filename)
Reads in bounded chunks, checks cancellation and keeps every byte as read, so CRLF line endings stay (as in MATLAB). The result is limited to 65536 UTF-16 units.
Example: d=tempname(pwd); mkdir(d); f=fullfile(d,'a.txt'); fid=fopen(f,'w'); fprintf(fid,'abc'); fclose(fid); text=fileread(f); rmdir(d,'s'); text   % abc
Differences from MATLAB: Only UTF-8 input is supported; non-UTF-8 files are rejected. Character arrays have the engine size limit.

## tempdir
Return the host temporary folder.
Syntax: folder = tempdir
The returned character row ends with a file separator.
Example: isdir(tempdir)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: none known for this form.

## tempname
Generate a unique temporary path without creating a file.
Syntax: name = tempname
Syntax: name = tempname(folder)
Uses the supplied folder or the host temporary folder. Names include process, time and sequence components. A name is not a reservation: another process can still create it.
Example: a=tempname(pwd); b=tempname(pwd); strcmp(a,b)   % 0
Differences from MATLAB: The generated name format differs from MATLAB.

## clock
Return the current local date and time.
Syntax: v = clock
Returns [year month day hour minute seconds], with fractional seconds.
Example: size(clock)   % [1 6]
Differences from MATLAB: none known for this form on supported Windows, Linux and macOS hosts.

## cputime
Return total process CPU time in seconds.
Syntax: t = cputime
Includes user and kernel CPU time from all threads in this process. It does not measure elapsed wall time.
Example: class(cputime)   % double
Differences from MATLAB: Measures the MatRust process, including other engines and desktop work in the same process.

## date
Return the current local date.
Syntax: s = date
Returns an eleven-character dd-mmm-yyyy row with an English month abbreviation.
Example: size(date)   % [1 11]
Differences from MATLAB: none known for this form.

## now
Return the current local time as a serial date number.
Syntax: n = now
Uses the same serial day numbering as datenum; the fraction represents time within the day.
Example: class(now)   % double
Differences from MATLAB: none known for this form.

## pause
Wait cooperatively or control timed pauses.
Syntax: pause
Syntax: pause(seconds)
Syntax: pause('on')
Syntax: pause('off')
Syntax: state = pause('query')
Syntax: pause(player)
Pausing an audio player preserves its position for resume.
Without an argument, waits until Enter is pressed in the CLI or any answer is given in the desktop Command Window. Zero and negative durations return immediately. Timed pauses check cancellation at least every 10 ms between sleeps. After pause('off') every pause returns at once. The on/off state belongs to the engine.
Example: pause(0); pause('query')   % on
Differences from MATLAB: Bare pause waits for a line (Enter), not a single key; in the browser console only pause(seconds) waits cooperatively.

## timeit
Estimate the elapsed time of a zero-input function handle.
Syntax: seconds = timeit(f)
Syntax: seconds = timeit(f, outputCount)
Warms up once and returns the median of five batches. Each batch performs at most 64 calls or 25 ms of work; a single call can take longer. Output count defaults to one. Ordinary execution budgets and cancellation apply. The function may run many times, so account for side effects.
Example: class(timeit(@() ones(10)))   % double (a fast-call warning may also appear)
Differences from MATLAB: Uses a bounded sampling algorithm rather than MATLAB calibration; interpreter overhead is included. Explicit output counts are limited to 0 through 16.

## isdir
True if a local directory exists.
Syntax: tf = isdir(path)
Resolves relative paths against the engine current folder and returns a logical scalar.
Example: isdir(pwd)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Network paths are not supported.

## isfile
True for names that are existing local files.
Syntax: tf = isfile(name)
Name is a character vector, string array or cell array of character vectors; the logical result has the size of a string or cell input. Relative names resolve against the engine current folder. Folders, missing or empty names give false.
Example: isfile(tempdir)   % 0
Differences from MATLAB: Network paths and URLs give false. The browser version has no files, so it always gives false.

## isfolder
True for names that are existing local folders.
Syntax: tf = isfolder(name)
Name is a character vector, string array or cell array of character vectors; the logical result has the size of a string or cell input. Relative names resolve against the engine current folder. Files, missing or empty names give false.
Example: isfolder(tempdir)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Network paths and URLs give false. The browser version has no files, so it always gives false.

## copyfile
Copy local files or directory trees.
Syntax: status = copyfile(source, destination)
Syntax: [status, message, id] = copyfile(source, destination, 'f')
Destination defaults to the current folder. A file copied to a directory keeps its basename; a directory source copies its contents into the destination. Wildcard sources create a missing destination folder. Supports final-component * and ? patterns. The f option permits replacing read-only files. Without outputs, failure raises an error.
Example: d=tempname(pwd); mkdir(d); f=fullfile(d,'a'); fclose(fopen(f,'w')); ok=copyfile(f,fullfile(d,'b')); rmdir(d,'s'); ok   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Local paths only; symbolic links are rejected. Copies are bounded to 256 MiB, 10000 entries and 64 levels. Each file is staged before replacement; cancellation or failure can leave a partially copied directory tree.

## movefile
Move local files or directory trees.
Syntax: status = movefile(source, destination)
Syntax: [status, message, id] = movefile(source, destination, 'f')
Uses an operating-system rename on the same filesystem. Across filesystems, copies using copyfile rules and removes the source after the copy completes. Supports final-component wildcard patterns. Without outputs, failure raises an error.
Example: d=tempname(pwd); mkdir(d); f=fullfile(d,'a'); fclose(fopen(f,'w')); ok=movefile(f,fullfile(d,'b')); rmdir(d,'s'); ok   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Across filesystems, the copyfile bounds apply and interruption can leave both copies. Symbolic links are rejected.

## delete
Delete local files.
Syntax: delete(filename)
Syntax: delete(pattern1, pattern2, ...)
Supports * and ? in the final path component and at most 64 patterns. A missing file emits a warning. Use rmdir to remove directories. delete(h) with a handle object of a classdef class deletes the object instead (see classdef).
Example: d=tempname(pwd); mkdir(d); f=fullfile(d,'a'); fclose(fopen(f,'w')); delete(f); n=exist(f,'file'); rmdir(d); n   % 0
Differences from MATLAB: Local file deletion only; graphics-object deletion is not supported by this function.

## movmax
Moving maximum.
