RadialDistortion is [k1 k2] or [k1 k2 k3] (default [0 0]), TangentialDistortion [p1 p2] (default [0 0]) and Skew a scalar (default 0). Properties: FocalLength, PrincipalPoint, ImageSize, RadialDistortion, TangentialDistortion, Skew and K = [fx s cx; 0 fy cy; 0 0 1]; the older IntrinsicMatrix property is K.'. All properties are read-only: make a new object to change one. Method: worldToImage.
Example: c = cameraIntrinsics([800 810], [320 240], [480 640]); c.K   % [800 0 320; 0 810 240; 0 0 1]
Example: c = cameraIntrinsics([800 0 320; 0 800 240; 0 0 1], [480 640], 'RadialDistortion', [-0.2 0.05 0.01]); c.RadialDistortion
Differences from MATLAB: the 6-element (rational) RadialDistortion and fisheyeIntrinsics are not supported yet.

## cameraParameters
Calibration result of one camera: intrinsics, pattern extrinsics and accuracy (value class).
Syntax: params = cameraParameters
Syntax: params = cameraParameters(Name, Value, ...)
Names: K or IntrinsicMatrix (= K.'), default eye(3); RadialDistortion ([0 0]); TangentialDistortion ([0 0]); ImageSize ([]); RotationVectors and TranslationVectors (P-by-3, one row per pattern); WorldPoints (M-by-2, or M-by-3); WorldUnits ('mm'); EstimateSkew (false); NumRadialDistortionCoefficients (2 or 3; follows RadialDistortion when that is given); EstimateTangentialDistortion (false); ReprojectionErrors (M-by-2-by-P). Read-only derived properties: Intrinsics (a cameraIntrinsics), FocalLength, PrincipalPoint, Skew, K, RotationMatrices (3-by-3-by-P, rotationVectorToMatrix of each row: postmultiply, the transpose of the Rodrigues matrix), NumPatterns, MeanReprojectionError (mean distance of the ReprojectionErrors rows, NaN without them) and ReprojectedPoints (M-by-2-by-P: WorldPoints projected with each pattern's extrinsics and the lens distortion). All properties are read-only. Method: worldToImage.
Example: p = cameraParameters('K', [800 0 320; 0 800 240; 0 0 1], 'ImageSize', [480 640]); p.FocalLength   % [800 800]
Example: p = cameraParameters('RotationVectors', [0 0 pi/2], 'TranslationVectors', [0 0 100]); p.RotationMatrices   % [0 1 0; -1 0 0; 0 0 1]
Differences from MATLAB: PatternExtrinsics (rigidtform3d), multi-pattern calibrations and the 6-element RadialDistortion are not supported yet.

## generateCheckerboardPoints
World coordinates of the inner corners of a checkerboard calibration pattern.
Syntax: worldPoints = generateCheckerboardPoints(boardSize, squareSize)
boardSize is [rows cols] in squares (each at least 2) and squareSize the side of one square in world units. The result is M-by-2 [x y] with M = (rows-1)*(cols-1); [0 0] is the lower-right corner of the top-left square, x grows along a row of the board and y down a column. Points run down the first column of corners first (y varies fastest), then the next column.
Example: generateCheckerboardPoints([3 4], 10)   % [0 0; 0 10; 10 0; 10 10; 20 0; 20 10]
Example: size(generateCheckerboardPoints([5 7], 25))   % [24 2]

## worldToImage
Project world points into the image of a camera.
Syntax: imagePoints = worldToImage(intrinsics, rotationMatrix, translationVector, worldPoints)
Syntax: [imagePoints, validIndex] = worldToImage(___, 'ApplyDistortion', tf)
intrinsics is a cameraIntrinsics or cameraParameters object; rotationMatrix is 3-by-3 and translationVector 1-by-3 in the postmultiply convention: camera coordinates [Xc Yc Zc] = [X Y Z] * R + t. worldPoints is M-by-3, or M-by-2 for points on the plane z = 0. imagePoints (M-by-2 [x y]) is [fx*x + s*y + cx, fy*y + cy] with x = Xc/Zc, y = Yc/Zc. With 'ApplyDistortion' true (default false) x and y first get radial (k1..k3) and tangential (p1, p2) distortion: r2 = x^2 + y^2, xd = x(1 + k1 r2 + k2 r2^2 + k3 r2^3) + 2 p1 x y + p2 (r2 + 2 x^2), yd = y(1 + ...) + p1 (r2 + 2 y^2) + 2 p2 x y. validIndex is true for points in front of the camera (Zc > 0) that land inside the image ([0.5, ncols+0.5] by [0.5, nrows+0.5]).
Example: c = cameraIntrinsics([800 800], [320 240], [480 640]); worldToImage(c, eye(3), [0 0 10], [1 2 0])   % [400 400]
Example: c = cameraIntrinsics([800 800], [320 240], [480 640]); [p, ok] = worldToImage(c, eye(3), [0 0 -10], [1 2 0]); ok   % false (behind the camera)
Differences from MATLAB: the rigidtform3d form worldToImage(intrinsics, tform, worldPoints) and fisheye cameras are not supported yet; the validIndex image bounds are MatRust's reading of the reference page.

## rotationVectorToMatrix
Rotation matrix of an axis-angle rotation vector (postmultiply convention).
Syntax: R = rotationVectorToMatrix(rotationVector)
rotationVector is a 3-element axis scaled by the angle in radians. R is the transpose of the Rodrigues matrix, for row points p * R (the convention of cameraParameters.RotationMatrices and worldToImage); rotvec2mat3d returns the premultiply form R.'.
Example: rotationVectorToMatrix(pi/2 * [0 0 1])   % [0 1 0; -1 0 0; 0 0 1]

## rotationMatrixToVector
Axis-angle rotation vector of a rotation matrix (postmultiply convention).
Syntax: v = rotationMatrixToVector(R)
Inverse of rotationVectorToMatrix: v is 1-by-3 with the angle in [0, pi] as its length. R is first replaced by its nearest rotation (orthogonal polar factor); a singular or reflecting R is an error.
Example: rotationMatrixToVector([0 1 0; -1 0 0; 0 0 1])   % [0 0 pi/2]

## rotvec2mat3d
Rotation matrix of an axis-angle rotation vector (premultiply convention).
Syntax: R = rotvec2mat3d(rotationVector)
R is the Rodrigues matrix for column points R * p: R = cos(a) I + (1 - cos(a)) k k' + sin(a) [k]x for the unit axis k and angle a = norm(rotationVector).
Example: rotvec2mat3d(pi/2 * [0 0 1])   % [0 -1 0; 1 0 0; 0 0 1]
Differences from MATLAB: one 3-element vector per call (no N-by-3 input).

## rotmat2vec3d
Axis-angle rotation vector of a rotation matrix (premultiply convention).
Syntax: v = rotmat2vec3d(R)
Inverse of rotvec2mat3d: v is 1-by-3 with the angle in [0, pi] as its length; R is first replaced by its nearest rotation.
Example: rotmat2vec3d([0 -1 0; 1 0 0; 0 0 1])   % [0 0 pi/2]
Differences from MATLAB: one 3-by-3 matrix per call (no 3-by-3-by-N input).

## imwarp
Apply a 2-D geometric transformation or a displacement field to an image.
Syntax: B = imwarp(A, tform)
Syntax: [B, RB] = imwarp(A, RA, tform)
Syntax: B = imwarp(A, D)
Syntax: B = imwarp(..., interp, 'OutputView', R, 'FillValues', f, 'SmoothEdges', tf)
A is M-by-N or M-by-N-by-P (each plane warped alike) of class double, single, logical or an integer class; B has the class of A (integers rounded and saturated, logical thresholded at 0.5). tform is an affinetform2d, rigidtform2d, simtform2d, transltform2d or affine2d object mapping input world coordinates to output world coordinates; RA (default imref2d(size(A))) places A in the world. Each output pixel centre is mapped back through the inverse transformation (inverse mapping) and sampled with interp: 'linear' (default), 'nearest' or 'cubic' (cubic convolution, a = -0.5); 'InterpolationMethod', interp is the same. Without OutputView the output covers the bounding box of the transformed image (outputLimits) at the pixel extent of RA, rounded up to whole pixels and centred; RB is the imref2d of the output. Points outside the pixel centres of A get FillValues (default 0; a scalar or one value per channel). 'SmoothEdges', true pads A with FillValues first, so the edges ramp to the fill value. D is M-by-N-by-2: B(r, c) samples A at column c + D(r, c, 1) and row r + D(r, c, 2), and B has the size of D.
Example: B = imwarp(magic(4), rigidtform2d(90, [0 0]))   % rot90(magic(4), -1)
Example: [B, RB] = imwarp(ones(4), simtform2d(1.5, 0, [0 0])); RB.XWorldLimits   % [0.75 6.75]
Example: B = imwarp([2 4 6 8], transltform2d(0.5, 0), 'OutputView', imref2d([1 4]), 'FillValues', 10, 'SmoothEdges', true)   % [6 3 5 7]
Example: B = imwarp(magic(3), cat(3, ones(3), zeros(3)))   % columns shift left; last column 0
Differences from MATLAB: the reference page does not give the edge rules or the rounding of the default output size; MatRust chooses these: a sample point is interpolated only inside the pixel-centre hull [1, N] x [1, M] (within 1e-9 pixel), cubic taps past the border repeat the edge pixel, SmoothEdges pads by 2 pixels, and the default size is ceil(extent / pixel extent) with the limits widened evenly. Categorical images, 3-D transformations (imref3d, affinetform3d), projective transformations and the Warper object are not supported yet.

## imregtform
Estimate the geometric transformation that aligns two 2-D images (intensity-based registration).
Syntax: tform = imregtform(moving, fixed, transformType, optimizer, metric)
Syntax: tform = imregtform(moving, Rmoving, fixed, Rfixed, transformType, optimizer, metric)
Syntax: tform = imregtform(..., 'DisplayOptimization', tf, 'InitialTransformation', tform0, 'PyramidLevels', n)
moving and fixed are 2-D grayscale images of class single, double, int8, int16, int32, uint8, uint16 or uint32 (their sizes may differ); Rmoving and Rfixed (imref2d objects, default imref2d(size(image))) place them in world coordinates. transformType 'translation', 'rigid', 'similarity' or 'affine' (any case, a unique prefix is accepted) gives a transltform2d, rigidtform2d, simtform2d or affinetform2d. tform maps moving world coordinates to fixed world coordinates, so imwarp(moving, Rmoving, tform, 'OutputView', Rfixed) lines moving up with fixed (imregister does exactly this). optimizer and metric come from imregconfig, and any optimizer works with any metric. 'monomodal' gives registration.optimizer.RegularStepGradientDescent and registration.metric.MeanSquares, the mean of the squared differences over the fixed pixels that land inside the moving image (linear interpolation; the half pixel beyond the outer pixel centres repeats the edge value). 'multimodal' gives registration.optimizer.OnePlusOneEvolutionary and registration.metric.MattesMutualInformation, minus the mutual information of the joint histogram of fixed and moving values (NumberOfHistogramBins bins per image over each image's value range, a fixed value counts in its bin, a moving value spreads over four bins with a cubic B-spline), which also aligns images whose brightness differs (for example an inverted image); it uses every fixed pixel, or with UseAllPixels false NumberOfSpatialSamples pixels drawn per pyramid level with a fixed seed. The search runs on an image pyramid of PyramidLevels levels (default 3), coarse to fine, each level half the size of the next; every dimension of both images needs at least 4*2^(PyramidLevels-1) pixels. At each level the regular step gradient descent starts with steps of MaximumStepLength, multiplies the step by RelaxationFactor whenever the gradient direction reverses, and stops when the gradient magnitude is below GradientMagnitudeTolerance, when the step is below MinimumStepLength or after MaximumIterations iterations. Step lengths are in pixels of the current level: each parameter is scaled by the root-mean-square distance a unit change of it moves the pixels, so one step length suits rotation, scale, shear and translation; GradientMagnitudeTolerance is compared with the gradient of the metric per pixel of movement, so for images with values in [0, 1] and little detail it can end the search a few tenths of a pixel early, because the tolerance is absolute like the documented property (lower it, for example to 1e-6, or scale the images to 0-255 for a finer result). The one-plus-one evolutionary optimizer tries one random step (normal variates from a fixed seed, so results repeat) from the current estimate per iteration and keeps it when the metric is lower; the search widens along the step by GrowthFactor after a success and narrows by GrowthFactor^(-1/4) after a failure. Each level starts with a search radius of InitialRadius and stops when the radius is at most Epsilon or after MaximumIterations iterations; InitialRadius and Epsilon are in the same pixel units as the step lengths, so the default InitialRadius (6.25e-3) starts with very small steps: for warps of more than a pixel or two raise MaximumIterations (300 recovers the examples here). InitialTransformation (default: no change) is the starting estimate; it can be any 2-D transformation object whose matrix has the form of transformType (a pure translation for 'translation', a rotation plus translation for 'rigid', ...). DisplayOptimization true prints, for every pyramid level, one line per iteration (metric value, gradient magnitude and step length; for OnePlusOneEvolutionary the best metric value and the search radius) and the reason the level stopped.
Example: [x, y] = meshgrid(1:64); fixed = exp(-((x - 26).^2 + (y - 34).^2)/60) + 0.8*exp(-((x - 40).^2 + (y - 24).^2)/30) + 0.6*exp(-((x - 38).^2 + (y - 44).^2)/40); [optimizer, metric] = imregconfig('monomodal'); moving = imwarp(fixed, transltform2d(2.5, -1.5), 'OutputView', imref2d(size(fixed))); tform = imregtform(moving, fixed, 'translation', optimizer, metric); tform.Translation   % about [-2.5 1.5]
Example: [x, y] = meshgrid(1:64); fixed = exp(-((x - 26).^2 + (y - 34).^2)/60) + 0.8*exp(-((x - 40).^2 + (y - 24).^2)/30) + 0.6*exp(-((x - 38).^2 + (y - 44).^2)/40); [optimizer, metric] = imregconfig('monomodal'); moving = imwarp(fixed, rigidtform2d(3, [1 -2]), 'OutputView', imref2d(size(fixed))); optimizer.GradientMagnitudeTolerance = 1e-6; tform = imregtform(moving, fixed, 'rigid', optimizer, metric, 'PyramidLevels', 2); tform.RotationAngle   % about -3 (-2.96; -2.45 with the default tolerance)
Example: [x, y] = meshgrid(1:64); fixed = exp(-((x - 26).^2 + (y - 34).^2)/60) + 0.8*exp(-((x - 40).^2 + (y - 24).^2)/30) + 0.6*exp(-((x - 38).^2 + (y - 44).^2)/40); [optimizer, metric] = imregconfig('multimodal'); optimizer.MaximumIterations = 300; moving = 1 - imwarp(fixed, transltform2d(2.5, -1.5), 'OutputView', imref2d(size(fixed))); tform = imregtform(moving, fixed, 'translation', optimizer, metric); tform.Translation   % about [-2.5 1.5] (inverted brightness)
Differences from MATLAB: the reference pages do not give the algorithm; MatRust chooses these: the pyramid filter ([1 3 3 1]/8 over pixel pairs) and the minimum image size, the parameter scaling and step units above (so OnePlusOneEvolutionary settings tuned for MATLAB can behave differently), metric gradients from central differences, the random generators and seeds, and the DisplayOptimization text. NumberOfHistogramBins is at most 4096. Results can differ from MATLAB's in the digits and, for hard cases, in the optimum found. 3-D volumes (imref3d), imregcorr, imregdemons and feature-based registration are not supported yet.

## imregister
Register two 2-D images by intensity: align moving with fixed.
Syntax: movingReg = imregister(moving, fixed, transformType, optimizer, metric)
Syntax: [movingReg, Rreg] = imregister(moving, Rmoving, fixed, Rfixed, transformType, optimizer, metric)
Syntax: [movingReg, Rreg] = imregister(..., 'DisplayOptimization', tf, 'InitialTransformation', tform0, 'PyramidLevels', n)
Estimates tform as imregtform does (same inputs and options) and returns movingReg = imwarp(moving, Rmoving, tform, 'OutputView', Rfixed) with linear interpolation: movingReg has the size of fixed and the class of moving, and pixels that map outside moving are 0. Rreg is Rfixed (imref2d(size(fixed)) when no referencing objects are given). Use imregtform to get the transformation itself, and imshowpair or imfuse to compare movingReg with fixed.
Example: [x, y] = meshgrid(1:64); fixed = exp(-((x - 26).^2 + (y - 34).^2)/60) + 0.8*exp(-((x - 40).^2 + (y - 24).^2)/30) + 0.6*exp(-((x - 38).^2 + (y - 44).^2)/40); [optimizer, metric] = imregconfig('monomodal'); moving = imwarp(fixed, rigidtform2d(3, [1 -2]), 'OutputView', imref2d(size(fixed))); movingReg = imregister(moving, fixed, 'rigid', optimizer, metric); max(max(abs(movingReg(8:56, 8:56) - fixed(8:56, 8:56))))   % about 0.02
Example: [x, y] = meshgrid(1:64); fixed = exp(-((x - 26).^2 + (y - 34).^2)/60) + 0.8*exp(-((x - 40).^2 + (y - 24).^2)/30) + 0.6*exp(-((x - 38).^2 + (y - 44).^2)/40); [optimizer, metric] = imregconfig('monomodal'); moving = imwarp(fixed, transltform2d(2, 1), 'OutputView', imref2d(size(fixed))); [movingReg, Rreg] = imregister(uint8(255*moving), uint8(255*fixed), 'translation', optimizer, metric); class(movingReg)   % 'uint8'
Differences from MATLAB: the estimate follows the choices listed under imregtform. 3-D volumes are not supported yet.

## fspecial
Create a predefined 2-D filter.
Syntax: h = fspecial(type)
Syntax: h = fspecial(type, parameters)
'average' (hsize, default 3): ones(hsize)/numel. 'gaussian' (hsize 3, sigma 0.5): exp(-(x^2+y^2)/(2 sigma^2)) normalised to sum 1. 'log' (hsize 5, sigma 0.5): (x^2+y^2-2 sigma^2) hg/(sigma^4 sum(hg)), shifted so the kernel sums to 0. 'laplacian' (alpha 0.2): 4/(alpha+1) [alpha/4 (1-alpha)/4 alpha/4; (1-alpha)/4 -1 (1-alpha)/4; alpha/4 (1-alpha)/4 alpha/4]. 'unsharp' (alpha 0.2): 1/(alpha+1) [-alpha alpha-1 -alpha; alpha-1 alpha+5 alpha-1; -alpha alpha-1 -alpha]. 'prewitt' [1 1 1; 0 0 0; -1 -1 -1] and 'sobel' [1 2 1; 0 0 0; -1 -2 -1] (horizontal edges; transpose for vertical). hsize is n or [rows cols].
Example: fspecial('average', 2)   % 0.25 * ones(2)
Example: fspecial('sobel')   % [1 2 1; 0 0 0; -1 -2 -1]
Example: fspecial('gaussian', 5, 1)
Differences from MATLAB: 'disk' and 'motion' are not supported yet.

## imfilter
Filter an image with a 2-D kernel.
Syntax: B = imfilter(A, h)
Syntax: B = imfilter(A, h, options...)
Correlation by default ('conv' turns the kernel by 180 degrees). The kernel centre is floor((size(h)+1)/2). Boundary: a numeric value X (default 0), 'symmetric' (mirror including the edge pixel), 'replicate' (repeat the edge pixel) or 'circular' (periodic). Size: 'same' (default) or 'full' (size(A) + size(h) - 1). Each plane of an M-by-N-by-C image is filtered with the 2-D kernel. The output class is the input class: integers rounded half away from zero and saturated, logical results true where nonzero.
Example: imfilter([1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9], ones(3)/9)
Example: imfilter(uint8([200 50 5]), 2)   % uint8 [255 100 10]
Example: imfilter(magic(4), [1 -1], 'replicate', 'full')
Differences from MATLAB: N-D kernels and the GPU and frequency options are not supported yet.

## imgaussfilt
2-D Gaussian filtering of an image.
Syntax: B = imgaussfilt(A)
Syntax: B = imgaussfilt(A, sigma, 'FilterSize', n, 'Padding', p)
Correlates with a Gaussian kernel normalised to sum 1. sigma is a positive scalar or [sigma_rows sigma_cols] (default 0.5); FilterSize is an odd n or [rows cols] (default 2*ceil(2*sigma)+1); Padding is 'replicate' (default), 'circular', 'symmetric' or a number. 'FilterDomain' is accepted; the result is always computed in the spatial domain (two 1-D passes). The class is kept. FilterSize is at most 4096, so with the default size sigma is at most 1023.5.
Example: imgaussfilt(magic(4))
Example: imgaussfilt(uint8(magic(5)), 1, 'Padding', 'symmetric')
Differences from MATLAB: FilterSize is limited to 4096 (MATLAB has no published limit).

## medfilt2
2-D median filtering.
Syntax: B = medfilt2(A)
Syntax: B = medfilt2(A, [m n], padopt)
Each output is the median of the m-by-n neighbourhood (default 3-by-3) centred at floor(([m n]+1)/2). padopt: 'zeros' (default), 'symmetric' (mirror) or 'indexed' (1 for double images, 0 otherwise). For an even number of elements the median is the mean of the two middle values; integer classes discard the fraction, as the reference page states (its example gives 4 for [1 5; 4 8]). The class is kept.
Example: medfilt2([1 9 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 2])   % [0 3 0; 4 5 3; 0 4 0]
Example: medfilt2(uint8([1 5; 4 8]), [2 2])   % uint8 [4 2; 2 0]
Differences from MATLAB: only 2-D images; NaN values sort after every number.

## imregconfig
Configurations for intensity-based image registration.
Syntax: [optimizer, metric] = imregconfig(modality)
Syntax: optimizer = registration.optimizer.RegularStepGradientDescent(Name, Value, ...)
Syntax: optimizer = registration.optimizer.OnePlusOneEvolutionary(Name, Value, ...)
Syntax: metric = registration.metric.MeanSquares
Syntax: metric = registration.metric.MattesMutualInformation(Name, Value, ...)
modality 'monomodal' (images of similar brightness and contrast) gives a registration.optimizer.RegularStepGradientDescent optimizer and a registration.metric.MeanSquares metric; 'multimodal' gives registration.optimizer.OnePlusOneEvolutionary and registration.metric.MattesMutualInformation. The objects are values: o2 = o; o2.MaximumIterations = 300 changes o2 only. Properties and defaults: RegularStepGradientDescent GradientMagnitudeTolerance 1e-4, MinimumStepLength 1e-5, MaximumStepLength 0.0625 (positive numbers), MaximumIterations 100 (positive integer), RelaxationFactor 0.5 (between 0 and 1); OnePlusOneEvolutionary GrowthFactor 1.05, Epsilon 1.5e-6, InitialRadius 6.25e-3 (positive numbers), MaximumIterations 100 (these are MATLAB's documented defaults; with them a multimodal pair often stops short, so raise MaximumIterations to 300, as MATLAB's own multimodal example does, or set InitialRadius); MeanSquares has no properties; MattesMutualInformation NumberOfSpatialSamples 500 (positive integer), NumberOfHistogramBins 50 (integer of at least 5), UseAllPixels true. The constructors take property name-value pairs (names in any case). class, isa, properties, isequal and disp work on the objects. imregtform and imregister accept any optimizer with any metric.
Example: [optimizer, metric] = imregconfig('monomodal'); optimizer.MaximumIterations   % 100
Example: [optimizer, metric] = imregconfig('multimodal'); class(metric)   % 'registration.metric.MattesMutualInformation'
Example: o = registration.optimizer.OnePlusOneEvolutionary('InitialRadius', 0.009); o.InitialRadius   % 0.009
Differences from MATLAB: a unique prefix of the modality ('mono') is accepted.

## imfuse
Composite of two images.
Syntax: C = imfuse(A, B)
Syntax: C = imfuse(A, B, method)
Syntax: C = imfuse(..., 'Scaling', scaling, 'ColorChannels', channels)
Syntax: [C, RC] = imfuse(A, RA, B, RB, ...)
A and B are grayscale or truecolor images of class double, single, logical, uint8, uint16 or int16; C is uint8. method: 'falsecolor' (default) puts A and B in different colour channels of an RGB image, so equal intensities look gray and differences look green or magenta; 'blend' is the mean (A + B) / 2; 'diff' is the absolute difference |A - B|; 'montage' places A and B side by side, [A B]; 'checkerboard' takes alternating tiles from A and B. 'falsecolor' and 'diff' convert RGB images to grayscale with the rgb2gray weights; the other methods keep colour (a grayscale image beside an RGB one is repeated in the three channels). Images of different sizes are padded with zeros at the bottom and right to the larger height and width. Each image is first put on its class's 0..1 scale (as im2double); Scaling 'independent' (default) then stretches each image's smallest..largest value to 0..1, 'joint' stretches the smallest..largest value of both images together, and 'none' leaves the values; the composite is converted as im2uint8. ColorChannels (falsecolor only) is [R G B] with 1 for A, 2 for B and 0 for neither; 'green-magenta' (default) is [2 1 2] and 'red-cyan' is [1 2 2].
Example: imfuse(uint8([0 100; 200 255]), uint8([50 50; 150 250]))   % 2x2x3 uint8; green channel [0 100; 200 255]
Example: imfuse(uint8([20 40]), uint8([60 120]), 'blend', 'Scaling', 'joint')   % uint8 [51 153]
Example: imfuse(uint8([10 20 30]), uint8([40; 50]), 'montage', 'Scaling', 'none')   % uint8 [10 20 30 40 0 0; 0 0 0 50 0 0]
Differences from MATLAB: the reference page does not give the formulas; MatRust chooses these: padding comes before scaling, so padded zeros take part in the scaling range; an image (or, with 'joint', both images) whose values are all equal is not stretched; 'blend' uses equal weights; 'diff' is not stretched after the difference; 'checkerboard' uses tiles of ceil(rows/8) by ceil(cols/8) pixels with the top-left tile from A. imfuse(A, RA, B, RB) with imref2d RA and RB: the output covers the union of both world extents at RA's pixel extents (starting at the lower world limits, whole pixels); A and B are resampled onto that grid with linear interpolation (identity transformation; pixels outside an image get its class's zero on the unit scale: 0 for uint8, uint16, logical and floating images, 32768/65535 (about 0.5) for int16, which shows as 128 with 'Scaling', 'none'; otherwise the fill takes part in the scaling range like the padded zeros), then fused as above; RC is the imref2d of the output ('montage': twice as wide). The second output RC is given only for this form; referencing structs and other objects are not supported yet.

## imshowpair
Show two images as a composite.
Syntax: imshowpair(A, B)
Syntax: imshowpair(A, B, method)
Syntax: h = imshowpair(..., 'Scaling', scaling, 'ColorChannels', channels, 'Parent', ax)
Syntax: imshowpair(A, RA, B, RB, ...)
Shows imfuse(A, B, ...) with imshow in the current axes, or in the axes given by 'Parent'; methods 'falsecolor' (default), 'blend', 'diff', 'montage' and 'checkerboard' and the Scaling and ColorChannels options are those of imfuse. h is the image object; its CData is the uint8 composite. Works without a window: save the figure with saveas or exportgraphics.
Example: h = imshowpair(uint8(magic(4)), uint8(magic(4)'), 'diff'); size(h.CData)   % [4 4]
Example: imshowpair(rand(8), rand(8), 'montage', 'Scaling', 'joint')
Differences from MATLAB: 'Interpolation' ('nearest' or 'bilinear') is accepted and ignored; imshowpair(A, RA, B, RB) shows imfuse(A, RA, B, RB, ...) (the union of both world extents, see imfuse) as a plain image in pixel coordinates, not placed at RC's world limits.

## detectCheckerboardPoints
Detect checkerboard pattern corners in images.
Syntax: [imagePoints, boardSize] = detectCheckerboardPoints(I)
Syntax: [imagePoints, boardSize, imagesUsed] = detectCheckerboardPoints(imageFileNames)
Syntax: [imagePoints, boardSize, imagesUsed] = detectCheckerboardPoints(images)
Syntax: [...] = detectCheckerboardPoints(..., 'PartialDetections', tf, 'HighDistortion', tf)
I is a grayscale or truecolor image (double, single, logical, uint8, uint16 or int16); imageFileNames is a cell array or string array of image files; images is an H-by-W-by-N grayscale stack (N other than 3: H-by-W-by-3 is one truecolor image), or a 4-D H-by-W-by-1-by-N grayscale or H-by-W-by-3-by-N truecolor stack. imagePoints are the inner corners as [x y] in pixels (the centre of the first pixel is (1,1)), sub-pixel accurate, M-by-2 for one image and M-by-2-by-K for the K images used, with M = prod(boardSize - 1). boardSize is [height width] in squares. Point order is generateCheckerboardPoints's: the origin is the lower-right corner of the top-left square, which is black; x runs along the longer side of the board (the side with more squares), y is x turned 90 degrees clockwise on the image, and y varies fastest. Use a board with an even number of squares along one side and an odd number along the other so the orientation is unique. imagesUsed is an N-by-1 logical vector, true where the board was found; when sizes differ the most common board size is kept. No board gives imagePoints = [] and boardSize = [0 0].
Method: Hessian saddle response on the image smoothed with sigma 1.2, a ring test (four alternating dark/bright sectors with straight edges), growth of a corner grid from a 3-by-3 seed by whole rows and columns, alternating cell colours (each cell against the cells next to it, so uneven lighting across the board is allowed). The search runs on the image and on copies reduced 2, 4 and 8 times (while the smaller side keeps 150 pixels), which finds boards in soft and high-resolution images; the grid with the most corners wins. Then sub-pixel refinement on the full-size image by gradient orthogonality (as OpenCV's cornerSubPix) with a window half-width of 0.3 of the smallest corner spacing (2 to 48 pixels; smaller for a corner near the image border).
Example: I = ones(180, 240); I(21:160, 21:220) = kron(mod(repmat((0:6)', 1, 10) + repmat(0:9, 7, 1), 2), ones(20)); [p, b] = detectCheckerboardPoints(I); b   % [7 10]
Example: I = ones(180, 240); I(21:160, 21:220) = kron(mod(repmat((0:6)', 1, 10) + repmat(0:9, 7, 1), 2), ones(20)); p = detectCheckerboardPoints(I); p(1:2, :)   % [40.5 40.5; 40.5 60.5]
Differences from MATLAB: only whole boards are returned: corners the grid cannot reach are left out rather than given as NaN, so 'PartialDetections' true (the default) and false both behave like false. 'HighDistortion' is accepted and changes nothing. 'MinCornerMetric' and the stereo forms (two image sets) are not supported yet. Boards need at least 3-by-3 inner corners (4-by-4 squares) and squares at least about 10 pixels wide. Large or soft boards are found on the reduced copies (at most 8 times reduced): checked with 640-by-480 test images enlarged up to 12 times (squares up to about 400 pixels) and with Gaussian blur up to sigma 4 pixels plus noise; stronger blur at that size (sigma 6) loses most boards.

## estimateCameraParameters
Calibrate a single camera from views of a planar pattern.
Syntax: params = estimateCameraParameters(imagePoints, worldPoints)
Syntax: [params, imagesUsed, estimationErrors] = estimateCameraParameters(imagePoints, worldPoints, Name, Value, ...)
imagePoints is M-by-2-by-P: the [x y] pixel positions (the centre of the first pixel is (1,1)) of the M pattern points in each of P >= 2 views, as detectCheckerboardPoints returns them; worldPoints is the M-by-2 [x y] pattern points on the plane z = 0 (generateCheckerboardPoints). params is a cameraParameters with FocalLength, PrincipalPoint, Skew, RadialDistortion, TangentialDistortion, RotationVectors and TranslationVectors (one row per view used), WorldPoints, ReprojectionErrors (reprojected minus detected points, M-by-2-by-P) and MeanReprojectionError. Partially detected patterns: a point not detected in a view is [NaN NaN] in that view; it is left out of the fit, and its ReprojectionErrors rows are NaN (MeanReprojectionError leaves them out). imagesUsed is P-by-1 logical, false for a view with fewer than 4 points or without a homography (a warning names such views); the result arrays cover the used views only, and at least 2 are needed. estimationErrors is a cameraCalibrationErrors object: IntrinsicsErrors (an intrinsicsEstimationErrors with SkewError, FocalLengthError, PrincipalPointError, RadialDistortionError and TangentialDistortionError) and ExtrinsicsErrors (an extrinsicsEstimationErrors with RotationVectorsError and TranslationVectorsError, one row per used view), the standard errors of the estimates (0 for parameters not estimated); displayErrors prints them. Names: ImageSize ([mrows ncols], default []); WorldUnits ('mm'); EstimateSkew (false); NumRadialDistortionCoefficients (2 or 3, default 2); EstimateTangentialDistortion (false); InitialK (a 3-by-3 [fx s cx; 0 fy cy; 0 0 1] start for the intrinsics instead of the closed form) or InitialIntrinsicMatrix (the same as its transpose, the earlier form); InitialRadialDistortion (a start for the radial coefficients, NumRadialDistortionCoefficients elements; default zeros). The views must tilt the pattern in different directions: parallel poses (pattern planes within about 1 degree of each other) are degenerate and give an error.
Method: Zhang's method: a homography per view (normalised DLT), closed-form intrinsics and extrinsics, then Levenberg-Marquardt over all parameters minimising the reprojection error (distortion starts at zero). With 2 to 4 views, or when the closed form gives no camera, the fit is also started from the principal point at the image centre (the centroid of the points without ImageSize) with focal lengths from the homographies, and the fit with the smaller error is kept (with InitialK only that start is used). Standard errors are sqrt(diag(s2 * inv(J'*J))) at the solution, J the Jacobian of the reprojection residuals, s2 = sum of squared residuals / (2 * number of points - number of parameters).
Example: w = generateCheckerboardPoints([7 10], 25); c = cameraIntrinsics([800 790], [322 238], [480 640]); r = [0.3 0 0; 0 0.3 0; 0.2 -0.2 0.1]; ip = zeros(54, 2, 3); for k = 1:3, ip(:, :, k) = worldToImage(c, rotationVectorToMatrix(r(k, :)), [-100 -60 500], w); end; params = estimateCameraParameters(ip, w, 'ImageSize', [480 640]); round(params.FocalLength)   % [800 790]
Example: w = generateCheckerboardPoints([7 10], 25); c = cameraIntrinsics([800 790], [322 238], [480 640]); r = [0.3 0 0; 0 0.3 0; 0.2 -0.2 0.1]; ip = zeros(54, 2, 3); for k = 1:3, ip(:, :, k) = worldToImage(c, rotationVectorToMatrix(r(k, :)), [-100 -60 500], w); end; ip(1:5, :, 2) = NaN; [params, used] = estimateCameraParameters(ip, w, 'InitialK', [800 0 322; 0 790 238; 0 0 1]); used'   % [1 1 1]
Differences from MATLAB: stereo pairs, fisheye models, EstimateSkew together with fewer than 3 views and more than 100 views are not supported yet. Points with only one coordinate NaN, or Inf, are an error.

## displayErrors
Display standard errors of camera parameter estimates.
Syntax: displayErrors(estimationErrors, cameraParams)
estimationErrors is the cameraCalibrationErrors (third output) of estimateCameraParameters and cameraParams its cameraParameters. Prints each estimate with its standard error, value +/- error: focal length, principal point, skew (when estimated), radial and tangential (when estimated) distortion, then one row per view of rotation vectors and of translation vectors (in WorldUnits).
Example: w = generateCheckerboardPoints([7 10], 25); c = cameraIntrinsics([800 790], [322 238], [480 640]); r = [0.3 0 0; 0 0.3 0; 0.2 -0.2 0.1; -0.2 0.1 0]; ip = zeros(54, 2, 4); for k = 1:4, ip(:, :, k) = worldToImage(c, rotationVectorToMatrix(r(k, :)), [-100 -60 500], w) + 0.1 * sin((1:54)' * [k 2 * k]); end; [params, ~, est] = estimateCameraParameters(ip, w); displayErrors(est, params)
Differences from MATLAB: the table header is not indented with tabs; every view row is printed in full.

## showReprojectionErrors
Plot the reprojection errors of a camera calibration.
Syntax: showReprojectionErrors(params)
Syntax: ax = showReprojectionErrors(params, view, 'HighlightIndex', idx, 'Parent', ax)
params is a cameraParameters from estimateCameraParameters. view 'BarGraph' (default) draws one bar per pattern, the mean of the per-point error lengths hypot(ReprojectionErrors(:, 1, p), ReprojectionErrors(:, 2, p)), with a dashed line at MeanReprojectionError and the legend "Overall Mean Error: 0.xx pixels". 'ScatterPlot' draws the x and y error of every point, one colour per pattern. HighlightIndex draws those patterns in red (circles in the scatter plot); Parent draws into that axes instead of the current one. ax is the axes used.
Example: w = generateCheckerboardPoints([7 10], 25); c = cameraIntrinsics([800 790], [322 238], [480 640]); r = [0.3 0 0; 0 0.3 0; 0.2 -0.2 0.1]; ip = zeros(54, 2, 3); for k = 1:3, ip(:, :, k) = worldToImage(c, rotationVectorToMatrix(r(k, :)), [-100 -60 500], w); end; params = estimateCameraParameters(ip, w, 'ImageSize', [480 640]); figure; ax = showReprojectionErrors(params, 'ScatterPlot'); numel(get(ax, 'Children'))   % 3
Differences from MATLAB: highlighted bars are a second bar series drawn over the first. Stereo, fisheye and multi-camera parameters are not supported yet.

## showExtrinsics
Plot the calibration patterns and the camera in 3-D.
Syntax: showExtrinsics(params)
Syntax: ax = showExtrinsics(params, view, 'HighlightIndex', idx, 'Parent', ax)
params is a cameraParameters from estimateCameraParameters. view 'CameraCentric' (default) puts the camera at the origin and each pattern (the rectangle around its WorldPoints, numbered) at [X Y 0]*R + t with that pattern's RotationMatrices and TranslationVectors. 'PatternCentric' puts the pattern at the origin and one numbered camera per pattern, centred at -t*R'. HighlightIndex draws those patterns or cameras in red (patterns more opaque); Parent draws into that axes. Axes are labelled in WorldUnits. ax is the axes used.
Example: w = generateCheckerboardPoints([7 10], 25); c = cameraIntrinsics([800 790], [322 238], [480 640]); r = [0.3 0 0; 0 0.3 0; 0.2 -0.2 0.1]; ip = zeros(54, 2, 3); for k = 1:3, ip(:, :, k) = worldToImage(c, rotationVectorToMatrix(r(k, :)), [-100 -60 500], w); end; params = estimateCameraParameters(ip, w, 'ImageSize', [480 640]); figure; ax = showExtrinsics(params, 'PatternCentric'); numel(get(ax, 'Children'))   % 7
Differences from MATLAB: the plot uses plain camera/world axes (X right, Y, Z along the optical axis) rather than MATLAB's swapped, reversed-Z layout. Stereo, fisheye and multi-camera parameters and CameraIndex/PatternIndex are not supported yet.
## undistortImage
Correct lens distortion in an image.
Syntax: J = undistortImage(I, intrinsics)
Syntax: J = undistortImage(I, intrinsics, interp)
Syntax: [J, camIntrinsics] = undistortImage(___, 'OutputView', view, 'FillValues', fill)
I is M-by-N or M-by-N-by-3 (double, single, logical or an integer class; J has the class of I); intrinsics is a cameraIntrinsics or cameraParameters object. Each pixel (u, v) of J is normalized with the intrinsics of J, distorted (radial k1..k3, tangential p1, p2, as in worldToImage), mapped back with K and sampled from I with interp 'linear' (default), 'nearest' or 'cubic'. Samples outside the pixel centres of I get FillValues (default 0; a scalar or one value per channel). OutputView 'same' (default) keeps the size of I; 'full' is the whole-pixel box around the undistorted border of I; 'valid' is the largest such box with no fill pixels. camIntrinsics is a cameraIntrinsics for J: the same focal lengths and skew, the principal point moved by the whole-pixel offset of the view, ImageSize = size of J and no distortion.
Example: c = cameraIntrinsics([800 790], [322 238], [480 640], 'RadialDistortion', [-0.12 0.05]); J = undistortImage(ones(480, 640), c); size(J)   % [480 640]
Example: c = cameraIntrinsics([800 790], [322 238], [480 640], 'RadialDistortion', [-0.12 0.05]); [J, n] = undistortImage(ones(480, 640), c, 'OutputView', 'full'); n.ImageSize   % larger than [480 640]
Differences from MATLAB: fisheye (cameraIntrinsicsKB) cameras are not supported; the 'full' and 'valid' boxes are aligned to whole pixels of the 'same' view.

## undistortPoints
Correct lens distortion of image points.
Syntax: undistortedPoints = undistortPoints(points, intrinsics)
Syntax: [undistortedPoints, reprojectionErrors] = undistortPoints(points, intrinsics)
points is an M-by-2 matrix of [x y] pixel coordinates; intrinsics is a cameraIntrinsics or cameraParameters object. Each point is normalized with K, the distortion is inverted by Newton's method (at most 50 steps, to a normalized residual below 1e-10) and the result is mapped back with K. reprojectionErrors (M-by-1, pixels) is the distance from each input point to its undistorted point distorted again. Outputs are double for double points, otherwise single.
Example: c = cameraIntrinsics([800 790], [322 238], [480 640], 'RadialDistortion', [-0.12 0.05]); p = worldToImage(c, eye(3), [0 0 1], [0.3 0.2 0], 'ApplyDistortion', true); undistortPoints(p, c)   % [562 396]
Differences from MATLAB: fisheye (cameraIntrinsicsKB) cameras and point objects (cornerPoints, ...) are not supported.

## sound
Play an audio signal and return immediately.
Syntax: sound(y)
Syntax: sound(y, Fs)
Syntax: sound(y, Fs, nBits)
A row or column vector plays in mono. An N-by-2 matrix plays in stereo, with the left channel first. Fs defaults to 8192 Hz and nBits defaults to 16. Values outside [-1, 1] are clipped. Requires an audio-enabled build.
Example: sound(zeros(64,1), 8000);

## soundsc
Scale audio samples to [-1, 1] and play them asynchronously.
Syntax: soundsc(y)
Syntax: soundsc(y, Fs)
Syntax: soundsc(y, [low high])
Syntax: soundsc(y, Fs, [low high])
Syntax: soundsc(y, Fs, nBits, [low high])
By default, the smallest and largest finite samples map to -1 and 1 across all channels. A constant signal scales to silence. An explicit range replaces the minimum and maximum and clips samples outside that range. See sound for the default rate and bit depth.
Example: soundsc([0 0.001 0], 8000, [-1 1]);

## audioplayer
Create a handle for audio playback.
Syntax: p = audioplayer(y, Fs)
Syntax: p = audioplayer(y, Fs, nBits)
Syntax: p = audioplayer(y, Fs, nBits, ID)
Use play or playblocking to start playback. SampleRate, Tag and UserData are writable. BitsPerSample, NumChannels, DeviceID, TotalSamples, CurrentSample and Running are read-only. DeviceID defaults to -1, the default output device. With no output device, playback follows the clip's timing in silence.
Example: p = audioplayer(zeros(64,1), 8000); if isobject(p); disp(p); end

## play
Start an audio player's playback and return immediately.
Syntax: play(p)
Syntax: play(p, start)
Syntax: play(p, [start finish])
Each call starts a new playback. Sample indices start at 1 and both endpoints are included.
Example: p = audioplayer(zeros(64,1), 8000); play(p, [2 16]);

## playblocking
Play audio and wait for playback to finish.
Syntax: playblocking(p)
Syntax: playblocking(p, start)
Syntax: playblocking(p, [start finish])
The wait is cancellable. Playback is timed when the system has no output device.
Example: p = audioplayer(zeros(64,1), 8000); playblocking(p);

## resume
Continue paused audio playback from its current position.
Syntax: resume(p)
Null playback resumes at the paused sample; on an output device the audible position depends on device buffering.
Example: p = audioplayer(zeros(64,1), 8000); if isobject(p); play(p); pause(p); resume(p); end

## stop
Stop audio playback or recording.
Syntax: stop(p)
Syntax: stop(r)
Playback resets to the first sample. Recording retains the samples already captured.
Example: p = audioplayer(zeros(64,1), 8000); stop(p);

## isplaying
Check whether an audio player is currently playing.
Syntax: tf = isplaying(p)
A paused or stopped player returns false.
Example: p = audioplayer(zeros(64,1), 8000); if isobject(p); disp(isplaying(p)); end

## audiorecorder
Create a handle for recording audio from the default input device.
Syntax: r = audiorecorder
Syntax: r = audiorecorder(Fs, nBits, nChannels)
The defaults are 8000 Hz, 8 bits and one channel. Bit depths are 8, 16 or 24 and the channel count is 1 or 2. The recorder opens a device when recording starts.
Example: r = audiorecorder(8000, 16, 1);

## record
Start recording audio and return immediately.
Syntax: record(r)
Syntax: record(r, seconds)
Call stop(r) to end an ongoing recording. Ongoing recordings also stop when the sample buffer reaches its limit. A usable audio input device is required.

## recordblocking
Record audio for a specified duration and wait for it to finish.
Syntax: recordblocking(r, seconds)
The wait is cancellable. A usable audio input device is required.

## getaudiodata
Return captured audio samples as a column for each channel.
Syntax: y = getaudiodata(r)
Syntax: y = getaudiodata(r, datatype)
Data types include double (default), single, int16, int8 and uint8. Use stop before reading to get the complete capture.
Example: r = audiorecorder(8000,16,1); y = getaudiodata(r);

## getplayer
Create an audio player from a recorder's captured samples.
Syntax: p = getplayer(r)
Example: r = audiorecorder(8000,16,1); p = getplayer(r);

## audioread
Read a WAV audio file.
Syntax: [y, Fs] = audioread(filename)
Syntax: [y, Fs] = audioread(filename, [start finish], datatype)
Returns samples by channels. 'double' (default) scales to [-1, 1); 'native' keeps uint8, int16, int32 (24-bit data shifted left by 8) or single.
Example: f=[tempname(pwd) '.wav']; audiowrite(f, [0; 0.5], 8000); y=audioread(f); delete(f); y   % [0; 0.5]
Differences from MATLAB: Only WAV files (PCM 8/16/24/32-bit and 32/64-bit float); FLAC, Ogg and MPEG-4 are not supported yet.

## audiowrite
Write a WAV audio file.
Syntax: audiowrite(filename, y, Fs)
Syntax: audiowrite(filename, y, Fs, 'BitsPerSample', b, 'Title', t, 'Artist', a, 'Comment', c)
y is samples by channels (a row vector is one channel) of class uint8, int16, int32, single or double. BitsPerSample is 8, 16 (default), 24, 32 or 64; 32 and 64 write floating point (int32 data writes 32-bit integers). Floating-point data outside [-1, 1] is clipped with a warning.
Example: f=[tempname(pwd) '.wav']; audiowrite(f, [0; 1], 8000); y=audioread(f, 'native'); delete(f); y   % [0; 32767] int16
Differences from MATLAB: Only .wav files; .flac, .ogg, .m4a and .mp4 are not supported yet.

## audioinfo
Information about a WAV audio file.
Syntax: info = audioinfo(filename)
Returns Filename, CompressionMethod, NumChannels, SampleRate, TotalSamples, Duration, Title, Comment, Artist ([] when absent) and BitsPerSample.
Example: f=[tempname(pwd) '.wav']; audiowrite(f, zeros(8,2), 8000); i=audioinfo(f); delete(f); i.NumChannels   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: Only WAV files.

## fileattrib
Get or set file and folder attributes.
Syntax: [status, values, msgid] = fileattrib(name)
Syntax: [status, msg, msgid] = fileattrib(name, attribs, users)
values has Name, archive, system, hidden, directory and the User, Group and Other read/write/execute fields; name may end in a wildcard (a struct array). With no outputs and no attribs, the attributes are displayed; bare fileattrib queries the current folder. attribs such as '+w' or '-h' set or clear attributes: a, h, s, w on Windows, r, w, x (users u, g, o, a) elsewhere. With outputs, failures return status 0 and a message instead of an error.
Example: s=fileattrib(pwd)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: The recursive 's' option is not supported yet.

## bsxfun
Apply a two-input function with singleton expansion.
Syntax: C = bsxfun(fun, A, B)
fun must be a function handle. A dimension of size 1 in one input is repeated to match the other input. Handles to built-in functions such as @plus receive the expanded arrays at once; user functions and anonymous handles receive one column (or a column and a scalar) at a time.
Example: bsxfun(@plus, [1 2 3], [10; 20])   % [11 12 13; 21 22 23]
Differences from MATLAB: Two-dimensional arrays only.

## builtin
Call the built-in version of a function.
Syntax: [varargout] = builtin(name, args...)
name must name a function MATLAB implements as a built-in; toolbox M-files such as mean are rejected. A user function of the same name is skipped, so an overload can call the built-in.
Example: builtin('sum', [1 2 3])   % 6
Differences from MATLAB: none known for these forms.

## which
Locate a function or variable.
Syntax: s = which(name); c = which(name, '-all'); which name
Returns 'variable' for a workspace variable, the full path of a function file in the current folder or on the search path, built-in (...) for built-in functions and keywords, and '' when nothing is found. Called inside a file, a function in that file's private folder is found first (see addpath); at the Command Window private functions are not found. A package-qualified name (which pkg.fn) gives the file of that package, and a name on the import list gives the package file it stands for (see import).
Example: s = which('zz_nonexistent_fn')   % ''
Differences from MATLAB: Built-in and toolbox locations are reported under the MatRust installation folder; '-all' lists one location.

## what
List the MATLAB files in a folder.
Syntax: s = what; s = what(folder); what folder
Returns a struct with fields path, m, mlapp, mat, mex, mdl, slx, p, classes and packages; each list is a sorted column cell. A missing folder gives a 0x1 struct.
Example: w = what(pwd); class(w.m)   % cell
Differences from MATLAB: Folders are looked up from the current folder only, not on a search path.

## isobject
True for MATLAB objects.
Syntax: tf = isobject(A)
True for objects of classdef classes and for MException, onCleanup and inline objects; false for numbers, structs, cells and function handles.
Example: isobject(MException('a:b', 'c'))   % true
Differences from MATLAB: none known for these classes.

## ismethod
True if a name is a method of an object's class.
Syntax: tf = ismethod(obj, name)
obj may also be a class name such as 'containers.Map'. For a classdef class it is true for the public methods, the constructor included. Methods of numeric, logical and char values are the supported built-in functions.
Example: ismethod(inline('t'), 'formula')   % true
Differences from MATLAB: Method lists are fixed tables for inline, MException, containers.Map and the built-in value classes.

## methods
List the public methods of a class.
Syntax: methods(obj); methods('Name')
Syntax: names = methods(obj); names = methods('Name')
For an object of a classdef class, or the name of a class file in the Current Folder, returns the public methods sorted by character code (upper case before lower case), as a column cell. The constructor is included, also the default one of a class without a constructor. Without an output it prints "Methods for class Name:" and one name per line, indented four spaces, with a blank line before and after the heading. For inline, MException and containers.Map objects (or those class names) it lists their fixed method tables.
Example: m = methods('MException'); m{1}   % 'MException'
Differences from MATLAB: The listing prints one name per line. Other built-in classes such as double are not supported yet. The -full option is not supported.

## isprop
True if a name is a property of an object.
Syntax: tf = isprop(obj, name)
For an object of a classdef class (or the name of its class file) it is true for every property the class defines, whatever its access, Constant ones included, as GNU Octave answers. For a graphics handle it checks the documented properties of the handle's class (Line, Axes, Figure, ...) without regard to case, as get and set do; an array of handles gives one logical per handle. For MException and the other struct-backed language objects it checks their public properties.
Example: isprop(MException('a:b', 'c'), 'message')   % true
Example: h = plot(1:3); isprop(h, 'LineWidth')   % true
Differences from MATLAB: Other values (numbers, structs, cells, text that names no class file) report "isprop: this call form is not supported yet" where MATLAB answers false. Only scalar classdef objects.

## classdef
Define a value or handle class in a class file.
Syntax: classdef Name ... end
Syntax: classdef (Sealed) Name ... end
Syntax: classdef Name < handle ... end
Syntax: classdef Name < Super1 & Super2 ... end
Put the definition in Name.mr or Name.m in the Current Folder, as for a function file; comments and blank lines may come before classdef. Name(args) calls the constructor, the method named like the class, function obj = Name(args), where obj starts as the default object. A class without a constructor makes the default object from Name().
A file Pt.m with these lines:
    classdef Pt
      properties
        x = 0
        label = 'a'
      end
      properties (Constant)
        Origin = 0
      end
      methods
        function obj = Pt(x)
          if nargin > 0
            obj.x = x;
          end
        end
        function obj = shift(obj, d)
          obj.x = obj.x + d;
        end
      end
      methods (Static)
        function p = unit()
          p = Pt(1);
        end
      end
    end
lets you write p = Pt(3), p = p.shift(1), p = shift(p, 2), u = Pt.unit() and Pt.Origin.
Blocks: properties takes (Access, GetAccess or SetAccess = public, protected or private), (SetAccess = immutable), (Constant), (Dependent), (Hidden) and (Transient); each line is name, optional validation `(dims) class {validators}` and optional `= expression` default. Property validation converts class, checks size, and runs validators on defaults and on every property assignment (including constructor, indexed assignment `obj.P(i) = v`, and `set(obj, 'P', v)` for handle classes). All defaults, Constant or not, are evaluated in declaration order once per run, when the class is first loaded (the first Name(...), Name.Const, Name.method(...), methods('Name'), properties('Name') or use of an object from an earlier run, not at each construction), in a workspace with no variables; a default may call functions and read Name.Const of the same class. A default that makes a handle object gives every new object that same handle, as in MATLAB. methods takes (Static), (Access = ...) and (Abstract); every method ends with end (in a class folder a signature without a body names a method kept in its own file, see below). Local functions may follow the classdef end; only the class's methods see them.
Value objects: b = a; b.x = 1 leaves a unchanged, and a method must return the changed object (p = p.shift(1)). p.x, p.x(i), p.x.f and the same forms on the left of = read and assign properties. obj.method(args) and method(obj, args) call a method, and a class method wins over current-folder and path functions and builtins of that name (imported, local and private functions of the calling file come first, as in MATLAB); [a, b] = obj.method() takes several outputs, also when obj is an expression (s.p.method(), c{1}.method(), method(Pt(3)), method(make())), evaluated once. Inside a method, nargin and nargout count obj. Name.method(args) calls a Static method and Name.Const reads a Constant property.
Handle classes: classdef Name < handle makes a class whose objects carry identity. b = a copies the reference, so b.x = 1 changes a.x too, and a method changes the object without returning it (function move(obj, d) obj.x = obj.x + d; end, called as h.move(1)). a == b and a ~= b (eq, ne) compare identity; isequal(a, b) is true for the same object and for two objects of one class whose properties are all equal. delete(h) (or h.delete()) runs the class's delete method, then those of its superclasses, and invalidates every copy: isvalid(h) is then false, any property use errors "Invalid or deleted object." and the display reads "handle to deleted Name". An error inside a delete method becomes a warning and the object is deleted anyway. A delete method declared in methods (Access = private) can be called only by the class's own methods (protected: also by subclass methods); from elsewhere delete(h) and h.delete() both error "Cannot access private method 'delete' of class 'Name'." When the last reference to a handle object goes (cleared, overwritten, never stored), the object is freed silently at a statement boundary, reference cycles included; its delete method runs only on an explicit delete. isa(h, 'handle') is true; handle itself cannot be constructed. methods lists delete, eq, isvalid and ne for a handle class. A subclass of a handle class is a handle class.
Inheritance: classdef B < A, or classdef C < A & B for several superclasses (their class files in the same folder). The subclass has every property and method of its superclasses; its own properties come first in displays and listings, then each superclass's, left to right; a class reached through two superclasses (a common base) counts once. Method lookup takes the subclass's own method first, then the superclasses' in order; a method that two superclasses define differently and the subclass does not is ambiguous, and calling it errors "Method 'm' of class 'C' is ambiguous: the superclasses 'A' and 'B' both define it; define m in C to choose." (MATLAB rejects such a class when it is loaded; here the other methods stay usable). In a constructor, obj = obj@A(args) calls A's constructor on the object being built (for a handle class obj@A(args); alone is enough); superclasses whose constructor is not called that way get an implicit call without arguments first, left to right. In a method, m@A(obj, args) calls A's version of m (any method of the subclass may call it). Protected members can be used in the class and its subclasses; private ones only in the defining class, even on a subclass object. isa(obj, 'A') is true up the chain, superclasses(obj) or superclasses('Name') lists every superclass (depth first, left to right, handle last), and methods, properties and fieldnames include inherited members. A class cannot derive from both handle and value classes; a Sealed class cannot be subclassed ("class 'A' is Sealed and cannot be subclassed"); a superclass that is missing, not a class file, or the class itself (directly or through others) is an error naming the file and line. methods (Abstract) lists method signatures without bodies (r = area(obj), [a, b] = f(obj, x), or name); a class with an abstract method it does not implement, declared or inherited, cannot be constructed: "Cannot create an object of the abstract class 'Shape': it does not implement the abstract methods area." A subclass implementing them can.
Property get and set methods: function v = get.x(obj) runs for every read of obj.x and function obj = set.x(obj, v) for every assignment to it (in a handle class the set method needs no output), from outside and from other methods alike, the constructor included (defaults are stored without it); obj.x(i) = v reads through the get method, changes the value and passes it to the set method. Inside get.x and set.x themselves, obj.x reads and writes the stored value without calling them again. A set method of a value class must return the object. A Dependent property has no stored value: reading it needs a get method ("In class 'C', no get method is defined for Dependent property 'x'. A Dependent property needs a get method to access its value.") and assigning it a set method (the same text with set), which usually stores other properties; displays show its get value. get and set methods are written in a methods block without attributes, only for properties of the same class.
Other attributes: SetAccess = immutable properties can be set only by the defining class's constructor (not by methods it calls) and read as GetAccess says ("Cannot set immutable property 'id' of class 'B' outside the constructor of 'B'."); Hidden properties work as usual but are not listed by properties and fieldnames or shown by the display; Transient is accepted and has no effect until objects can be saved.
Private and protected members, a constructor declared in methods (Access = private) included, can be used only inside the class's methods (protected: also in subclasses); outside access fails with "Cannot access private property 'k' of class 'Pt'." and similar messages. A Constant property cannot be set. An unknown name gives "Unrecognized method, property, or field 'y' for class 'Pt'." (assignment: "Unrecognized property 'y' for class 'Pt'.").
Without a semicolon an object displays like this (loose format):
    p = 
    
      Pt with properties:
    
             x: 3
         label: 'a'
        Origin: 0
    
The public properties appear in declaration order, Constant ones included, formatted like struct fields: the names are right-aligned, as struct display does here (MATLAB's class display left-aligns them). disp(p) prints the text from the "Pt with properties:" line on. A class without public properties shows "  Pt with no properties.". A method named disp replaces the text, also when it is private: p = ... then prints the "p =" line, a blank line and what the method prints.
class(p) is 'Pt'; isa, isobject, properties, methods, isprop, ismethod, fieldnames (the public properties), isequal (same class and equal properties) and whos (Class column Pt) know the class. isstruct(p) is false. struct(p) returns every stored property, private ones included, as a struct and prints a one-line warning. An object has no struct fields: numfields(p) is 0, isfield(p, name) is false, getfield(p, 'x') and setfield(p, 'x', v) follow the property rules above (a private property or a Constant one fails as p.x does), and rmfield, orderfields and struct2cell are not defined for it. subsref(p, substruct('.', 'x')) and p = subsasgn(p, substruct('.', 'x'), v) read and assign like p.x and p.x = v, with the same rules; a '()' step after a method name passes its arguments (subsref(p, substruct('.', 'shift', '()', {1}))). subsasgn is available for these objects only.
Class folders: a folder named @Name directly inside the current folder, a search path folder or a package folder (+pkg/@Name is the class pkg.Name) holds the class file Name.m and, each in its own file, further methods: every other function file @Name/method.m is a method of the class, called as method(obj, ...) or obj.method(...), found before current-folder and path functions and builtins of that name when the first argument is an object of the class (an imported, local or private function of that name still comes first; obj.method(...) always calls the method), inherited by subclasses and listed by methods and ismethod. Such a method is public and not Static unless a methods block of the class file declares its signature without a body (r = method(obj, x) in methods (Static) or methods (Access = private)); a declaration without a body is accepted only in a class folder. The constructor and the get/set methods stay in the class file; a method defined both there and in its own file is an error naming both files. A folder @Name/private is visible to the class file and to the method files. Folders are searched in lookup order (current folder, then the path): when one folder holds both Name.m and @Name/Name.m the class folder wins, and otherwise the first folder with either wins, so a plain Name.m of the current folder comes before a class folder on the path. An object keeps its class: a later import of a class with the same name changes what Name(...) constructs, not the methods of existing objects. genpath leaves @ folders off the path. Method files are read when first called; a new or edited one is used from the next run. Old-style class folders, where @Name/Name.m is a function calling class(s, 'Name'), are not supported: Name(...) errors "Old-style @Name class folders (class() constructors) are not supported; use a classdef file."
Editing a class file takes effect on the next run, also for objects made earlier; inside one run the definition first loaded stays.
Example: iskeyword('classdef')   % true
Differences from MATLAB: Behaviour follows the MATLAB documentation; GNU Octave 10.3 confirms handle aliasing, isequal on handles, superclass constructor and method calls, protected access and get/set methods, and where it differs (Octave has no isvalid, superclasses or handle ==, resolves ambiguous inherited methods to the first superclass, runs delete methods when an object is freed and leaves an object usable after delete(obj) inside its own class) the documentation wins. Not supported yet (each reports an error naming the file and line): property listeners (SetObservable, GetObservable), and class attributes other than Sealed. Also not supported yet: overloading operators and functions other than disp (plus, eq, subsref, subsasgn, size, numel methods), object arrays ([a b], a(2)), old-style @folder classes, @folder methods for built-in classes (@double/f.m) and saving objects (save reports "objects of class 'Pt' cannot be saved yet"). A handle object's delete method does not run when the object is freed implicitly. A classdef typed in the console or in a script is rejected as before. With several outputs, a method named like a function or builtin wins for name(expr, ...) only when expr is a variable, a path into one (s.p, c{1}) or a constructor call; for another expression, such as a function's result, the function or builtin runs.

## isvalid
True for a handle object that has not been deleted.
Syntax: tf = isvalid(h)
For an object of a handle class (classdef Name < handle) it is false after delete(h), for every copy of the object. containers.Map and inputParser objects answer the same way.
Example: m = containers.Map; isvalid(m)   % true
Differences from MATLAB: Only scalar objects; a value-class object errors "Undefined function 'isvalid' for input arguments of type 'Name'.".

## superclasses
Names of the superclasses of a class.
Syntax: superclasses(obj); superclasses('Name')
Syntax: names = superclasses(obj); names = superclasses('Name')
For an object of a classdef class or the name of a class file in the Current Folder, every superclass, direct or not, depth first and left to right as the classdef line lists them, each once, handle last. Without an output it prints "Superclasses for class Name:" and one name per line; a class without superclasses prints "No superclasses for class Name". With an output, a column cell.
Example: c = superclasses('handle')   % {} (0x1)
Differences from MATLAB: Only classdef classes in the Current Folder and handle.

## events
Events of a handle class.
Syntax: events(obj); events('Name'); names = events(obj)
An events block in a handle class file names the events its objects can send:
    classdef Sensor < handle
      events
        Changed
      end
    end
Without an output it prints "Events for class Name:" and one event per line; with an output, a column cell. Inherited events are listed after the class's own. Only handle classes can define events.
Example: iskeyword('events')   % false
Differences from MATLAB: Event attributes (ListenAccess, NotifyAccess, Hidden) are accepted and not enforced.

## addlistener
Listen to an event of a handle object.
Syntax: lh = addlistener(obj, 'EventName', @callback)
After addlistener(s, 'Changed', @(src, evt) disp(src.Value)), every notify(s, 'Changed') calls the callback with the object and an event data struct with the fields Source and EventName. Listeners run in the order they were added and go away with the object.
Example: exist('addlistener')   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: The listener returned is a struct (Source, EventName, Callback, Enabled), not an event.listener object: deleting it or setting Enabled does not stop the callback. Property events (PreSet, PostSet) and the listener(...) function are not supported yet.

## notify
Send an event of a handle object to its listeners.
Syntax: notify(obj, 'EventName'); notify(obj, 'EventName', data)
Calls each listener of that event with the object and an event data struct with the fields Source and EventName; the fields of a scalar struct data are added to it. The event must be declared in an events block of the class or a superclass. An error in a callback is shown as a warning and the other listeners still run.
Example: exist('notify')   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: Event data is a struct; event.EventData subclasses are not supported yet.

## enumeration
Members of an enumeration class.
Syntax: enumeration('Name'); enumeration(obj); [m, names] = enumeration('Name')
An enumeration block lists the members, each optionally with constructor arguments:
    classdef Color
      properties
        R, G, B
      end
      methods
        function c = Color(r, g, b), c.R = r; c.G = g; c.B = b; end
      end
      enumeration
        Red (1, 0, 0)
        Blue (0, 0, 1)
      end
    end
Color.Red is the member: its properties read as usual, char(c) is 'Red', and c == Color.Red or c == 'Red' compare members. Without an output enumeration lists the member names; m holds the members and names their names as a column cell.
Example: iskeyword('enumeration')   % false
Differences from MATLAB: Object arrays are not supported yet, so m is a column cell of members rather than an array. Enumeration classes derived from numeric types (classdef C < int32) and handle enumeration classes are not supported yet.

## metaclass
Description of a class.
Syntax: mc = metaclass(obj)
For an object of a classdef class, a struct with the fields Name, Sealed, HandleCompatible, Enumeration, and the lists PropertyList, MethodList, EventList, EnumerationMemberList and SuperclassList (struct arrays with a Name field). For example, {mc.PropertyList.Name} lists the property names.
Example: exist('metaclass')   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: The result is a struct, not a meta.class object; the ?Name operator is not supported yet, so use metaclass on an object.

## handle
Base class of handle classes.
Syntax: classdef Name < handle ... end
Objects of a class derived from handle carry identity: copies refer to one object, == compares identity and delete invalidates every copy (see classdef). handle itself is abstract: handle() errors.
Example: iskeyword('classdef')   % true
Differences from MATLAB: The handle methods available are delete, eq, ne, isvalid, addlistener and notify; findobj, findprop and the ordering operators are not supported yet.

## iskeyword
True for MATLAB keywords.
Syntax: tf = iskeyword(s); list = iskeyword
Without an input it returns the 20 keywords as a column cell.
Example: iskeyword('for')   % true
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## genvarname
Construct a valid, unique variable name.
Syntax: name = genvarname(candidate); name = genvarname(candidate, protected)
Spaces are removed and the next letter capitalized, other invalid characters become 0xHH codes, an initial non-letter or a keyword gets an x prefix, and a number is appended until the name differs from protected names. A cell input gives a cell of mutually unique names.
Example: genvarname('my var')   % myVar
Differences from MATLAB: none known for these forms.

## namelengthmax
Maximum length of a MATLAB name.
Syntax: n = namelengthmax
Example: namelengthmax   % 63
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## clearvars
Clear selected workspace variables.
Syntax: clearvars v1 v2 ...; clearvars ... -except k1 k2 ...; clearvars -regexp pattern ...; clearvars -global ...
Names may contain * wildcards. -regexp makes the following names regular expressions; -except keeps matching variables; -global selects among all global variables, including those declared only inside functions, and clears their global values.
Example: a = 1; b = 2; clearvars a; exist('a')   % 0
Differences from MATLAB: none known for these forms.

## functions
Information about a function handle.
Syntax: s = functions(fh)
Named handles give fields function, type ('simple') and file. A handle made inside a file to one of its local functions has type 'scopedfunction', that file and parentage. Anonymous handles add workspace (a cell holding a struct of the captured variables) and within_file_path.
Example: s = functions(@(t) t + 1); s.type   % anonymous
Differences from MATLAB: Nested functions are not supported, so there are no 'nested' handles.

## localfunctions
Handles to the local functions of the running file.
Syntax: c = localfunctions
Inside a function file it returns a column cell of handles to the file's local functions in file order; elsewhere it returns {}.
Example: localfunctions   % {}
Differences from MATLAB: A handle made by localfunctions is resolved by name when it is called.

## dbstack
Show the stack of named function and script calls.
Syntax: st = dbstack; st = dbstack(n); st = dbstack('-completenames'); [st, k] = dbstack; dbstack
Returns a column struct array with fields file, name and line, innermost call first. The argument n skips that many frames. At the command line the stack is empty.
Example: numel(dbstack)   % 0
Differences from MATLAB: dbstack omits anonymous function frames.

## isequalwithequalnans
Equality that treats NaN values as equal.
Syntax: tf = isequalwithequalnans(A, B, ...)
The same as isequaln.
Example: isequalwithequalnans([1 NaN], [1 NaN])   % true
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## bitmax
Removed function; use flintmax.
Syntax: bitmax
Every call raises MATLAB's error "BITMAX has been removed. Use FLINTMAX instead."
Example: flintmax   % 9.0072e+15
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## inline
Construct an inline function object.
Syntax: f = inline(expr); f = inline(expr, arg1, arg2, ...); f = inline(expr, n)
Without names the arguments are the variables found in expr, in alphabetical order (x when there are none); n gives x, P1, ..., Pn. Call it as f(args) or feval(f, args); formula, argnames, char, vectorize and nargin inspect it.
Example: f = inline('t^2 + 1'); f(3)   % 10
Differences from MATLAB: Display inside cells and structs shows the underlying fields.

## argnames
Argument names of an inline function.
Syntax: c = argnames(f)
Example: argnames(inline('a*x + b'))   % {'a'; 'b'; 'x'}
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## formula
Expression of an inline function.
Syntax: s = formula(f)
Example: formula(inline('sin(t)'))   % sin(t)
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## mexext
MEX-file extension of the platform.
Syntax: ext = mexext; s = mexext('all')
mexext('all') returns a 1x4 struct with fields arch and ext.
Example: s = mexext('all'); s(4).ext   % mexw64
Differences from MATLAB: MatRust cannot load MEX files.

## maxNumCompThreads
Number of computational threads (deprecated).
Syntax: n = maxNumCompThreads; old = maxNumCompThreads(n); old = maxNumCompThreads('automatic')
Every call warns that the function will be removed. The query returns the stored setting, by default the number of processors.
Example: n = maxNumCompThreads;   % number of threads, with a deprecation warning
Differences from MATLAB: The setting is only stored; it does not change how many workers MatRust uses.

## usejava
True if a Java feature is available.
Syntax: tf = usejava(feature)
Example: usejava('jvm')   % false
Differences from MATLAB: MatRust has no Java, so every feature is false.

## isstudent
True for the MATLAB Student Version.
Syntax: tf = isstudent
Example: isstudent   % false
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## diary
Record command-window output in a file.
Syntax: diary filename; diary(filename); diary on; diary off; diary
Output is appended to the file while the diary is on; diary without arguments toggles it. get(0, 'Diary') and get(0, 'DiaryFile') report the state. A file that cannot be opened or written is an error and leaves the diary off.
Example: diary off; get(0, 'Diary')   % off
Differences from MATLAB: The commands typed are not recorded, only the output. Output captured by evalc is recorded too (MATLAB turns the diary off inside evalc).

## ode113
Solve nonstiff differential equations, variable order (Adams-Bashforth-Moulton PECE).
Syntax: [t, y] = ode113(@(t,y) -y, tspan, y0)
Syntax: [t, y] = ode113(@f, tspan, y0, options, p1, p2, ...)
Syntax: [t, y, te, ye, ie] = ode113(@f, tspan, y0, odeset('Events', @ev))
Syntax: sol = ode113(@f, tspan, y0)
Integrates dy/dt = f(t, y) with a variable-step, variable-order (1 to 12) Adams
predictor-corrector using modified divided differences and local extrapolation,
as described by Shampine and Gordon (1975) and Hairer, Norsett and Wanner (1993,
sections III.5 and III.7). Error estimates select the step size and order; steps,
statistics and numerical values can differ from MATLAB.
tspan = [t0 tf] returns the solver steps; a longer tspan returns y at exactly those
times, interpolated. Options from odeset: RelTol, AbsTol, NormControl, MaxStep,
InitialStep, Refine, Stats, Events, Mass. See odeset for event outputs and extra
arguments after options.
One output with a handle gives a solution structure for deval and odextend.
Example: [t, y] = ode113(@(t,y) -y, [0 1], 1); y(end)   % 0.3679
Differences from MATLAB: OutputFcn, OutputSel and NonNegative (including with
Mass) are supported. sol.idata keeps phi3d as a 2-D neq-by-(14*N) matrix.

## ode15s
Solve stiff differential equations and DAEs, variable order (NDF/BDF 1 to 5).
Syntax: [t, y] = ode15s(@f, tspan, y0)
Syntax: [t, y] = ode15s(@f, tspan, y0, odeset('Jacobian', J, 'Mass', M))
Syntax: [t, y, te, ye, ie] = ode15s(@f, tspan, y0, odeset('Events', @ev))
Syntax: [t, y] = ode15s(@f, tspan, y0, options, p1, p2, ...)
Syntax: sol = ode15s(@f, tspan, y0)
Uses the numerical differentiation formulas of Shampine and Reichelt (1997,
section 2), or backward differentiation formulas with odeset('BDF','on'),
of orders 1 through MaxOrder (at most 5). Backward differences provide error
estimates and polynomial interpolation; quasi-constant steps and order changes
control the error. A simplified Newton iteration reuses a finite-difference or
user Jacobian and its linear-system factors when possible. Mass may be a constant
matrix or a function M(t, y). Constant diagonal singular mass matrices support
index-1 DAEs, with consistent initial values obtained by solving the algebraic
constraints (Shampine, Reichelt and Kierzenka, 1999, sections 3–4).
Stats 'on' prints the six counters.
See odeset for event outputs and extra arguments after options.
Example: [t, y] = ode15s(@(t,y) [-y(1); -1000*y(2)], [0 1], [1; 1]); y(end, 1)   % approximately 0.368
Differences from MATLAB: adaptive steps, order choices, statistics and rounded
solution values can differ. Consistent initial conditions are computed only for
constant diagonal mass matrices. OutputFcn, OutputSel and NonNegative are
supported, except NonNegative with a Mass matrix stops with an error.

## ode23s
Solve stiff differential equations, low order (modified Rosenbrock 2(3)).
Syntax: [t, y] = ode23s(@f, tspan, y0)
Syntax: [t, y] = ode23s(@f, tspan, y0, odeset('Jacobian', @J, 'Mass', M))
Syntax: [t, y] = ode23s(@f, tspan, y0, options, p1, p2, ...)
Syntax: [t, y, te, ye, ie] = ode23s(@f, tspan, y0, odeset('Events', @eventFcn))
Syntax: sol = ode23s(@f, tspan, y0)
Modified Rosenbrock (2,3) pair of Shampine and Reichelt (1997), used as a W-method: each
step forms the Jacobian (numerical unless the Jacobian option is given), a finite-difference
df/dt and one LU factorization of M - h*d*J, d = 1/(2+sqrt(2)); the third stage gives the
error estimate and the solution has a quadratic continuous extension. The mass matrix must be
constant and nonsingular.
See odeset for event outputs and extra arguments after options.
Example: [t, y] = ode23s(@(t,y) -y, [0 1], 1); y(end)   % about 0.3677
Differences from MATLAB: the initial step and step-size controller are this implementation's
own, so steps, statistics and the last digits of solution values can differ.

## ode23t
Solve moderately stiff differential equations and DAEs (trapezoidal rule).
Syntax: [t, y] = ode23t(@f, tspan, y0)
Syntax: [t, y] = ode23t(@f, tspan, y0, odeset('Mass', M))
Syntax: [t, y] = ode23t(@f, tspan, y0, options, p1, p2, ...)
Syntax: [t, y, te, ye, ie] = ode23t(@f, tspan, y0, odeset('Events', @eventFcn))
Syntax: sol = ode23t(@f, tspan, y0)
The trapezoidal rule, solved for the scaled derivative h*y' by a simplified Newton iteration
whose Jacobian is refreshed only when the iteration fails to converge. The local error is
estimated from the difference between the corrector and an explicit second-order predictor
that uses the previous step's derivative (Milne's device); the solution between steps is the
cubic Hermite interpolant. Constant, singular diagonal or function mass matrices are accepted.
See odeset for event outputs and extra arguments after options.
Example: [t, y] = ode23t(@(t,y) -y, [0 1], 1); y(end)   % about 0.368
Differences from MATLAB: the error estimate, initial step and iteration-matrix updates are this
implementation's own, so steps, statistics and the last digits of solution values can differ.

## ode23tb
Solve stiff differential equations (TR-BDF2, implicit Runge-Kutta).
Syntax: [t, y] = ode23tb(@f, tspan, y0)
Syntax: [t, y] = ode23tb(@f, tspan, y0, odeset('Mass', @(t,y) M))
Syntax: [t, y] = ode23tb(@f, tspan, y0, options, p1, p2, ...)
Syntax: [t, y, te, ye, ie] = ode23tb(@f, tspan, y0, odeset('Events', @eventFcn))
Syntax: sol = ode23tb(@f, tspan, y0)
TR-BDF2 (Bank et al. 1985; Hosea and Shampine 1996): a trapezoidal stage to t + (2-sqrt(2))h
followed by a BDF2 stage, both solved with the same iteration matrix, and the error estimate of
the companion third-order formula. The solution between steps is the quadratic through the
step's three solution values. Constant or function mass matrices are accepted.
See odeset for event outputs and extra arguments after options.
Example: [t, y] = ode23tb(@(t,y) -y, [0 1], 1); y(end)   % about 0.3677
