Differences from MATLAB: the initial step and step-size controller are this implementation's
own, so steps, statistics and the last digits of solution values can differ.

## ode15i
Solve fully implicit differential equations f(t, y, y') = 0 (variable-order BDF).
Syntax: [t, y] = ode15i(@(t,y,yp) f, tspan, y0, yp0)
Syntax: [t, y] = ode15i(@f, tspan, y0, yp0, options, p1, p2, ...)
Syntax: [t, y, te, ye, ie] = ode15i(@f, tspan, y0, yp0, odeset('Events', @eventFcn))
Syntax: sol = ode15i(@f, tspan, y0, yp0)
Variable-order (1 to MaxOrder, at most 5) variable-coefficient backward differentiation
formulas for index-1 implicit equations, following Brenan, Campbell and Petzold (1996,
chapters 3 and 5) and the interpolation and initialisation mathematics of Shampine (2002).
Newton iterations use finite-difference Jacobians df/dy and df/dy'. Divided differences
control the step size and order. Use decic for consistent y0 and yp0. The interpolant
is the polynomial through the last k+1 solution points. An event callback can
take (t, y, yp) or declare the fixed input list (t, y) without the derivative.
Put any extra parameters after these inputs. See odeset for event outputs.
Example: [t, y] = ode15i(@(t,y,yp) yp + y, [0 1], 1, -1); y(end)   % approximately exp(-1)
Differences from MATLAB: values, steps, orders and statistics can differ.
Jacobian, NormControl 'on' and NonNegative options are not supported; OutputFcn
and OutputSel are supported.

## decic
Compute consistent initial conditions for ode15i.
Syntax: [y0new, yp0new] = decic(@f, t0, y0, fixed_y0, yp0, fixed_yp0)
Syntax: [y0new, yp0new, resnrm] = decic(@f, t0, y0, fixed_y0, yp0, fixed_yp0, options)
Adjusts the components of y0 and yp0 whose fixed flags are 0 so that f(t0, y0, yp0) = 0,
by damped Newton iterations with finite-difference Jacobians. Singular value decomposition
gives minimum-norm corrections in the free components (Golub and Van Loan, Matrix
Computations, 2013, section 5.5). Fixed components remain unchanged; failure to reduce
the residual reports a convergence error. At most numel(y0) components may be fixed.
Example: [y0, yp0] = decic(@(t,y,yp) yp + y, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0)   % y0 = 1, yp0 = -1
Differences from MATLAB: nonlinear iteration paths, the chosen consistent solution and
the final residual can differ.

## deval
Evaluate the solution of a differential equation.
Syntax: sxint = deval(sol, xint)
Syntax: sxint = deval(sol, xint, idx)
Syntax: [sxint, spxint] = deval(sol, xint)
Syntax: sxint = deval(xint, sol)
Evaluates a solution structure from ode45, ode23, ode113, ode15s, ode23s, ode23t,
ode23tb, ode15i, bvp4c, bvp5c, dde23 or ddesd at the points xint with the solver's own
interpolant. Each column of sxint is the solution at one point; idx selects components.
The second output is the derivative.
Example: sol = ode45(@(t,y) -y, [0 1], 1); deval(sol, 0.5)   % 0.6065
Differences from MATLAB: error messages leave the argument name blank, as MATLAB does
inside evalc. The derivative of the stiff and ode113 interpolants is a central difference.

## odextend
Extend the solution of an initial value problem.
Syntax: solext = odextend(sol, odefun, tfinal)
Syntax: solext = odextend(sol, [], tfinal, yinit, options)
Continues the integration of sol from sol.x(end) to tfinal with the same solver (a new
odefun, initial values or options may be given) and returns the joined solution.
Example: sol = ode45(@(t,y) -y, [0 1], 1); sol2 = odextend(sol, [], 2); deval(sol2, 2)   % 0.1353
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## bvpinit
Form the initial guess for bvp4c and bvp5c.
Syntax: solinit = bvpinit(x, yinit)
Syntax: solinit = bvpinit(x, @guess, parameters)
x is the initial mesh (monotonic, repeated points allowed); yinit is a constant vector or
a function returning the guess at a mesh point. Returns a structure with fields solver,
x, y, parameters (when given) and yinit.
Example: s = bvpinit([0 0.5 1], [1 2]); s.y   % [1 1 1; 2 2 2]
Differences from MATLAB: extending a previous solution (bvpinit(sol, ...)) is not
supported yet; use bvpxtend.

## bvpset
Create or alter options for bvp4c and bvp5c.
Syntax: options = bvpset('name1', value1, ...)
Syntax: options = bvpset(oldopts, 'name1', value1, ...)
Syntax: options = bvpset(oldopts, newopts)
Fields: AbsTol, RelTol, SingularTerm, FJacobian, BCJacobian, Stats, Nmax, Vectorized.
Names match by case-insensitive unique prefix; unset fields are [].
Example: o = bvpset('RelTol', 1e-4); o.RelTol   % 1.0000e-04
Differences from MATLAB: bvpset with no arguments does not print the property list.

## bvpget
Get an option from a bvpset structure.
Syntax: v = bvpget(options, 'name')
Syntax: v = bvpget(options, 'name', default)
Returns the field, or the default (or []) when it is unset.
Example: bvpget(bvpset('RelTol', 1e-4), 'AbsTol', 1e-7)   % 1.0000e-07
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## bvp4c
Solve boundary value problems (3-stage Lobatto IIIa collocation).
Syntax: sol = bvp4c(@odefun, @bcfun, solinit)
Syntax: sol = bvp4c(@odefun, @bcfun, solinit, options, p1, p2, ...)
The three-stage Lobatto IIIA method of Kierzenka and Shampine (2001) uses a C1
cubic collocated at the endpoints and midpoint of each interval. Damped Newton
iterations solve the collocation and boundary equations together. Five-point
Lobatto quadrature estimates each subinterval's L2 norm of the ODE residual,
scaled by max(abs(odefun), AbsTol/RelTol), for mesh refinement. Unknown parameters come from
solinit.parameters (odefun(x,y,p), bcfun(ya,yb,p)). sol has fields solver, x, y, yp,
parameters (if any) and stats; deval evaluates the cubic and its derivative.
Example: sol = bvp4c(@(x,y) [y(2); -y(1)], @(a,b) [a(1); b(1)-1], bvpinit(linspace(0,pi/2,5), [0 0])); deval(sol, 1)   % [0.8414; 0.5403]
Differences from MATLAB: mesh selection, stopping tests, residual estimates, values
and evaluation counts can differ. The dense pivoted LU solve allows at most 3000
unknowns. Multipoint problems and SingularTerm are not supported.

## bvp5c
Solve boundary value problems (4-stage Lobatto IIIa collocation).
Syntax: sol = bvp5c(@odefun, @bcfun, solinit)
Syntax: sol = bvp5c(@odefun, @bcfun, solinit, options)
The four-stage Lobatto IIIA method of Kierzenka and Shampine (2008, sections 2–3)
collocates a quartic at the four Lobatto points of each interval. Damped Newton
iterations solve for mesh values, interior stages and any unknown parameters.
The mesh is refined using the sampled ODE residual multiplied by interval length
and scaled relative to local solution magnitudes with RelTol and AbsTol. This
controls the error asymptotically for smooth, well-conditioned problems. sol has
fields solver, x, y, idata, parameters (if any) and stats (maxerr, the scaled
residual estimate); deval evaluates the quartic and its derivative.
Example: sol = bvp5c(@(x,y) [y(2); -y(1)], @(a,b) [a(1); b(1)-1], bvpinit(linspace(0,pi/2,5), [0 0])); deval(sol, 1)   % [0.8415; 0.5403]
Differences from MATLAB: mesh selection, stopping tests, error estimates, values
and evaluation counts can differ. The dense solve has the same 3000-unknown
limit as bvp4c, including interior stages. Multipoint problems and SingularTerm
are not supported.

## bvpxtend
Extend a boundary value solution to a longer interval.
Syntax: solinit = bvpxtend(sol, xnew)
Syntax: solinit = bvpxtend(sol, xnew, ynew)
Syntax: solinit = bvpxtend(sol, xnew, 'constant' | 'linear' | 'solution')
Adds the point xnew before or after the mesh with ynew, or with the end value
('constant', the default), a linear extrapolation using the end slope, or the last
interval's cubic extrapolated ('solution').
Example: sol = bvp4c(@(x,y) [y(2); -y(1)], @(a,b) [a(1); b(1)-1], bvpinit(linspace(0,pi/2,5), [0 0])); s = bvpxtend(sol, 2); s.x(end)   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## dde23
Solve delay differential equations with constant delays.
Syntax: sol = dde23(@(t,y,Z) f, lags, history, tspan)
Syntax: sol = dde23(@f, lags, @history, tspan, options)
Uses the Bogacki-Shampine 2(3) pair with cubic Hermite history, following Shampine
and Thompson, "Solving DDEs in MATLAB" (2001), sections 2 and 4-7. Potential
discontinuities from initial history jumps and Jumps are propagated through three
delay additions and included in the mesh. A continuous restart from a previous
solution does not introduce a new initial jump. Steps longer than a delay use bounded fixed-point
iteration; unsuccessful steps are reduced. history is a constant vector, a
function of t, or a previous solution. Z(:,j) is y(t - lags(j)). sol has fields
solver, history, discont, x, y, stats and yp (and xe, ye, ie with Events).
Example: sol = dde23(@(t,y,Z) -Z, 1, 1, [0 2]); deval(sol, 2)   % -0.5000
Differences from MATLAB: step sizes, statistics and last-digit rounding can differ;
NormControl and OutputFcn are not supported.

## ddesd
Solve delay differential equations with general delays.
Syntax: sol = ddesd(@(t,y,Z) f, @(t,y) d, history, tspan)
Syntax: sol = ddesd(@f, lags, history, tspan, options)
The delays are a function returning the delayed times d(t, y) <= t, or constant lags.
Uses classical four-stage Runge-Kutta steps and a cubic Hermite interpolant with
sampled residual control, following the approach of Shampine, "Solving ODEs and
DDEs with residual control" (2005), sections 2.1 and 3. The residual compares the
interpolant's derivative with the differential equation at interior points.
Short delays use bounded fixed-point iteration. sol has fields solver, history,
x, y, stats and yp
(and xe, ye, ie with Events).
Example: sol = ddesd(@(t,y,Z) -Z, @(t,y) t - 1, 1, [0 2]); deval(sol, 1.5)   % -0.3750
Differences from MATLAB: residual sampling, step sizes, statistics and numerical
results can differ.

## ddeset
Create or alter options for dde23 and ddesd.
Syntax: options = ddeset('name1', value1, ...)
Syntax: options = ddeset(oldopts, 'name1', value1, ...)
Fields: AbsTol, Events, InitialStep, InitialY, Jumps, MaxStep, NormControl, OutputFcn,
OutputSel, Refine, RelTol, Stats. Names match by case-insensitive unique prefix.
Example: o = ddeset('RelTol', 1e-4); o.RelTol   % 1.0000e-04
Differences from MATLAB: ddeset with no arguments does not print the property list.

## ddeget
Get an option from a ddeset structure.
Syntax: v = ddeget(options, 'name')
Syntax: v = ddeget(options, 'name', default)
Returns the field, or the default (or []) when it is unset.
Example: ddeget(ddeset('RelTol', 1e-4), 'RelTol')   % 1.0000e-04

## fftn
N-dimensional discrete Fourier transform of a vector or matrix.
Syntax: Y = fftn(X)
Syntax: Y = fftn(X, [m n])
Transforms along both dimensions. A size vector pads with zeros or truncates first. Real input gives the Hermitian result of a real-to-complex transform; a result whose imaginary parts are all zero is real. Single input gives a single result.
Example: fftn([1 2; 3 4])   % [10 -2; -4 0]
Differences from MATLAB: MatRust has no N-D arrays: a size vector may not have entries other than 1 beyond the second. Integer input is rejected as in MATLAB. Lengths up to 4 reproduce MATLAB's rounding; longer dimensions use MatRust's fft, whose last-digit rounding is not FFTW's.

## ifftn
N-dimensional inverse discrete Fourier transform of a vector or matrix.
Syntax: X = ifftn(Y)
Syntax: X = ifftn(Y, [m n])
Syntax: X = ifftn(..., 'symmetric')
Transforms back along both dimensions and divides by the number of elements. Conjugate-symmetric input, or the 'symmetric' flag, gives a real result.
Example: ifftn([10 -2; -4 0])   % [1 2; 3 4]
Differences from MATLAB: Two-dimensional arrays only (no N-D arrays). 'symmetric' reads the first half of the spectrum (along dimension 1, or along the length of a vector) and rebuilds the rest by conjugate symmetry, as the MATLAB documentation describes.

## convn
N-dimensional convolution of vectors and matrices.
Syntax: C = convn(A, B)
Syntax: C = convn(A, B, shape)
shape is 'full' (default), 'same' or 'valid', as for conv2. An empty B gives zeros the size of A.
Example: convn([1 2 3], [1 1])   % [1 3 5 3]
Differences from MATLAB: Two-dimensional arrays only (no N-D arrays).

## flow
Generate the sample scalar flow volume and its coordinate grids.
Syntax: V = flow(n)
Syntax: [X, Y, Z, V] = flow(n)
The default n is 25. The generated grid has n rows, 2*n columns and n pages.
Example: size(flow(4))   % [4 8 4]

## smooth3
Smooth a three-dimensional volume with a box or Gaussian kernel.
Syntax: W = smooth3(V, method, size, sd)
The default method is 'box', size is 3 and Gaussian standard deviation is 0.65. Method names are case-insensitive. Borders are replicated. Single input returns single output.
Example: size(smooth3(ones(3, 3, 3)))   % [3 3 3]

## reducevolume
Retain regularly spaced samples of a volume.
Syntax: W = reducevolume(V, R)
Syntax: [X, Y, Z, W] = reducevolume(X, Y, Z, V, R)
R is a positive integer scalar or [Rx Ry Rz]. The sampled arrays retain their input classes.
Example: size(reducevolume(ones(4, 4, 4), 2))   % [2 2 2]

## subvolume
Extract a rectangular region from a volume.
Syntax: W = subvolume(V, limits)
Syntax: [X, Y, Z, W] = subvolume(X, Y, Z, V, limits)
Limits are [xmin xmax ymin ymax zmin zmax]; NaN leaves a bound unrestricted. The extracted arrays retain their input classes.
Example: size(subvolume(ones(4, 4, 4), [1 2 1 2 1 2]))   % [2 2 2]

## volumebounds
Return coordinate and color limits for a volume.
Syntax: limits = volumebounds(V)
Syntax: limits = volumebounds(X, Y, Z, V)
Example: volumebounds(ones(2, 3, 4))   % [1 3 1 2 1 4 1 1]

## interp3
Interpolate three-dimensional gridded data in meshgrid layout.
Syntax: Vq = interp3(V, Xq, Yq, Zq)
Syntax: Vq = interp3(X, Y, Z, V, Xq, Yq, Zq, method, extrapval)
Methods are 'linear', 'nearest', 'cubic' and 'spline'. Method names are case-insensitive and accept a leading '*'. Nearest selects the higher grid point at a tie. Cubic uses cubic convolution on uniform grids and spline uses a not-a-knot spline. Outside points return NaN unless extrapval is given. Single V returns single values.
Example: interp3(ones(3, 3, 3), 1.5, 1.5, 1.5)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: Grids must be increasing. Cubic uses a spline on nonuniform grids and supports two-point axes. Queries must have equal sizes. Spline uses the same outside fill as the other methods.

## interpn
Interpolation on a one- or two-dimensional grid in ndgrid layout.
Syntax: Vq = interpn(X, V, Xq)
Syntax: Vq = interpn(X1, X2, V, Y1, Y2)
Syntax: Vq = interpn(V, Y1, Y2)
Syntax: Vq = interpn(V, ntimes)
Syntax: Vq = interpn(..., method, extrapval)
method is 'linear' (default), 'nearest', 'cubic', 'spline' or 'pchip'. Points outside the grid get extrapval (NaN by default). interpn(V, ntimes) refines the grid ntimes times between the points (once when ntimes is omitted). Query arrays of different shapes that are vectors are expanded as grid vectors.
Example: interpn([1 2 3], [10 20 30], 2.5)   % 25
Example: interpn(magic(3), 1.5, 2.5)   % 4.7500
Differences from MATLAB: One- and two-dimensional grids only (no N-D arrays). 'cubic' on a non-uniform grid uses 'spline' (not checked against MATLAB).

## griddata
Interpolate scattered two-dimensional data.
Syntax: vq = griddata(x, y, v, xq, yq)
Syntax: vq = griddata(x, y, v, xq, yq, method)
Syntax: [xq, yq, vq] = griddata(...)
method is 'linear' (default), 'nearest', 'natural', 'cubic' or 'v4'. A row xq with a column yq is expanded to a grid. Duplicate points are merged and their values averaged, with a warning. Query points outside the convex hull give NaN, except with 'v4'. 'cubic' is C1 (smooth across triangle edges) and reproduces linear data exactly.
Example: griddata([0 1 1 0 0.5], [0 0 1 1 0.5], [0 1 2 1 0.75], 0.25, 0.75)   % 0.8750
Example: griddata([0 1 1 0 0.5], [0 0 1 1 0.5], [1 3 6 4 3.5], 0.25, 0.75, 'cubic')   % 3.7500
Differences from MATLAB: 'cubic' is a Clough-Tocher interpolant with minimum norm network gradient estimates (Nielson, Renka and Cline). MATLAB's own gradient estimate is not identified, so results can differ from MATLAB's in the third decimal place. The three-dimensional form griddata(x, y, z, v, xq, yq, zq) is not supported.

## griddatan
Interpolate scattered data given as rows of points.
Syntax: yi = griddatan(X, y, XI)
Syntax: yi = griddatan(X, y, XI, method)
method is 'linear' (default) or 'nearest'. Linear interpolation outside the convex hull gives NaN.
Example: griddatan([0 0; 1 0; 0 1], [1; 2; 3], [0.2 0.2])   % 1.6000
Differences from MATLAB: Two-column (two-dimensional) points only.

## delaunay
Delaunay triangulation of two-dimensional points.
Syntax: T = delaunay(x, y)
Syntax: T = delaunay(P)
Each row of T holds the indices of one triangle, counter-clockwise. Duplicate points are used once. Four co-circular points are split as MATLAB splits them.
Example: delaunay([0 1 0], [0 0 1])   % [1 2 3]
Differences from MATLAB: The rows come in a different order, and start at a different vertex, than MATLAB's; the set of triangles and their orientation match MATLAB. Three-dimensional points are not supported.

## delaunayn
Delaunay triangulation of points given as rows.
Syntax: T = delaunayn(X)
Syntax: T = delaunayn(X, options)
X has one or two columns. Qhull options are accepted and ignored. Three collinear points give the single row [1 2 3], as in MATLAB.
Example: delaunayn([0 0; 1 0; 0 1])   % [1 2 3]
Differences from MATLAB: Points in three or more dimensions are not supported. Rows are ordered by their vertex indices; MATLAB's Qhull order can differ, with the same triangles.

## convhull
Convex hull of two- or three-dimensional points.
Syntax: K = convhull(x, y)
Syntax: K = convhull(P)
Syntax: [K, A] = convhull(..., 'simplify', tf)
Syntax: [K, V] = convhull(x, y, z)
For two-dimensional points K lists the hull points counter-clockwise as a closed column, starting at the smallest index. Points on hull edges are kept unless 'simplify' is true. A is the enclosed area. For three-dimensional points (x, y, z or a three-column P) each row of K is one triangle of the hull surface, counter-clockwise seen from outside, and V is the enclosed volume. A flat face is split into triangles on its corners; duplicate points and points on faces or edges are not used.
Example: convhull([0 1 1 0 0.5], [0 0 1 1 0.5])'   % [1 2 3 4 1]
Example: [K, V] = convhull([0 0 0; 1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 1; 0.2 0.2 0.2])   % K = [1 2 4; 1 3 2; 1 4 3; 2 3 4], V = 0.1667
Differences from MATLAB: For three-dimensional points the rows are ordered by their vertex indices and a flat face can be split along other diagonals than MATLAB's. Points on faces and edges are left out with or without 'simplify'. A point closer to a face than about 1e-13 times the largest coordinate counts as on it; points that are coplanar within that distance are refused.

## convhulln
Convex hull of points given as rows.
Syntax: K = convhulln(X)
Syntax: [K, V] = convhulln(X, options)
For two-column X each row of K is one hull edge, counter-clockwise from the smallest index; points on hull edges are left out. V is the enclosed area. For three-column X each row of K is one triangle of the hull surface, counter-clockwise seen from outside, and V is the enclosed volume, as for convhull. Qhull options are accepted and ignored.
Example: convhulln([0 0; 1 0; 1 1; 0 1])   % [1 2; 2 3; 3 4; 4 1]
Example: [K, V] = convhulln([0 0 0; 1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 1])   % K = [1 2 4; 1 3 2; 1 4 3; 2 3 4], V = 0.1667
Differences from MATLAB: Points in four or more dimensions are not supported. Every triangle of a three-dimensional hull is oriented outward and the rows are ordered by their vertex indices; MATLAB lists Qhull's facets in Qhull's order and orientation. A flat face can be split along other diagonals.

## dsearchn
Nearest data point to each query point.
Syntax: k = dsearchn(X, XI)
Syntax: [k, d] = dsearchn(X, T, XI)
Syntax: k = dsearchn(X, T, XI, outval)
k holds the row of X nearest to each row of XI and d the distance. With a triangulation T and outval, query points outside the triangulation get outval.
Example: dsearchn([0 0; 1 0; 0 1], [0.9 0.2])   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: Exact ties go to the first point without a triangulation and to the last with one, matching MATLAB.

## tsearchn
Enclosing simplex of each query point.
Syntax: [t, p] = tsearchn(X, T, XI)
t holds the first row of T whose simplex contains each row of XI (NaN outside) and p its barycentric coordinates.
Example: tsearchn([0 0; 1 0; 0 1], [1 2 3], [0.25 0.25])   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: none known for these forms.

## delaunayTriangulation
Create a two-dimensional Delaunay triangulation object.
Syntax: DT = delaunayTriangulation(P)
Syntax: DT = delaunayTriangulation(x, y)
Points stores the unique sites in first-occurrence order. ConnectivityList stores one triangle per row as indices into Points. Constraints is empty. Use DT(i,j) to index the connectivity list and size(DT) to get its dimensions. Only unconstrained 2-D inputs are supported.
Example: DT = delaunayTriangulation([0 0; 1 0; 0 1]); DT.ConnectivityList

## pointLocation
Find the triangle containing each query point.
Syntax: [ID, B] = pointLocation(DT, Q)
Each row of Q contains an x and y coordinate. ID indexes the rows of DT.ConnectivityList. B contains the barycentric weights in that row's vertex order. Outside points return NaN in both outputs.
Example: DT = delaunayTriangulation([0 0; 1 0; 0 1]); [id, b] = pointLocation(DT, [0.25 0.25])

## nearestNeighbor
Find the closest triangulation vertex to each query point.
Syntax: [ID, D] = nearestNeighbor(DT, Q)
Each row of Q contains an x and y coordinate. ID indexes the rows of DT.Points and D contains Euclidean distances.
Example: DT = delaunayTriangulation([0 0; 1 0; 0 1]); [id, d] = nearestNeighbor(DT, [0.1 0.2])

## edges
List the unique edges of a Delaunay triangulation.
Syntax: E = edges(DT)
Each row of E contains two indices into DT.Points.
Example: DT = delaunayTriangulation([0 0; 1 0; 0 1]); edges(DT)

## neighbors
Find the neighboring triangles of a Delaunay triangulation.
Syntax: N = neighbors(DT)
N(i,j) gives the triangle across the edge opposite vertex j of triangle i. Boundary edges have NaN neighbors.
Example: DT = delaunayTriangulation([0 0; 1 0; 1 1; 0 1]); neighbors(DT)

## convexHull
Find the boundary of a Delaunay triangulation.
Syntax: K = convexHull(DT)
Syntax: [K, A] = convexHull(DT)
K is a closed counterclockwise sequence of indices into DT.Points and A is the enclosed area.
Example: DT = delaunayTriangulation([0 0; 1 0; 0 1]); [k, a] = convexHull(DT)

## vertexAttachments
List the triangles attached to each vertex of a Delaunay triangulation.
Syntax: C = vertexAttachments(DT)
C is a column cell array with one cell per point. Cell i is a row of ascending indices into DT.ConnectivityList for the triangles that use point i.
Example: DT = delaunayTriangulation([0 0; 4 0; 1 3; 1.5 1]); C = vertexAttachments(DT)

## voronoi
Plot the input sites and finite edges of their two-dimensional Voronoi diagram.
Syntax: voronoi(x, y)
Syntax: H = voronoi(x, y)
Syntax: [VX, VY] = voronoi(x, y)
H contains the handles for the point markers and edge lines. With two outputs, each column of VX and VY gives the two endpoints of an edge and no figure is created.
Example: voronoi([0 1 1 0 0.5], [0 0 1 1 0.5])
Example: [vx, vy] = voronoi([0 1 1 0 0.5], [0 0 1 1 0.5])

## voronoin
Voronoi diagram of two-dimensional points.
Syntax: [V, C] = voronoin(X)
Syntax: [V, C] = voronoin(X, options)
V starts with a point at infinity, then holds the circumcentres of the Delaunay triangles. C{i} lists the vertices of the cell of point i; unbounded cells include 1. Qhull options are accepted and ignored.
Example: [v, c] = voronoin([0 0; 2 0; 1 2; 1 0.7]); c{4}   % [4 2 3]
Differences from MATLAB: Points in three or more dimensions are not supported. Vertex order follows the checked cases; it is not checked against Qhull for unbounded cells with more than two finite vertices.

## quad2d
Numerically integrate over a planar region.
Syntax: q = quad2d(fun, a, b, c, d)
Syntax: [q, errbnd] = quad2d(fun, a, b, c, d, name, value, ...)
fun(x, y) must accept arrays. c and d are numbers or functions of x. Options are 'AbsTol' (1e-10), 'RelTol' (1e-6), 'MaxFunEvals' (2000), 'Singular' (true) and 'FailurePlot' (ignored).
Example: quad2d(@(x, y) x.*y, 0, 1, 0, 1)   % 0.2500
Differences from MATLAB: The last digits of the tiled sum can differ from MATLAB's. Complex integrands are not supported yet. Reaching MaxFunEvals gives no warning, as in MATLAB.

## quadl
Numerically integrate with adaptive Gauss-Lobatto quadrature.
Syntax: q = quadl(fun, a, b)
Syntax: [q, fcnt] = quadl(fun, a, b, tol, trace, p1, p2, ...)
fun must accept a vector and return a vector of the same length. tol defaults to 1e-6; extra arguments are passed to fun.
Example: quadl(@(t) exp(t), 0, 1)   % 1.7183
Differences from MATLAB: The trace argument is ignored. Complex integrands are not supported yet.

## quadv
Vectorized adaptive Simpson quadrature of an array-valued function.
Syntax: Q = quadv(fun, a, b)
Syntax: [Q, fcnt] = quadv(fun, a, b, tol, trace, p1, p2, ...)
fun is called with one scalar at a time and may return an array of any fixed size.
Example: quadv(@(t) [t t.^2], 0, 1)   % [0.5000 0.3333]
Differences from MATLAB: The trace argument is ignored. Complex integrands are not supported yet.

## freqspace
Frequency spacing for frequency responses.
Syntax: f = freqspace(n)
Syntax: f = freqspace(n, 'whole')
Syntax: [f1, f2] = freqspace(n)
Syntax: [x1, y1] = freqspace(n, 'meshgrid')
One output gives n/2+1 points from 0 to 1 ('whole': n points from 0 up to 2). Two outputs give centred two-dimensional frequencies; n may be [rows cols].
Example: freqspace(4)   % [0 0.5000 1.0000]
Differences from MATLAB: none known for these forms.

## iqr
Interquartile range.
Syntax: r = iqr(X)
Syntax: r = iqr(X, dim)
The difference of the 75th and 25th percentiles (midpoint rule, as prctile). NaN values are ignored; iqr([]) is NaN.
Example: iqr([1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8])   % 4
Differences from MATLAB: Two-dimensional arrays only (no N-D arrays).

## eigs
A few eigenvalues and eigenvectors.
Syntax: d = eigs(A)
Syntax: d = eigs(A, k)
Syntax: d = eigs(A, k, sigma)
Syntax: d = eigs(A, k, sigma, opts)
Syntax: [V, D, flag] = eigs(A, B, k, sigma, opts)
Returns the k (default 6) eigenvalues selected by sigma: 'lm' (default), 'sm', 'la', 'sa', 'lr', 'sr', 'li', 'si', 'be' or a number (closest to it). flag is 0 when the eigenvalues were found.
Example: eigs(diag(1:10), 2)   % [10; 9]
Differences from MATLAB: Computed with a dense eigensolver instead of ARPACK, so results agree with MATLAB to about 1e-12 relative, not to every digit. Sparse input is not supported.

## svds
A few singular values and vectors.
Syntax: s = svds(A)
Syntax: s = svds(A, k)
Syntax: s = svds(A, k, sigma)
Syntax: [U, S, V, flag] = svds(A, k, sigma, opts)
Returns the k (default 6) largest singular values, or those nearest sigma (0 gives the smallest).
Example: svds(diag([3 1 2]), 1)   % 3
Differences from MATLAB: Computed densely, so results agree with MATLAB to about 1e-12 relative, not to every digit. Sparse input is not supported.

## condeig
Condition numbers of eigenvalues.
Syntax: c = condeig(A)
Syntax: [V, D, c] = condeig(A)
c(k) is 1/|cos| of the angle between the left and right eigenvectors of the k-th eigenvalue.
Example: condeig([1 2; 0 3])   % [1.4142; 1.4142]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digit.

## funm
Evaluate a general matrix function.
Syntax: F = funm(A, fun)
Syntax: F = funm(A, fun, options)
Syntax: [F, exitflag, output] = funm(...)
Uses the Schur-Parlett algorithm. fun is a handle such as @exp, @log, @sin, @cos, @sinh, @cosh, or a function fun(x, k) returning the k-th derivative. options may set TolBlk, TolTay, MaxTerms, MaxSqrt and Ord. MaxTerms must be an integer from 1 to 1000000; nonempty Ord must have one integer label in 1:n per eigenvalue. MaxSqrt is accepted for compatibility and has no effect, because every atomic block is evaluated with a Taylor series. output has fields terms, ind, ord and T.
Example: funm([1 0; 0 2], @exp)   % [2.7183 0; 0 7.3891]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digit.

## polyeig
Polynomial eigenvalue problem.
Syntax: e = polyeig(A0, A1, ..., Ap)
Syntax: [X, e] = polyeig(A0, A1, ..., Ap)
Syntax: [X, e, s] = polyeig(A0, A1, ..., Ap)
Solves (A0 + lambda*A1 + ... + lambda^p*Ap)*x = 0 through its companion linearisation. X has unit-norm columns; s holds the eigenvalue condition numbers.
Example: polyeig(-6, 11, -6, 1)   % [1; 2; 3]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digits, and eigenvectors can differ by a complex phase.

## qz
Generalized Schur (QZ) factorization.
Syntax: [AA, BB, Q, Z] = qz(A, B)
Syntax: [AA, BB, Q, Z, V, W] = qz(A, B, flag)
Q*A*Z = AA and Q*B*Z = BB with AA, BB upper triangular (quasi-triangular for flag 'real'). flag is 'complex' (default) or 'real'. V and W hold the right and left generalized eigenvectors.
Example: [AA, BB] = qz([1 2; 3 4], eye(2)); x = diag(AA)'   % [-0.3723 5.3723]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digit.

## ordschur
Reorder eigenvalues in a Schur factorization.
Syntax: [US, TS] = ordschur(U, T, select)
Syntax: [US, TS] = ordschur(U, T, keyword)
Syntax: [US, TS] = ordschur(U, T, clusters)
Moves the selected eigenvalues to the leading block. keyword is 'lhp', 'rhp', 'udi' or 'udo'; clusters gives a cluster index per eigenvalue (higher first).
Example: [U, T] = schur([1 2; 0 3]); [US, TS] = ordschur(U, T, [0 1]); x = diag(TS)'   % [3 1]
Differences from MATLAB: Results depend on schur, whose output can differ from MATLAB's in sign or the last digit.

## ordeig
Eigenvalues of a quasi-triangular matrix in their diagonal order.
Syntax: e = ordeig(T)
Syntax: e = ordeig(AA, BB)
Reads the eigenvalues from the 1x1 and 2x2 diagonal blocks, in order.
Example: ordeig([1 2; 0 3])'   % [1 3]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digit.

## ordqz
Reorder eigenvalues in a QZ factorization.
Syntax: [AAS, BBS, QS, ZS] = ordqz(AA, BB, Q, Z, select)
Syntax: [AAS, BBS, QS, ZS] = ordqz(AA, BB, Q, Z, keyword)
Syntax: [AAS, BBS, QS, ZS] = ordqz(AA, BB, Q, Z, clusters)
Moves the selected generalized eigenvalues to the leading block; keyword is 'lhp', 'rhp', 'udi' or 'udo'.
Example: [AA, BB, Q, Z] = qz([1 2; 0 -3], eye(2)); [AAS, BBS] = ordqz(AA, BB, Q, Z, 'lhp'); x = ordeig(AAS, BBS)'   % [-3 1]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digit.

## gsvd
Generalized singular value decomposition.
Syntax: sigma = gsvd(A, B)
Syntax: [U, V, X, C, S] = gsvd(A, B)
Syntax: [U, V, X, C, S] = gsvd(A, B, 0)
A = U*C*X' and B = V*S*X' with C'*C + S'*S = I. One output returns the generalized singular values. The third argument 0 gives the economy-size decomposition.
Example: gsvd([1 2; 3 4], eye(2))'   % [0.3660 5.4650]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digit, and the economy form can return a singular-vector pair with the opposite sign.

## cholupdate
Rank-1 update of a Cholesky factorization.
Syntax: R1 = cholupdate(R, x)
Syntax: R1 = cholupdate(R, x, '+')
Syntax: [R1, p] = cholupdate(R, x, '-')
R1'*R1 = R'*R + x*x' ('+', default) or R'*R - x*x' ('-'). With two outputs a failed downdate returns p > 0 instead of an error.
Example: cholupdate(chol([4 2; 2 3]), [1; 0])   % [2.2361 0.8944; 0 1.4832]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digit.

## qrupdate
Rank-1 update of a QR factorization.
Syntax: [Q1, R1] = qrupdate(Q, R, u, v)
Q1*R1 = Q*R + u*v' for a full QR factorization [Q, R] = qr(A).
Example: [Q, R] = qr([1 2; 3 4]); [Q1, R1] = qrupdate(Q, R, [1; 0], [0; 1]); x = Q1*R1   % [1 3; 3 4]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digit.

## qrinsert
Insert a column or row into a QR factorization.
Syntax: [Q1, R1] = qrinsert(Q, R, j, x)
Syntax: [Q1, R1] = qrinsert(Q, R, j, x, 'col')
Syntax: [Q1, R1] = qrinsert(Q, R, j, x, 'row')
Returns the QR factorization of A with x inserted before column (or row) j.
Example: [Q, R] = qr([1 2; 3 4]); [Q1, R1] = qrinsert(Q, R, 3, [1; 1]); x = Q1*R1   % [1 2 1; 3 4 1]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digit.

## qrdelete
Delete a column or row from a QR factorization.
Syntax: [Q1, R1] = qrdelete(Q, R, j)
Syntax: [Q1, R1] = qrdelete(Q, R, j, 'col')
Syntax: [Q1, R1] = qrdelete(Q, R, j, 'row')
Returns the QR factorization of A with column (or row) j removed.
Example: [Q, R] = qr([1 2; 3 4; 5 6]); [Q1, R1] = qrdelete(Q, R, 1); x = Q1*R1   % [2; 4; 6]
Differences from MATLAB: Some results differ in the last printed digit.

## pcg
Preconditioned conjugate gradients for a symmetric positive definite system.
Syntax: x = pcg(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = pcg(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
A, M1 and M2 are dense or sparse matrices or function handles (afun(x) returns A*x, mfun(x) returns M\x). Defaults: tol 1e-6, maxit min(n,20). flag is 0 (converged), 1 (maxit reached), 2 (ill-conditioned preconditioner), 3 (stagnation) or 4 (breakdown). With one output it prints MATLAB's convergence message.
Example: [x, flag] = pcg([4 1; 1 3], [1; 2])   % x = [0.0909; 0.6364], flag = 0
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## gmres
Restarted generalized minimum residual method.
Syntax: x = gmres(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = gmres(A, b, restart, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
GMRES with Householder Arnoldi (Saad and Schultz, 1986), left preconditioned: relres and resvec measure M\(b - A*x) relative to M\b. With restart, iter is [outer inner] and maxit counts outer iterations. Defaults: no restart, tol 1e-6, maxit min(n,10).
Example: [x, flag, relres, iter] = gmres([4 1; 2 5], [1; 0])   % iter = [1 2]
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## bicg
Biconjugate gradients.
Syntax: x = bicg(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = bicg(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
A function handle is called as afun(x,'notransp') for A*x and afun(x,'transp') for A'*x; preconditioner functions likewise.
Example: [x, flag] = bicg([4 1; 2 5], [1; 2])   % flag = 0
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## bicgstab
Biconjugate gradients stabilized.
Syntax: x = bicgstab(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = bicgstab(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
iter can be a half iteration (for example 2.5); resvec has two entries per iteration.
Example: [x, flag, relres, iter] = bicgstab([4 1 0; 2 5 1; 0 1 3], [1; 2; 3])   % iter = 2.5
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## bicgstabl
Biconjugate gradients stabilized (l), with l = 2.
Syntax: x = bicgstabl(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = bicgstabl(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
iter counts quarter iterations (for example 1.25); resvec has four entries per iteration.
Example: [x, flag, relres, iter] = bicgstabl([4 1 0; 2 5 1; 0 1 3], [1; 2; 3])   % iter = 1.25
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## cgs
Conjugate gradients squared.
Syntax: x = cgs(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = cgs(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
Example: [x, flag] = cgs([4 1; 2 5], [1; 2])   % flag = 0
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## minres
Minimum residual method for a symmetric (possibly indefinite) system.
Syntax: x = minres(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec, resveccg] = minres(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
The preconditioner M = M1*M2 must be symmetric positive definite (flag 5 otherwise).
Example: [x, flag] = minres([2 1 0; 1 -3 1; 0 1 1], [1; 2; 3])   % x = [1/3; 1/3; 8/3]
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## lsqr
Least squares QR method for a rectangular or square system.
Syntax: x = lsqr(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec, lsvec] = lsqr(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
Solves min norm(b - A*x). A function handle is called as afun(x,'notransp') and afun(x,'transp'). Defaults: tol 1e-6, maxit min([size(A) 20]). lsvec holds the scaled estimates of norm(A'*r).
Example: [x, flag] = lsqr([1 2; 3 4; 5 6], [1; 2; 4])   % x = [0.6667; 0.0833]
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## qmr
Quasi-minimal residual method.
Syntax: x = qmr(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = qmr(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
A function handle is called as afun(x,'notransp') and afun(x,'transp').
Example: [x, flag] = qmr([4 1; 2 5], [1; 2])   % flag = 0
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## symmlq
Symmetric LQ method for a symmetric (possibly indefinite) system.
Syntax: x = symmlq(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec, resveccg] = symmlq(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
Returns the conjugate-gradient point when it has the smaller residual. The preconditioner must be symmetric positive definite (flag 5 otherwise).
Example: [x, flag] = symmlq([2 1 0; 1 -3 1; 0 1 1], [1; 2; 3])   % flag = 0
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## tfqmr
Transpose-free quasi-minimal residual method.
Syntax: x = tfqmr(A, b)
Syntax: [x, flag, relres, iter, resvec] = tfqmr(A, b, tol, maxit, M1, M2, x0, ...)
Each iteration has two half steps; resvec has an entry for each.
Example: [x, flag] = tfqmr([4 1; 2 5], [1; 2])   % flag = 0
Differences from MATLAB: Real dense or sparse matrices and real-valued function handles; complex systems are unsupported. A sparse A is used through sparse products (same values as full(A)); a sparse M1 or M2 is solved by substitution when triangular (same values as full) and otherwise factorized once per call by sparse LU. Singular dense preconditioners return flag 2 without MATLAB's singular-matrix warning.

## tf
Create a real-coefficient transfer-function value.
Syntax: G = tf(num, den, Ts); s = tf('s'); z = tf('z', Ts); G = tf(sys)

`G=tf(num,den[,Ts])`, `s=tf('s')`, `z=tf('z',Ts)`, `G=tf(sys)`.
Coefficients are finite real rows in descending powers, or ascending powers
with Variable 'z^-1' or 'q^-1'. For MIMO models, supply output-by-input cells
of coefficient rows. A numeric row is shared across all channels if the
other argument is a cell array. Numerator and Denominator are returned as
cells. Denominators keep their scale, and numerators are padded to at least
the corresponding denominator length.

The constructors tf, zpk and ss accept trailing property name-value pairs.
Use dot syntax, get(sys,'Property'), and set(sys,'Property',value). Use
copy=set(sys,...) to return a modified value. Common properties include Ts,
Variable, InputName, OutputName, Name, Notes, and UserData. Ts is zero for
continuous time, positive for a specified sample period, or -1 for unspecified
discrete time. Continuous variables are 's' and 'p'. Discrete variables are
'z', 'q', 'z^-1', and 'q^-1'. Signal names are stored as column cells.
InputDelay, OutputDelay and IODelay are finite, nonnegative SISO delays in
seconds or in whole sample periods for discrete time.
Use sys(outputs,inputs) to select channels by scalar, vector, or colon.
Use sys(i,j)=rhs to replace a channel in a tf or zpk model with a SISO model.
Copies have value semantics.
Example: G = tf({1,2},{[1 1],[1 2]}); size(G)
SISO models support +, -, *, /, unary minus, inv and integer ^ (-64..64),
including scalar numbers. Mixed representations promote ss > zpk > tf.
Polynomials are limited to degree 256. A nonproper model can be stored as tf
but cannot be converted to an ordinary ss realization. Complex coefficients
and arrays of separate LTI models are unsupported. A channel grid can have
up to 4096 ports per axis and 16384 channels.

## tf.bode
Return gain as an amplitude ratio and phase in degrees at angular frequencies w.
Syntax: [gain, phase] = bode(G, w)
Example: G = tf(1, [1 2]); [gain, phase] = bode(G, [0.1 1 10])
See also: tf

## tf.pzmap
Return the poles and zeros of a transfer function, or draw its pole-zero map.
Syntax: [p, z] = pzmap(G)
Syntax: pzmap(G)
Example: G = tf([1 3], [1 4 4]); [p, z] = pzmap(G)
See also: tf

## tf.impulse
Sample the impulse response of a transfer function on a uniform time grid.
Syntax: [y, t] = impulse(G, t)
Example: G = tf(1, [1 2]); [y, t] = impulse(G, 0:0.25:1)
See also: tf

## tf.lsim
Simulate the response of a transfer function to an input sampled at times t.
Syntax: y = lsim(G, u, t)
Example: G = tf(1, [1 2]); t = (0:0.25:1)'; y = lsim(G, sin(t), t)
See also: tf

## tf.series
Connect the outputs of transfer function G to the inputs of H.
Syntax: sys = series(G, H)
Example: G = tf(1, [1 2]); H = tf(2, [1 1]); sys = series(G, H); dcgain(sys)
See also: tf

## tf.step
Sample the unit-step response of a transfer function.
Syntax: [y, t] = step(G, t)
Example: G = tf(1, [1 2]); [y, t] = step(G, 0:0.25:1)
See also: tf

## tf.feedback
Close a negative feedback loop around transfer function G with feedback path H.
Syntax: sys = feedback(G, H)
Example: G = tf(1, [1 2]); sys = feedback(G, 1); pole(sys)
See also: tf

## zpk
Create a model from zeros, poles and gains.
Syntax: G = zpk(z, p, k, Ts); s = zpk('s'); G = zpk(sys)

`G=zpk(z,p,k[,Ts])`, `s=zpk('s')`, `G=zpk(sys)`.
Roots may be complex but must occur in conjugate pairs, giving real polynomial
coefficients. Empty root vectors describe constant factors. For MIMO models,
supply matching output-by-input zero and pole cells and a finite real gain
matrix. Properties Z and P are cells containing root columns with up to 256
roots each. K is the gain matrix. Z, P and K can be replaced with dot syntax.
See tf for common properties, arithmetic, and bounds. Factoring high-order or repeated roots is
numerically sensitive; a root list does not imply exact symbolic factors.

## ss
Create a finite real state-space value with SISO or MIMO inputs and outputs.
Syntax: S = ss(A, B, C, D, Ts); S = ss(sys)

`S=ss(A,B,C,D[,Ts])`, `S=ss(sys)`.
The model is x'=A*x+B*u, y=C*x+D*u in continuous time; sampled models advance
one interval instead of differentiating. A is n by n, B is n by inputs,
C is outputs by n, and D is outputs by inputs. Empty state matrices admit
static gains. A/B/C/D and StateName are readable and writable alongside the
common properties described under tf. StateName accepts one label per state.
Assignment shares immutable arrays until a property is replaced.

At most 1024 states and 1048576 total matrix entries. Augmented sampling
matrices are limited to 1024 dimensions. Ordinary realizations require proper
transfer functions. MIMO conversion from tf or zpk builds a direct sum of
channel realizations. Polynomial conversions have a 256-state bound and can
lose relative accuracy for nearly cancelling coefficients. Arithmetic,
feedback and zero require SISO. A model can have up to 4096 ports per axis.
Selecting I/O channels retains A and StateName. For static gains,
ss([],[],[],D) infers empty state dimensions from D. A scalar zero D expands
to the model's output-by-input zero matrix.

## ss.c2d
Discretize a continuous state-space model with a zero-order hold at sample interval Ts.
Syntax: sysd = c2d(sys, Ts)
Example: sys = ss(-2, 1, 1, 0); sysd = c2d(sys, 0.1); sysd.A
See also: ss

## tfdata
Extract numerator and denominator coefficients from an LTI value.
Syntax: [num, den, Ts] = tfdata(sys); [num, den, Ts] = tfdata(sys, 'v')

`[num,den,Ts]=tfdata(sys)` returns output-by-input coefficient cells and the timebase.
`[num,den,Ts]=tfdata(sys,'v')` returns numeric rows for SISO models. One or two outputs are
also allowed. TF coefficients keep their stored denominator scale and use
the model's Variable convention. Numerator rows are padded to the denominator
length. Conversion of internal-delay models requires pade first.
State-space conversion is limited to 256 states.

## zpkdata
Extract the zero/pole/gain description of an LTI value.
Syntax: [z, p, k, Ts] = zpkdata(sys); [z, p, k, Ts] = zpkdata(sys, 'v')

`[z,p,k,Ts]=zpkdata(sys)` returns output-by-input root cells, the gain matrix and the timebase.
`[z,p,k,Ts]=zpkdata(sys,'v')` returns numerical root columns for SISO models.
Fewer outputs are allowed. Repeated and high-order roots have the usual
floating-point polynomial-root sensitivity.

## ssdata
Extract the real state-space matrices and sampling interval.
Syntax: [A, B, C, D, Ts] = ssdata(sys)

`[A,B,C,D,Ts]=ssdata(sys)`; one through five outputs are accepted.
Existing state coordinates are retained for ss objects, including MIMO.
Proper tf/zpk models use controllable companion realizations for individual channels.

## feedback
Close a feedback loop between LTI models or static gains.
Syntax: R = feedback(G,H[,sign])
Syntax: R = feedback(G,H,feedin,feedout[,sign])

Feedback defaults to negative (-1). Use +1 for positive feedback. For indexed
feedback, select inputs and outputs of G in the order used by H. The result
keeps all inputs and outputs of G. Sampling intervals must agree, with static
gain and unspecified discrete exceptions. Model precedence is ss > zpk > tf.
A singular direct-feedthrough loop is rejected.
Example: G=ss([0 1;-2 -3],eye(2),eye(2),zeros(2)); R=feedback(G,eye(2));
Differences from MATLAB: Transport delays in feedback and name-based routing are unsupported.

## series
Connect two LTI models in sequence.
Syntax: R = series(G,H)
Syntax: R = series(G,H,out1,in2)

The full connection is H*G. In the indexed form, out1 and in2 pair selected
outputs of G with selected inputs of H. The result has all inputs of G and all
outputs of H. With the * operator, a SISO operand multiplies each MIMO channel.
Model precedence is ss > zpk > tf.
Example: G=tf({1;2},{[1 1];[1 2]}); H=tf({1,2},[1 1]); R=series(G,H,2,1);
Differences from MATLAB: Indexed and MIMO connections use ordinary delay-free state-space realizations. Name-based routing is unsupported.

## parallel
Connect two LTI models in parallel.
Syntax: R = parallel(G,H)
Syntax: R = parallel(G,H,in1,in2,out1,out2)

The full connection is G+H. The indexed form shares the paired inputs and sums
the paired outputs. Each result axis orders unpaired ports of G, paired ports
in index-vector order, then unpaired ports of H. The + and - operators expand a
SISO operand to every MIMO channel. Model precedence is ss > zpk > tf.
SISO systems with different transport delays retain separate internal paths.
Example: G=ss(eye(2)); H=ss([1 2;3 4]); R=parallel(G,H,2,1,1,2);
Differences from MATLAB: Indexed and MIMO connections use ordinary delay-free state-space realizations. Name-based routing is unsupported.

## append
Group LTI models by appending inputs and outputs.
Syntax: R = append(G,H,...)

The result has a block-diagonal input-to-output transfer matrix. Each model
keeps its own input and output ports, in argument order. Static numeric
gains can appear alongside LTI models. Model precedence is ss > zpk > tf.
Example: R=append(tf(1,[1 1]),ss(-2,1,1,0),eye(2)); size(R)
Differences from MATLAB: Multiple operands must be delay-free (no MIMO transport delays yet); improper tf/zpk operands are fine.

## pole
Return a column of LTI poles, including repeated poles.
Syntax: p = pole(sys)

`p=pole(sys)`. For ss, these are the eigenvalues of A, including hidden
uncontrollable or unobservable modes. For tf/zpk, denominator roots are
returned without cancellation. Eigenvalue/root ordering is not specified.
Continuous stability requires strictly negative real parts; discrete
stability requires strictly subunit magnitudes. Complex pairs are retained.

## zero
Return a column of numerator zeros of a SISO LTI model.
Syntax: z = zero(sys)

`z=zero(sys)`. Uses the numerator polynomial, without automatic cancellation.
Static and zero numerators return an empty column. MIMO transmission zeros,
zeros at infinity and generalized descriptor models are not implemented.

## dcgain
Evaluate the steady constant-input gain of an LTI model.
Syntax: k = dcgain(sys)

`k=dcgain(sys)` evaluates a SISO rational model at s=0 or z=1. An uncancelled
DC pole can give Inf or NaN; use minreal explicitly when cancellation is
intended. For MIMO ss, solves (-A)*X=B or (I-A)*X=B and returns D+C*X.
A singular MIMO DC solve is rejected; an explicit inverse is never formed.

## minreal
Reduce an LTI model while preserving its input-output transfer.
Syntax: R = minreal(sys); R = minreal(sys, tol)

`R=minreal(sys[,tol])`. The default tolerance is sqrt(machine epsilon).
Roots with abs(imag(r)) <= tol*(1+abs(r)) are first projected onto the real
axis. Remaining complex conjugate pairs cancel together, with both distances
at most tol*(1+abs(z)); real roots match individually to the closest pole.
tol must be finite and nonnegative. The gain is
preserved; a zero transfer function reduces to a constant zero model.
The result keeps its representation. MIMO tf and zpk reduction applies
cancellation to each channel. SISO ss uses polynomial cancellation and a
companion realization. MIMO ss reduces unreachable and unobservable states
using orthogonal projections.

## c2d
Convert a continuous LTI model to sampled time.
Syntax: R = c2d(sys, Ts); R = c2d(sys, Ts, method)

`R=c2d(sys,Ts[,method])`; method is 'zoh' (default), 'tustin', or 'foh'.
Ts must be positive and finite. Zero-order hold uses the exponential of
[A*Ts B*Ts; 0 0]. First-order hold integrates a linear input over each
interval and returns a causal state-coordinate realization. Tustin uses
linear solves for the bilinear substitution s=(2/Ts)*(z-1)/(z+1).
SISO models preserve their representation. SISO transport delays must be
integer multiples of Ts and become whole sample delays. Trailing model
property name-value pairs update the sampled model. Improper models and
sampling prewarping are unsupported.
Matrix functions use the engine's existing bounded numerical kernels.

## d2c
Recover a continuous model from a sampled LTI model.
Syntax: R = d2c(sys); R = d2c(sys, method)

`R=d2c(sys[,method])`; method is 'zoh' (default) or 'tustin'.
ZOH uses the principal matrix logarithm of [Ad Bd; 0 I], divided by Ts.
A singular logarithm or a materially complex result is rejected. Sampling
can alias different continuous systems to the same discrete model; d2c
selects the principal branch and cannot recover the original frequencies
beyond that branch. Tustin reverses the bilinear state-space transformation
using solves. Whole sample delays convert to seconds. FOH inversion and prewarping are unsupported.
Inverse Tustin clears a cancelled direct term only within a componentwise
64*n*epsilon roundoff envelope of the subtracted terms. Feedthrough below
that envelope cannot reliably be distinguished from cancellation error.

## isstable
Test strict asymptotic stability of an LTI model.
Syntax: ok = isstable(sys)

`ok=isstable(sys)` returns a logical scalar. Every pole must have negative
real part in continuous time or magnitude less than one in discrete time.
Boundary poles are unstable; no tolerance is applied. ss includes hidden
state modes. A static gain with no poles is stable.

## issiso
Test whether an LTI model has one input and one output.
Syntax: ok = issiso(sys)
Returns a logical scalar.
Example: issiso(tf(1,[1 2]))

## order
Count represented dynamic states or denominator poles.
Syntax: n = order(sys)

`n=order(sys)` returns the state dimension for ss, denominator degree for tf,
or number of poles for zpk. For MIMO tf and zpk models, the channel orders
are summed. Use minreal to reduce the model before counting.

## damp
Compute modal natural frequencies and damping ratios.
Syntax: [wn, zeta, p] = damp(sys)

`[wn,zeta,p]=damp(sys)` returns frequency, damping and represented poles as
columns, sorted by increasing natural frequency. Fewer outputs are allowed.
Continuous poles use wn=abs(p), zeta=-real(p)/wn. Discrete poles first map
to log(p)/Ts on the principal branch; p still contains the discrete poles.
An origin continuous pole has zero frequency and undefined damping (NaN).
A discrete zero pole has infinite natural frequency and unit damping.
Call damp(sys) with no outputs to print the modal table.

## pade
Approximate a continuous-time transport delay with a rational model.
Syntax: [num,den] = pade(T,N)
Syntax: sysx = pade(sys,N)
The first form returns the numerator and denominator of the diagonal Padé
approximation of exp(-s*T). T must be finite and nonnegative. N is an integer
from 0 to 32. The second form replaces the model's transport delay with its
rational approximation. Order zero removes the delay.
Example: [n,d] = pade(0.5,1)

## besself
Design an analog Bessel low-pass filter.
Syntax: [b,a] = besself(n, Wo)
Syntax: [z,p,k] = besself(n, Wo)
Syntax: [A,B,C,D] = besself(n, Wo)
Wo is a positive analog radian frequency; n is 1 through 20. The normalization is unit group delay at DC, matching the standard Thomson delay normalization. State-space output uses controllable canonical companion form.
Example: [b,a] = besself(4, 10)
Differences from MATLAB: Only analog low-pass designs through order 20 are supported.

## butter
Design a Butterworth IIR filter as transfer coefficients, zeros/poles/gain, or state space.
Syntax: [b,a] = butter(n, Wn)
Syntax: [z,p,k] = butter(n, Wn, ftype)
Syntax: [A,B,C,D] = butter(n, Wn, 's')
Wn is normalized to Nyquist for digital filters. A two-edge Wn defaults to bandpass; ftype is low, high, bandpass or stop. Append 's' for analog design. Orders range from 1 through 20 per low-pass prototype. State-space output uses controllable canonical companion form.
Example: [b,a] = butter(4, 0.25)
Append 'sos' for SOS output: one output includes the gain, while [sos,g] returns unit-gain sections and a separate scalar gain.
Differences from MATLAB: Only the listed output forms, frequency types and orders through 20 are supported.

## buttord
Choose a Butterworth order and cutoff from passband and stopband specifications.
Syntax: [n,Wn] = buttord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs)
Syntax: [n,Wn] = buttord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs, 's')
Wp and Ws are digital frequencies normalized to Nyquist; use 's' for analog radian frequencies. Rp is passband loss in dB and Rs is stopband attenuation in dB.
Example: [n,Wn] = buttord(0.2, 0.35, 1, 40)
Differences from MATLAB: Up to 20th order is supported; digital edge frequencies must be between zero and Nyquist.

## cheb2ord
Choose a Chebyshev type II order and cutoff from passband and stopband specifications.
Syntax: [n,Wn] = cheb2ord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs)
Syntax: [n,Wn] = cheb2ord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs, 's')
Rp and Rs are passband loss and stopband attenuation in dB. A two-edge Wp selects a band design.
Example: [n,Wn] = cheb2ord(0.2, 0.35, 1, 40)
Differences from MATLAB: Up to 20th order is supported; output is limited to order and edge frequency.

## cheby2
Design a Chebyshev type II IIR filter.
Syntax: [b,a] = cheby2(n, Rs, Ws)
Syntax: [z,p,k] = cheby2(n, Rs, Ws, ftype)
Syntax: [A,B,C,D] = cheby2(n, Rs, Ws, 's')
Rs is stopband attenuation in dB. A two-edge Ws defaults to bandpass; ftype is low, high, bandpass or stop. Append 's' for analog design. State-space output uses controllable canonical companion form.
Example: [b,a] = cheby2(5, 40, 0.3)
Append 'sos' for SOS output: one output includes the gain, while [sos,g] returns unit-gain sections and a separate scalar gain.
Differences from MATLAB: Only the listed output forms, frequency types and orders through 20 are supported.

## ellip
Design an elliptic IIR filter with passband and stopband ripple constraints.
Syntax: [b,a] = ellip(n, Rp, Rs, Wp)
Syntax: [z,p,k] = ellip(n, Rp, Rs, Wp, ftype)
Syntax: [A,B,C,D] = ellip(n, Rp, Rs, Wp, 's')
Rp and Rs are passband loss and stopband attenuation in dB. A two-edge Wp defaults to bandpass. Append 's' for analog design. State-space output uses controllable canonical companion form.
Example: [b,a] = ellip(5, 1, 40, 0.3)
Append 'sos' for SOS output: one output includes the gain, while [sos,g] returns unit-gain sections and a separate scalar gain.
Differences from MATLAB: The elliptic prototype is evaluated with bounded Jacobi AGM iterations; orders are limited to 20.

## ellipord
Choose an elliptic filter order and passband edges from specifications.
Syntax: [n,Wn] = ellipord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs)
Syntax: [n,Wn] = ellipord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs, 's')
A two-edge Wp selects a band design. Rp and Rs are passband loss and stopband attenuation in dB.
Example: [n,Wn] = ellipord(0.2, 0.35, 1, 40)
Differences from MATLAB: Up to 20th order is supported; output is limited to order and edge frequency.

## cheb1ord
Choose a Chebyshev type I order and cutoff from passband and stopband specifications.
Syntax: [n,Wn] = cheb1ord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs)
Syntax: [n,Wn] = cheb1ord(Wp, Ws, Rp, Rs, 's')
Rp and Rs are passband ripple and stopband attenuation in dB. A two-edge Wp selects a band design.
Example: [n,Wn] = cheb1ord(0.2, 0.35, 1, 40)
Differences from MATLAB: Up to 20th order is supported; output is limited to order and edge frequency.

## tf2ss
Convert a SISO transfer function into controllable canonical state space.
Syntax: [A,B,C,D] = tf2ss(b, a)
Coefficients are in descending powers. The result uses the controllable companion form.
Example: [A,B,C,D] = tf2ss([1 2], [1 3 2])
Differences from MATLAB: Only real SISO systems of order 40 or less are supported.

## tf2zp
Convert SISO transfer coefficients into zeros, poles and gain.
Syntax: [z,p,k] = tf2zp(b, a)
Coefficients are in descending powers.
Example: [z,p,k] = tf2zp([1 2], [1 3 2])
Differences from MATLAB: Only real coefficient vectors are supported; degree is limited to 40.

## ss2tf
Convert a SISO state-space system into transfer coefficients.
Syntax: [b,a] = ss2tf(A, B, C, D)
The matrices use the controllable companion convention documented by tf2ss.
Example: [A,B,C,D] = tf2ss([1 2], [1 3 2]); [b,a] = ss2tf(A, B, C, D)
Differences from MATLAB: Only real SISO state spaces of order 40 or less are supported.

## ss2zp
Convert a SISO state-space system into zeros, poles and gain.
Syntax: [z,p,k] = ss2zp(A, B, C, D)
Example: [A,B,C,D] = tf2ss([1 2], [1 3 2]); [z,p,k] = ss2zp(A, B, C, D)
Differences from MATLAB: Only real SISO state spaces of order 40 or less are supported.

## sos2tf
Convert real second-order sections into one transfer function.
Syntax: [b,a] = sos2tf(sos)
Syntax: [b,a] = sos2tf(sos, g)
Multiplies the section numerators sos(:,1:3) and denominators sos(:,4:6) together (conv), then scales b by the gain g (default 1). b and a have 2L+1 coefficients for L sections.
Example: [b,a] = sos2tf([1 2 1 1 -0.5 0.2])
Example: b = sos2tf([1 1 0 1 -0.5 0; 1 0 0 1 0.2 0], 2)   % [2 2 0 0 0]
Differences from MATLAB: Only real SOS matrices with six columns are supported.

## sos2zp
Convert real second-order sections into zeros, poles and gain.
Syntax: [z,p,k] = sos2zp(sos)
Example: [z,p,k] = sos2zp([1 2 1 1 -0.5 0.2])
Differences from MATLAB: Only real SOS matrices with six columns are supported.

## tf2sos
Convert SISO transfer coefficients into real second-order sections.
Syntax: sos = tf2sos(b, a)
Syntax: [sos,g] = tf2sos(b, a)
Pairing selects the pole nearest the unit circle first, then pairs its zeros by nearest distance. Sections are emitted in reverse selection order, with the most critical poles last.
Example: sos = tf2sos([1 2 1], [1 -0.5 0.2])
Differences from MATLAB: Pairing follows a nearest-pole rule; output sections may differ from MATLAB scaling and ordering.

## zp2ss
Convert zeros, poles and gain into controllable canonical state space.
Syntax: [A,B,C,D] = zp2ss(z, p, k)
Example: [A,B,C,D] = zp2ss([], [-1 -2], 1)
Differences from MATLAB: Only real SISO systems of order 40 or less are supported.

## zp2tf
Convert zeros, poles and gain into transfer coefficients.
Syntax: [b,a] = zp2tf(z, p, k)
Coefficients are in descending powers.
Example: [b,a] = zp2tf([], [-1 -2], 1)
Differences from MATLAB: Only finite SISO pole and zero vectors are supported.

## bilinear
Bilinear transformation of an analog filter into a digital one.
Syntax: [bz, az] = bilinear(b, a, fs)
Syntax: [bz, az] = bilinear(b, a, fs, fp)
Syntax: [zd, pd, kd] = bilinear(z, p, k, fs)
Syntax: [zd, pd, kd] = bilinear(z, p, k, fs, fp)
Substitutes s = 2*fs*(z-1)/(z+1). With a match frequency fp (Hz, below fs/2) the scale is 2*pi*fp/tan(pi*fp/fs), so the analog and digital responses are equal at fp. b and a are row vectors in descending powers of s (numerator degree at most the denominator's); the result is normalized to az(1) = 1. In the zero-pole-gain form (p a column), each root maps to (1+r/(2fs))/(1-r/(2fs)) and missing zeros go to -1.
Example: [bz, az] = bilinear(1, [1 1], 10)   % bz = [1 1]/21, az = [1 -19/21]
Example: [zd, pd, kd] = bilinear([], -2*pi*50, 2*pi*50, 1000, 50);
Differences from MATLAB: the state-space form (A, B, C, D) is not supported.

## zp2sos
Convert zeros, poles and gain into real second-order sections.
Syntax: sos = zp2sos(z, p, k)
Syntax: [sos,g] = zp2sos(z, p, k)
Poles closest to the unit circle are paired first. For each section, the nearest remaining zeros are paired, including conjugates. Sections follow SciPy nearest ordering with the most critical poles last; gain is placed in the first section. Unpaired complex roots are rejected.
Example: sos = zp2sos([], [-1 -2], 1)
Differences from MATLAB: Nearest pairing is supported, so section order can differ. Fewer zeros than poles stay a degree deficit (leading numerator zeros, as in zp2tf), not roots at the origin. Equal zero and pole counts, including an odd-order trailing-zero section, are unchanged.

## ctrb
Build the controllability matrix.
Syntax: T = ctrb(A,B)
Syntax: T = ctrb(sys)
Returns [B A*B ... A^(n-1)*B]. rank(T) estimates controllability; powers can be ill-conditioned, so interpret numerical rank with care. LTI models are converted to state space.
Example: A=[0 1;0 0]; B=[0;1]; T=ctrb(A,B); rank(T)
Example: T=ctrb(ss([0 1;0 0],[0;1],[1 0],0));
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double matrices only; at most 128 states, 128 inputs and 1048576 output entries. No descriptor models.

## obsv
Build the observability matrix.
Syntax: O = obsv(A,C)
Syntax: O = obsv(sys)
Returns [C; C*A; ...; C*A^(n-1)]. rank(O) estimates observability; powers can be ill-conditioned. LTI models are converted to state space.
Example: O=obsv([0 1;0 0],[1 0]); rank(O)
Example: O=obsv(ss([0 1;0 0],[0;1],[1 0],0));
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double matrices only; at most 128 states, 128 outputs and 1048576 result entries. No descriptor models.

## care
Solve the continuous algebraic Riccati equation.
Syntax: [X,K,L] = care(A,B,Q)
Syntax: [X,K,L] = care(A,B,Q,R,S,E)
Solves A'*X+X*A-(X*B+S)*(R\(B'*X+S'))+Q=0. R defaults to identity and S to zero; [] selects either default. E must be identity or []. K=R\(B'*X+S') and L=eig(A-B*K). Uses Laub's balanced Hamiltonian real Schur method with stable eigenvalue reordering and a linear solve for the invariant subspace. A relative residual above 1e-10 triggers one Newton-Kleinman correction using a Lyapunov solve. Rejects non-stabilising results, nonfinite arithmetic, or a residual still above 1e-10 after refinement. Q and R must be symmetric to relative tolerance 1e-12; R must be positive definite.
Example: [X,K,L]=care([0 1;0 0],[0;1],eye(2),1);
Example: [X,K,L]=care(-1,1,2,1,0.1,1);
Differences from MATLAB: output order is X, feedback gain K, closed-loop poles L. Only finite real double data, positive definite R and identity E; at most 128 states and inputs. No scaling/status outputs or descriptor equations.

## dare
Solve the discrete algebraic Riccati equation.
Syntax: [X,K,L] = dare(A,B,Q)
Syntax: [X,K,L] = dare(A,B,Q,R,S,E)
Solves A'*X*A-X-(A'*X*B+S)*((R+B'*X*B)\(B'*X*A+S'))+Q=0. R defaults to identity, S to zero; [] selects defaults. E must be identity or []. K=(R+B'*X*B)\(B'*X*A+S') and L=eig(A-B*K). Uses a balanced symplectic pencil with ordered QZ (Pappas, Laub and Sandell), including singular A, rather than an inverse of A. A relative residual above 1e-10 triggers one Newton correction using a discrete Lyapunov equation, converted to a Sylvester equation by a bilinear transform. Rejects non-stabilising results, nonfinite arithmetic, or a residual still above 1e-10 after refinement. Q and R must be symmetric to relative tolerance 1e-12; R must be positive definite.
Example: [X,K,L]=dare([1 1;0 1],[0;1],eye(2),1);
Example: [X,K,L]=dare(0.8,1,2,1,0.1,1);
Differences from MATLAB: output order is X, feedback gain K, closed-loop poles L. Only finite real double data, positive definite R and identity E; at most 128 states and inputs. No scaling/status outputs or descriptor equations.

## lqr
Design optimal quadratic state feedback.
Syntax: [K,S,P] = lqr(A,B,Q,R,N)
Syntax: [K,S,P] = lqr(sys,Q,R,N)
N is optional and defaults to zero. Minimizes the infinite-horizon quadratic cost with state weight Q, input weight R and cross term 2*x'*N*u. Feedback is u=-K*x; S is the Riccati solution and P the closed-loop poles. Matrix inputs use continuous time; an LTI model uses its sampling time to select CARE or DARE. R must be positive definite; the Riccati residual must pass 1e-10 relative tolerance.
Example: [K,S,P]=lqr([0 1;0 0],[0;1],eye(2),1);
Example: [K,S,P]=lqr(ss(0.8,1,1,0,0.1),1,1);
Differences from MATLAB: only finite real double data, identity descriptor and positive definite R, with at most 128 states and inputs; no output-weighted lqry form.

## dlqr
Design discrete quadratic state feedback.
Syntax: [K,S,P] = dlqr(A,B,Q,R,N)
N is optional and defaults to zero. Feedback u=-K*x minimizes the infinite sum of x'*Q*x+u'*R*u+2*x'*N*u for x_next=A*x+B*u. S is the stabilising DARE solution and P=eig(A-B*K). Uses ordered symplectic QZ; the relative Riccati residual must be at most 1e-10.
Example: [K,S,P]=dlqr([1 1;0 1],[0;1],eye(2),1);
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double matrices only, positive definite R and at most 128 states and inputs. Use lqr(sys,Q,R) for discrete LTI objects.

## place
Assign closed-loop poles by state feedback.
Syntax: K = place(A,B,p)
Chooses K so eig(A-B*K) matches p. For rank(B)=1, computes the effective gain directly with Ackermann's formula in orthogonal Hessenberg coordinates, without forming controllability powers or solving for closed-loop eigenvectors. Otherwise uses KNV method 0 projections for real poles, with a conjugate-preserving two-column determinant maximization for complex pairs. Uses four deterministic starts and up to 80 sweeps per start, stopping at relative determinant change below 1e-8. Multi-input gains are not unique. Complex poles must come in conjugate pairs (relative tolerance 1e-12); requested multiplicity may not exceed numerical rank(B). Numerical rank uses 1e-12*max(size)*largest singular value. Checks achieved poles to 1e-8*(1+abs(p)); exceeding this target issues a warning and returns the gain, because sensitive eigenvalues can limit accuracy even for a valid gain. Uncontrollability, failed solves and nonfinite results still produce errors.
Example: A=[0 1;0 0]; B=[0;1]; K=place(A,B,[-2 -3]); eig(A-B*K)
Example: K=place([1 2;3 4],eye(2),[-1+2i -1-2i]);
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double A,B only, at most 128 states and inputs; complex pairs use a two-column extension of KNV0. Only K is returned. Conditioning can limit achievable accuracy.

## acker
Assign single-input poles with Ackermann's formula.
Syntax: K = acker(A,b,p)
Evaluates the desired characteristic polynomial at A and solves a transposed controllability system for the feedback u=-K*x. b must have one column; p has n entries and complex poles must come in conjugate pairs. Warning: controllability powers and polynomial evaluation are often severely ill-conditioned, especially at high order or with widely separated poles; prefer place for numerical work. Repeated poles are allowed here.
Example: A=[0 1;0 0]; b=[0;1]; K=acker(A,b,[-2 -3]); eig(A-b*K)
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double A,b only, at most 128 states. Rejects numerical uncontrollability at 1e-12*max(size)*largest singular value; no accuracy guarantee for ill-conditioned polynomial calculations.

## rlocus
Compute or plot a SISO root locus.
Syntax: [r,k] = rlocus(sys)
Syntax: [r,k] = rlocus(sys,k)
Syntax: rlocus(sys)
Each column of r contains the closed-loop roots of den+k*num for one gain. Supplied gains are finite nonnegative vectors, preserved in their given order. With no outputs, draws each branch separately (a point marker for one gain), open-loop poles as x and zeros as o. Successive roots are greedily matched to the nearest unused previous root; labels at crossings or repeated roots are ambiguous. Automatic gains start with zero plus 81 logarithmic values from 1e-4 to 1e4 times max(abs(den))/max(abs(num)). An interval is bisected when branch movement exceeds 5% of 1+min(endpoint magnitudes), or midpoint chord error exceeds 1% of 1+midpoint magnitude. Refinement stops after 12 rounds or 4096 gains. A zero numerator uses scale 1; scale is bounded to [1e-100,1e100].
Example: [r,k]=rlocus(tf(1,[1 3 2]),[0 0.1 1 10 100]);
Example: rlocus(tf([1 2],[1 4 5 0]),[0 0.1 1 10 100]);
Differences from MATLAB: proper real SISO models only, at most 128 poles and 4096 gains; plots also obey the graphics limit of 64 total branch/marker series. A gain cancelling the leading coefficient is rejected because infinite poles are not represented. The finite adaptive grid and greedy branch labels can differ; branches beyond the selected range are not guaranteed to reach their asymptotes.

## step
Unit-step responses of a continuous or discrete LTI model.
Syntax: [y,t,x] = step(sys[,t_or_final_time])
Syntax: step(sys1,sys2,...[,t_or_final_time])
The outputs y and x have time in the first dimension, output or state in the second, and the excited input in the third. t is a time column. Without outputs, draws one axes per I/O pair with a shared time axis; several systems overlay. Continuous uniform-grid propagation uses one augmented matrix exponential and exact constant-input recursion, up to floating-point rounding. Discrete propagation uses the model matrices at Ts. SISO transport delays shift the response; the automatic horizon includes the delay.
Automatic time: poles with abs(p)<=1e-10 are treated as integrators and contribute 10; other stable poles contribute 7/abs(real(p)); other unstable or purely imaginary poles contribute 10/abs(p). Use the largest contribution (10 if there are no poles). For discrete poles, p means log(z)/Ts, and a zero pole contributes no rate. Rates above the integrator threshold with abs(real(p))<=1e-10*abs(p) are treated as purely imaginary and contribute 10/abs(p), including rates obtained from discrete poles. Continuous grids use clamp(ceil(25*Tfinal*fastest_pole_rate)+1,100,10000) samples. Default discrete grids clamp floor(Tfinal/Ts)+1 to 100..10000 samples at Ts, extending or truncating the pole-derived horizon; static models use 101 samples. Explicit scalar final times use floor(Tfinal/Ts)+1 and requests exceeding 10000 samples are rejected. A supplied time vector must be uniform, start at zero and have 2..10000 samples; discrete spacing must equal Ts. A scalar positive final time uses the same sampling rule. Responses are limited to 256 states, 64 ports, 4 million combined state/output entries and bounded work.
Example: G=tf(1,[1 0.4 1]); [y,t]=step(G,0:0.1:10)
Example: G=tf(1,[1 1]); step(G,G,0:0.1:5)
Differences from MATLAB: Time vectors must be uniform and start at zero. Automatic grids and plot styling differ. No response options or model arrays.

## impulse
Impulse responses of an LTI model.
Syntax: [y,t,x] = impulse(sys[,t_or_final_time])
Syntax: impulse(sys1,sys2,...[,t_or_final_time])
The outputs y and x have time in the first dimension, output or state in the second, and the excited input in the third. t is a time column. Without outputs, plots or overlays the responses with a shared time axis. Continuous responses return the regular part C*exp(A*t)*B; a direct-feedthrough Dirac delta is omitted. Discrete input is 1/Ts at the first sample and zero thereafter, so its sampled area is one. SISO transport delays shift the response.
Automatic time and bounds follow step: poles with abs(p)<=1e-10 are treated as integrators and contribute 10; other stable poles contribute 7/abs(real(p)), other unstable or imaginary poles 10/abs(p). Use the largest contribution; fallback 10 for static continuous models, 100*Ts for static discrete models. Discrete poles use log(z)/Ts. Rates above the integrator threshold with abs(real(p))<=1e-10*abs(p) are treated as purely imaginary and contribute 10/abs(p), including rates obtained from discrete poles. Continuous grids have clamp(ceil(25*Tfinal*fastest_pole_rate)+1,100,10000) points; discrete grids use floor(Tfinal/Ts)+1 at Ts (at most 10000). Default discrete counts are clamped to 100..10000 while keeping Ts, extending or truncating the horizon. Explicit grids must start at zero, be uniform and have 2..10000 points; discrete spacing is Ts.
Example: G=tf(1,[1 0.4 1]); [y,t]=impulse(G,0:0.1:10)
Differences from MATLAB: Continuous feedthrough impulses are omitted, and automatic grids differ. No impulse configuration options.

## initial
Zero-input state response from an initial state.
Syntax: [y,t,x] = initial(sys,x0[,t_or_final_time])
Syntax: initial(sys1,sys2,...,x0[,t_or_final_time])
Requires state-space models and a real vector x0 with one entry per state. Rows are times, with columns for outputs in y and states in x. Without outputs, draws one axes per output; multiple systems overlay using the same x0. Continuous propagation uses a matrix exponential; discrete propagation recurses at Ts.
Automatic time follows step: poles with abs(p)<=1e-10 are treated as integrators and contribute 10; other stable poles contribute 7/abs(real(p)), other unstable or imaginary poles 10/abs(p). Use the largest contribution, with a static fallback of 10 (100*Ts if discrete). Discrete poles use log(z)/Ts. Rates above the integrator threshold with abs(real(p))<=1e-10*abs(p) are treated as purely imaginary and contribute 10/abs(p), including rates obtained from discrete poles. Continuous grids use clamp(ceil(25*Tfinal*fastest_pole_rate)+1,100,10000) points; discrete grids have floor(Tfinal/Ts)+1 points at Ts, at most 10000. Default discrete counts are clamped to 100..10000 while keeping Ts, extending or truncating the horizon. Explicit time must start at zero and be uniform, with 2..10000 points and spacing Ts for discrete models.
Example: G=ss([0 1;-1 -0.4],[0;1],[1 0],0); [y,t]=initial(G,[1;0],0:0.1:10)
Differences from MATLAB: Only state-space models are accepted. Automatic grids differ, and nonuniform or nonzero-start time vectors are rejected.

## lsim
Simulate an LTI model with sampled inputs.
Syntax: [y,t,x] = lsim(sys,u,t[,x0][,'zoh'|'foh'])
Syntax: lsim(sys1,sys2,...,u,t[,x0][,'zoh'|'foh'])
Each row of u is a time sample and each column is an input. SISO input may also be a row vector. The default initial state is zero. y and x have one row per time, and columns for outputs and states. Without outputs, plots y with one axes per output. Continuous ZOH holds u(k,:) until the next sample; FOH interpolates linearly between successive samples. Both use a single augmented exponential and exact propagation up to rounding. Discrete models use direct recursion at Ts; interpolation options have no effect on discrete recursion. SISO transport delays use the selected hold at the shifted input times.
No automatic time vector: t must be uniform, start at zero, and contain 2..10000 samples. Discrete spacing must equal Ts. Work and storage bounds are the same as step.
Example: G=ss(-2,1,1,0); t=(0:0.1:5)'; [y,t,x]=lsim(G,sin(t),t,0,'foh')
Differences from MATLAB: Default interpolation is always ZOH. Nonuniform times and automatic interpolation selection are unsupported; inputs must be finite real doubles.

## stepinfo
Measure sampled step-response characteristics.
Syntax: S = stepinfo(sys[,t_or_final_time])
Syntax: S = stepinfo(y,t)
Returns RiseTime (first 10% to first 90% sample), SettlingTime (first sample after the last error of at least 2%), Overshoot and Undershoot (percent of absolute final value), Peak (absolute amplitude), PeakTime, SettlingMin and SettlingMax (extrema from the first 90% crossing, including the final value). Models use DC gain as the final value; data use the last sample. A MIMO model returns an outputs-by-inputs struct array; data return one struct per column.
