Undefined crossings and unsettled responses yield NaN; zero final values have undefined normalized metrics. No interpolation between time samples.
For models the automatic time rule is the one in step: poles with abs(p)<=1e-10 are treated as integrators and contribute 10; other stable poles contribute 7/abs(real(p)), other poles 10/abs(p). Use the largest contribution. Static models use 10 (100*Ts if discrete). Discrete poles use log(z)/Ts; continuous grids have clamp(ceil(25*Tfinal*fastest_pole_rate)+1,100,10000) points, discrete grids floor(Tfinal/Ts)+1 at Ts, at most 10000. Default discrete counts are clamped to 100..10000 while keeping Ts, extending or truncating the horizon. Explicit model grids start at zero and are uniform; data times may be nonuniform but must be strictly increasing.
Example: G=tf(1,[1 0.4 1]); S=stepinfo(G,0:0.01:40); S.Overshoot
Example: S=stepinfo([0;0.2;0.8;1;1],[0;1;2;3;4]); S.RiseTime
Differences from MATLAB: Thresholds are fixed at 10%-90% and 2%. Only the listed fields are returned; no threshold or final-value options. Accuracy depends on the supplied sampling and duration.

## bode
Magnitude and unwrapped phase of an LTI frequency response.
Syntax: [mag,phase,w] = bode(sys[,w])
Syntax: bode(sys1,sys2,...[,w])
mag is absolute amplitude and phase is unwrapped degrees. MIMO arrays have dimensions outputs by inputs by frequencies. SISO samples are returned as frequency columns. Without outputs, plots magnitude in dB above phase with logarithmic frequency, one pair of axes per I/O pair. Several systems overlay. Continuous evaluation uses s=j*w; discrete evaluation uses z=exp(j*w*Ts), with w in radians per model time unit. State-space evaluation reduces A to Hessenberg form once, then solves each shifted system without inversion; Rational models use polynomial evaluation for each channel. Transport delays contribute -w*tau radians, where tau is the total delay in seconds.
Automatic frequency: 1000 logarithmic points from one decade below floor(log10(smallest pole/zero magnitude above 1e-10)) to one decade above ceil(log10(largest magnitude)); if no finite scales above 1e-10 exist use 0.01..100. Discrete scales are abs(log(z))/Ts; the upper endpoint is always exactly pi/Ts, evaluated at z=-1, and the lower endpoint is at least two decades below it. MIMO models use pole scales only. Explicit w is a strictly increasing nonnegative real vector of at most 10000 points; discrete frequencies cannot exceed pi/Ts.
Models with zero inputs or zero outputs are rejected with an error; at least one input and one output are required.
Example: G=tf(1,[1 0.4 1]); [mag,phase,w]=bode(G,logspace(-2,2,50))
Example: G=tf(1,[1 1]); bode(G)
Differences from MATLAB: SISO responses are frequency columns. Automatic grids and plots differ. No plot-option objects or model arrays.

## nyquist
Real and imaginary frequency response of an LTI model.
Syntax: [re,im,w] = nyquist(sys[,w])
Syntax: nyquist(sys1,sys2,...[,w])
MIMO arrays have dimensions outputs by inputs by frequencies. SISO samples are returned as frequency columns. Without outputs, draws one axes per I/O pair, a dashed conjugate mirror and a marker at -1. Several systems overlay. Continuous frequencies evaluate s=j*w; discrete frequencies evaluate z=exp(j*w*Ts).
Automatic frequency uses 1000 log points, one decade below the rounded-down smallest pole/zero magnitude above 1e-10 through one decade above the rounded-up largest magnitude, or 0.01..100 if no finite scales above 1e-10 exist. MIMO uses poles only. Discrete scales use abs(log(z))/Ts; the upper endpoint is always exactly pi/Ts, evaluated at z=-1, with the lower endpoint at least two decades below it. Explicit frequencies must be increasing, nonnegative and at most 10000 points (at most pi/Ts for discrete models).
Models with zero inputs or zero outputs are rejected with an error; at least one input and one output are required.
Example: G=tf(1,[1 0.4 1]); [re,im,w]=nyquist(G,logspace(-2,2,50))
Differences from MATLAB: No contour indentation around imaginary-axis poles; exact poles are rejected. SISO responses are frequency columns. The mirror is drawn for real-coefficient models.

## freqresp
Evaluate a frequency grid and return complex LTI responses.
Syntax: H = freqresp(sys,w)
MIMO arrays have dimensions outputs by inputs by frequencies. SISO samples are returned as frequency columns. Continuous models evaluate s=j*w and discrete models evaluate z=exp(j*w*Ts). State-space models use one Hessenberg reduction followed by a pivoted solve per frequency. Exact poles are rejected.
No automatic frequency grid: supply an increasing nonnegative vector of 1..10000 finite frequencies in radians per model time unit; discrete frequencies must not exceed pi/Ts. bode and nyquist provide automatic grids based on pole/zero decades.
Models with zero inputs or zero outputs are rejected with an error; at least one input and one output are required.
Example: G=tf(1,[1 1]); H=freqresp(G,[0 1 10])
Differences from MATLAB: SISO responses are frequency columns. Frequency units and multidimensional model arrays are unsupported.

## evalfr
Evaluate an LTI model at one complex-plane point.
Syntax: H = evalfr(sys,s)
For continuous models s is a Laplace-plane point. For discrete models it is a z-plane point directly, without an exponential mapping. H has one row per output and one column per input. Evaluation solves (s*I-A)*X=B and forms C*X+D, or evaluates rational coefficients channel by channel. A point coinciding with a pole is rejected.
No automatic time or frequency grid is used.
Models with zero inputs or zero outputs are rejected with an error; at least one input and one output are required.
Example: G=tf(1,[1 1]); H=evalfr(G,1i)
Differences from MATLAB: Only finite scalar evaluation points and real-coefficient LTI models are supported; poles raise an error instead of returning an infinite response.

## margin
Classical SISO gain and phase margins.
Syntax: [Gm,Pm,Wcg,Wcp] = margin(sys)
Syntax: [Gm,Pm,Wcg,Wcp] = margin(mag,phase,w)
Gm is an absolute gain factor at the negative-real-axis crossing Wcg; Pm is degrees from -180 at the unity-magnitude crossing Wcp. Frequencies are radians per model time unit. Among multiple crossings, selects gain closest to unity on a logarithmic scale and phase closest to zero. An absent crossing returns Inf for its margin and NaN for its frequency. Model crossings are bracketed on the automatic grid and refined by bisection; data crossings interpolate log magnitude and phase against log frequency (linear frequency when the left sample is zero).
Automatic frequency starts with the 1000-point bode grid based on pole/zero scales above 1e-10 (default 0.01..100). Continuous models expand both ends to bounds for the finite nonzero gain and phase crossing frequencies, with one extra decade on each side. Models with delays also sample the
delay-induced phase turns within the bounded search grid. The expanded grid retains at least the original logarithmic density, up to 10000 points; requests exceeding this bound or representable coefficient/range limits require sampled frequency data. Discrete scales are abs(log(z))/Ts; the upper endpoint is always exactly pi/Ts, evaluated at z=-1, with at least two decades of span. A negative real H(-1) counts as a gain-margin crossing at that endpoint. Without outputs, both forms draw a Bode plot with margins in the title; multiple SISO models overlay. Data require nonnegative absolute magnitudes, unwrapped phase in degrees and strictly increasing nonnegative frequencies, all with equal length 2..10000.
Models with zero inputs or zero outputs are rejected with an error; at least one input and one output are required.
Example: G=tf(10,[1 6 11 6]); [Gm,Pm,Wcg,Wcp]=margin(G)
Example: G=tf(2,[1 1 0]); margin(G)
Differences from MATLAB: SISO only. Grid bracketing can miss tangential or closely spaced crossings; supply a denser sampled-data response when needed. The discrete Nyquist endpoint is included: for 1/(z-0.5), Gm=1.5 at pi/Ts, whereas python-control 0.10.2 returns Inf. No frequency-range options; allmargin lists every crossing.

Classifier overload: Syntax: m = margin(mdl,X,Y)
Returns true-class score minus maximal other-class score for each observation, in observation order.
Example: m=fitcknn([0;2],[1;2]); margin(m,[0;2],[1;2])
Differences from MATLAB: Custom observation weights and learner subsets are unsupported.


## allmargin
All gain, phase and delay margins of a loop transfer.
Syntax: S = allmargin(sys)
Syntax: S = allmargin(sys, 'Focus', [fmin fmax])
Syntax: S = allmargin(mag, phase, w[, ts])
S has the fields GainMargin, GMFrequency, PhaseMargin, PMFrequency, DelayMargin, DMFrequency and Stable. Every -180 degree (modulo 360) phase crossing gives a gain margin 1/|L| at GMFrequency; every unity-gain crossing gives a phase margin in degrees (phase + 180, in [-180, 180)) at PMFrequency, and a delay margin (PM mod 360)*pi/180/w: seconds for continuous models, sample periods for discrete ones; DMFrequency repeats PMFrequency. Each field is a 1-by-k row sorted by frequency, 1-by-0 when there is no such crossing. Stable is 1 when the loop closed by unit negative feedback is stable, 0 when not, NaN when the closed loop is ill-posed or for frequency data. The crossings are those margin finds (same grid, bisection refinement), so margin returns the dominant entries of allmargin. A square MIMO loop gives an M-by-1 struct array: loop j with every other loop closed by unit negative feedback. 'Focus' keeps crossings with fmin <= w <= fmax.
Example: S = allmargin(tf(1,[1 3 3 1]))   % GainMargin 8 at sqrt(3)
Example: S = allmargin(tf(0.5,[1 0.2 1])); S.PMFrequency
Differences from MATLAB: grid bracketing can miss tangential or closely spaced crossings and a crossing exactly at zero frequency; delayed closed-loop stability may be undefined. Model arrays and non-square MIMO loops are unsupported.

## nichols
Nichols response: open-loop gain in dB against phase.
Syntax: [mag,phase,w] = nichols(sys[,w])
Syntax: nichols(sys1[,LineSpec1],sys2[,LineSpec2],...[,w])
mag, phase and w are the arrays bode returns (absolute magnitude, unwrapped degrees, the same automatic grid). w may be a frequency vector or a range {wmin, wmax} (1000 logarithmic points, wmax clipped at pi/Ts for discrete models). Without outputs, plots 20*log10(mag) against phase on one axes per I/O pair with the title Nichols chart; several systems overlay with optional line specifications. The grid is off; ngrid adds Nichols grid lines.
Example: G=tf(1,[1 0.4 1]); [mag,phase,w]=nichols(G,logspace(-1,1,20))
Example: nichols(tf(4,[1 2 1 0])); ngrid
Differences from MATLAB: MIMO responses use flattened 2-D columns like bode; automatic grids and plots differ. No plot-option objects or model arrays.

## ngrid
Nichols chart grid lines on the current axes.
Syntax: ngrid
Syntax: ngrid('new')
Draws contours of constant closed-loop magnitude (6 3 1 0.5 0.25 0 -1 -3 -6 -12 -20 -40 ... -240 dB) and constant closed-loop phase (-1 to -359 degrees) of T = L/(1+L) as light dotted lines with small labels, repeated over every 360-degree turn of the visible phase range. On empty axes the limits become [-360 0] by [-40 40]; otherwise the phase limits round out to whole turns and the gain limits cover at least -40..40 dB (explicit limits are kept). 'new' clears the axes first and leaves hold on.
Example: nichols(tf(1,[1 1 1])); ngrid
Example: ngrid
Differences from MATLAB: the contour levels, labels and colours are MatRust's own; at most 10 turns are drawn.

## sigma
Singular values of a frequency response.
Syntax: [sv,w] = sigma(sys[,w])
Syntax: sv = sigma(sys,w,type)
Syntax: sigma(sys1[,LineSpec1],sys2,...[,w][,type])
sv is min(ny,nu)-by-numel(w): the singular values of H(jw) (H(exp(j*w*Ts)) for discrete models) in descending order, absolute units. type 1 gives the singular values of inv(H), 2 of I+H and 3 of I+inv(H) (square systems only); w = [] keeps the automatic grid. Type 1 uses the reciprocals of the singular values of H and type 3 an LU solve, without forming an inverse; a singular H gives Inf. w may be a vector or {wmin, wmax}. Without outputs, plots every singular value in dB against logarithmic frequency on one axes.
Example: [sv,w] = sigma(tf(1,[1 0.4 1]), [0.1 1 10])
Example: sv = sigma(ss([-1 2;-3 -4],eye(2),eye(2),zeros(2)), [0.1 1], 2)
Differences from MATLAB: automatic grids and plots differ; no plot-option objects or model arrays.

## lyap
Solve continuous Lyapunov and Sylvester equations.
Syntax: X = lyap(A,Q)
Syntax: X = lyap(A,B,C)
lyap(A,Q) solves A*X + X*A' + Q = 0; lyap(A,B,C) solves the Sylvester equation A*X + X*B + C = 0 with C of size rows(A) by rows(B). Bartels-Stewart method: real Schur forms of A and B (made triangular with rsf2csf) and complex back-substitution; O(m^3+n^3) work, no Kronecker matrix or inverse. A unique solution exists only when lambda_i(A) + lambda_j(B) is nonzero for every eigenvalue pair; otherwise the error names that condition (a pair counts as zero below 100*eps*(norm(A,'fro')+norm(B,'fro'))).
Example: A=[-1 2;0 -3]; Q=eye(2); X=lyap(A,Q); norm(A*X+X*A'+Q)
Example: X=lyap([-1 0;1 -2],-4,[1;2])
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double matrices with at most 512 rows. The generalized form lyap(A,Q,[],E) is not supported yet. Q is not required to be symmetric and X is not symmetrized.

## dlyap
Solve discrete Lyapunov and Stein (discrete Sylvester) equations.
Syntax: X = dlyap(A,Q)
Syntax: X = dlyap(A,B,C)
dlyap(A,Q) solves A*X*A' - X + Q = 0; dlyap(A,B,C) solves A*X*B - X + C = 0 with C of size rows(A) by rows(B). Bartels-Stewart method on the triangular Schur forms of A and B (column-by-column back-substitution), no Kronecker matrix or inverse. A unique solution exists only when lambda_i(A)*lambda_j(B) differs from 1 for every eigenvalue pair; otherwise the error names that condition (relative tolerance 100*eps).
Example: A=[0.5 0.2;0 -0.4]; X=dlyap(A,eye(2)); norm(A*X*A'-X+eye(2))
Example: X=dlyap(0.5*eye(2),0.2,ones(2,1))
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double matrices with at most 512 rows. The generalized form dlyap(A,Q,[],E) is not supported yet.

## gram
Controllability or observability gramian of a stable LTI model.
Syntax: Wc = gram(sys,'c')
Syntax: Wo = gram(sys,'o')
gram(sys,'c') solves A*Wc + Wc*A' + B*B' = 0 (continuous) or A*Wc*A' - Wc + B*B' = 0 (discrete); gram(sys,'o') solves the dual equations with A' and C'*C. tf and zpk models are realized as ss first. The result is symmetrized. Every pole must be strictly stable (Re(p) < 0, or abs(p) < 1 for discrete models); otherwise gram reports an error.
Example: W = gram(ss([-1 0;1 -2],[1;0],[0 1],0),'c')
Example: W = gram(ss([0.5 0.1;0 -0.3],[1;1],[1 0],0,0.1),'o')
Differences from MATLAB: the Cholesky factor types 'cf' and 'of', model arrays and descriptor models are not supported yet.

## hsvd
Hankel singular values of an LTI model.
Syntax: hsv = hsvd(sys)
Syntax: hsv = hsvd(sys,'Offset',alpha)
hsv is a column vector: sqrt(eig(Wc*Wo)) of the stable part, computed as the singular values of Lo'*Lc for factors Wc = Lc*Lc' and Wo = Lo*Lo', in descending order. Unstable modes are split off with an ordered Schur form and reported first as Inf. A pole counts as stable when Re(p) < -alpha*max(1,abs(Im(p))) (continuous) or abs(p) < 1-alpha (discrete); alpha defaults to 1e-8.
Example: hsv = hsvd(tf([1 2],[1 3 3 1]))
Example: hsv = hsvd(zpk([],[1 -2 -3],1))
Differences from MATLAB: no plot without outputs, no hsvdOptions object and no BALDATA output.

## balreal
Balanced state-space realization.
Syntax: sysb = balreal(sys)
Syntax: [sysb,g,T,Ti] = balreal(sys)
Square-root balancing (Laub et al.) of the stable part: the gramians of sysb are both diag(g). xb = T*x and Ti = inv(T) is formed from the factors without an explicit inverse. Unstable modes are kept unchanged as the first states with g = Inf. The stable part must be minimal (no zero Hankel singular value); otherwise use minreal or balred. 'Offset',alpha moves the stability boundary as in hsvd.
Example: [sysb,g] = balreal(ss([-1 0;1 -2],[1;0],[0 1],0))
Example: [sysb,g,T,Ti] = balreal(tf(1,[1 3 2]))
Differences from MATLAB: no balredOptions object; the result is always an ss model.

## balred
Reduce model order by balanced truncation or singular perturbation.
Syntax: rsys = balred(sys,r)
Syntax: rsys = balred(sys,r,opts)
Syntax: rsys = balred(sys,r,'StateElimMethod',method)
Syntax: rsys = balred(sys,r,'Offset',alpha)
method is 'MatchDC' (default, singular perturbation that keeps the DC gain) or 'Truncate'. opts is a struct from balredOptions; its StateProjection field selects the same method. The name/value form 'StateElimMethod',method is also accepted. The stable part is balanced and its weakest states removed; unstable modes are always kept, so r must be at least their number. For the stable part the H-infinity error is at most twice the sum of the discarded Hankel singular values. States with zero Hankel singular value are removed first, so the result may have fewer than r states.
Example: rsys = balred(tf(1,[1 6 11 6]),1)
Example: rsys = balred(ss(diag([-1 -5 -20]),[1;1;1],[1 1 1],0),2,'StateElimMethod','Truncate')
Differences from MATLAB: r must be a scalar (a vector of orders, which returns a model array, is an error); no plot without outputs; opts is a struct and only StateProjection is read from it; the result is always an ss model.

## balredOptions
Options for balanced truncation.
Syntax: opts = balredOptions
Syntax: opts = balredOptions(Name,Value,...)
Returns a struct whose StateProjection field is 'MatchDC' (default; singular perturbation that keeps the DC gain) or 'Truncate' (drop the weakest states and leave the others unchanged). The older name 'StateElimMethod' sets the same field. Other names are an error. Pass the struct as the third argument of balred. Names are case-insensitive.
Example: opts = balredOptions
Example: opts = balredOptions('StateProjection','Truncate')
Example: rsys = balred(tf(1,[1 6 11 6]),1,balredOptions('StateElimMethod','Truncate'))
Differences from MATLAB: returns a struct, not an options object. ErrorBound, Regularization, Offset, FreqIntervals and TimeIntervals are not accepted here; Offset remains a name/value argument of balred.

## modred
Eliminate chosen states of a state-space model.
Syntax: rsys = modred(sys,elim)
Syntax: rsys = modred(sys,elim,method)
elim lists state indices or is a logical vector of length order(sys). method 'MatchDC' (default) sets the derivatives (continuous) or increments (discrete) of the eliminated states to zero, which keeps the DC gain; 'Truncate' deletes them. The remaining states keep their order. A singular eliminated block is an error for 'MatchDC'. 'mdc' and 'del' are accepted as older names.
Example: rsys = modred(ss(diag([-1 -10]),[1;1],[1 1],0),2)
Example: rsys = modred(ss(diag([-1 -10]),[1;1],[1 1],0),[false true],'Truncate')
Differences from MATLAB: the result is always an ss model.

## filtord
Order of a digital filter.
Syntax: n = filtord(b,a)
Syntax: n = filtord(sos)
Syntax: n = filtord(d)
n is the degree in z^-1 of B(z)/A(z) without pole/zero cancellation: trailing zero coefficients are ignored, leading zeros count as delay. filtord(b) uses a = 1. A K-by-6 matrix is read as second-order sections [b0 b1 b2 a0 a1 a2] (a single 1-by-6 row only when a0 = 1); its order is the larger of the summed numerator and denominator section degrees. d is a digitalFilter from designfilt.
Example: n = filtord([1 2 1],[1 -0.5])   % 2
Example: n = filtord([1 1 0 1 0.5 0; 1 0 1 1 0 0.25])   % 3
Example: n = filtord(fir1(20,0.3))   % 20
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## pzmap
Pole-zero map of LTI models.
Syntax: pzmap(sys)
Syntax: pzmap(sys1,sys2,...)
Syntax: pzmap(ax,...)
Syntax: [p,z] = pzmap(sys)
With outputs, returns pole(sys) and zero(sys) as column vectors and draws nothing. Without outputs, draws poles as x markers and zeros as o markers on the current (or given) axes with the ordinary plot function, dashed lines along the real and imaginary axes, and for discrete models the dotted unit circle. Title 'Pole-Zero Map', axis labels 'Real Axis' and 'Imaginary Axis'.
Example: [p,z]=pzmap(tf([1 2],[1 4 5]))
Example: pzmap(zpk(-1,[-2 -3],1), tf(1,[1 0.5],0.1))
Differences from MATLAB: the axis lines and unit circle are ordinary line series, so legend lists them; no grid of damping/natural-frequency lines and no data tips. At most 16 overlaid models.

## zplane
Zero-pole plot of a discrete-time filter.
Syntax: zplane(z, p)
Syntax: zplane(b, a)
Syntax: zplane(sos)
Column vectors are zeros z and poles p; row vectors are numerator b and denominator a coefficients in powers of z^-1 (the shorter one is padded with trailing zeros, which places the extra roots at the origin); an L-by-6 matrix with L >= 2 is second-order sections. Draws zeros as 'o' and poles as 'x' in the current axes, with dashed real and imaginary axes, the dotted unit circle, axis labels and equal axis scaling.
Example: zplane([1 1], [1 -0.5 0.25])
Example: zplane([0.5; -0.5], [0.9i; -0.9i])
Example: zplane([1 2 1 1 -0.5 0.3; 1 -1 0.5 1 0.2 0.4])
Differences from MATLAB: no output handles, no multiplicity labels and no filter-object input.

## pid
Parallel-form PID controller object.
Syntax: C = pid(Kp)
Syntax: C = pid(Kp,Ki)
Syntax: C = pid(Kp,Ki,Kd)
Syntax: C = pid(Kp,Ki,Kd,Tf)
Syntax: C = pid(Kp,Ki,Kd,Tf,Ts)
Syntax: C = pid(Cstd)
C = Kp + Ki/s + Kd*s/(Tf*s+1); missing gains are zero, Tf = 0 means an unfiltered derivative. Properties Kp, Ki, Kd, Tf, Ts, IFormula, DFormula, InputName and OutputName are read and assigned with dot syntax (assignments are validated). Discrete controllers (Ts > 0) use the forward-Euler integrator Ts/(z-1) for both the integral and the derivative filter. C converts to a transfer function in one place, so tf(C), zpk(C), ss(C), C*G, feedback, series, step, bode and margin work as for that transfer function. pid(Cstd) converts a pidstd object.
Example: C=pid(2,1,0.5,0.1); G=tf(1,[1 2 1]); T=feedback(C*G,1); [y,t]=step(T,0:0.1:5);
Example: C=pid(1,2); C.Ki=4; tf(C)
Example: Cd=pid(1,0.5,0,0,0.1)
Differences from MATLAB: scalar SISO controllers only (no arrays of controllers, delays or time units); IFormula and DFormula accept only 'ForwardEuler', other formulas are not supported yet. ss(C) of an unfiltered derivative is rejected (improper).

## pidstd
Standard-form PID controller object.
Syntax: C = pidstd(Kp)
Syntax: C = pidstd(Kp,Ti)
Syntax: C = pidstd(Kp,Ti,Td)
Syntax: C = pidstd(Kp,Ti,Td,N)
Syntax: C = pidstd(Kp,Ti,Td,N,Ts)
Syntax: C = pidstd(Cpar)
C = Kp*(1 + 1/(Ti*s) + Td*s/((Td/N)*s+1)); Ti = Inf (default) removes the integral term, Td = 0 (default) the derivative and N = Inf (default) its filter. Properties Kp, Ti, Td, N, Ts, IFormula, DFormula, InputName and OutputName. Conversions and arithmetic behave as for pid; discrete forms use the forward-Euler integrator. pidstd(Cpar) converts a pid object with nonzero Kp.
Example: C=pidstd(2,4,0.5,10); tf(C)
Example: C=pidstd(1,2); Cp=pid(C)
Differences from MATLAB: same limits as pid; only the 'ForwardEuler' formulas.

## pidtune
Tune a PID controller for a SISO plant by a documented phase-margin rule.
Syntax: [C,info] = pidtune(G,type)
Syntax: [C,info] = pidtune(G,type,wc)
Syntax: [C,info] = pidtune(G,type,opts)
Syntax: [C,info] = pidtune(G,type,wc,opts)
type is 'P', 'I', 'PI', 'PD', 'PDF', 'PID' or 'PIDF'. Returns a parallel pid object and info with fields Stable, CrossoverFrequency and PhaseMargin. opts comes from pidtuneOptions; its PhaseMargin (default 60 degrees) sets the target, and wc = [] keeps the default crossover. The gains differ from MATLAB's pidtune, which uses a different (unpublished) method. Rule used here: at the crossover wc the loop must satisfy abs(C(jwc)*G(jwc)) = 1 and angle = PhaseMargin - 180 degrees (-120 for the default 60). Integral types fix Ki = Kp*wc/10 (a 5.71 degree lag at wc), except PI with a given wc, which solves Kp and Ki for the target when the needed phase lies between -90 and 0 degrees; PDF and PIDF fix Tf = 1/(10*wc). P, I and PI have one free gain at the default wc: Kp (or Ki for I) gives abs(C*G) = 1, and the default wc is the frequency where the phase of G equals the target minus the controller's own phase (0 for P, -90 for I, -5.71 for PI), so the margin is exactly the target; with a given wc, P and I reach whatever margin results. PD, PDF, PID and PIDF solve Kp and Kd in closed form from the complex target; their default wc is where the phase of G is the target minus 30 degrees (-150 for a 60 degree margin). If the required phase never occurs, wc falls back to the gain crossover of G, then to 1 rad/s. The closed loop feedback(C*G,1) is checked; an unstable result (or one that needs negative gains) is an error.
Example: G=tf(1,[1 3 3 1]); [C,info]=pidtune(G,'PID')
Example: [C,info]=pidtune(tf(1,[1 2 0]),'PI',0.5);
Example: [C,info]=pidtune(tf(1,[1 3 3 1]),'PIDF',[],pidtuneOptions('PhaseMargin',45));
Differences from MATLAB: different tuning method and gains; continuous SISO plants only; DesignFocus is accepted but does not change the design; no 2-DOF types; unstable results are errors instead of warnings.

## pidtuneOptions
Options for pidtune: target phase margin and design focus.
Syntax: opts = pidtuneOptions
Syntax: opts = pidtuneOptions(Name,Value,...)
Returns a struct with PhaseMargin (degrees, default 60, between 0 and 180) and DesignFocus ('balanced' by default, 'reference-tracking' or 'disturbance-rejection'). Pass it as the last argument of pidtune. Names are case-insensitive.
Example: opts = pidtuneOptions('PhaseMargin',45)
Example: [C,info] = pidtune(tf(1,[1 3 3 1]),'PI',pidtuneOptions('PhaseMargin',50));
Differences from MATLAB: returns a struct, not an options object; DesignFocus is validated but does not change the design; NumUnstablePoles is not supported.

## periodogram
Windowed single-segment power spectrum or density.
Syntax: [pxx,w] = periodogram(x,window,nfft)
Syntax: [pxx,f] = periodogram(x,window,nfft,fs,'onesided','psd')
Optional arguments may be omitted or replaced by []. Defaults: rectangular window covering x, nfft=max(256,next power of two of length(x)), no detrending, one-sided for real input and two-sided for complex input. Without fs, frequency is radians/sample and density is power per radian/sample; with fs it is Hz and power/Hz. Trailing 'onesided', 'twosided', or 'centered' selects the range; 'power' divides by squared window sum instead of fs times window energy. Interior one-sided powers double, excluding DC and an even-length Nyquist bin. Matrix columns are independent channels. With no outputs, plots dB versus frequency.
Example: [p,w] = periodogram([1 0 -1 0],[],16);
Example: [p,f] = periodogram(1:16,[],32,100,'centered','power');
Differences from MATLAB: only finite 2-D arrays; window must cover the entire signal, FFT length must be at least window length, and frequency vectors as FFT specifications are unsupported. FFT length is limited to 1048576, with additional work and memory limits.

## pwelch
Average overlapping windowed periodograms.
Syntax: [pxx,w] = pwelch(x,window,noverlap,nfft)
Syntax: [pxx,f] = pwelch(x,window,noverlap,nfft,fs)
Defaults (also selected by []): symmetric Hamming window of max(1,floor(2*N/9)) samples to target eight segments, overlap=floor(window length/2), nfft=max(256,next power of two of window length), no detrending, PSD scaling, one-sided for real input. A scalar window specifies its length; a vector supplies its weights. Incomplete trailing segments are discarded. Columns are independent channels. Without fs, frequency is radians/sample and density is power per radian/sample; with fs it is Hz and power/Hz. Trailing 'onesided', 'twosided', 'centered', 'psd', 'power' work as in periodogram. With no outputs, plots dB versus frequency.
Example: [p,w] = pwelch(1:64);
Example: [p,f] = pwelch([(1:64)' (64:-1:1)'],hamming(16),8,32,100);
Differences from MATLAB: no confidence intervals, reassignment, frequency-vector grids, or alternative averaging; finite arrays only. FFT length must be at least window length and at most 1048576; work and memory limits also apply. Short inputs can yield a segment count other than eight.

## cpsd
Cross power density from overlapping windowed transforms.
Syntax: [pxy,w] = cpsd(x,y,window,noverlap,nfft)
Syntax: [pxy,f] = cpsd(x,y,window,noverlap,nfft,fs)
Uses mean(conj(FFT(x))*FFT(y)), preserving cross-spectrum phase. Defaults, empty placeholders, scalar or vector window, frequency ranges, PSD/power scaling, and incomplete-tail handling match pwelch: symmetric Hamming, eight target segments, 50 percent overlap, nfft at least 256, no detrending. Real inputs default to one-sided; complex inputs to two-sided. Columns must match. Without fs, frequency is radians/sample and density is power per radian/sample; fs selects Hz and power/Hz. No outputs plots cross-spectrum magnitude in dB.
Example: [p,w] = cpsd(1:64,filter([1 0.5],1,1:64));
Differences from MATLAB: unequal signal lengths and channel counts are rejected; no confidence intervals or frequency-vector grids. FFT, work, and memory limits match pwelch.

## mscohere
Magnitude-squared coherence from averaged auto and cross spectra.
Syntax: [cxy,w] = mscohere(x,y,window,noverlap,nfft)
Syntax: [cxy,f] = mscohere(x,y,window,noverlap,nfft,fs)
Returns abs(Pxy)^2/(Pxx*Pyy), between zero and one, with NaN where either autospectrum is zero. Defaults and segment options match pwelch: symmetric Hamming, eight target segments, 50 percent overlap, nfft at least 256, no detrending, one-sided for real inputs. Frequency is radians/sample without fs, Hz with fs. Matching columns are processed independently. Trailing range and scaling flags are accepted; scaling cancels in the ratio. With no outputs, plots coherence versus frequency.
Example: [c,w] = mscohere(1:64,1:64);
Differences from MATLAB: no confidence intervals, frequency-vector grids, or unequal input lengths; finite arrays and the pwelch resource limits apply.

## tfestimate
H1 transfer estimate from overlapping windowed spectra.
Syntax: [txy,w] = tfestimate(x,y,window,noverlap,nfft)
Syntax: [txy,f] = tfestimate(x,y,window,noverlap,nfft,fs)
Returns Pxy/Pxx with Pxy=mean(conj(FFT(x))*FFT(y)); x is the input and y the output. Defaults and segment options match pwelch: symmetric Hamming, eight target segments, 50 percent overlap, nfft at least 256, no detrending, one-sided for real inputs. Frequency is radians/sample without fs, Hz with fs. Matching columns are independent. Trailing range and scaling flags are accepted; scaling cancels in the ratio. Zero input power gives undefined bins. With no outputs, plots 20*log10(abs(txy)).
Example: [h,w] = tfestimate(1:64,filter([0.5 0.5],1,1:64));
Differences from MATLAB: only H1 is implemented; no H2 estimator, confidence intervals, or frequency-vector grids. Finite arrays and pwelch resource limits apply. Finite segments can bias comparisons with a filter's exact response.

## spectrogram
Complex short-time transforms and optional per-frame power density.
Syntax: [s,f,t] = spectrogram(x,window,noverlap,nfft)
Syntax: [s,f,t,ps] = spectrogram(x,window,noverlap,nfft,fs)
Returns raw windowed FFTs in columns, frequencies in a column and frame-center times in a row. Required segment parameters accept [] for pwelch defaults: symmetric Hamming of max(1,floor(2*N/9)) samples, 50 percent overlap, nfft=max(256,next power of two of window length). A scalar window selects a Hamming length. Uses complete frames, no boundary padding and no detrending. Default range is one-sided for real input, two-sided for complex input; trailing 'onesided', 'twosided', 'centered' select it. The fourth output is abs(s)^2/(fs*sum(window.^2)) with one-sided interior doubling. Without fs, frequency is radians/sample, times are samples, and density is power per radian/sample. 'power' selects squared-window-sum normalization. With fs, frequency is Hz and times are seconds. Request outputs; image plotting is unavailable.
Example: [s,f,t,ps] = spectrogram(sin(1:128),hamming(32),16,64,100);
Differences from MATLAB: vectors only; no image plots, reassignment, or frequency-vector grids. FFT length must be at least window length and at most 1048576; work and memory limits apply.

## stft
Short-time Fourier transform with boundary padding.
Syntax: [s,f,t] = stft(x)
Syntax: [s,f,t] = stft(x,fs,'Window',w,'OverlapLength',n,'FFTLength',m)
Returns raw windowed FFTs in columns, frequencies in a column, and center times in a row. Defaults: symmetric Hann window of min(128,length(x)) samples, overlap=floor(3*window length/4), FFT length=window length, two-sided centered frequency ordering, no detrending. 'FrequencyRange' accepts 'centered', 'twosided', 'onesided' (real input only). Pads floor(window length/2) zeros at both ends and pads the tail to a whole hop. The first frame is centered at sample zero. Without fs, frequency is radians/sample and time is samples; fs selects Hz and seconds. Optional fourth output gives per-frame PSD. Request outputs; image plotting is unavailable.
Example: [s,f,t] = stft(sin(1:128));
Example: [s,f,t] = stft(1:64,100,'Window',hann(16),'OverlapLength',8,'FFTLength',32);
Differences from MATLAB: vectors only, raw FFT normalization, explicit zero boundary padding, no image plots or timetable inputs. Output length after inversion can include padded tail samples. FFT, work, and memory limits apply.

## istft
Reconstruct a signal by weighted overlap-add of short-time transforms.
Syntax: [x,t] = istft(s)
Syntax: [x,t] = istft(s,fs,'Window',w,'OverlapLength',n,'FFTLength',m)
Uses inverse FFT, multiplies by the synthesis window, and divides by accumulated squared windows. Supply the same window, overlap, FFT length, sample rate and 'FrequencyRange' used by stft. Defaults: symmetric Hann of min(128,inferred FFT length), 75 percent overlap rounded down, FFT length inferred from frequency bins, centered range. For one-sided input, FFT length is inferred as 2*(number of bins-1); otherwise it is the number of bins. Explicit FFTLength also sets the default window length; specify it for odd one-sided transforms. Removes floor(window length/2) boundary samples at each end. A whole-hop input round trips to rounding accuracy under COLA; NOLA windows also reconstruct when all retained weights are nonzero. 'OutputLength' trims padded tail samples when the original length was not a whole hop. Output time is samples without fs, seconds with fs. Complex signals are retained; exactly conjugate-symmetric spectra produce real reconstructions.
Example: s=stft(sin(1:128)); [x,t]=istft(s);
Example: s=stft(1:63,'Window',hamming(16),'OverlapLength',8); [x,t]=istft(s,'Window',hamming(16),'OverlapLength',8,'OutputLength',63);
Differences from MATLAB: raw-FFT input, zero-padding convention paired with this stft, vectors only, and no timetable or alternate synthesis methods. Uncovered output samples error. FFT length is at most 1048576; work and memory limits apply.

## findpeaks
Find interior maxima, their locations, widths and prominences.
Syntax: [pks,locs,w,p] = findpeaks(y[,x],Name,Value,...)
Syntax: findpeaks(y[,x],Name,Value,...)
Use finite real vectors; x must increase strictly and match y. Without x, locations are one-based sample indices. Endpoints are excluded. A flat top uses its first sample. Prominence is peak height minus the higher of the two minima reached before a strictly higher sample or an endpoint; equal-height peaks do not stop the search. WidthReference 'halfprom' (default) measures width at peak height minus half its prominence, bounded by those minima. 'halfheight' uses half the absolute height and may extend to the signal endpoints; nonpositive peaks have zero half-height width. Crossings use linear interpolation in x. Widths and distances use x units.
Options: MinPeakHeight (default -Inf), MinPeakProminence (0), MinPeakDistance (0), Threshold (0), NPeaks (all), SortStr ('none', 'ascend', 'descend'), WidthReference ('halfprom', 'halfheight'), MinPeakWidth (0), MaxPeakWidth (Inf). MinPeakHeight is strict: a peak equal to the limit is excluded. Threshold requires both drops from a flat top to its adjacent samples to meet the threshold. Height, threshold, prominence and width gates precede greedy distance suppression. Tallest peaks win; ties choose the first sample. SortStr orders the surviving peaks before NPeaks truncation. All four outputs are row vectors. With no output, plot the signal and mark the selected peaks.
Example: [p,l,w,q] = findpeaks([0 2 0 1 0],'MinPeakProminence',1);
Example: findpeaks([0 2 0 1 0]);
Differences from MATLAB: finite real vectors only; flat tops and selection order follow the definitions above. No sample-rate scalar, datetime coordinates or annotation options. At most 1048576 samples; prominence, width and distance searches use bounded O(N log N) work and linear scratch storage.

## resample
Change a signal's sample rate with a delay-compensated polyphase FIR.
Syntax: y = resample(x,p,q[,n,beta])
Reduce positive integer p/q by their greatest common divisor. Design a 2*n*max(p,q)+1-tap Kaiser-windowed sinc with cutoff 1/max(p,q), unit DC gain before scaling by p, default n=10 and beta=5. Evaluate only the necessary convolution phases and remove the integer FIR group delay. The input is zero outside its extent; output length is ceil(length*p/q). Row vectors retain orientation; matrices operate down columns.
Example: y = resample([0 1 0 -1 0],3,2);
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double inputs only, no time coordinates or supplied filter form. n is positive, beta is 0..100, ratios at most 65536, FIR order at most 4096, and input/output at most 1048576 elements.

## decimate
Lowpass filter then reduce the sample rate by an integer factor.
Syntax: y = decimate(x,r[,n,'fir'|'iir'])
Default: order-8 Chebyshev I lowpass, 0.05 dB ripple and cutoff 0.8/r relative to Nyquist. Forward/backward SOS filtering uses steady-state initial conditions and odd reflection of 3*(n+1) samples at each end, then selects samples 1,1+r,... . The 'fir' form defaults to order 30, a Hamming-windowed sinc at cutoff 1/r with delay compensation and zero extension. This form requires even n. Matrices operate down columns.
Example: y = decimate(sin(0:0.1:12.7),4);
Example: y = decimate([0 1 0 -1 0],2,30,'fir');
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double inputs only, r is 2..1024. IIR orders must be 1..20 and require more than 3*(n+1) samples. Odd FIR orders and streaming-state forms are rejected.

## interp
Interpolate by an integer factor with a windowed-sinc lowpass.
Syntax: y = interp(x,r[,l,alpha])
Use a 2*l*r+1-tap Kaiser-windowed cardinal sinc (beta=5), cutoff 1/r relative to the output Nyquist and exact delay compensation. The sinc has center tap one and zeros at every other original sample position; it is not normalized for DC, so original samples are preserved. interp(x,1) returns x. Defaults: l=4, alpha=0.5. alpha declares the input band of interest [0,alpha], rather than moving the cutoff into that band. This fixed-window design uses the same taps for each alpha; increase l for a narrower transition and better fidelity between original samples near input Nyquist. Output has r times as many samples. Input is zero outside its extent. Matrices operate down columns.
Example: y = interp([0 1 0 -1 0],4);
Differences from MATLAB: this is a windowed-sinc design, not the Oetken/Parks/Schuessler design. Finite real double inputs only; 1<=r<=1024, 1<=l<=2048, 0<alpha<=1, order at most 4096 and output at most 1048576 elements.

## hilbert
Construct the complex analytic signal by Fourier projection.
Syntax: z = hilbert(x)
Keep DC and the even-length Nyquist bin, double positive-frequency bins and zero negative-frequency bins, then inverse transform. Row vectors retain orientation; matrices operate down columns. The finite input is treated as one period, so nonperiodic endpoint discontinuities affect the result.
Example: z = hilbert([1 0 -1 0]);
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double input only; no transform-length argument. At most 1048576 elements. Uses the shared bounded FFT implementation.

## envelope
Compute upper and lower analytic, RMS or peak envelopes.
Syntax: [up,lo] = envelope(x[,n,'analytic'|'rms'|'peak'])
Default 'analytic': subtract each column's mean, take the magnitude of its FFT analytic signal, then add/subtract this magnitude about that mean. n defaults to 3 and is validated but does not alter the exact FFT projection. 'rms': centered length-n root-mean-square, truncating the window at the ends, with lower envelope equal to -up; even windows include one extra sample to the left. 'peak': piecewise-linear interpolation through local maxima/minima and endpoints; nearby extrema less than n samples apart keep the more extreme of the adjacent pair, choosing the first on ties. Matrices operate down columns.
Example: [up,lo] = envelope([0 1 0 -1],3,'analytic');
Example: [up,lo] = envelope([0 1 0 -1 0],3,'rms');
Example: [up,lo] = envelope([0 2 0 -2 0 2 0],1,'peak');
Differences from MATLAB: analytic uses a periodic FFT rather than a length-n FIR; peak uses linear interpolation rather than splines. Finite real doubles only, 1<=n<=4097; no dimension argument.

## medfilt1
Filter each signal column with a centered running median.
Syntax: y = medfilt1(x[,n][,'zeropad'|'truncate'])
Default n=3 and 'zeropad' (zero padding at each endpoint). 'truncate' omits samples outside the input. Even n uses offsets -n/2 through n/2-1 and averages the two middle sorted values. Row vectors retain their orientation.
Example: y = medfilt1([1 9 2 3 4],3);
Example: y = medfilt1([1 9 2 3 4],4,'truncate');
Example: y = medfilt1([1 9 2 3 4],3,'zeropad');
Differences from MATLAB: finite real doubles only; no NaN policy or dimension options. At most 1048576 input elements and window length 1..4097. The work cap is 2000000000 estimated sorting operations: numel(x)*n*(floor(log2(n))+1). For example, n=101 is supported at the full input limit; n=4097 on a million samples exceeds the cap. Computation remains cancellable.

## sgolay
Construct Savitzky-Golay polynomial smoothing and coefficient matrices.
Syntax: [b,g] = sgolay(order,framelen)
Fit powers of the centered sample offset by least squares (Savitzky and Golay, 1964). Use a scaled Vandermonde matrix and SVD. b is the framelen-by-framelen projection onto fitted polynomials. Column k+1 of g estimates the coefficient of offset^k; multiply by k! for a kth derivative per sample. Smoothing weights are the center row of b, or the first column of g.
Example: [b,g] = sgolay(3,7);
Differences from MATLAB: unweighted real double design only. framelen must be positive, odd and at most 255; 0<=order<framelen and order<=20. Very high orders may lose accuracy due to conditioning.

## sgolayfilt
Smooth signals by local least-squares polynomial fits.
Syntax: y = sgolayfilt(x,order,framelen)
Use the center fit inside the signal. Near each endpoint, fit the first/last full frame and evaluate the polynomial at the current sample. This preserves polynomials through the requested order, including at the endpoints. Matrices operate down columns; each column needs at least framelen samples. See sgolay for design bounds.
Example: y = sgolayfilt([1 4 9 16 25 36 49],2,5);
Differences from MATLAB: finite real double inputs, unweighted smoothing only; no dimension or weighting arguments.

## lowpass
Apply a delay-compensated Kaiser FIR lowpass.
Syntax: [y,d] = lowpass(x,wpass[,fs],'Steepness',s,'StopbandAttenuation',a)
Default fs=2 makes wpass relative to Nyquist. The transition extends upward from wpass by (1-s)*(Nyquist-wpass). Place the design cutoff at its midpoint. Defaults s=0.85, a=60 dB; use Kaiser's order estimate ceil((a-8)/(2.285*pi*normalized_transition_width)), rounded up to an even order, and a Kaiser window. Remove the integer group delay and use zero extension. d is a struct with order, coefficients and type. Matrices operate down columns.
Example: [y,d] = lowpass([0 1 0 -1 0],0.3,'Steepness',0.75);
Differences from MATLAB: FIR only with the stated transition rule; finite real doubles, 0<s<1, 21<=a<=160 dB, order<=4096 and at most 1048576 input elements. Convolution work is capped at numel(x)*(order+1)<=2000000000 multiply-add terms; cancellation remains available. Common default designs, including bandpass(x,[0.1 0.2]), support the full input limit. Attenuation is an approximate design target; finite-window ripple can slightly exceed it.

## highpass
Apply a delay-compensated Kaiser FIR highpass.
Syntax: [y,d] = highpass(x,wpass[,fs],'Steepness',s,'StopbandAttenuation',a)
The transition extends downward from wpass by (1-s)*wpass; use its midpoint as cutoff. Defaults, Kaiser order formula, zero extension, column behavior and d fields follow lowpass.
Example: [y,d] = highpass([0 1 0 -1 0],0.6,'StopbandAttenuation',50);
Differences from MATLAB: FIR only, with the stated transition rule and lowpass's finite-input, order and option bounds.

## bandpass
Apply a delay-compensated Kaiser FIR bandpass.
Syntax: [y,d] = bandpass(x,[flo fhi][,fs],'Steepness',s,'StopbandAttenuation',a)
Passband edges increase strictly inside Nyquist. Each transition extends outward by (1-s)*min(flo,Nyquist-fhi); use the transition midpoints as design cutoffs. Defaults, Kaiser order formula, zero extension, column behavior and d fields follow lowpass.
Example: [y,d] = bandpass([0 1 0 -1 0],[0.3 0.6]);
Differences from MATLAB: FIR only, with the stated transition rule and lowpass's finite-input, order and option bounds.

## bandstop
Apply a delay-compensated Kaiser FIR bandstop.
Syntax: [y,d] = bandstop(x,[flo fhi][,fs],'Steepness',s,'StopbandAttenuation',a)
Passbands lie below flo and above fhi. Each transition extends into the stopband by (1-s)*(fhi-flo)/2; use its midpoint as design cutoff. Defaults, Kaiser order formula, zero extension, column behavior and d fields follow lowpass.
Example: [y,d] = bandstop([0 1 0 -1 0],[0.3 0.6]);
Differences from MATLAB: FIR only, with the stated transition rule and lowpass's finite-input, order and option bounds.

## fir2
Design a symmetric FIR by frequency sampling and windowing.
Syntax: b = fir2(n,f,m[,npt,lap,window])
Syntax: b = fir2(n,f,m,window)
Syntax: b = fir2(n,f,m,npt,window)
f and m give a piecewise-linear desired response on [0,1] relative to Nyquist; f must start at 0 and end at 1. Default npt is max(512,next_power_of_two(n+1)), specifying npt+1 mesh points. Inverse-transform the response with linear phase n/2, retain n+1 taps and multiply by a symmetric Hamming window, or the supplied n+1 window values. A repeated interior frequency represents a jump: lap spreads the pair by lap/(2*npt) on each side; default lap=0 uses machine epsilon. Only paired repeats are accepted.
Example: b = fir2(32,[0 0.3 0.5 1],[1 1 0 0]);
Example: b = fir2(16,[0 0.4 0.4 1],[1 1 0 0],512,4,hann(17));
Example: b = fir2(16,[0 0.3 0.5 1],[1 1 0 0],512,hann(17));
Differences from MATLAB: the stated mesh and jump conventions are explicit. Odd n requires zero desired Nyquist gain. 1<=n<=4096, n<npt<=65536, lap<=npt/2, at most 8192 breakpoints and bounded inverse-transform work. No antisymmetric design option.

## firpm
Design an equiripple FIR by iterative Remez exchange.
Syntax: b = firpm(n,f,a[,w][,'bandpass'|'hilbert'|'differentiator'])
Each increasing pair in f defines a constrained band relative to Nyquist; a supplies the two endpoint amplitudes per band and interpolates linearly inside it. w supplies one positive error weight per band, default one. 'bandpass' selects symmetric linear phase (also for lowpass, highpass and multiband responses). 'hilbert' selects antisymmetry. 'differentiator' also uses a(f) itself as the desired amplitude, with error weight w/f on bands with nonzero desired amplitudes; [0 pi] over [0 1] requests magnitude omega in radians/sample. Odd/even tap counts cover symmetry types I-IV. Follows alternating-error exchange (McClellan, Parks and Rabiner, 1973), using barycentric Lagrange interpolation on a dense mesh of 128 points per independent coefficient. Both edges of every band are candidates; the exchange retains the largest alternating errors. A failed or unconverged exchange returns an error.
Example: b = firpm(32,[0 0.3 0.45 1],[1 1 0 0]);
Example: b = firpm(31,[0.1 1],[1 1],'hilbert');
Example: b = firpm(21,[0 1],[0 pi],'differentiator');
Differences from MATLAB: finite real designs only, order 1..256, at most 32 bands and 100 iterations under a bounded work budget; no custom response callbacks or diagnostic outputs. Exact endpoint gains must respect the chosen symmetry. Grid rounding and convergence can differ from other Remez implementations.


## string
Convert supported values to strings.
Syntax: s = string(x)
Accepts char rows/matrices, cellstr, numeric and logical values. Numbers use shortest round-trip text.
Example: string({'a','b'})
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## strings
Create an array of empty strings.
Syntax: s = strings(n,m)
Two-dimensional arrays only; each element contains empty text.
Example: strings(2,3)
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## missing
Create a missing string scalar.
Syntax: s = missing
Missing propagates through text operations; comparisons are false except ~=.
Example: ismissing(missing)
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## ismissing
Identify numeric NaNs, empty char rows in cellstr, or missing string elements.
Syntax: tf = ismissing(s)
Returns a logical array with the same shape.
Example: ismissing(["a" missing])
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## isstring
Test whether a value has string class.
Syntax: tf = isstring(x)
Character arrays are a separate class.
Example: isstring("abc")
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## strlength
Count UTF-16 code units in each string.
Syntax: n = strlength(s)
Missing elements return NaN.
Example: strlength(["abc" "x"])
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## strip
Remove edge whitespace or chosen characters.
Syntax: s = strip(s,side,characters)
side is left, right or both; default both removes Unicode whitespace, but keeps significant whitespace char(133), char(160), char(8199) and char(8239) unless that character is named. strip(s,'-') strips '-' from both ends. Char and cellstr inputs retain their type.
Example: strip("--a--",'both','-')
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## contains
Test for text within each string, or for points inside an imref2d.
Syntax: tf = contains(s,pattern,'IgnoreCase',flag)
Syntax: tf = contains(R, xWorld, yWorld)
Each subject matches if any pattern matches; the result has the subject's shape. With an imref2d R, tf is a logical array of the size of xWorld that is true where the point lies inside or on the border of R.XWorldLimits by R.YWorldLimits.
Example: contains(["ABC" "def"],"b",'IgnoreCase',true)
Example: contains(imref2d([2 3]), [1 3.5 4], [1 2.5 1])   % [1 1 0]
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## count
Count occurrences of patterns in text.
Syntax: n = count(str, pat)
Syntax: n = count(str, pat, 'IgnoreCase', flag)
str is a character vector, cellstr or string array; pat is text or a list of patterns. The text is scanned from left to right; at each position the patterns are tried in order and a match consumes its characters, so a segment is counted at most once. n is a double array with the shape of str (a character vector counts as one element); missing strings count 0 and empty patterns never match.
Example: count("the cat sat on the mat", "at")   % 3
Example: count({'aaaa', 'abab'}, 'aa')   % [2 0]
Example: count('abcabc', {'bc', 'a'})   % 4
Example: count("Hello hello", "hello", 'IgnoreCase', true)   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: pattern objects (digitsPattern etc.) are not supported.

## startsWith
Test the beginning of each string.
Syntax: tf = startsWith(s,pattern,'IgnoreCase',flag)
IgnoreCase defaults to false.
Example: startsWith(["abc" "def"],"a")
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## endsWith
Test the end of each string.
Syntax: tf = endsWith(s,pattern,'IgnoreCase',flag)
IgnoreCase defaults to false.
Example: endsWith(["abc" "def"],"f")
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## replace
Replace literal text within each string.
Syntax: s = replace(s,old,new)
Each old/new pair is applied in order to every subject. Char and cellstr inputs retain their type.
Example: replace(["ab" "ac"],"a","z")
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## split
Split text into strings, or cellstr for char/cellstr input.
Syntax: s = split(s,delimiter)
Syntax: [y,m,d] = split(cd,{'years','months','days'})
For calendarDuration input, split returns numeric years, months and days, and optionally a duration for the time unit; units must be unique and in calendar order.
Example: [y,m,d] = split(calendarDuration(1,2,3),{'years','months','days'})
A scalar becomes a column. Column vectors add a second axis with equal piece counts. Row vectors and matrices requiring a third axis are unsupported. Repeated delimiters collapse by default; pass 'CollapseDelimiters',false to retain empty pieces.
Example: split("a,b",",")
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## join
Join strings along their last nonsingleton axis.
Syntax: s = join(s,delimiter)
The default delimiter is a space. Missing values propagate.
Example: join(["a" "b";"c" "d"],"-")
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## compose
Format each row using successive data columns.
Syntax: s = compose(format,values,...)
For one data array, each format consumes successive columns across a row; a single conversion retains the input shape. Data columns must be a multiple of the format input count. Inputs expand along singleton axes; format syntax follows sprintf. A char format returns cellstr; a string format returns strings.
Example: compose("x=%d",[1 2])
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## extractBefore
Extract text before a pattern or position.
Syntax: s = extractBefore(s,boundary)
Positions count UTF-16 code units, starting at one. A position splitting a surrogate pair is unsupported.
Example: extractBefore("abc",2)
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## extractAfter
Extract text after a pattern or position.
Syntax: s = extractAfter(s,boundary)
Positions count UTF-16 code units, starting at one. A position splitting a surrogate pair is unsupported.
Example: extractAfter("abc",1)
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## extractBetween
Extract text between boundaries.
Syntax: s = extractBetween(s,start,stop)
Text boundaries are excluded and every nonoverlapping pair is returned (a column for scalar input). Array elements must have equal match counts; results requiring N-D strings are unsupported. Numeric endpoints in UTF-16 code units are included. A position splitting a surrogate pair is unsupported.
Example: extractBetween("<abc>","<",">")
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## insertBefore
Insert text before a pattern or position.
Syntax: s = insertBefore(s,boundary,text)
Inserts at every text match; absent boundaries leave the input unchanged. Numeric positions count UTF-16 code units; a position splitting a surrogate pair is unsupported.
Example: insertBefore("abc",2,"!")
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## insertAfter
Insert text after a pattern or position.
Syntax: s = insertAfter(s,boundary,text)
Inserts at every text match; absent boundaries leave the input unchanged. Numeric positions count UTF-16 code units; a position splitting a surrogate pair is unsupported.
Example: insertAfter("abc",1,"!")
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## erase
Remove literal text within strings.
Syntax: s = erase(s,pattern)
Every pattern is removed in order from each subject. Char and cellstr inputs retain their type.
Example: erase(["ab" "ac"],"a")
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## reverse
Reverse the Unicode code points in each string.
Syntax: s = reverse(s)
Combining marks are separate code points, not grapheme clusters.
Example: reverse(["ab" "cd"])
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## pad
Pad each string to a minimum width.
Syntax: s = pad(s,width,side,character)
side defaults to right; character defaults to a space. pad(s,4,'-') pads with '-'. both assigns an odd extra character to the right.
Example: pad("a",4,'both','-')
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.


## newline
Return a newline character.
Syntax: c = newline
Returns one LF character, code 10.
Example: double(newline)
Differences from MATLAB: bounded 2-D string storage (65536 elements, 2 MiB text); MAT persistence and N-D strings are not implemented.

## prctile
Percentiles of data.
Syntax: P = prctile(X, p)
Syntax: P = prctile(X, p, dim)
p holds percentages from 0 to 100. Each sorted value is assigned a percentile by the midpoint rule: the k-th of n values is the 100*(k-0.5)/n percentile. Percentiles between two such points interpolate linearly; percentiles below the first or above the last point give the smallest or largest value. NaN values are ignored, and a lane with no values gives NaN. For a vector X the result has the orientation of p; for a matrix X each row of the result holds one percentile per column (dim 1, the default for matrices) or each column one percentile per row (dim 2). prctile([], p) is NaN. X is double, single or logical: single input gives single results (computed in double, then rounded), and integer input is an error, as the published page lists single and double only.
Example: prctile([6 3 2 10 1], [5 50 95])   % [1 3 10]
Differences from MATLAB: Only the midpoint method; no 'Method' option, 'all' or vector dimensions. Real 2-D data only; dim 3 or higher works only for a single percentage.

## quantile
Quantiles of data.
Syntax: Q = quantile(X, p)
Syntax: Q = quantile(X, p, dim)
Syntax: Q = quantile(X, N)
p holds cumulative probabilities from 0 to 1, computed with the same midpoint rule as prctile: the k-th of n sorted values is the (k-0.5)/n quantile, with linear interpolation between and the extreme values outside. An integer N greater than 1 asks for the N quantiles at the probabilities (1:N)/(N+1). NaN values are ignored. Shapes follow prctile; so does the class rule (single in, single out; integers rejected).
Example: quantile([1 2 3 4], [0.25 0.5 0.75])   % [1.5 2.5 3.5]
Example: quantile(1:10, 3)   % [3 5.5 8]
Differences from MATLAB: Only the midpoint method; no 'Method' option, 'all' or vector dimensions. Real 2-D data only.

## zscore
Standardized z-scores.
Syntax: Z = zscore(X)
Syntax: Z = zscore(X, flag)
Syntax: Z = zscore(X, flag, dim)
Syntax: [Z, mu, sigma] = zscore(...)
Subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation along dim (default: the first dimension whose size is not 1). flag 0 or [] (default) uses the sample standard deviation (divide by n-1), flag 1 the population one (divide by n). mu and sigma are the mean and standard deviation that were used. When a standard deviation is 0 (for example constant data), Z is computed with 1 instead, so that Z is all zeros, while sigma still reports 0. NaN values are not skipped: a vector containing NaN gives NaN z-scores. Single input gives single Z, mu and sigma (computed in double, then rounded); integer input is an error, as the published page lists single and double only. Every output count follows the same rule.
Example: zscore([1 2 3])   % [-1 0 1]
Example: [z, mu, sigma] = zscore([2 4 4 4 5 5 7 9], 1)   % mu = 5, sigma = 2
Differences from MATLAB: No 'all' or vector dimensions. Real 2-D data only.

## skewness
Sample skewness.
Syntax: y = skewness(X)
Syntax: y = skewness(X, flag)
Syntax: y = skewness(X, flag, dim)
The third central moment divided by the second central moment to the power 1.5, both with divisor n. flag 1 or [] (default) gives this biased value; flag 0 multiplies it by sqrt(n*(n-1))/(n-2), which needs at least 3 values (NaN otherwise). NaN values are ignored. Constant data gives NaN (0/0). skewness([]) is NaN. X is double, single or logical: single input gives single results (computed in double, then rounded), and integer input is an error, as the published page lists single and double only.
Example: skewness([1 2 3 10])   % 1.0182
Example: skewness([1 2 3 10], 0)   % 1.7636
Differences from MATLAB: No 'all' or vector dimensions. Real 2-D data only.

## kurtosis
Sample kurtosis.
Syntax: k = kurtosis(X)
Syntax: k = kurtosis(X, flag)
Syntax: k = kurtosis(X, flag, dim)
The fourth central moment divided by the squared second central moment, both with divisor n. This is not the excess kurtosis: a normal distribution has kurtosis 3. flag 1 or [] (default) gives the biased value; flag 0 gives the bias-corrected value (n-1)/((n-2)(n-3)) * ((n+1)k - 3(n-1)) + 3, which needs at least 4 values (NaN otherwise). NaN values are ignored. Constant data gives NaN. X is double, single or logical: single input gives single results (computed in double, then rounded), and integer input is an error, as the published page lists single and double only.
Example: kurtosis([1 2 3 10])   % 2.2304
Example: kurtosis([1 2 3 4 10], 0)   % 6.1520
Differences from MATLAB: No 'all' or vector dimensions. Real 2-D data only.

## mad
Mean or median absolute deviation.
Syntax: y = mad(X)
Syntax: y = mad(X, flag)
Syntax: y = mad(X, flag, dim)
flag 0 or [] (default) gives the mean absolute deviation mean(abs(X - mean(X))); flag 1 gives the median absolute deviation median(abs(X - median(X))). No scale factor is applied. NaN values are ignored. mad([]) is NaN. X is double, single or logical: single input gives single results (computed in double, then rounded), and integer input is an error, as the published page lists single and double only.
Example: mad([1 2 3 4 100])   % 31.2
Example: mad([1 2 3 4 100], 1)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: No 'all' or vector dimensions. Real 2-D data only.

## normalize
Center and scale data.
Syntax: N = normalize(A)
Syntax: N = normalize(A, dim)
Syntax: N = normalize(..., method)
Syntax: N = normalize(..., method, type)
Syntax: N = normalize(..., 'center', c, 'scale', s)
Works along dim (default: the first dimension whose size is not 1); the result is (A - C) ./ S with a center C and scale S per vector. Methods: 'zscore' (default) with type 'std' (mean and sample standard deviation, default) or 'robust' (median and median absolute deviation); 'norm' with p (default 2, Inf allowed): divide by the p-norm; 'scale' with 'std' (default), 'mad' (median absolute deviation), 'first' (the first value), 'iqr' (interquartile range, midpoint rule) or a number; 'range' with [a b] (default [0 1]): a + (A - min)./(max - min).*(b - a); 'center' with 'mean' (default), 'median' or a number; 'medianiqr': median and interquartile range. A numeric center or scale may also have one value per vector. NaN values are ignored when the center and scale are computed and stay NaN. A zero scale is not replaced, so constant data gives NaN (0/0), except 'range', which gives a for constant data. Single input gives a single result; integer input is an error (the published page lists double and single only).
Example: normalize([1 2 3])   % [-1 0 1]
Example: normalize([2 4 6], 'range', [-1 1])   % [-1 0 1]
Example: normalize([1 2 3; 4 6 8], 2, 'center', 'median')   % [-1 0 1; -2 0 2]
Differences from MATLAB: No table inputs, 'DataVariables', 'ReplaceValues' or the C and S outputs. A numeric center or scale is a scalar or one value per vector. Real 2-D data only.

## rescale
Rescale data to an interval.
Syntax: R = rescale(A)
Syntax: R = rescale(A, l, u)
Syntax: R = rescale(..., 'InputMin', inmin, 'InputMax', inmax)
Maps inmin to l and inmax to u linearly: l + (A - inmin)./(inmax - inmin).*(u - l), after values below inmin or above inmax are moved to those bounds. The defaults are l = 0, u = 1, and inmin and inmax the smallest and largest non-NaN values of the whole array. l, u, inmin and inmax may be scalars or arrays that expand along singleton dimensions (for example one value per column). Where inmin equals inmax (constant data) the result is l. NaN values stay NaN, and a NaN inmin or inmax gives NaN. Single input gives a single result; every other class (integer, logical) gives double.
Example: rescale([1 2 3 5])   % [0 0.25 0.5 1]
Example: rescale([-30 1 2 3 4 5 70], 'InputMin', 1, 'InputMax', 5)   % [0 0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1 1]
Differences from MATLAB: Real 2-D data only.

## smoothdata
Smooth noisy data.
Syntax: B = smoothdata(A)
Syntax: B = smoothdata(A, dim)
Syntax: B = smoothdata(..., method)
Syntax: B = smoothdata(..., method, window)
Syntax: B = smoothdata(..., nanflag)
Syntax: B = smoothdata(..., 'SmoothingFactor', f)
Syntax: B = smoothdata(..., 'sgolay', window, 'Degree', d)
Syntax: [B, window] = smoothdata(...)
Smooths each vector along dim (default: the first dimension whose size is not 1). Methods: 'movmean' (default, moving mean), 'movmedian' (moving median), 'gaussian' (Gaussian-weighted moving mean with standard deviation window/5), 'lowess' and 'loess' (local linear and quadratic least squares fits with tricube weights (1-(|t|/d)^3)^3, where d is one more than the largest offset t in the window), 'rlowess' and 'rloess' (the same followed by five robustness passes that weight each sample by the bisquare of its residual over six median absolute residuals, stopping early when that median is 0; residuals below 1e-12 times the largest magnitude count as 0), and 'sgolay' (unweighted local polynomial fit of degree 'Degree', default 2, which must be less than the window length). A scalar window k centers each window, with one extra sample behind for even k; [kb kf] gives the samples before and after. Windows shrink at the ends. 'omitnan' (default) skips NaN values; 'includenan' gives NaN for every window that holds a NaN. Without a window, the window is the smallest moving-mean length k whose frequency response removes at least the fraction f (default 0.25) of the energy of the mean-removed data (pooled over all vectors, NaN counted as the mean); every k from 1 up is tried, because the removed energy does not grow steadily with k (alternating data loses all of it at k = 2 but not at k = 3). For 'sgolay' it is at least Degree+1. The second output is the window used (double). Single input gives a single result; integer input gives a double result (the published page does not state the class).
Example: smoothdata([1 5 2 8 3], 'movmean', 3)   % [3 2.6667 5 4.3333 5.5]
Example: [b, w] = smoothdata([1 5 2 8 3 9 4], 'movmedian', 3)   % w = 3
Example: smoothdata([1 2 3 4 20 6 7], 'rlowess', 5)
Differences from MATLAB: MATLAB does not publish its default window algorithm or its local-regression weights and robustness iterations, so default windows and the lowess, loess, rlowess, rloess and gaussian results can differ from MATLAB's. No 'SamplePoints', non-integer windows, tables or N-D arrays.

## isoutlier
Find outliers in data.
Syntax: TF = isoutlier(A)
Syntax: TF = isoutlier(A, method)
Syntax: TF = isoutlier(A, 'percentiles', [lo hi])
Syntax: TF = isoutlier(A, movmethod, window)
Syntax: TF = isoutlier(..., dim)
Syntax: TF = isoutlier(..., Name, Value)
Syntax: [TF, L, U, C] = isoutlier(...)
Works along dim (default: the first dimension whose size is not 1) of numeric vectors and matrices, or on the numeric variables of tables and timetables. Methods: 'median' (default; more than k = 3 scaled MAD from the median, scaled MAD = c*median(abs(A-median(A))) with c = -1/(sqrt(2)*erfcinv(3/2))), 'mean' (more than k = 3 standard deviations from the mean), 'quartiles' (outside [Q1-k*IQR, Q3+k*IQR], k = 1.5, quartiles as quantile computes them; center (Q1+Q3)/2), 'percentiles' (outside the given percentiles; center their midpoint), 'grubbs' (two-sided Grubbs test removing one outlier per iteration at significance alpha = 0.05) and 'gesd' (generalized extreme Studentized deviate test with at most MaxNumOutliers outliers, default the integer nearest to 10 percent of the elements, at least 1); for these two the thresholds are mean +- critical value * std of the points kept and the center is their mean. 'movmedian' and 'movmean' apply the median and mean rules with local statistics over a window: a scalar k covers sample points in [t-k/2, t+k/2) (k samples centered, one extra behind for even k), [kb kf] covers [t-kb, t+kf]; windows shrink at the ends. NaN is never an outlier and is ignored by the statistics. L, U and C are the lower threshold, upper threshold and center: one value per vector, or one per element for moving methods. Options: 'ThresholdFactor' (k; alpha for grubbs and gesd), 'SamplePoints' (sorted unique numeric, datetime or duration vector; a timetable uses its row times and needs a duration window), 'DataVariables' (names, indices or a logical mask), 'OutputFormat' ('logical' gives a logical matrix of the table size, 'tabular' a table) and 'MaxNumOutliers'.
Example: isoutlier([2 3 2 4 3 50 3 2])
Example: [TF, L, U, C] = isoutlier([1 2 3 4 100], 'quartiles')
Example: isoutlier([1 1.2 0.9 6 1.1 1 0.8], 'movmedian', 3)
Differences from MATLAB: no N-D arrays, function-handle DataVariables or multicolumn table variables. MATLAB does not publish every center and threshold rule, so C for 'quartiles', 'grubbs' and 'gesd' and the gesd default count follow the definitions above.

## filloutliers
Detect and replace outliers in data.
Syntax: B = filloutliers(A, fillmethod)
Syntax: B = filloutliers(A, fillmethod, findmethod)
Syntax: B = filloutliers(A, fillmethod, movmethod, window)
Syntax: B = filloutliers(..., dim)
Syntax: B = filloutliers(..., Name, Value)
Syntax: [B, TF, L, U, C] = filloutliers(...)
Detects outliers as isoutlier does (same methods and options) and replaces them. fillmethod: a numeric scalar, 'center' (the detection center), 'clip' (the threshold that was crossed), 'previous', 'next' or 'nearest' (non-outlier neighbour; ties go to the next one; an outlier without such a neighbour is kept), or 'linear', 'spline', 'pchip' and 'makima' (interp1 over the non-outlier points at the sample points, extrapolating at the ends; at least two such points are needed). NaN values stay NaN and are never used as neighbours. 'OutlierLocations' (a logical array of the data size) replaces detection; then 'center', 'clip' and the L, U, C outputs are not available. TF marks the outliers. Integer and single data keep their class.
Example: filloutliers([2 3 2 40 3 2], 'linear')
Example: [B, TF] = filloutliers([1 2 3 4 100], 'clip', 'quartiles')
Differences from MATLAB: no 'ReplaceValues' false, N-D arrays or multicolumn table variables.

## rmoutliers
Detect and remove outliers from data.
Syntax: B = rmoutliers(A)
Syntax: B = rmoutliers(A, method)
Syntax: B = rmoutliers(A, movmethod, window)
Syntax: B = rmoutliers(..., dim)
Syntax: B = rmoutliers(..., Name, Value)
Syntax: [B, TFrm, TFoutlier, L, U, C] = rmoutliers(...)
Detects outliers as isoutlier does along dim (default: the first dimension whose size is not 1), then removes the rows (dim 1) or columns (dim 2) holding at least 'MinNumOutliers' outliers (default 1): elements of a vector, rows of a matrix, table or timetable. TFrm marks the removed rows or columns, TFoutlier the outliers. 'OutlierLocations' replaces detection; 'DataVariables' chooses the table variables checked.
Example: rmoutliers([2 3 2 40 3 2])
Example: [B, TFrm] = rmoutliers([1 2; 2 3; 50 4; 3 2; 2 3], 'MinNumOutliers', 1)
Differences from MATLAB: no N-D arrays or multicolumn table variables.

## bounds
Smallest and largest elements.
Syntax: [S, L] = bounds(A)
Syntax: [S, L] = bounds(A, dim)
Syntax: [S, L] = bounds(..., nanflag)
S is min(A) and L is max(A) along dim (default: the first dimension whose size is not 1), computed together. 'omitnan' (default) ignores NaN values; 'includenan' gives NaN for every vector that holds a NaN. Empty input gives the same empty results as min and max. S and L keep the class of A as min and max do (integer values are selected exactly), for one output or two.
Example: [s, l] = bounds([3 NaN 1 7])   % s = 1, l = 7
Example: [s, l] = bounds([1 5; 4 2], 2)   % s = [1; 2], l = [5; 4]
Differences from MATLAB: No 'all' or vector dimensions. Complex data is not supported yet.

## rms
Root-mean-square level.
Syntax: y = rms(x)
Syntax: y = rms(x, dim)
Syntax: y = rms(x, vecdim)
Syntax: y = rms(x, 'all')
Syntax: y = rms(..., nanflag)
The square root of the mean of abs(x).^2 along dim (default: the first dimension whose size is not 1), over the dimensions in vecdim, or over every element with 'all'. 'includenan' (default) gives NaN for a vector holding a NaN; 'omitnan' leaves NaN values out. Complex input uses the magnitude. rms([]) is NaN. x is double, single, logical or char: single input gives single results (computed in double, then rounded), and integer input is an error.
Example: rms([3 4])   % 3.5355
Example: rms([1 2; 3 4], 2)   % [1.5811; 3.5355]
Example: rms([1 NaN 3], 'omitnan')   % 2.2361

## text
Place a text label at data coordinates in the current axes.
Syntax: t = text(x, y, str)
Syntax: t = text(x, y, z, str)
Syntax: t = text(ax, x, y, str, Name, Value)
x and y give the anchor point in data units; vectors place one label per point. str is character text or a cell array with one string per point. Properties: String, Position, Color, FontSize (points, default 10), FontWeight, HorizontalAlignment (left, center, right), VerticalAlignment (middle, top, bottom, baseline, cap), Rotation (degrees), Visible. Change them later with set or dot syntax, for example t.Color = 'r'. Unlike plot, text never replaces what the axes already show.
Example: plot(1:5); t = text(2, 3, 'peak', 'Color', 'r', 'FontSize', 12); t.Rotation = 30;
Example: t = text([1 2], [1 4], {'a', 'b'}); numel(t)   % 2
Interpreter defaults to tex; none draws source text literally and latex renders a $...$ / $$...$$ math subset (fractions, sub/superscripts, Greek, \sqrt, \mathrm/\mathbf, \left/\right, \sum/\int and common symbols; unsupported syntax falls back to plain text). Only data Units. Text objects and colorbars are not stored in .fig or session files yet.

## colormap
Set or query the colormap of the current figure or axes.
Syntax: colormap name
Syntax: colormap(map)
Syntax: colormap(target, map)
Syntax: map = colormap
name is one of viridis, parula, gray, hot, cool, jet, hsv, bone, copper or default; map is an n-by-3 matrix of RGB values in [0,1]. With a figure (or no) target the map applies to every axes of the figure; with an axes handle only to that axes. colormap with no arguments returns the current map, 256 rows by default.
Example: colormap('hot'); m = colormap; size(m)   % [256 3]
Example: colormap(gray(8)); m = colormap; m(end,:)   % [1 1 1]
Differences from MATLAB: The default map is viridis (van der Walt and Smith, CC0), not parula; the name parula gives viridis too. colormap(...) only returns a value in the no-argument form.

## colororder
Set or query the colour order of the current figure or axes.
Syntax: colororder(map)
Syntax: colororder(name)
Syntax: colororder(target, map)
Syntax: c = colororder
Sets the axes or figure colour order from an n-by-3 RGB matrix in [0,1] or a supported palette name ('gem', 'default', or a built-in colormap name). Subsequent plots cycle through the new colours.
Example: colororder([1 0 0; 0 0 1]); c = colororder; size(c)   % [2 3]
Differences from MATLAB: Only 'gem', 'default', and built-in colormap names are supported as named palettes.

## image
Display an image from an array of colour data.
Syntax: image(C)
Syntax: image(x, y, C)
Syntax: h = image(..., 'CDataMapping', 'scaled')
C is m-by-n (one colour per element) or m-by-n-by-3 (truecolor RGB: 0 to 1 for double, 0 to 255 for uint8). m-by-n doubles index the colormap from 1; integer classes index it from 0. x and y give the centres of the first and last column and row. On axes that are not held, image shows the 2-D view with y = 1 at the top (axis ij). The handle has CData, XData, YData, CDataMapping and Visible.
Example: image([1 2; 3 4]); colormap(gray(4))
Example: h = image(magic(8)); h.CDataMapping   % 'direct'
Differences from MATLAB: AlphaData and the low-level image() form are not supported; images are not saved in .fig files yet.

## imagesc
Display an image with colours scaled to the colormap.
Syntax: imagesc(C)
Syntax: imagesc(x, y, C)
Syntax: imagesc(..., clims)
Like image with CDataMapping 'scaled': the smallest value of C takes the first colormap row and the largest the last. clims = [cmin cmax] sets the colour limits instead (see clim). Use colorbar to show the scale.
Example: imagesc(peaks(20)); colorbar
Example: imagesc(magic(4), [0 20]); clim   % [0 20]
Differences from MATLAB: AlphaData is not supported; images are not saved in .fig files yet.

## imshow
Display an image (Image Processing Toolbox style).
Syntax: imshow(I)
Syntax: imshow(I, [low high])
Syntax: imshow(I, [])
Syntax: imshow(RGB)
Syntax: imshow(X, map)
Syntax: imshow(filename)
A grayscale image shows in gray over the range of its class (0 to 1 for double, 0 to 255 for uint8). [low high] sets that range; [] uses the image's own minimum and maximum. An m-by-n-by-3 array is truecolor; imshow(X, map) shows an indexed image with its colormap; imshow(filename) reads the file with imread. imshow keeps pixels square and hides the axes (axis image, axis off).
Example: imshow(rand(64))
Example: I = uint8(reshape(0:255, 16, 16)); h = imshow(I, []); h.CDataMapping   % 'scaled'
Differences from MATLAB: InitialMagnification and Border are accepted and ignored; the figure is not resized to the image.

## colorbar
Show a colour scale next to the current axes.
Syntax: cb = colorbar
Syntax: cb = colorbar(location)
Syntax: cb = colorbar(ax, 'Location', location)
Syntax: colorbar off
