location is eastoutside (vertical, the default) or southoutside (horizontal). The bar shows the axes colormap across its colour limits (see clim). The handle has Limits, Label, Location, Orientation, FontSize and Visible; cb.Label.String sets its label.
Example: plot(1:3); cb = colorbar; cb.Label.String = 'Level'; cb.Limits   % [0 1]
Example: cb = colorbar('southoutside'); cb.Orientation   % 'horizontal'
Differences from MATLAB: Only the eastoutside and southoutside positions. Ticks follow the limits automatically; Ticks and TickLabels cannot be set yet.

## clim
Set or query the colour limits of the current axes.
Syntax: clim([cmin cmax])
Syntax: lim = clim
Syntax: clim('auto')
Syntax: clim(ax, [cmin cmax])
The colour limits map the first and last colormap rows to data values; the colorbar shows this range. Without colour-mapped data the automatic limits are [0 1].
Example: plot(1:3); clim([-2 5]); clim   % [-2 5]
Differences from MATLAB: No plot kind maps data to colours yet, so the limits only affect the colorbar scale.

## caxis
Older name for clim: set or query the colour limits.
Syntax: caxis([cmin cmax])
Syntax: lim = caxis
Syntax: caxis('auto')
Works exactly like clim.
Example: caxis([0 10]); caxis   % [0 10]
Differences from MATLAB: Same as clim.

## yyaxis
Give the current axes a second y-axis on the right and choose the active side.
Syntax: yyaxis left
Syntax: yyaxis right
Syntax: yyaxis(ax, side)
After yyaxis right, plot, ylim, ylabel and the YLim and YColor properties act on the right axis; yyaxis left switches back. Each side has its own limits and colour (the first and second ColorOrder colours), and a plot without hold replaces only the series of the active side. One legend lists the series of both sides.
Example: x = 1:10; yyaxis left; plot(x, x.^2); yyaxis right; plot(x, sqrt(x)); ylim([0 4]); r = ylim()   % [0 4]
Differences from MATLAB: Linear y-axes only. ax.YAxis rulers are not available; use YLim and YColor while the side is active. Both sides share one line-style cycle.

## drawnow
Update figures and process queued UI callbacks.
Syntax: drawnow
Syntax: drawnow limitrate
Syntax: drawnow nocallbacks
Syntax: drawnow update
Syntax: drawnow expose
In the desktop app a running script refreshes its figures and UI windows when drawnow runs, and drains queued UI callbacks (such as button clicks or uiprogressdlg Cancel). drawnow nocallbacks, drawnow update, and drawnow expose refresh the display without draining callbacks. pause also refreshes figures and drains queued UI callbacks. In -batch mode and SVG export drawnow does nothing.
Example: h = plot(1:3); h.YData = [3 2 1]; drawnow
Differences from MATLAB: limitrate is accepted and behaves like plain drawnow; nocallbacks, update, and expose skip callback draining but do not rate-limit or defer rendering.

## ishandle
True for valid graphics handles or open figure numbers.
Syntax: tf = ishandle(h)
Returns true where h holds a handle to an object that still exists. For a number, true when a figure with that number is open.
Example: plot(1:3); ax = gca; ishandle(ax)   % true
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet. Other values give false.

## viridis
Viridis colormap: dark blue through green to yellow.
Syntax: map = viridis
Syntax: map = viridis(n)
Returns an n-by-3 matrix of RGB rows (256 by default), interpolated from the published 256-entry viridis table (van der Walt and Smith, 2015, released CC0). It is MatRust's default colormap.
Example: m = viridis(3); size(m)   % [3 3]
Differences from MATLAB: MATLAB has no viridis function; it is provided because its table may be reproduced.

## parula
Default colormap under MATLAB's name; gives viridis in MatRust.
Syntax: map = parula
Syntax: map = parula(n)
Returns the same rows as viridis(n), so scripts written for MATLAB's default map run.
Example: isequal(parula(4), viridis(4))   % true
Differences from MATLAB: The colours are viridis, not MATLAB's parula table, which is not published under terms MatRust may reproduce.

## gray
Grayscale colormap from black to white.
Syntax: map = gray(n)
Returns n RGB rows with equal components rising linearly from 0 to 1 (256 rows by default).
Example: gray(3)   % [0 0 0; 0.5 0.5 0.5; 1 1 1]
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## hot
Black-red-yellow-white colormap.
Syntax: map = hot(n)
Red rises over the first 3/8 of the rows, green over the next 3/8 and blue over the rest (256 rows by default).
Example: m = hot(8); m(end,:)   % [1 1 1]
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet.

## cool
Cyan-to-magenta colormap.
Syntax: map = cool(n)
Row k is [t 1-t 1] with t rising linearly from 0 to 1 (256 rows by default).
Example: cool(2)   % [0 1 1; 1 0 1]
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## jet
Blue-cyan-yellow-red colormap.
Syntax: map = jet(n)
The classic piecewise-linear rainbow ramp, from dark blue through cyan, yellow and red to dark red (256 rows by default).
Example: m = jet(9); m(5,:)   % [0.5 1 0.5]
Differences from MATLAB: Built from the piecewise-linear definition; individual rows can differ slightly from MATLAB's table for some n.

## hsv
Hue colormap around the colour wheel.
Syntax: map = hsv(n)
Fully saturated colours with the hue going once round from red (256 rows by default), so the first and last rows are close.
Example: m = hsv(6); m(3,:)   % [0 1 0]
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## bone
Grayscale colormap with a blue tint.
Syntax: map = bone(n)
Seven parts gray to one part reversed hot, which gives light blue highlights (256 rows by default).
Example: m = bone(4); m(end,:)   % [1 1 1]
Differences from MATLAB: Not checked against MATLAB yet.

## copper
Black-to-copper colormap.
Syntax: map = copper(n)
Rows rise linearly from black with the channel ratios 1.25 : 0.7812 : 0.4975, clipped at 1 (256 rows by default).
Example: m = copper(5); m(1,:)   % [0 0 0]
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## histogram
Histogram plot.
Syntax: h = histogram(X)
Syntax: h = histogram(X, nbins)
Syntax: h = histogram(X, edges)
Syntax: h = histogram(..., Name, Value)
Bins all elements of X and draws one bar per bin. Bins are [edges(k), edges(k+1)) and the last bin is closed; NaN values are not counted. Automatic bins: integer data spanning at most 50 gets one bin per integer, other data Scott's rule with "nice" edges. BinLimits [lo hi] with NumBins n gives n equal bins over the limits; BinWidth w alone aligns the edges to multiples of w. Options: NumBins, BinEdges, BinWidth, BinLimits, BinMethod, Normalization (count, probability, pdf, cdf, countdensity, cumcount), DisplayStyle (bar or stairs), FaceColor, EdgeColor, FaceAlpha, DisplayName and LineWidth. The handle answers get for Values, BinCounts, BinEdges, NumBins, BinWidth, BinLimits, Normalization, BinMethod, DisplayStyle, Data, FaceColor and FaceAlpha; set recomputes the bins.
Example: h = histogram([1 2 2 3 3 3]); get(h, 'Values')   % [1 2 3]
Example: h = histogram(randn(1, 200), 'Normalization', 'pdf', 'NumBins', 12);
Differences from MATLAB: FaceAlpha is drawn as an opaque tint toward white. The probability, pdf and cdf normalizations divide by numel(X). Categorical data and the Orientation property are not supported.

## errorbar
Line plot with error bars.
Syntax: e = errorbar(y, err)
Syntax: e = errorbar(x, y, err)
Syntax: e = errorbar(x, y, neg, pos)
Syntax: e = errorbar(x, y, yneg, ypos, xneg, xpos)
Syntax: e = errorbar(..., ornt)
Syntax: e = errorbar(..., linespec, Name, Value)
Draws y against x with a bar from y-neg to y+pos at every point and a cap at each end. ornt works with every form: 'vertical' (default) draws the deltas as vertical bars, 'horizontal' as horizontal bars and 'both' as both. The six-input form draws both directions; there 'vertical' or 'horizontal' keeps only the bars of that direction. Matrix data gives one errorbar per column. Options: CapSize (points, default 6), Color, LineWidth, LineStyle and DisplayName. get and set work for XData, YData, YNegativeDelta, YPositiveDelta, XNegativeDelta, XPositiveDelta, CapSize, Color and LineWidth.
Example: e = errorbar([1 2 3], [2 4 3], [0.5 1 0.5]); get(e, 'CapSize')   % 6
Example: errorbar(1:3, [2 4 3], [1 1 1], 'horizontal');
Example: e = errorbar([2 4 3], [0.5 1 0.5], 'both'); get(e, 'XNegativeDelta')   % [0.5 1 0.5]
Differences from MATLAB: cap lengths are fixed in data units for the default figure size when the chart is drawn, so they scale with zooming.

## area
Filled area plot.
Syntax: h = area(Y)
Syntax: h = area(X, Y)
Syntax: h = area(..., basevalue)
Syntax: h = area(..., Name, Value)
Fills the region between each column of Y and the one below it: the columns are stacked, so the top of the last area is the row sum. The first area is filled down to basevalue (default 0). Options: BaseValue, FaceColor, EdgeColor, LineWidth and DisplayName. get answers XData, YData and BaseValue.
Example: h = area([1 2 3], [1 2; 3 4; 5 6]); get(h(2), 'YData')   % [2 4 6]
Differences from MATLAB: at most 3000 rows and 24 columns. Face colours come from the plot palette.

## barh
Horizontal bar plot.
Syntax: b = barh(y)
Syntax: b = barh(x, y)
Syntax: b = barh(..., width)
Syntax: b = barh(..., 'grouped')
Syntax: b = barh(..., 'stacked')
Syntax: b = barh(..., Name, Value)
Draws one horizontal bar per element of y at the positions x (default 1:n). A matrix y gives one bar series per column, grouped side by side or stacked. Options: BarWidth (default 0.8), BaseValue, BarLayout, FaceColor, EdgeColor, LineWidth and DisplayName. get answers XData, YData, BarWidth, BaseValue, BarLayout and Horizontal.
Example: b = barh([3 5 2]); get(b, 'Horizontal')   % 'on'
Example: barh([1 2; 3 4], 'stacked');
Differences from MATLAB: at most 2500 groups and 32 series. No baseline object.

## pie
Pie chart.
Syntax: p = pie(x)
Syntax: p = pie(x, explode)
Syntax: p = pie(x, labels)
Syntax: p = pie(x, explode, labels)
Draws one slice per nonzero element of x, clockwise from 12 o'clock. When sum(x) is less than 1 the values are fractions and the pie is partial. Slices are labelled with their percentage (round(100*x/sum(x)), "< 1%" for tiny slices), inside the slice from 6 % up and outside below 6 %; labels is a cell array of texts used instead. Nonzero explode entries offset their slices. p holds a patch and a text handle per slice.
Example: p = pie([1 2 3 4]); numel(p)   % 8
Example: pie([0.2 0.3], [1 0], {'first', 'second'});
Differences from MATLAB: slice colours come from the plot palette, not the colormap. Labels are figure textboxes placed for the default figure size. The pie is drawn on Cartesian axes with the tick labels hidden.

## fill
Filled 2-D polygons.
Syntax: p = fill(x, y, c)
Syntax: p = fill(x1, y1, c1, x2, y2, c2, ...)
Syntax: p = fill(..., Name, Value)
Fills the polygon with corners (x, y) in colour c (a colour letter, colour name or RGB triple) with a black outline. Matrix x and y give one polygon per column. Options: FaceColor, EdgeColor, LineStyle, LineWidth and DisplayName. Returns patch handles.
Example: p = fill([0 1 1 0], [0 0 1 1], 'r'); get(p, 'Type')   % 'patch'
Differences from MATLAB: colour data (scalars or per-vertex values mapped through a colormap) is not supported; polygons have at most 3000 vertices.

## polarplot
Plot in polar coordinates.
Syntax: p = polarplot(theta, rho)
Syntax: p = polarplot(theta, rho, linespec)
Syntax: p = polarplot(theta1, rho1, ..., thetaN, rhoN)
Syntax: p = polarplot(rho)
Syntax: p = polarplot(..., Name, Value)
Draws lines at angles theta (radians) and radii rho on polar axes with a circle grid, spokes every 30 degrees labelled in degrees, and radius labels. With hold on, further polarplot calls add lines and rescale the grid; without hold, a later plot, bar or other chart replaces the polar axes with Cartesian ones. set and get on the axes (gca) support RLim, RLimMode, ThetaZeroLocation ('right', 'top', 'left', 'bottom') and ThetaDir ('counterclockwise', 'clockwise'). Options: Color, LineWidth, LineStyle and DisplayName; the line handles answer ThetaData and RData.
Example: p = polarplot(linspace(0, 2*pi, 50), 1 + cos(linspace(0, 2*pi, 50))); get(p, 'Type')   % 'line'
Differences from MATLAB: the polar grid is drawn on Cartesian axes with the tick labels hidden. Equal scaling and label placement assume the default figure size. Points with rho below the lower RLim are not drawn.

## fplot
Plot a function of x.
Syntax: fp = fplot(f)
Syntax: fp = fplot(f, [xmin xmax])
Syntax: fp = fplot(..., linespec, Name, Value)
Evaluates the function handle f on [xmin xmax] (default [-5 5]) and draws the curve. Sampling starts with MeshDensity (default 23) equally spaced points including both limits; each round tests the midpoint of every interval and keeps bisecting where the midpoint deviates from the chord by more than 0.1 % of the y range, at most 10 rounds and 5000 points. Handles that are not vectorized (the call on the vector of x values errors, as @(x) x^2 does, or returns the wrong number of values) are evaluated point by point. get answers Function, XRange, MeshDensity, XData and YData; set of XRange or MeshDensity resamples.
Example: fp = fplot(@(x) x.^2, [-1 2]); x = get(fp, 'XData'); [x(1) x(end)]   % [-1 2]
Differences from MATLAB: parametric fplot(funx, funy) and automatic pole detection are not supported; the curve is not resampled when the axes are zoomed.

## contour3
3-D contour plot.
Syntax: contour3(Z)
Syntax: contour3(X, Y, Z)
Syntax: contour3(..., n)
Syntax: contour3(..., v)
Syntax: contour3(..., LineSpec)
Syntax: [C, h] = contour3(...)
Same inputs, levels, options and handle as contour; each level's line is drawn at the height Z = level, and an axes that is not held switches to view(3). C equals contourc's.
Example: [C, h] = contour3(peaks(20), 5); h.LevelList
Differences from MATLAB: ShowText and clabel labels are not drawn in 3-D.

## line
Add a line to the current axes.
Syntax: h = line(x, y)
Syntax: h = line(x, y, z)
Syntax: h = line(..., Name, Value)
Syntax: h = line('XData', x, 'YData', y, 'ZData', z, ...)
Draws like plot (matrices give one line per column) but always adds to the current axes, whatever hold says, and never resets the axes. Missing XData or YData default to [0 1]. Name,Value pairs are plot's line properties. When Color is omitted, line uses an inherited DefaultLineColor if set. High-level plot uses the axes ColorOrder for automatic colors.
Example: plot(1:3); h = line([1 3], [3 1], 'Color', 'r'); numel(get(gca, 'Children'))   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: 'Parent' is not supported (select the axes first). Without an inherited default color, the line takes the next colour of the axes ColorOrder.

## quiver
Arrow plot of a vector field.
Syntax: q = quiver(U, V)
Syntax: q = quiver(X, Y, U, V)
Syntax: q = quiver(..., scale)
Syntax: q = quiver(..., LineSpec)
Syntax: q = quiver(..., Name, Value)
Draws an arrow (U,V) at every point (X,Y); vector X and Y next to a matrix U are expanded as meshgrid(X,Y), and quiver(U,V) uses the column and row numbers. Arrows are scaled as in GNU Octave: 0.9 (or scale) times the grid spacing over the longest arrow; a scale of 0, 'off' or 'AutoScale','off' draws them unscaled. Heads are 1/3 of the arrow (MaxHeadSize 0.2); a marker in the LineSpec marks the arrow bases and hides the heads, as in Octave. Options: AutoScale, AutoScaleFactor, MaxHeadSize, ShowArrowHead, Color, LineStyle, LineWidth, DisplayName. Returns one line whose XData/YData hold the shafts and heads, NaN-separated.
Example: [x, y] = meshgrid(-2:2); q = quiver(x, y, -y, x); q.Type   % 'line'
Differences from MATLAB: returns a line, not a Quiver object, so UData/VData and AutoScaleFactor cannot be read or set afterwards; Alignment is 'tail' only.

## quiver3
3-D arrow plot.
Syntax: q = quiver3(Z, U, V, W)
Syntax: q = quiver3(X, Y, Z, U, V, W)
Syntax: q = quiver3(..., scale)
Syntax: q = quiver3(..., LineSpec, Name, Value)
The 3-D form of quiver: an arrow (U,V,W) at every point (X,Y,Z), scaled as in GNU Octave (the grid spacing includes the Z range). Same options as quiver; an axes that is not held switches to view(3).
Example: [x, y] = meshgrid(1:3); q = quiver3(x, y, zeros(3), zeros(3), zeros(3), ones(3)); size(q.ZData)
Differences from MATLAB: returns a line, not a Quiver object.

## fsurf
Surface plot of a function.
Syntax: s = fsurf(f)
Syntax: s = fsurf(f, [min max])
Syntax: s = fsurf(f, [xmin xmax ymin ymax])
Syntax: s = fsurf(funx, funy, funz, [umin umax vmin vmax])
Syntax: s = fsurf(..., 'MeshDensity', n, Name, Value)
Evaluates f(x,y) on an n-by-n grid (MeshDensity, default 35) over the interval (default [-5 5] for x and y) and draws it with surf; three functions give the parametric surface (x(u,v), y(u,v), z(u,v)). The function is called once on the whole grid; when that errors, returns the wrong size or disagrees with scalar calls (x*y instead of x.*y), it is evaluated point by point. Other Name,Value pairs are surf's.
Example: s = fsurf(@(x, y) x.^2 - y.^2, [-1 1]); size(s.ZData)   % [35 35]
Differences from MATLAB: returns a surface; the grid is not refined adaptively or resampled when the axes are zoomed.

## fimplicit
Plot an implicit curve f(x,y) = 0.
Syntax: h = fimplicit(f)
Syntax: h = fimplicit(f, [min max])
Syntax: h = fimplicit(f, [xmin xmax ymin ymax])
Syntax: h = fimplicit(..., LineSpec, 'MeshDensity', n, Name, Value)
Evaluates f on an n-by-n grid (MeshDensity, default 151) over the interval (default [-5 5]) and draws the zero contour as one line (pieces NaN-separated, colour from the color order); the axes limits are set to the interval. Evaluation as in fsurf.
Example: h = fimplicit(@(x, y) x.^2 + y.^2 - 1); h.Type   % 'line'
Differences from MATLAB: returns a line; the curve is not resampled when the axes are zoomed.

## animatedline
Line for points added in a loop.
Syntax: h = animatedline
Syntax: h = animatedline(x, y)
Syntax: h = animatedline(x, y, z)
Syntax: h = animatedline(..., 'MaximumNumPoints', n, Name, Value)
Adds an empty (or initial) line to the current axes, whatever hold says. addpoints appends points, getpoints returns them, clearpoints removes them; when more than MaximumNumPoints are stored, the oldest are dropped. Call drawnow to show the new points while a loop runs. Other Name,Value pairs are plot's line properties.
Example: h = animatedline(); for k = 1:10, addpoints(h, k, k^2); end; [x, y] = getpoints(h); y(end)   % 100
Differences from MATLAB: the handle's Type is 'line'; MaximumNumPoints can only be given when the line is created (at most 1000000).

## addpoints
Add points to an animated line.
Syntax: addpoints(h, x, y)
Syntax: addpoints(h, x, y, z)
Appends the points to the animatedline h, keeping its newest MaximumNumPoints points.
Example: h = animatedline; addpoints(h, [1 2 3], [4 5 6]); [x, y] = getpoints(h); y   % [4 5 6]

## getpoints
Points of an animated line.
Syntax: [x, y] = getpoints(h)
Syntax: [x, y, z] = getpoints(h)
Returns the points of the animatedline h as row vectors; z is zeros for a 2-D line.
Example: h = animatedline(1:3, [2 4 6]); [x, y] = getpoints(h); x   % [1 2 3]

## clearpoints
Remove all points of an animated line.
Syntax: clearpoints(h)
Example: h = animatedline(1:3, 1:3); clearpoints(h); numel(getpoints(h))   % 0

## print
Save a figure to a file.
Syntax: print(filename, '-dformat')
Syntax: print(fig, filename, '-dformat', '-rdpi')
Syntax: print -dpng filename
Writes the current (or given) figure: -dpng, -djpeg, -dtiff, -dpdf and -dsvg through exportgraphics, -depsc through saveas. The device's extension is added when the filename has none; a filename with another extension is kept as given. Without -d the extension picks the format (default PNG). -rN sets the resolution (-r0 = 96 dpi); -fN selects figure N; -painters, -opengl, -vector, -image, -noui, -bestfit, -fillpage and -loose are accepted and ignored.
Example: plot(1:3); print('-dpng', 'plot.png')   % writes plot.png
Differences from MATLAB: printing to a printer, the clipboard and other devices (-dbmp, -dmeta, -dps ...) is not supported yet; PDF output is the tight figure, not a full page. Needs a build with the plot-export feature (on in the desktop build).

## heatmap
Heatmap of a matrix.
Syntax: h = heatmap(cdata)
Syntax: h = heatmap(xvalues, yvalues, cdata)
Syntax: h = heatmap(..., Name, Value)
Draws one coloured cell per element of cdata, row 1 at the top, with the value written in each cell and a colour scale on the right. xvalues and yvalues (cell arrays of texts or numbers) label the columns and rows. Options: ColorLimits, CellLabelColor ('none' hides the cell values), ColorbarVisible, Title, XLabel and YLabel. NaN cells are grey. get answers ColorData, ColorLimits and CellLabelColor.
Example: h = heatmap([1 2; 3 4]); get(h, 'ColorData')   % [1 2; 3 4]
Example: heatmap({'a', 'b'}, {'x', 'y'}, magic(2), 'Title', 'Counts');
Differences from MATLAB: the colour scale is a 16-step sequential ramp from the first plot-palette colour, not a colormap. Labels are figure textboxes (at most 64 per figure): cell values are left out when they do not fit, and category labels too for large matrices. At most 100 by 100 cells. The cells are drawn on Cartesian axes with the tick labels hidden.

## contourc
Contour matrix of a grid, without drawing.
Syntax: C = contourc(Z)
Syntax: C = contourc(Z, n)
Syntax: C = contourc(Z, v)
Syntax: C = contourc(x, y, Z)
Syntax: C = contourc(x, y, Z, n)
Syntax: C = contourc(x, y, Z, v)
Traces the lines where Z crosses each level, by linear interpolation along the cell edges (marching squares). x and y are vectors with one entry per column and per row of Z (default 1:columns and 1:rows), or matrices of Z's size (meshgrid output, or a general mesh: the lines are traced in index space and mapped onto it bilinearly). Level rule: a count n gives n levels evenly spaced strictly inside the data range, linspace(min(Z(:)), max(Z(:)), n+2) without its two ends, NaN ignored; the default is n = 10. A vector v gives its sorted distinct values as the levels, so [k k] is the single level k. Layout of C: one block per line, a column [level; npoints] followed by the npoints [x; y] columns. Per level, lines that start on the top and bottom edges come first, then those on the left and right edges, then closed lines (which repeat their first point at the end). Cells with a NaN corner have no crossings on the edges that touch it. Constant Z or levels outside the data range give an empty 2-by-0 C.
Example: C = contourc([1 2; 3 4], [2.5 2.5])   % [2.5 1 2; 2 1.75 1.25] (one line, two points)
Example: size(contourc(peaks(20)))
Differences from MATLAB: the level rule and line order are GNU Octave's (the reference for the tests). Z must be real and finite or NaN, with at most 1000000 elements; at most 2000000 contour points; n is at most 1000.

## contour
Contour lines of a matrix.
Syntax: contour(Z)
Syntax: contour(X, Y, Z)
Syntax: contour(..., n)
Syntax: contour(..., v)
Syntax: contour(..., LineSpec)
Syntax: contour(..., Name, Value)
Syntax: contour(ax, ...)
Syntax: [C, h] = contour(...)
Draws the contour lines of contourc (same inputs, level rule and C layout): one line object per level, coloured from the axes colormap at that level. When the axes colour limits are automatic, contour sets CLim to [min max] of the levels of all contours on the axes ([k-1 k+1] for a single level), so colorbar shows the levels; with hold on a second contour shares that scale and the earlier ones are redrawn with it. A CLim you set yourself (clim([a b]), set CLim) is kept. A colour in LineSpec or LineColor draws every level in that colour. Options: LineColor (a colour, 'flat' or 'none'), LineWidth (default 0.5), LineStyle ('-', '--', ':', '-.' or 'none'; 'none' hides the lines and leaves LineColor as it is), LevelList (the levels), ShowText ('on' writes the level, as %g, at the midpoint of every line, in the axes font size) and DisplayName. get, set and dot syntax on h support LevelList, LineColor, LineWidth, LineStyle, ShowText, ZData and Visible (each set redraws the contour; the labels follow Visible); Fill ('off') and Type ('contour') are read-only; ContourMatrix, XData and YData can be read.
Example: [C, h] = contour(peaks(20)); h.Type   % 'contour'
Example: [~, h] = contour(peaks(20), [-2 0 2], 'k--'); get(h, 'LevelList')   % [-2 0 2]
Example: [~, h] = contour(peaks(20)); set(h, 'LevelList', [0 1]); h.LevelList   % [0 1]
Example: contour(peaks(20), 'ShowText', 'on'); colorbar;
Differences from MATLAB: the level rule and line order are GNU Octave's (Octave's contour also lists min(Z) first in LevelList, a level that never has a line; matrust lists the drawn levels only); the line colours are fixed when the contour is drawn (a later colormap call does not recolour them) and CLimMode reads 'manual' after contour set the limits (so clim('manual') straight after a contour still counts as automatic until you give other limits). One legend entry per contour. At most 64 series per axes (one per level with lines), 1000000 line points per figure and 256 labels per axes. A saved .mrfig holds the drawn lines and bands, not a contour object: reopening shows the same lines and fills, but the reopened objects are plain lines and patches (no LevelList), and labels are left out because .mrfig does not store axes text objects yet. No 3-D contours (contour3), fcontour, LabelSpacing or label gaps in the lines.

## contourf
Filled contour plot.
Syntax: contourf(Z)
Syntax: contourf(X, Y, Z)
Syntax: contourf(..., n)
Syntax: contourf(..., v)
Syntax: contourf(..., LineSpec)
Syntax: contourf(..., Name, Value)
Syntax: [C, h] = contourf(...)
Same inputs, options and handle properties as contour, with the regions between levels filled: the band from one level up to the next has the colormap colour of the lower level. Levels as in GNU Octave: a count n (default 10) gives min(Z(:)) followed by contourc's n levels, so h.LevelList has n+1 entries, CLim is [min(Z) highest level] and the band from the minimum up to the first line gets the first colormap row, every other band its own colour; min(Z) never has a line, so C is contourc's. A vector v gives v's levels only: CLim spans them and the region below the first level stays unfilled. The bands are built cell by cell (whole cells as rectangles, cut cells as triangles; saddle cells split at the centre average) and the contour lines are drawn on top in black; 'LineColor', 'none' hides them. NaN cells stay empty. h.Fill is 'on'.
Example: [C, h] = contourf(peaks(20), 5); h.Fill   % 'on'
Example: [~, h] = contourf(magic(4), 2); h.LevelList   % [1 6 11]
Example: contourf(peaks(20), 'LineColor', 'none'); colorbar;
Differences from MATLAB: the band faces share the figure's patch budget of 100000 faces, so large grids with many levels report an error (use a coarser grid or fewer levels). The same limits and .mrfig behaviour as contour apply.

## clabel
Contour labels.
Syntax: t = clabel(C)
Syntax: t = clabel(C, v)
Syntax: t = clabel(C, h)
Syntax: t = clabel(C, h, v)
Writes the level of every contour line, formatted with %g, at the line's midpoint by arc length, as a text object in the axes font size (centred, no background). With h (from contour or contourf) the labels belong to that contour and follow it when its levels change, like ShowText 'on'; v labels only those levels. Without h the labels are placed on the current axes from C alone. With h and a C that is not the contour's own, the labels sit on the lines of that C. A C that is not a contour matrix (a block without points, a count beyond the matrix) is an error. Returns the text handles.
Example: [C, h] = contour(peaks(20), [0 2]); t = clabel(C, h); get(t(1), 'String')
Example: C = contourc(peaks(20), [1 1]); t = clabel(C);
Differences from MATLAB: no '+' markers, no manual placement, no LabelSpacing; the lines are not broken under the labels. At most 256 text objects per axes.

## alphamap
Query or set the figure opacity alphamap.
Syntax: a = alphamap
Syntax: alphamap(map)
Syntax: alphamap(option)
Syntax: alphamap(option, delta)
Syntax: alphamap(fig, ...)
Options are 'rampup', 'rampdown', 'vup', 'vdown', 'default', 'increase' and 'decrease' (with optional delta, default 0.1). Returns an n-by-1 vector in [0, 1].
Example: alphamap('rampdown'); a = alphamap;
Differences from MATLAB: Volume.Alphamap is independent of the figure alphamap.

## volshow
Display a 3-D volume with an orthographic raycaster.
Syntax: v = volshow(V)
Syntax: v = volshow(V, Name=Value)
Syntax: v = volshow(V, 'Name', Value)
Accepts 3-D logical, integer, single or double arrays. Supported properties: Data, RenderingStyle ('VolumeRendering', 'MaximumIntensityProjection', 'MinimumIntensityProjection', 'Isosurface', 'SlicePlanes'), Colormap, Alphamap, DataLimits, IsosurfaceValue, IsosurfaceColor (default [0.7 0.7 0.7]), SlicePlaneValues (k-by-4 [a b c d] planes, default three centre planes), Transformation (voxel spacing scale), Visible, Parent, OverlayData (empty default, or numeric/logical/categorical array matching Data size), OverlayRenderingStyle ('LabelOverlay' default or 'VolumeOverlay'), OverlayColormap, OverlayAlphamap (scalar or vector in [0, 1], default 0.5), and OverlayDisplayRange (for 'VolumeOverlay').
Parent is a live scalar axes handle. Assign v.Parent or use set(v, 'Parent', ax) to move the volume to another axes.
Example: V = reshape(1:27, 3, 3, 3); v = volshow(V, RenderingStyle='MaximumIntensityProjection');
Example: V = reshape(1:27, 3, 3, 3); v = volshow(V, RenderingStyle='Isosurface', IsosurfaceValue=14, IsosurfaceColor=[0.2 0.6 0.9]);
Differences from MATLAB: CPU orthographic raycaster with a single headlight for Isosurface.

## sliceViewer
Display 2-D slices of a 3-D volume.
Syntax: s = sliceViewer(V)
Syntax: s = sliceViewer(V, Name=Value)
Syntax: s = sliceViewer(V, 'Name', Value)
Accepts 2-D or 3-D numeric or logical arrays. Supported properties: SliceNumber (default centre slice), SliceDirection ([0 0 1] default, [1 0 0], [0 1 0], 'X', 'Y', or 'Z'), Colormap (gray(256) default), DisplayRange (data limits default; [] for auto), ScaleFactors ([1 1 1] default), Parent, Visible and Tag.
Example: V = reshape(1:27, 3, 3, 3); s = sliceViewer(V, 'SliceNumber', 2, 'Colormap', 'hot');
Differences from MATLAB: 4-D RGB volumes and SliderValueChanging/SliderValueChanged listeners are not supported yet.

## orthosliceViewer
Display orthogonal XY, YZ and XZ slices of a 3-D volume.
Syntax: o = orthosliceViewer(V)
Syntax: o = orthosliceViewer(V, Name=Value)
Syntax: o = orthosliceViewer(V, 'Name', Value)
Accepts 2-D or 3-D numeric or logical arrays. Supported properties: SliceNumbers ([x y z] default centres), CrosshairEnabled ('on' default or 'off'), Colormap (gray(256) default), DisplayRange (data limits default; [] for auto), ScaleFactors ([1 1 1] default), Parent, Visible and Tag.
Example: V = reshape(1:27, 3, 3, 3); o = orthosliceViewer(V, 'SliceNumbers', [1 2 3], 'CrosshairEnabled', 'on');
Differences from MATLAB: 4-D RGB volumes and SliderValueChanging/SliderValueChanged listeners are not supported yet.

## getAxesHandles
Return the axes handle or handles of a slice viewer.
Syntax: ax = getAxesHandles(s)
Syntax: [hXY, hYZ, hXZ] = getAxesHandles(o)
Returns the single axes handle for a sliceViewer, or the three pane axes handles (XY, YZ, XZ) for an orthosliceViewer.
Example: V = reshape(1:27, 3, 3, 3); o = orthosliceViewer(V); [hXY, hYZ, hXZ] = getAxesHandles(o);
Differences from MATLAB: Only SliceViewer and OrthosliceViewer handles are supported.

## contourslice
Draw contours through volume slices.
Syntax: h = contourslice(V, xslice, yslice, zslice)
Syntax: h = contourslice(X, Y, Z, V, xslice, yslice, zslice)
Syntax: h = contourslice(V, Xi, Yi, Zi)
Syntax: h = contourslice(..., nlevels)
Syntax: h = contourslice(..., levels)
Syntax: h = contourslice(..., method)
Syntax: h = contourslice(ax, ...)
Scalar or vector positions select axis-aligned planes. Use [] to omit an axis, or supply equal-sized Xi, Yi, Zi matrices for a surface. The interpolation methods are 'nearest' (default for planes), 'linear' (default for a surface) and 'cubic'.
By default, each slice has ten levels spaced inside its sampled data range. A positive integer changes the count, and a vector supplies explicit levels. Use [k k] for a single level k. Each contour line returns a patch handle with FaceColor 'none', EdgeColor 'flat' and CData equal to the contour level. Existing plots are retained.
Example: [X,Y,Z] = meshgrid(1:4,1:4,1:4); V = X+2*Y+3*Z; h = contourslice(X,Y,Z,V,[],[],2,[10 13]); view(3);
Differences from MATLAB: Coordinates and methods have the same limits as interp3. Each line counts toward the figure's 64-series limit.

## slice
Draw slices through three-dimensional gridded data.
Syntax: h = slice(V, xslice, yslice, zslice)
Syntax: h = slice(X, Y, Z, V, xslice, yslice, zslice, method)
Syntax: h = slice(ax, ...)
Scalar or vector positions draw planes; [] omits an axis. Three matrices of equal size specify a surface. The method is 'linear' (default), 'nearest' or 'cubic'. Handles are returned in x, y, z order. Surfaces support the same properties and limits as surf.
Example: h = slice(ones(3,3,3), [], [], 2);
Differences from MATLAB: Coordinates must be increasing meshgrid axes; interpolation has the same limitations as interp3.

## surf
3-D surface plot.
Syntax: surf(Z)
Syntax: surf(Z, C)
Syntax: surf(X, Y, Z)
Syntax: surf(X, Y, Z, C)
Syntax: surf(..., Name, Value)
Syntax: surf(ax, ...)
Syntax: h = surf(...)
Draws the surface through the grid points (X(j), Y(i), Z(i,j)) as one surface object of (rows-1)*(columns-1) quadrilateral faces. Z is a real matrix of at least 2-by-2 (at most 1000000 elements); X and Y are vectors with one value per column and per row of Z, or matrices of Z's size; surf(Z) uses X = 1:columns and Y = 1:rows. C (default Z) is the colour data: with FaceColor 'flat' a face takes the CData of its first vertex (row i, column j for the face between rows i..i+1 and columns j..j+1), mapped through the axes colormap with CDataMapping 'scaled'. While CLim is automatic it spans [min max] of the finite CData of every surface in the axes; a CLim set with clim or caxis is kept. colormap, clim and caxis recolour the faces; colorbar shows the mapping.
A face with NaN or Inf in any of its four vertices (X, Y, Z or C) is left out (a hole). Faces are painted far to near by the mean depth of their projected corners (painter's algorithm) after every view change, across all surfaces of the axes. With hold off the axes switches to view(3) = (-37.5, 30); with hold on the current view is kept.
Defaults: FaceColor 'flat', EdgeColor black, LineStyle '-', LineWidth 0.5, FaceAlpha 1, FaceLighting 'flat'. Name-value pairs and h's properties: XData, YData, ZData, CData (setting them redraws), FaceColor ('flat', 'interp', 'none', an RGB triplet or colour name), EdgeColor ('flat', 'interp', 'none', RGB or name), FaceAlpha (scalar 0..1), LineStyle, LineWidth, FaceLighting ('none', 'flat', 'gouraud' or 'phong'), DisplayName and Visible. h.Type is 'surface'. FaceLighting is stored and returned; it does not change the drawn colours. legend lists one entry per surface; .mrfig files keep the face colours, FaceAlpha and the view.
Errors: "surf: Z exceeds 1000000 elements", "surf: Z must be a matrix of at least 2-by-2", "surf: X must be a vector with one value per column of Z, or a matrix of Z's size", "surf: C must be the same size as Z", "surf: the surface needs N faces and the figure already holds M; a figure holds at most 100000 patch faces".
Example: [X, Y] = meshgrid(-2:0.25:2); Z = X .* exp(-X.^2 - Y.^2); surf(X, Y, Z)
Example: h = surf(magic(4)); h.Type   % 'surface'
Example: h = surf(magic(4)); h.FaceAlpha = 0.5; h.EdgeColor = 'none';
Differences from MATLAB: FaceColor and EdgeColor 'interp' are approximated: each face (or face outline) takes the mean of its four vertices' mapped colours, without per-vertex gradients. The depth sort is per face (painter's algorithm), so intersecting faces can overlap wrongly where a depth buffer would cut them. EdgeColor 'flat' draws a face's whole outline in that face's colour. A figure holds at most 100000 patch faces in total (surfaces, contourf bands, patches); low-level patch objects keep their own 10000-face budget. FaceAlpha 'flat'/'interp', AlphaData, CDataMapping 'direct', true-colour CData, material and camlight are not supported yet, nor are surfc, meshc, meshz, waterfall, ribbon and hidden off. FaceLighting does not light the faces. The low-level function is surface.

## surface
Low-level grid surface.
Syntax: surface(Z)
Syntax: surface(Z, C)
Syntax: surface(X, Y, Z)
Syntax: surface(X, Y, Z, C)
Syntax: surface(..., Name, Value)
Syntax: surface(ax, ...)
Syntax: h = surface(...)
Adds one surface to the current axes. Unlike surf, it does not clear existing series and does not change the view, including when hold is off. With no axes yet, the new axes keep the 2-D view. Z is a real matrix of at least 2-by-2 (at most 1000000 elements). X is a vector with one value per column of Z, or a matrix of Z's size; Y is a vector with one value per row of Z, or a matrix of Z's size. A vector and the matching matrix describe the same quadrilaterals: point (i, j) is (X(j), Y(i), Z(i, j)), or (X(i, j), Y(i, j), Z(i, j)) when X and Y are matrices. C defaults to Z. Face colours, holes, the face limit and the other properties are the same as surf. h is a scalar graphics handle and h.Type is 'surface'.
FaceLighting accepts 'none', 'flat', 'gouraud' or 'phong' (default 'flat'). get returns that word. The drawn colours stay the flat or interpolated CData colours; light objects are not simulated.
Example: h = surface([10 20 30], [1; 2], [1 2 3; 4 5 6]); h.Type
Example: h = surface([1 2 3; 4 5 6], 'EdgeColor', 'none', 'LineStyle', 'none', 'FaceLighting', 'phong'); h.FaceLighting
Differences from MATLAB: the same colour approximation and face limit as surf. FaceLighting does not light the faces.

## mesh
3-D mesh (wireframe) surface.
Syntax: mesh(Z)
Syntax: mesh(Z, C)
Syntax: mesh(X, Y, Z)
Syntax: mesh(X, Y, Z, C)
Syntax: mesh(..., Name, Value)
Syntax: mesh(ax, ...)
Syntax: h = mesh(...)
Same inputs, properties and limits as surf, with mesh defaults: EdgeColor 'flat' (each face's outline in the colormap colour of its first vertex's CData) and FaceColor the axes background colour, so lines behind the mesh are hidden as with MATLAB's hidden on. h.Type is 'surface'; shading changes the EdgeColor of a mesh and keeps its faces.
Example: mesh(peaks(25))
Example: h = mesh(magic(4)); h.EdgeColor   % 'flat'
Example: [X, Y] = meshgrid(1:10); mesh(X, Y, sin(X / 2) .* cos(Y / 3), 'LineWidth', 1)
Differences from MATLAB: the face colour is the background colour when the mesh is drawn (a later change of the axes Color recolours it). hidden off, meshc, meshz and waterfall are not supported yet; EdgeColor 'interp' uses the mean of the four vertex colours of a face.

## shading
Surface colour shading.
Syntax: shading flat
Syntax: shading faceted
Syntax: shading interp
Syntax: shading(ax, mode)
Sets the colouring of every surface in the current axes, or in axes ax: 'flat' gives FaceColor 'flat' and EdgeColor 'none'; 'faceted' (surf's default) gives FaceColor 'flat' and black edges; 'interp' gives FaceColor 'interp' and EdgeColor 'none'. On a mesh, 'flat' and 'faceted' set EdgeColor 'flat' and 'interp' sets EdgeColor 'interp'; the mesh faces are kept.
Example: surf(peaks(20)); shading interp
Example: h = surf(magic(4)); shading flat; h.EdgeColor   % 'none'
Differences from MATLAB: 'interp' colours each face with the mean of its four vertex colours (no gradients within a face). Patch objects are not changed.

## pcolor
Draw a grid of coloured cells.
Syntax: h = pcolor(C)
Syntax: h = pcolor(X, Y, C)
Returns a surface with zero ZData and CData from C. New plots use the 2-D view with flat colours and black edges. Each face takes its colour from its first vertex, so the last row and column of C supply no flat face colours. With C alone, X is the column index and Y is the row index. Grid sizes and surface properties follow surf.
Example: h = pcolor([1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9]); h.Type   % 'surface'

## sphere
Create a sampled unit sphere or draw it as a surface.
Syntax: [X, Y, Z] = sphere
Syntax: [X, Y, Z] = sphere(n)
Syntax: sphere(n)
Returns three (n+1)-by-(n+1) coordinate arrays, with n = 20 by default. Rows run from the south pole to the north pole. A call without outputs draws the surface. Coordinate generation accepts integer n from 1 to 999. Drawing also uses the figure's 100000-face limit.
Example: [X, Y, Z] = sphere(4); size(Z)   % [5 5]
Example: sphere

## surfl
Draw a surface with colours based on its slope.
Syntax: h = surfl(Z)
Syntax: h = surfl(X, Y, Z)
Returns a surface. CData is computed from the surface normals and a fixed light direction. Grid sizes, surface properties and the axes view follow surf.
Example: h = surfl(peaks(20)); h.Type   % 'surface'

## trisurf
Draw filled triangular faces as a patch.
Syntax: h = trisurf(T, X, Y, Z)
Syntax: h = trisurf(T, X, Y, Z, C)
Each row of T contains three one-based vertex indices. The live patch exposes T as Faces and the coordinate columns as Vertices. A face takes its colour from the first vertex using the axes colormap at creation. C supplies one scalar per vertex and defaults to Z.
Example: h = trisurf([1 2 3], [0 1 0], [0 0 1], [0 1 2]); h.Faces

## trimesh
Draw triangular edges as a patch.
Syntax: h = trimesh(T, X, Y, Z)
Syntax: h = trimesh(T, X, Y, Z, C)
Uses the coordinate and connectivity inputs of trisurf. Each triangle has coloured edges and an open face.
Example: h = trimesh([1 2 3], [0 1 0], [0 0 1], [0 1 2]); h.Type   % 'patch'

## tetramesh
Draw the triangular faces of tetrahedra as a patch.
Syntax: h = tetramesh(T, X)
T has four one-based vertex indices per tetrahedron. X has one vertex per row and three coordinate columns. The patch contains four faces per tetrahedron and shares the Vertices table across all faces.
Example: h = tetramesh([1 2 3 4], [0 0 0; 1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 1]); size(h.Faces)   % [4 3]

## eqtflength
Equalize the lengths of two transfer-function coefficient vectors.
Syntax: [b, a] = eqtflength(num, den)
Returns row vectors after padding the shorter input on the right and discarding trailing coefficients that are zero in both vectors. Accepts real or complex double vectors.
Example: [b, a] = eqtflength([1 2], [1 2 3 0])   % b = [1 2 0], a = [1 2 3]

## jsondecode
Decode JSON text into arrays, structs and cells.
Syntax: v = jsondecode(txt)
Syntax: v = jsondecode(txt, 'makeValidName', false)
txt is a character vector or string scalar holding one JSON value. An object becomes a scalar struct; member names that are not valid field names are changed the way matlab.lang.makeValidName does it (spaces removed with the next letter capitalized, other bad characters replaced by '_', an 'x' put in front of names that do not start with a letter), and repeated names get _1, _2, ... added. With 'makeValidName', false an invalid name is an error. null becomes [], true and false become logical scalars, numbers become double and strings become character vectors. An array of numbers becomes a column vector (null inside it is NaN), an array of booleans a logical column, and nested arrays of equal length become a matrix or N-D array whose first dimension is the outer array. An array of objects that all have the same member names becomes an N-by-1 struct array; any other array becomes an N-by-1 cell array. The words NaN, Inf, Infinity and -Infinity are accepted as numbers.
Example: s = jsondecode('{"name":"pump","rate":[1.5,2,null],"on":true}')   % struct with fields name, rate (3x1, NaN last) and on
Example: m = jsondecode('[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]')   % 2-by-3 double
Example: c = jsondecode('[1,"two",[3,4]]')   % 3-by-1 cell
Example: s = jsondecode('{"first name":1,"2nd":2}')   % fields firstName and x2nd
Differences from MATLAB: Arrays of objects nested inside arrays become cells of struct columns, not N-D struct arrays. An array holding only nulls becomes a cell of [] values. Results obey this engine's bounds: character vectors up to 65536 characters and cells or structs nested at most 16 levels; JSON text up to 64 MiB.

## jsonencode
Encode a value as JSON text.
Syntax: txt = jsonencode(v)
Syntax: txt = jsonencode(v, 'PrettyPrint', true)
Syntax: txt = jsonencode(v, 'ConvertInfAndNaN', false)
Returns a character vector. Numeric and logical scalars become numbers and true/false, vectors become flat JSON arrays, matrices become arrays of rows and N-D arrays arrays nested by dimension. Character vectors and string scalars become JSON strings (a missing string becomes null, a char matrix an array of row strings). A cell array becomes a JSON array of its elements in column order, a scalar struct an object, a struct array an array of objects and a containers.Map an object of its keys and values. Empty arrays, cells and structs become []. NaN and Inf become null unless 'ConvertInfAndNaN' is false, which writes NaN, Infinity and -Infinity. 'PrettyPrint', true adds line breaks and two-space indentation.
Example: jsonencode(struct('a',[1 2 3],'b','text'))   % '{"a":[1,2,3],"b":"text"}'
Example: jsonencode({1, true, 'x', []})   % '[1,true,"x",[]]'
Example: jsonencode([1 NaN Inf])   % '[1,null,null]'
Example: jsonencode(magic(3), 'PrettyPrint', true)
Differences from MATLAB: Numbers use the shortest text that reads back exactly, with exponent form (1e+300 is written 1e300) outside 1e-5 to 1e15. Complex values, function handles, graphics handles and other objects are errors. N-D input must sit inside a struct or cell field; an N-D array passed directly is rejected. The result is a character vector, so it can hold at most 65536 characters.

## readcell
Read a text or spreadsheet file into a cell array.
Syntax: C = readcell('data.csv')
Syntax: C = readcell('data.txt', 'Delimiter', ';', 'NumHeaderLines', 1)
Syntax: C = readcell('data.csv', 'Range', 'B2:C5')
Syntax: C = readcell('book.xlsx', 'Sheet', 2, 'Range', 'A1:D10')
Syntax: C = readcell(filename, opts)
With import options from detectImportOptions, the selected variables are converted to their types (numbers, text, datetime, duration, categorical, logical) and each value fills one cell; empty and unconvertible fields take the variable's FillValue unless MissingRule or ImportErrorRule omit them.
Returns one cell per field. Fields that read as numbers (including Inf and NaN) become doubles, other text becomes character vectors with surrounding spaces removed, and empty fields become missing. Quoted fields stay text and may contain the delimiter, line breaks and doubled quotes. Without Delimiter, the most frequent of comma, tab, semicolon and bar outside quotes in the first lines is used. If none occurs, space is used. Set Delimiter to ' ', 'space', 'whitespace' or a list such as {' ', '\t'} to join runs of spaces and tabs and ignore leading and trailing whitespace. Blank lines are skipped and short rows are padded with missing. NumHeaderLines skips leading lines; Range ('A1:C10' or a start cell 'B2') counts lines and fields of the file, and blank lines inside it become rows of missing. For .xlsx, .xlsm, .xlsb and .xls files (or 'FileType', 'spreadsheet') numbers become doubles, logical cells logical, text character vectors and empty cells missing; Sheet picks a sheet by name or 1-based index, and NumHeaderLines counts sheet rows from row 1.
Example: writecell({'name','size';'bolt',4},'parts.csv'); C = readcell('parts.csv')   % 2-by-2 cell: {'name','size';'bolt',4}
Differences from MATLAB: Missing entries hold a missing string (class string), not a missing object. Dates, durations and complex numbers in text files stay text; spreadsheet dates read as Excel serial numbers. NumHeaderLines and Range cannot be combined. Results are limited to 65536 cells; text files to 64 MiB. An .xls workbook is read whole and is limited to 16777216 cells over all its sheets.

## writecell
Write a cell array to a delimited text file.
Syntax: writecell(C, 'out.csv')
Syntax: writecell(C, 'out.txt', 'Delimiter', 'tab')
Syntax: writecell(C, 'out.csv', 'QuoteStrings', true)
Each cell must hold a numeric or logical scalar, text (character vector or string scalar) or an empty value. Numbers are written in the shortest form that reads back exactly (logical as 1 or 0, NaN and Inf by name); text that contains the delimiter, a quote or a line break is put in double quotes with inner quotes doubled, and 'QuoteStrings', true quotes all text. Delimiter is comma (default), semicolon, tab, bar or space, given as the character or its name. Use a .csv, .txt or .dat name, or add 'FileType', 'text'; a name without an extension gets .txt. Call it as a statement.
Example: writecell({'a',1;'b',2},'pairs.csv')   % writes a,1 and b,2
Differences from MATLAB: Overwrites the file only (no append). Writing spreadsheets (.xlsx, .xls) is not supported yet and gives an error. Cells holding arrays, cells, structs or datetimes are rejected.

## xlsread
Read numbers, text and raw cells from a spreadsheet (legacy form).
Syntax: num = xlsread('book.xlsx')
Syntax: [num, txt, raw] = xlsread('book.xlsx', sheet)
Syntax: [num, txt, raw] = xlsread('book.xlsx', sheet, 'A1:C10')
Syntax: num = xlsread('book.xlsx', 'B2:D5')
Reads .xlsx, .xlsm, .xlsb or .xls files. sheet is a sheet name or 1-based index ('' or omitted: the first sheet); a single text argument containing ':' is a range of the first sheet. num is the smallest rectangle holding every numeric or logical cell, with NaN for the others; txt is the smallest rectangle holding every text cell, with '' for the others; raw is every cell of the read area, with numbers as double, logical cells as logical, text as character vectors and empty cells as NaN. A fourth input 'basic' is accepted and changes nothing.
Example: [num, txt] = xlsread('book.xlsx', 'Data')   % numbers and header text of sheet Data
Differences from MATLAB: No Excel automation: no interactive selection (-1), no custom processing function and no formula evaluation (stored cached results are read). Error cells read as NaN; dates read as Excel serial numbers. raw is limited to 65536 cells; an .xls workbook is read whole and is limited to 16777216 cells over all its sheets.

## xlswrite
Write a matrix or cell array to a spreadsheet (legacy form).
Syntax: xlswrite('book.xlsx', A)
Syntax: xlswrite('book.xlsx', A, sheet)
Syntax: xlswrite('book.xlsx', A, 'B2:D5')
Syntax: xlswrite('book.xlsx', A, sheet, 'B2')
Syntax: status = xlswrite(...)
Writes an .xlsx workbook (a name without an extension gets .xlsx). A is a numeric, logical, character vector, string or cell array; cells of a cell array hold real scalars, text or empty values. sheet is a sheet name or 1-based index ('' or omitted: the first sheet); a sheet that does not exist is added (an index past the last sheet adds sheets named Sheet1, Sheet2, ...). A range that is one cell is the top-left corner; a rectangle clips A to its size. A single text argument containing ':' is a range on the first sheet. An existing workbook keeps its other sheets and the cells outside the written area. NaN, Inf and empty values clear their cells. status is true when the file was written.
Example: xlswrite('book.xlsx', magic(3))   % 3x3 block at A1 of Sheet1
Example: xlswrite('book.xlsx', {'x', 'y'; 1, 2}, 'Data', 'B2')   % header row and values on sheet Data
Differences from MATLAB: No Excel automation: only .xlsx is written (not .xls, .xlsm or .xlsb). Updating an existing workbook keeps cell values only: formatting, formulas, charts, merged cells and defined names are not kept. No message output and no "Added specified worksheet" warning. A rectangle larger than A leaves the extra cells as they were instead of filling #N/A.

## webread
Read content from a web service (HTTP or HTTPS GET).
Syntax: data = webread(url)
Syntax: data = webread(url, name1, value1, ...)
Syntax: data = webread(..., options)
Name/value pairs are added to the URL as a percent-encoded query (numeric values as comma-separated numbers). options comes from weboptions. With ContentType 'auto', a JSON response (application/json or +json) is decoded as jsondecode does, a text response (text/*, XML, JavaScript) is returned as a character vector and anything else as a uint8 column vector of the bytes. ContentType 'text', 'json' and 'binary' force one of these; 'raw' returns text responses as text without decoding JSON. Redirects are followed (at most 10). A status of 400 or more is an error.
Example: data = webread('https://api.example.org/items', 'page', 2)   % decoded JSON struct
Example: html = webread('https://example.org', weboptions('Timeout', 20))
Differences from MATLAB: Requests run through the system curl program (Windows 10 and later, macOS and most Linux systems include it); there is no webread in the browser console. GET only; no Username/Password, key or certificate options. Images, audio, tables and XML documents are not parsed (ContentType 'image', 'audio', 'table', 'xmldom'); image and audio responses come back as uint8 bytes. Responses are limited to 64 MiB.

## websave
Save content from a web service to a file.
Syntax: outfilename = websave(filename, url)
Syntax: outfilename = websave(filename, url, name1, value1, ...)
Syntax: outfilename = websave(..., options)
Downloads the response body unchanged into filename (relative names are in the current folder) and returns the full path. Query pairs and options are as in webread. The download goes to a temporary file in the same folder that replaces filename only when the request succeeded, so a failed request leaves an existing file untouched.
Example: f = websave('data.csv', 'https://example.org/data.csv')
Differences from MATLAB: Requests run through the system curl program; there is no websave in the browser console. GET only; no authentication options. No extension is added from the content type when filename has none. Downloads are limited to 4 GiB.

## weboptions
Settings for webread and websave.
Syntax: options = weboptions
Syntax: options = weboptions(name1, value1, ...)
Returns a struct with the fields CharacterEncoding ('auto': from the response, else UTF-8), UserAgent ('MatRust/<version>'), Timeout (seconds, default 5), ContentType ('auto', 'text', 'json', 'binary' or 'raw') and HeaderFields (an n-by-2 cell array of extra request header names and values). Change a field with dot assignment or give name/value pairs.
Example: options = weboptions('Timeout', 30, 'HeaderFields', {'Accept', 'application/json'})
Differences from MATLAB: options is a struct, not a weboptions object. Username, Password, KeyName, KeyValue and CertificateFilename are errors; MediaType, ArrayFormat and ContentReader are accepted and ignored; RequestMethod can only be 'get'.

## h5read
Read data from an HDF5 dataset.
Syntax: data = h5read(filename, ds)
Syntax: data = h5read(filename, ds, start, count)
Syntax: data = h5read(filename, ds, start, count, stride)
ds is the dataset path, such as '/group/data' (the leading / is optional). The size is the reverse of the HDF5 (C-order) dimensions, so a dataset that h5py or h5dump shows as 3x4 reads as 4x3; a one-dimensional dataset reads as a column. Doubles read as double, floats as single, integers as their integer class, HDF5 booleans (h5py bool) as logical and text (variable or fixed length) as a cell array of character vectors. start (one-based), count (Inf: to the end) and stride select a hyperslab, one value per MATLAB dimension. Deflate, shuffle and Fletcher32 filters are read.
Example: m = h5read('data.h5', '/m')
Example: part = h5read('data.h5', '/m', [2 1], [2 Inf])   % rows 2 and 3, every column
Differences from MATLAB: Compound, enum (other than boolean), reference, opaque and array types are not supported; text datasets cannot be read in parts. External filter plugins, external and virtual storage are not used. Reads are limited to 2 GiB. Not in the browser build.

## h5create
Create an HDF5 dataset.
Syntax: h5create(filename, ds, sz)
Syntax: h5create(filename, ds, sz, Name, Value)
Creates the file when it does not exist and any missing groups on the path. sz is the MATLAB size (stored reversed, as h5write and h5read expect). Options: 'Datatype' ('double' default, 'single' or an integer class), 'ChunkSize' (one value per dimension, required by 'Deflate'), 'Deflate' (0 to 9) and 'FillValue'. Creating a dataset that exists is an error.
Example: h5create('out.h5', '/results/x', [100 3], 'Datatype', 'single')
Differences from MATLAB: No unlimited (Inf) dimensions, no 'Fletcher32', 'Shuffle', 'TextEncoding' or 'CustomFilter' options, and no string datasets. A chunk is limited to 8 MiB. Not in the browser build.

## h5write
Write data to an existing HDF5 dataset.
Syntax: h5write(filename, ds, data)
Syntax: h5write(filename, ds, data, start, count)
Syntax: h5write(filename, ds, data, start, count, stride)
Without start and count, data must have the dataset's size (as h5read returns it; a one-dimensional dataset takes a row or a column). With them, data fills the hyperslab: count must equal size(data). Values are converted to the dataset type: integer datasets round half away from zero and saturate, as int16() and the other integer conversions do; NaN becomes 0.
Example: h5create('out.h5', '/x', [3 4]); h5write('out.h5', '/x', rand(3, 4))
Example: h5write('out.h5', '/x', [1; 2], [2 3], [2 1])   % rows 2-3 of column 3
Differences from MATLAB: Text, complex and struct data cannot be written. Datasets do not grow. Not in the browser build.

## ncread
Read a variable from a NetCDF file.
Syntax: vardata = ncread(source, varname)
Syntax: vardata = ncread(source, varname, start, count)
Syntax: vardata = ncread(source, varname, start, count, stride)
Reads NetCDF classic files (CDF-1, 64-bit offset CDF-2 and 64-bit data CDF-5) and NetCDF-4 files. The size is the reverse of the order ncdump lists the dimensions, with the record (unlimited) dimension last. Values keep their class (double, single, integer, char for NC_CHAR). Values equal to the _FillValue or missing_value attribute become NaN in floating data; with scale_factor or add_offset the result is double, unpacked as value*scale_factor+add_offset, with fill and missing values NaN. start (one-based), count (Inf: to the end) and stride select part of the variable.
Example: t = ncread('weather.nc', 'temp')
Example: first = ncread('weather.nc', 'temp', [1 1 1], [Inf Inf 1])   % the first record
Differences from MATLAB: URLs (OPeNDAP) are not read. Integer data with a fill value but no scale or offset keeps the fill value. NetCDF-4 user-defined (compound, enum, vlen) and string variables are not supported; group variables are named 'group/var'. Not in the browser build.

## sparse
Create a sparse array.
Syntax: S = sparse(A)
Syntax: S = sparse(m, n)
Syntax: S = sparse(i, j, v)
Syntax: S = sparse(i, j, v, m, n)
Syntax: S = sparse(i, j, v, m, n, nzmax)
sparse(A) stores the nonzeros of a full double or logical matrix; sparse(m,n) is an m-by-n all-zero sparse array; sparse(i,j,v,m,n) puts v(k) at row i(k), column j(k). A scalar v, or an i or j of length 1, is expanded to the common length. Repeated subscripts are summed in input order (logical v: combined with or), and sums of zero are not stored. Without m and n the size is max(i)-by-max(j). nzmax is checked and then ignored.
Example: S = sparse([1 2 3], [1 2 3], [4 5 6])   % 3x3 with three nonzeros
Example: full(sparse([1 1 2], [1 1 2], [2 3 4]))   % [5 0; 0 4]
Example: S = sparse(2)   % 1x1 sparse
Storage: compressed columns. Each column keeps its row indices in increasing order with their values (double, or logical for a logical sparse array). Zeros are never stored, including sums that cancel and rounding results that become 0. Only two dimensions. Assigning a sparse variable shares its storage; a write builds a new copy.
Results (scalar means 1-by-1, full or sparse): S+S and S-S are sparse; S+F, S-F, F-S and S+scalar are full. S.*S, S.*F, F.*S, S*scalar, scalar*S, S/scalar, S./scalar and scalar\S are sparse; multiplying or dividing by a scalar changes the stored values only. S*S is sparse; S*F and F*S are full. S\F and F/S with a square sparse S (not 1-by-1) solve without converting S: a triangular S by substitution, a symmetric S with a positive diagonal by sparse Cholesky (AMD ordering), otherwise sparse LU (COLAMD ordering, partial pivoting); the results are full, and S\S and S/S are sparse. A singular S, stored NaN or Inf, or a non-finite right-hand side uses the full solver when n*n fits the sparse-to-full limit (same values and warnings as full(S)\F) and is an error above it. A rectangular S, and S/X and X\S with a full non-scalar X, convert to full and use the full solver. S&S, S&F and F&S are logical sparse. -S, +S, S', S.', abs, round, floor, ceil and fix are sparse; sqrt is sparse when no stored value is negative. sum, max, min (one output), any and all are sparse; implicit zeros take part in max and min. double and logical keep sparse storage. [S, F], [F; S] and cat(1 or 2, ...) are sparse. find and nonzeros give full columns. Indexing a sparse array (S(i,j), S(k), S(:), masks, end) gives a sparse result, 1-by-1 included.
Converted to full first: every other function given a sparse input, including S./F, F./S, scalar./S, S.^p, p.^S, S|F, ~S, xor, the comparisons ==, ~=, <, <=, >, >=, [m,i] = max(S), max(S,F) and max(S,scalar). Their results are full.
Indexed writes: S(i,j) = v stores nonzeros and deletes entries set to 0; subscripts beyond the size grow the array (S(5,6) = 0 grows a 3-by-2 array to 5-by-6 and stores nothing). S(:,j) = [] and S(i,:) = [] delete columns and rows. Linear growth of a matrix beyond its number of elements is an error, as for full matrices. When an index repeats, the last value wins.
Bytes (whos and the workspace limit): 16 per stored double entry, 9 per stored logical entry, plus 8 per column pointer (number of columns + 1). This is MatRust's count, not MATLAB's.
Display: one line per stored entry in column order, (row,col) followed by the value as the current format shows a column of the stored values; an array without nonzeros shows All zero sparse: m-by-n.
MAT files: -v6 and -v7 save and load double and logical sparse arrays, also inside cell arrays.
Differences from MATLAB: The functions listed above as converted to full return full results where MATLAB keeps some of them sparse (S./F, S.^p, comparisons, ~S, S|F). A sparse array with more than 16777216 elements cannot be converted to full yet (the error names the function). Complex, single and integer sparse arrays are not supported; complex sparse variables in MAT files are reported and skipped while the other variables load. nzmax equals nnz. Sparse variables cannot be saved to v7.3 files yet. No sparse factorizations, eigs, svds, spfun or sprand yet.

## issparse
True for a sparse array.
Syntax: tf = issparse(A)
Example: issparse(speye(3))   % true
Example: issparse(eye(3))   % false
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## speye
Sparse identity matrix.
Syntax: S = speye(n)
Syntax: S = speye(m, n)
Syntax: S = speye([m n])
Ones on the main diagonal of an m-by-n sparse array; speye with no input is 1-by-1.
Example: S = speye(3)   % three stored ones
Example: nnz(speye(2, 4))   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## spalloc
All-zero sparse array with room for nonzeros.
Syntax: S = spalloc(m, n, nz)
Returns sparse(m,n). nz must be a nonnegative integer; storage grows when entries are added, so nz is otherwise ignored.
Example: S = spalloc(3, 4, 5)   % All zero sparse: 3x4
Differences from MATLAB: nz does not reserve storage, and nzmax(S) is 0 until entries are stored.

## spdiags
Sparse matrix from diagonals.
Syntax: S = spdiags(B, d, m, n)
Column k of B becomes diagonal d(k) of the m-by-n result (0 is the main diagonal, positive above, negative below). When m >= n, element B(j,k) goes to column j of the result; when m < n, to row j.
Example: full(spdiags(reshape(1:12, 4, 3), [-1 0 1], 5, 4))   % [5 10 0 0; 1 6 11 0; 0 2 7 12; 0 0 3 8; 0 0 0 4]
Example: full(spdiags([1 2 3]', 0, 3, 3))   % diag([1 2 3])
Differences from MATLAB: Only the create form spdiags(B,d,m,n) is supported yet; the extraction and replacement forms give an error.

## spones
Replace the nonzeros of an array by ones.
Syntax: R = spones(S)
Returns a double sparse array with ones where S has nonzeros.
Example: full(spones(sparse([0 5; -2 0])))   % [0 1; 1 0]
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## sprand
Random sparse matrix with uniformly distributed stored values.
Syntax: S = sprand(m, n, density)
Syntax: R = sprand(S)
Draws round(density*m*n) positions, merges duplicate draws, and stores uniform values strictly between 0 and 1. The one-input form keeps the nonzero pattern of S.
Example: S = sprand(4, 5, 0.3); issparse(S)
Differences from MATLAB: Positions are drawn first and values second, so the random-stream consumption is documented and deterministic here.

## sprandn
Random sparse matrix with normally distributed stored values.
Syntax: S = sprandn(m, n, density)
Syntax: R = sprandn(S)
Draws a sparse pattern as sprand does, with normal stored values. The one-input form keeps the nonzero pattern.
Example: S = sprandn(4, 5, 0.3); issparse(S)
Differences from MATLAB: Positions are drawn first and values second; normal draws use MatRust's rng implementation.

## sprandsym
Random symmetric sparse matrix.
Syntax: S = sprandsym(n, density)
Draws the lower triangle with normal values and mirrors it across the diagonal.
Example: S = sprandsym(5, 0.4); norm(full(S-S.'))
Differences from MATLAB: Positions are drawn first and values second; the density controls draws in the lower triangle.

## spfun
Apply a function to sparse stored values.
Syntax: R = spfun(fun, S)
Calls fun once with a column vector of S's nonzeros. R is sparse with the same pattern, except output zeros are omitted.
Example: full(spfun(@exp, sparse([0 1; -1 0])))
Differences from MATLAB: fun must return a real vector with the same length as the stored values.

## amd
Approximate minimum degree permutation.
Syntax: p = amd(A)
Syntax: p = amd(A, opts)
Returns a 1-based row permutation for the pattern of A+A'.
Example: p = amd(sparse([4 1 0; 1 4 1; 0 1 4]))
Differences from MATLAB: opts is accepted and ignored.

## colamd
Column approximate minimum degree permutation.
Syntax: p = colamd(S)
Syntax: p = colamd(S, opts)
Returns a 1-based column permutation for the pattern of S.
Example: p = colamd(sparse([1 0 1; 0 1 1]))
Differences from MATLAB: opts is accepted and ignored.

## symamd
Symmetric approximate minimum degree permutation.
Syntax: p = symamd(S)
Syntax: p = symamd(S, opts)
Returns a 1-based permutation for a square matrix pattern.
Example: p = symamd(sparse([4 1 0; 1 4 1; 0 1 4]))
Differences from MATLAB: opts is accepted and ignored; this uses AMD on S+S'.

## symrcm
Symmetric reverse Cuthill-McKee permutation.
Syntax: p = symrcm(S)
Returns a 1-based permutation found by a pseudo-peripheral breadth-first traversal of S+S'.
Example: p = symrcm(sparse([1 1 0; 1 1 1; 0 1 1]))
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## ichol
Incomplete Cholesky factorization of a sparse matrix.
Syntax: L = ichol(A)
Syntax: L = ichol(A, opts)
Returns a sparse lower triangular L with L*L' close to A, using only the lower triangle of A. opts fields: type 'nofill' (default, the pattern of tril(A)) or 'ict' (fill kept above droptol*norm(A(j:end,j),1)); droptol (default 0); michol 'off' (default) or 'on' (dropped values go to the diagonal so that L*L'*e equals A*e); diagcomp alpha (factors A + alpha*diag(diag(A))); shape 'lower' (default) or 'upper' (returns R with R'*R close to A, using the upper triangle). A nonpositive pivot is an error. Use L as the preconditioner of pcg: pcg(A,b,tol,maxit,L,L').
Example: A = gallery('poisson',30); L = ichol(A); x = pcg(A, ones(900,1), 1e-8, 200, L, L');
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## ilu
Incomplete LU factorization of a sparse matrix.
Syntax: W = ilu(A)
Syntax: [L, U] = ilu(A, setup)
Syntax: [L, U, P] = ilu(A, setup)
L is unit lower triangular and U upper triangular with L*U close to A; one output gives W = L+U-speye(n). setup fields: type 'nofill' (default, the pattern of A), 'crout' or 'ilutp' (fill kept above droptol times the 2-norm of the column of A); droptol (default 0, a complete factorization); milu 'off' (default), 'row' or 'col' (dropped values go to the diagonal of U so that row or column sums match A); udiag 1 replaces a zero pivot of 'ilutp' by the local drop tolerance; thresh (default 1) is the 'ilutp' pivot threshold: the diagonal is kept when it is at least thresh times the largest candidate. For 'ilutp', P*A is close to L*U; with two outputs L is returned as P'*L. A zero pivot is an error.
Example: A = gallery('tridiag',100); [L, U] = ilu(A); x = gmres(A, ones(100,1), 20, 1e-10, 10, L, U);
Differences from MATLAB: milu 'row' is not supported with type 'ilutp'.

## nzmax
Storage allocated for nonzeros.
Syntax: n = nzmax(S)
For a sparse array MatRust allocates exactly the stored entries, so nzmax(S) equals nnz(S). For a full array it is numel(A).
Example: nzmax(sparse([1 0 2]))   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: MATLAB can report more than nnz(S) after spalloc or sparse(...,nzmax).

## table
Table of named variables (columns) of a common height.
Syntax: T = table(v1, v2, ...)
Syntax: T = table(..., 'VariableNames', names, 'RowNames', rows)
Syntax: T = table()
Each input is one variable; every variable must have the same number of rows (a variable may have several columns, such as a 3x2 matrix). Variable names come from the input variable names, else Var1, Var2, ... by position. 'VariableNames' (cellstr or string array) and 'RowNames' (one unique name per row) set them explicitly; 'DimensionNames' renames the two dimensions (default {'Row', 'Variables'}). A variable name must be nonempty, at most 63 characters, unique, and may not be 'Properties' or a dimension name (table(1, 'VariableNames', {'Row'}) is an error); dimension names must be valid identifiers.
Access: T.Var, T.(name), T.Var(i), T.Var(i,j) read a variable; T.Var = v replaces or appends a variable (its height must match; a 0x0 table takes the height), T.Var(i) = v writes into it, T.Var = [] deletes it. T(rows, vars) is a table and T{rows, vars} the selected values side by side (an error for incompatible types). Rows are numbers, a logical mask, ':' or row names; variables are numbers, a logical mask, ':', a name, a cellstr or a string array. T(rows, vars) = T2 (same size; T2's variables are matched to the selected ones by name, in any order), T(rows, vars) = {...} and T{rows, vars} = value write; T(rows, :) = [] deletes rows, T(:, vars) = [] deletes variables, and T(end+1, :) = {...} appends a row.
Properties: T.Properties.VariableNames, RowNames, DimensionNames, Description, VariableUnits and VariableDescriptions are read and set (VariableNames must stay unique valid names that differ from 'Properties' and from the two dimension names, so T.Properties and T.Row never return a variable; RowNames unique; '' or {} removes the row names); T.Properties alone is a struct of them.
Functions on tables: istable, class ('table'), height, width, size (rows by variables), numel (height times width), isempty, head, tail, sortrows, isequal, horzcat/vertcat ([T1, T2] needs distinct names and the same height, and when both have row names the same set, which T2's rows then follow in T1's order; [T1; T2] needs the same names in any order, which follow T1), table2array, table2cell, table2struct, writetable. whos shows Class table.
Display: a size line, then each variable under its name and a rule of underscores as wide as the column, four spaces apart. Numbers are right-aligned and printed as the current format prints a scalar; logicals show true/false, cellstr elements {'text'}, strings "text", datetime and duration values their text. Row names are a first column without a header. Trailing blanks are trimmed.
Example: T = table([31; 45], {'Ann'; 'Bob'}, 'VariableNames', {'Age', 'Name'})   % 2x2 table
Example: Age = [31; 45]; T = table(Age); T.Height = [1.6; 1.8]; T.Age(2)   % 45
Example: T = table([1; 2; 3], 'RowNames', {'a', 'b', 'c'}); T({'c', 'a'}, :)   % rows c and a
Example: T = table([3; 1; 2], [10; 20; 30]); S = T(T.Var1 > 1, :)   % 2x2 table
Example: T = table([1; 2]); T(end+1, :) = {3}; height(T)   % 3
Differences from MATLAB: Part 1 of tables. Not supported yet (planned): joins (join, innerjoin, outerjoin), groupsummary, varfun and rowfun, timetable, readtable datetime detection, xlsx tables, categorical variables, the 'Size'/'VariableTypes' constructor, nested tables, sparse, function handle and graphics handle variables (a cell variable may hold handles) and growing a table by assigning past the end of one variable. Tables cannot be saved to MAT files yet. A brace write into a cell variable takes a non-cell value as the content of one cell. Wide tables are not wrapped to the console width.

## table.disp
Display table variable names and their row values.
Syntax: disp(T)
Example: T = table([18; 22], 'VariableNames', {'Temperature'}); disp(T)
See also: table

## array2table
Table with one variable per column of an array.
Syntax: T = array2table(A)
Syntax: T = array2table(A, 'VariableNames', names, 'RowNames', rows)
The variables are named after the input variable and the column number (array2table(M) gives M1, M2, ...), or Var1, Var2, ... for an expression.
Example: M = [1 2; 3 4]; T = array2table(M); T.M2   % [2; 4]
Example: T = array2table(magic(3), 'VariableNames', {'a', 'b', 'c'})   % 3x3 table
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## cell2table
Table from the columns of a cell array.
Syntax: T = cell2table(C)
Syntax: T = cell2table(C, 'VariableNames', names, 'RowNames', rows)
A column whose cells all hold numeric (or logical) scalars of one class becomes a column vector of that class; any other column stays a cell column. Names follow array2table.
Example: T = cell2table({'Ann', 31; 'Bob', 45}, 'VariableNames', {'Name', 'Age'}); T.Age   % [31; 45]
Differences from MATLAB: Columns of text, datetimes or mixed values stay cell columns.

## struct2table
Table from a struct array or a scalar struct.
Syntax: T = struct2table(S)
Syntax: T = struct2table(S, 'VariableNames', names, 'RowNames', rows)
For a struct vector each field becomes a variable with one row per element (numeric or logical scalars of one class join into a column, other values form a cell column). For a scalar struct each field is one variable taken as it is, so all fields need the same number of rows.
Example: S = struct('a', {1, 2}, 'b', {'x', 'y'}); T = struct2table(S); T.a   % [1; 2]
Example: s.a = [1; 2]; s.b = [3; 4]; T = struct2table(s)   % 2x2 table
Differences from MATLAB: No 'AsArray' option.

## table2array
Values of all table variables side by side.
Syntax: A = table2array(T)
The same as T{:, :}: the variables are concatenated horizontally; numeric and logical variables mix, other classes must match (an error otherwise).
Example: A = table2array(table([1; 2], [3; 4]))   % [1 3; 2 4]
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## table2cell
Cell array of the table's values.
Syntax: C = table2cell(T)
C is height-by-width; C{i,j} holds row i of variable j (the text itself for a cellstr variable).
Example: C = table2cell(table([1; 2], {'a'; 'b'}))   % {1, 'a'; 2, 'b'}
Differences from MATLAB: At most 65536 cells.

## table2struct
Struct array of the table's rows.
Syntax: S = table2struct(T)
Syntax: S = table2struct(T, 'ToScalar', true)
S is height-by-1 with one field per variable; 'ToScalar', true gives one struct whose fields are the whole variables.
Example: S = table2struct(table([1; 2], 'VariableNames', {'x'})); S(2).x   % 2
Example: s = table2struct(table([1; 2], 'VariableNames', {'x'}), 'ToScalar', true)   % s.x = [1; 2]
Differences from MATLAB: Row names are not returned.

## istable
True for a table.
Syntax: tf = istable(x)
Example: tf = istable(table([1; 2]))   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## height
Number of rows.
Syntax: n = height(T)
The table height, or size(A, 1) for any other array.
Example: n = height(table([1; 2; 3]))   % 3
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## width
Number of variables of a table, or columns of an array.
Syntax: n = width(T)
Example: n = width(table([1; 2], [3; 4]))   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## head
First rows of a table or array.
Syntax: B = head(T)
Syntax: B = head(T, k)
k defaults to 8 and is cut to the height.
Example: B = head(table((1:10)'), 3)   % rows 1 to 3
Example: B = head(magic(4), 2)   % [16 2 3 13; 5 11 10 8]
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## tail
Last rows of a table or array.
Syntax: B = tail(T)
Syntax: B = tail(T, k)
k defaults to 8 and is cut to the height.
Example: B = tail(table((1:10)'), 2)   % rows 9 and 10
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## addvars
Add variables to a table.
Syntax: T2 = addvars(T, var1, ..., varN)
Syntax: T2 = addvars(T, ..., 'Before', loc)   or   'After', loc
Syntax: T2 = addvars(T, ..., 'NewVariableNames', names)
New variables go at the end unless 'Before' or 'After' names one variable (name or index). Default names are the argument's variable name, else VarK by position; a table argument adds each of its variables.
Example: T = table([1;2]); z = [3;4]; T = addvars(T, z, 'Before', 1)   % variables z, Var1
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## removevars
Remove variables from a table.
Syntax: T2 = removevars(T, vars)
vars is a name, a list of names, indices or a logical mask.
Example: T = removevars(table([1;2], [3;4]), 'Var1')
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## renamevars
Rename table variables.
Syntax: T2 = renamevars(T, vars, newNames)
Example: T = renamevars(table([1;2]), 'Var1', 'x')
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## movevars
Move table variables.
Syntax: T2 = movevars(T, vars)
Syntax: T2 = movevars(T, vars, 'Before', loc)   or   'After', loc
Without a location the variables move to the end.
Example: T = movevars(table(1, 2, 3), 'Var3', 'Before', 1)   % Var3 Var1 Var2
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## innerjoin
Rows of two tables whose keys match.
Syntax: [T, ileft, iright] = innerjoin(Tleft, Tright)
Syntax: ... = innerjoin(Tleft, Tright, 'Keys', k, 'LeftKeys', lk, 'RightKeys', rk, 'LeftVariables', lv, 'RightVariables', rv)
Keys default to the variables both tables share. The result holds every matching pair, sorted by key, with the left variables then the right non-key variables; clashing names get _<input name> (or _left/_right) suffixes. Missing keys (NaN, '', <missing>) never match.
Example: L = table([1;2], {'a';'b'}, 'VariableNames', {'id','s'}); R = table([2;1], [20;10], 'VariableNames', {'id','v'}); innerjoin(L, R)
Differences from MATLAB: Row-name keys are not supported.

## outerjoin
Join two tables keeping unmatched rows.
Syntax: [T, ileft, iright] = outerjoin(Tleft, Tright, 'Type', 'full'|'left'|'right', 'MergeKeys', tf, ...)
Takes the innerjoin options. Unmatched rows get missing values (NaN, '', <missing>, NaT; false/0 for logical and integer variables) and index 0. Without MergeKeys both key variables are kept with _<input name> suffixes; with MergeKeys one key variable holds the key of either side.
Example: outerjoin(table([1;2], 'VariableNames', {'id'}), table([2;3], [20;30], 'VariableNames', {'id','v'}), 'MergeKeys', true)   % id 1, 2, 3
Differences from MATLAB: Row-name keys and empty input tables are not supported.

## findgroups
Group numbers of the unique values or value combinations.
Syntax: [G, ID1, ..., IDn] = findgroups(A1, ..., An)
Syntax: [G, TID] = findgroups(T)
Groups are numbered in sorted order of their values (numbers ascending, text in code-point order). Rows with a missing value get NaN. Inputs: numeric, logical, cellstr, string, char matrix rows, datetime, duration, table variables.
Example: [G, ID] = findgroups({'b';'a';'b'})   % G = [2;1;2], ID = {'a';'b'}
