Supports Style 'pushbutton' (default), 'togglebutton', 'edit', 'text', 'slider', 'checkbox', 'radiobutton', 'popupmenu', and 'listbox', with String, Value, Min, Max, Position, Units ('pixels', 'normalized'), Callback, Enable, Visible, Tag, UserData, BackgroundColor, ForegroundColor, FontSize, HorizontalAlignment, and Tooltip/TooltipString.
Example: fig = figure('Visible', 'off'); b = uicontrol(fig, 'Style', 'pushbutton', 'String', 'Go', 'Tag', 'go'); b.String; close(fig)
Differences from MATLAB: 'frame' style, reparenting after creation, Units other than 'pixels' and 'normalized', and GUIDE .fig files are not supported.

## gcbo
Return handle of the object whose callback is currently executing.
Syntax: h = gcbo
Returns the source UI component or uicontrol handle inside a running callback, or [] when no callback is executing.
Example: isempty(gcbo)
Differences from MATLAB: Two-output form [h, fig] = gcbo is not supported yet; use gcbf for the enclosing figure.

## gcbf
Return handle of the figure containing the object whose callback is currently executing.
Syntax: f = gcbf
Returns the enclosing figure handle inside a running callback, or [] when no callback is executing.
Example: isempty(gcbf)
Differences from MATLAB: Only tracks callbacks dispatched by UI components and uicontrols.

## createCallbackFcn
Create a UI component callback wrapper for an AppBase app method.
Syntax: cb = createCallbackFcn(app, @callbackFcn)
Syntax: cb = createCallbackFcn(app, @callbackFcn, requiresEvent)
Returns a function handle suitable for UI component callback properties (such as ButtonPushedFcn or ValueChangedFcn) that invokes callbackFcn(app, event) when requiresEvent is true, or callbackFcn(app) when requiresEvent is false (default), with access to private methods of app's class.
Example: d = tempname; mkdir(d); addpath(d); writelines(["classdef CbHelpApp < matlab.apps.AppBase","properties","UIFigure matlab.ui.Figure","Btn matlab.ui.control.Button","end","methods (Access = private)","function onPush(app, ~)","end","end","methods","function app = CbHelpApp","app.UIFigure = uifigure('Visible','off');","app.Btn = uibutton(app.UIFigure);","app.Btn.ButtonPushedFcn = createCallbackFcn(app, @onPush, true);","registerApp(app, app.UIFigure);","end","end","end"], fullfile(d, "CbHelpApp.m")); a = CbHelpApp; isa(a.Btn.ButtonPushedFcn, 'function_handle'); delete(a); rmpath(d); rmdir(d, 's')
Differences from MATLAB: App Designer visual editor, .mlapp packaging, App Testing Framework (matlab.uitest), web apps, and ComponentContainer are not supported.

## registerApp
Register a UIFigure with an AppBase app instance.
Syntax: registerApp(app, fig)
Links a matlab.apps.AppBase subclass instance app with its uifigure handle fig so deleting or closing fig (without a vetoing CloseRequestFcn) deletes app, deleting app deletes fig, and clearing app inside a zero-output constructor keeps the app alive while fig remains open.
Example: d = tempname; mkdir(d); addpath(d); writelines(["classdef RegHelpApp < matlab.apps.AppBase","properties","UIFigure matlab.ui.Figure","end","methods","function app = RegHelpApp","app.UIFigure = uifigure('Visible','off');","registerApp(app, app.UIFigure);","end","end","end"], fullfile(d, "RegHelpApp.m")); a = RegHelpApp; f = a.UIFigure; close(f); ~isvalid(a); rmpath(d); rmdir(d, 's')
Differences from MATLAB: Only registers uifigure handles; classic figure handles and App Designer RunningAppInstance lifecycle hooks are not supported.

## runStartupFcn
Execute an AppBase app's startup function.
Syntax: runStartupFcn(app, @startupFcn)
Syntax: runStartupFcn(app, @(app)startupFcn(app, varargin{:}))
Calls the startup function handle with app, granting access to private methods of app's class. If the startup function errors, app is deleted before the error propagates.
Example: d = tempname; mkdir(d); addpath(d); writelines(["classdef StartHelpApp < matlab.apps.AppBase","properties","UIFigure matlab.ui.Figure","Ready logical = false","end","methods (Access = private)","function startupFcn(app, flag)","app.Ready = flag;","end","end","methods","function app = StartHelpApp(varargin)","app.UIFigure = uifigure('Visible','off');","registerApp(app, app.UIFigure);","runStartupFcn(app, @(app)startupFcn(app, varargin{:}));","end","end","end"], fullfile(d, "StartHelpApp.m")); a = StartHelpApp(true); a.Ready; delete(a); rmpath(d); rmdir(d, 's')
Differences from MATLAB: App Designer visual editor and RunningAppInstance tracking are not supported.


## categorical
Create an array of category codes and names.
Syntax: C = categorical(A); C = categorical(A,valueset,catnames,'Ordinal',true)
Numeric, logical, string, cellstr and character-row inputs are supported. Missing inputs become undefined; valueset fixes category order. Assignment to a nonordinal array can append categories.
Example: C = categorical([1 3 2],1:3,{'red','green','blue'}); cellstr(C)
Differences from MATLAB: two dimensions only; duplicate category names are rejected. Protected, summary, file persistence and categorical plots are not supported yet.

## categories
Return category names in category order.
Syntax: names = categories(C)
Names are returned as a column cell array of character vectors, including unused categories.
Example: categories(categorical([2 1 2]))
Differences from MATLAB: two-dimensional categorical arrays only.

## countcats
Count defined elements in each category.
Syntax: counts = countcats(C); counts = countcats(C,dim)
The default dimension is the first nonsingleton dimension. Undefined elements do not contribute to the counts.
Example: countcats(categorical([1;3;2;1;3;1],1:3))
Differences from MATLAB: dim must be 1 or 2.

## iscategorical
Test whether a value is a categorical array.
Syntax: tf = iscategorical(A)
Returns one logical scalar.
Example: iscategorical(categorical({'a','b'}))
Differences from MATLAB: none for supported array types.

## isundefined
Find undefined categorical elements.
Syntax: mask = isundefined(C)
Returns a logical array with the same dimensions as C.
Example: isundefined(categorical([1 NaN 2]))
Differences from MATLAB: categorical input only.

## boxplot
Box plot of data columns or groups.
Syntax: boxplot(x)
Syntax: boxplot(x, g)
Syntax: h = boxplot(x, 'Labels', labels, 'Whisker', w)
Each column of a matrix, or each group of g (numbers, text or categorical), gets one box at x = 1, 2, ...: the box spans the 25th to 75th percentiles (prctile midpoint rule), a red line marks the median, dashed whiskers reach the most extreme points within w (default 1.5) interquartile ranges, and red + marks the outliers beyond them. h is 7-by-k: upper and lower whisker, upper and lower adjacent value, box, median, outliers.
Example: h = boxplot([1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 30]');   % 30 is an outlier
Differences from MATLAB: Group labels are not drawn as tick labels yet; notches, 'PlotStyle', 'Orientation' and other options are not supported yet.

## histfit
Histogram with a fitted distribution curve.
Syntax: histfit(data)
Syntax: histfit(data, nbins)
Syntax: h = histfit(data, nbins, dist)
Draws a histogram of data with nbins bins (default ceil(sqrt(n))) and the density of the distribution fitted by fitdist (default 'normal'), scaled to the bar heights by n times the bin width. NaN values are ignored. h holds the bar handles followed by the line handle.
Example: rng(0); h = histfit(randn(100,1) + 5, 10);
Differences from MATLAB: Uses equal-width bins between the data minimum and maximum; kernel fits are not supported.

## perfcurve
ROC curve or other classifier performance curve.
Syntax: [X, Y, T, AUC] = perfcurve(labels, scores, posclass)
Syntax: [X, Y, T, AUC] = perfcurve(labels, scores, posclass, 'XCrit', xc, 'YCrit', yc)
Thresholds T are the distinct scores in descending order; at each one, observations with score >= T count as positive. The first point is the reject-all point (0,0) for the default false positive rate X and true positive rate Y. Criteria: fpr, tpr, tnr, fnr, ppv (prec), npv, accu, reca, tp, fp, tn, fn. AUC is the trapezoidal area under Y(X). Labels may be numeric, logical, text cells or categorical.
Example: [X, Y, T, AUC] = perfcurve([1 1 0 1 0]', [0.9 0.8 0.7 0.6 0.5]', 1);   % AUC = 5/6
Differences from MATLAB: The (0,0) point carries the largest score as its threshold; confidence bounds, weights, 'Prior', 'Cost' and other options are not supported yet.

## gplot
Plot a graph from its adjacency matrix.
Syntax: gplot(A, xy)
Syntax: gplot(A, xy, LineSpec)
Syntax: [X, Y] = gplot(A, xy)
Draws a segment from xy(i,:) to xy(j,:) for each nonzero A(i,j), as one line broken by NaN. With outputs it returns the X and Y vectors without plotting. A may be sparse.
Example: [X, Y] = gplot([0 1; 1 0], [0 0; 1 1]);   % X = [1;0;NaN;0;1;NaN]
Differences from MATLAB: None known.

## makedist
Create a probability distribution value object.
Syntax: pd = makedist(name)
Syntax: pd = makedist(name, parameter, value, ...)
Creates a scalar object for Normal, Uniform, Exponential, Gamma, Beta, Chisquare, T, F, Lognormal, Weibull, Rayleigh, ExtremeValue, Binomial, Poisson, Geometric, NegativeBinomial, Logistic, Loglogistic, Rician, Nakagami, GeneralizedExtremeValue, GeneralizedPareto, tLocationScale, InverseGaussian, BirnbaumSaunders or HalfNormal. Family and parameter names are case-insensitive. Parameters use MATLAB names: mu/sigma, Lower/Upper, a/b, nu, nu1/nu2, A/B, B, N/p, lambda, p, R/P, s/sigma (Rician), mu/omega (Nakagami), k/sigma/mu (GEV), k/sigma/theta (GP), mu/sigma/nu (tLocationScale), mu/lambda (InverseGaussian), beta/gamma (BirnbaumSaunders) as appropriate. Defaults are zero location, unit scale/shape, Uniform [0,1], Binomial N=1/p=0.5, Geometric p=0.5, NegativeBinomial R=1/P=0.5, GEV k=0, GeneralizedPareto k=sigma=theta=1 and tLocationScale nu=5.
Read parameters with pd.mu, pd.ParameterNames or pd.ParameterValues; pd.DistributionName gives the family and class(pd) the prob.*Distribution name. Use pdf, cdf, icdf, random, mean, std, var, median, paramci and negloglik on objects. Assignment shares the immutable value.
Example: pd = makedist('Normal','mu',2,'sigma',3); [pdf(pd,2), mean(pd), std(pd)]
Example: pd = makedist("Gamma","a",2,"b",3); pd.ParameterValues
Example: pd = makedist('GeneralizedExtremeValue','k',0.2,'sigma',2,'mu',1); [cdf(pd,3), icdf(pd,0.9)]
Differences from MATLAB: properties are read-only; create a changed object with makedist. Only scalar objects and the listed families are supported; Chisquare, T and F objects extend the named-kernel interface. Parameters must be finite and in the family kernel's domain (Nakagami accepts any mu > 0). No no-argument listing, custom distributions, truncation or object persistence.

## fitdist
Fit a probability distribution object to data.
Syntax: pd = fitdist(x, name)
Syntax: pd = fitdist(x, name, Name, Value)
Syntax: [pd, gn, gl] = fitdist(x, name, 'By', groupvar, Name, Value)
Fits Normal, Exponential, Gamma, Weibull, Lognormal, Poisson, Binomial ('NTrials'), Beta, Rayleigh, ExtremeValue, NegativeBinomial, Logistic, Loglogistic, Rician, Nakagami, GeneralizedExtremeValue, GeneralizedPareto ('Theta', default 0), tLocationScale, InverseGaussian, BirnbaumSaunders, HalfNormal ('mu', default 0) by maximum likelihood, and Kernel ('Kernel' normal|box|triangle|epanechnikov, 'Bandwidth' or 'Width', 'Support' 'unbounded'|'positive'|[lower upper]). A real row or column is one sample; NaN observations are ignored. Normal sigma and Lognormal log-sigma are unbiased (divided by n-1) for uncensored data. Options: 'Censoring' (1 = right-censored, continuous parametric families), 'Frequency' (nonnegative counts or weights), 'Options' (statset: MaxIter, MaxFunEvals, TolX, TolFun) and 'By': pd is then a 1-by-g cell of objects and gn, gl are g-by-1 cell arrays of the group names in sorted order.
Fitted objects add ParameterCovariance (inverse observed information; analytic for Normal/Lognormal at the unbiased sigma, Poisson, Binomial and Exponential), ParameterIsFixed, ParameterDescription, InputData (data, cens, freq), NLogL, Truncation and IsTruncated; the display lists each parameter with its 95% confidence interval (see paramci). Kernel objects have Kernel, BandWidth and Support; their default bandwidth is Silverman's rule sigma*(4/(3n))^(1/5) with sigma = MAD/0.6745, the kernels are scaled to unit variance and bounded supports are mapped by log(x) or log((x-L)/(U-x)).
Example: pd = fitdist([1 2 3 4 NaN], 'Normal'); [pd.mu, pd.sigma]
Example: pd = fitdist([0 1 2 3], 'Binomial', 'NTrials', 5); mean(pd)
Example: pd = fitdist([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1 1.7]', 'Weibull', 'Censoring', [0 0 0 0 1 0]')
Example: [pd, gn] = fitdist([4.1 5.3 4.4 6.0 4.8 5.1]', 'Normal', 'By', [1 1 1 2 2 2]');
Example: pd = fitdist([1.2 0.4 2.2 0.9 3.1 1.7]', 'Kernel', 'Support', 'positive'); pdf(pd, 1)
Differences from MATLAB: at most 1000000 observations; Burr and Stable are not supported; left censoring, truncation and kernel censoring are not supported. Normal/Lognormal need at least two observations; families with two or three free parameters need that many distinct uncensored values. Iterative fits use tighter default tolerances than MATLAB's statset defaults, so last digits can differ. 'By' groups are ordered by sorted value or text.

## dendrogram
Draw a hierarchical linkage tree as U-shaped lines.
Syntax: H = dendrogram(Z)
Syntax: [H, T, outperm] = dendrogram(Z, P)
Z is the three-column linkage matrix. Each displayed merge creates one line object whose height is the linkage distance. Leaves follow left-to-right child order; ticks show their labels. The default P=30 contracts the earliest merges until at most 30 leaves remain. P=0 shows every leaf. T is a column assigning each original observation its displayed leaf label; outperm is a row of those labels in plotted order. Contracted leaves are numbered by their earliest original observation.
Example: Z = linkage([0;1;4;6], 'average'); [H,T,outperm] = dendrogram(Z,0);
Differences from MATLAB: vertical layout only; axes arguments, colors, labels, reordering and other name/value options are unsupported. Existing plot bounds permit at most 65 visible leaves (64 merge lines); choose P accordingly. Custom leaf ticks are transient, as are other axes decorations.

## designfilt
Design a digital FIR or IIR filter object from a response type and specifications.
Syntax: d = designfilt(response, 'FilterOrder', n, Name, Value, ...)
Responses: lowpassfir, highpassfir, bandpassfir, bandstopfir (CutoffFrequency or CutoffFrequency1/2, Hamming window design like fir1); lowpassiir, highpassiir, bandpassiir, bandstopiir (HalfPowerFrequency or HalfPowerFrequency1/2 gives Butterworth; StopbandFrequency plus StopbandAttenuation gives Chebyshev II). Frequencies are in Hz with 'SampleRate', otherwise normalised to the Nyquist frequency. Band IIR orders count both edges, like MATLAB. The digitalFilter works with filter, filtfilt, freqz, grpdelay, phasez, impz, filtord and [b,a] = tf(d); IIR Coefficients is an SOS matrix with the gain in the first section.
Example: d = designfilt('lowpassfir','FilterOrder',20,'CutoffFrequency',150,'SampleRate',1000); y = filter(d, randn(1,100));
Differences from MATLAB: FilterOrder is required; passband/stopband-ripple specification sets, other windows and design methods (equiripple, kaiserwin, cheby1, ellip), the filter designer dialog and fvtool are not supported.

## dfilt.df1
Create a direct-form I digital filter from its coefficients.
Syntax: H = dfilt.df1(b,a)
Supply the numerator b and denominator a as nonempty, finite real vectors. The first denominator coefficient must be nonzero. Use filter(H,x) to apply the filter or freqz(H,w) to evaluate its frequency response.
Example: H = dfilt.df1([1 2],1); filter(H,[1 0 0])   % [1 2 0]
Differences from MATLAB: Both coefficient vectors are required.

## isfir
Test whether a digital filter has a finite impulse response.
Syntax: tf = isfir(H)
For a dfilt.df1 filter, returns logical true when every denominator coefficient after the first is zero. Also accepts a filter from designfilt.
Example: isfir(dfilt.df1([1 2],[1 0]))   % true
Example: isfir(dfilt.df1(1,[1 -0.5]))   % false
Differences from MATLAB: Takes one digital filter object.

## fitlm
Fit a numeric linear regression model with coefficient inference.
Syntax: mdl = fitlm(X,y); mdl = fitlm(X,y,modelspec); mdl = fitlm(tbl,formula); mdl = fitlm(...,'Intercept',false)
Adds an intercept by default and solves least squares with column-pivoted QR. A table uses its last variable as the response unless a formula names another variable. Numeric scalar table columns and real numeric predictor matrices are supported. Model specifications are 'linear', 'interactions', 'quadratic', 'purequadratic' and 'constant'. Formulas support +, -1, x1:x2, x1*x2 and x1^2 (which adds both x1 and its square). Other syntax and unknown options raise errors. NaN observations in used variables are omitted; Fitted and Residuals.Raw retain their original row positions. Coefficients has Estimate, SE, tStat and pValue columns and named rows. Other properties include Rsquared.Ordinary, Rsquared.Adjusted, RMSE, NumObservations, DFE, SSE, SST, SSR, Fitted, Residuals, CoefficientNames, Formula, LogLikelihood and ModelCriterion.AIC/BIC. Model properties are read-only and assignments share immutable storage.
Example: mdl=fitlm([0;1;2;3;4],[1;3;4;8;9]); mdl.Coefficients
Differences from MATLAB: only numeric predictors and the documented formula subset/options are supported; no categorical expansion, weights, robust fits, term matrices or feval. Formulas are character text. Normal log likelihood uses the fitted residual mean squared error; AIC/BIC penalize the number of estimated coefficients. Rank deficient fits set dependent coefficients to zero, with NaN standard errors for them and NaN prediction intervals. Fits require positive residual degrees of freedom. Designs are bounded to 1000000 rows, 256 terms, 2000000 elements and 100000000 QR work units; large workspaces can hit the host evaluation budget earlier.

## fitglm
Fit a numeric generalized linear regression model by IRLS.
Syntax: mdl = fitglm(X,y,'Distribution',d); mdl = fitglm(...,'Link',link); mdl = fitglm(tbl,formula,...)
Returns a GeneralizedLinearModel with Coefficients, Deviance, Dispersion and the model statistics and residual properties provided by fitlm. Supported distributions are 'normal' (default identity link), 'binomial' (default logit link) and 'poisson' (default log link). Normal also supports the log link; binomial supports probit; poisson supports identity. Dispersion is estimated for normal and fixed to one for binomial and poisson. Binomial and poisson coefficient p-values use the standard normal distribution; normal uses Student's t. predict returns the mean response on the response scale. Model specifications, intercept control and numeric table input follow fitlm.
Example: mdl=fitglm([-2;-1;0;1;2;3],[0;1;0;1;0;1],'Distribution','binomial'); predict(mdl,[0;1])
Differences from MATLAB: no grouped binomial counts, trial sizes, weights, offsets, categorical predictors, custom links or other distributions. Unsupported links and incompatible combinations raise errors. IRLS uses at most 100 iterations with deviance step halving; separated data, singular weights or failure to converge raise errors. The fitlm design limits also apply. Normal likelihood uses the fitted dispersion. Normal dispersion uses residual degrees of freedom.

## stepwiselm
Select a numeric linear model by forward and backward partial F tests.
Syntax: mdl = stepwiselm(X,y); mdl = stepwiselm(...,'PEnter',0.05,'PRemove',0.10); mdl = stepwiselm(...,'Upper','linear')
Starts from an intercept-only model and considers main effects and two-way interactions by default. Additions use the smallest partial F-test p-value below PEnter; removals use the largest p-value above PRemove. Lower-order terms remain while their interactions are present. Prints each accepted adding/removing step and returns a LinearModel. Optional initial model specifications and numeric tables follow fitlm. All candidates use the same complete observations from the upper model.
Example: mdl=stepwiselm([0;1;2;3;4;5],[1;3;4;7;9;10]); mdl.Coefficients
Differences from MATLAB: numeric predictors only; selection supports the F-test criterion, PEnter, PRemove and Upper. Requires 0 < PEnter < PRemove < 1 and an intercept. At most 16 predictors and 1024 candidate fits are allowed; fitlm workspace limits also apply. Other selection criteria and Lower are unsupported.

## fit
Fit a curve or surface model to data by least squares or interpolation.
Syntax: fitobject = fit(x, y, fitType)
Syntax: fitobject = fit([x y], z, fitType)
Syntax: [fitobject, gof, output] = fit(x, y, fitType, fitOptions, Name, Value, ...)
fitType is a library model name (poly1..poly9, poly00..poly55, exp1, exp2, fourier1..fourier8, gauss1..gauss8, power1, power2, rat01..rat55, sin1..sin8, weibull, linearinterp, nearestinterp, pchipinterp, cubicinterp, smoothingspline), a custom equation such as 'a*exp(-b*x)+c', a cell array of linear terms, an anonymous function or a fittype. Polynomial and linear models are solved by column-pivoted QR; nonlinear models by a bounded Levenberg-Marquardt (trust-region) iteration from a start point computed from the data (custom equations without StartPoint use a fixed pseudo-random start and warn). Name-value options: StartPoint, Lower, Upper, Weights, Exclude (logical mask or indices), Normalize ('on' centers and scales x by its mean and standard deviation; coefficients then refer to the scaled x), Robust ('off', 'LAR', 'Bisquare'), Algorithm ('Trust-Region', 'Levenberg-Marquardt'), MaxIter, MaxFunEvals, TolFun, TolX, Display, SmoothingParam (smoothingspline only; between 0 and 1, default from the data as in csaps) and problem (values of problem parameters). gof has sse, rsquare, dfe, adjrsquare and rmse; output has numobs, numparam, residuals, Jacobian, exitflag, iterations, funcCount, firstorderopt, algorithm and message, plus p (the smoothing parameter used) for smoothingspline.
Example: f = fit((1:5)', [2.1 3.9 6.2 7.8 10.1]', 'poly1'); coeffvalues(f)
Example: [f, ~, out] = fit((0:5)', [0 1.1 1.9 3.2 3.8 5.1]', 'smoothingspline', 'SmoothingParam', 0.8); out.p   % 0.8
Example: [f, gof] = fit((0:0.5:3)', 2*exp(0.7*(0:0.5:3))', 'exp1'); gof.dfe   % 5
Differences from MATLAB: converged nonlinear fits take a few extra Gauss-Newton steps, so results are the least-squares optimum even with loose TolFun/TolX. Rows as well as columns are accepted for curve data. Problem parameters are scalars. Lowess and loess, biharmonic and thin-plate interpolants, surface interpolants and fittype 'options' are not supported yet. Interpolant and smoothing-spline fits average repeated x values (smoothing splines with the weights summed); a smoothing spline's gof has dfe 0, like an interpolant. Robust fits use leverage-adjusted residuals with the MAD/0.6745 scale about the median; their confidence bounds use the final robust weights.

## fittype
Create a curve or surface model for fit.
Syntax: ft = fittype(libraryModelName)
Syntax: ft = fittype(expression, 'independent', 'x', 'dependent', 'y', 'coefficients', {'a','b'}, 'problem', {'c'})
Syntax: ft = fittype({'term1', 'term2', ...})
Syntax: ft = fittype(@(a, b, x) a*exp(b*x))
In an equation the coefficients are the names that are not independent variables, problem parameters or functions, in order of first appearance; *, / and ^ act elementwise. A cell array of terms gives a linear model a*term1 + b*term2 + ... solved by linear least squares. For an anonymous function the last input is the independent variable unless 'independent' names others. Call ft(coefficients..., problems..., x) to evaluate. formula, coeffnames, argnames, numcoeffs, type, category and islinear describe the model.
Example: ft = fittype('a*exp(-b*x)+c'); coeffnames(ft)
Example: ft = fittype('poly2'); ft(1, 2, 3, [0 1 2])   % [3 6 11]
Differences from MATLAB: the 'options' argument is not supported yet; give fit options to fit.

## fitoptions
Create or change the options of a curve or surface fit.
Syntax: opts = fitoptions(libraryModelName or fittype)
Syntax: opts = fitoptions('Method', methodName, Name, Value, ...)
Syntax: opts = fitoptions(opts, Name, Value, ...)
Methods are NonlinearLeastSquares, LinearLeastSquares, LinearInterpolant, NearestInterpolant, PchipInterpolant, CubicSplineInterpolant, SmoothingSpline and None. Every method has Normalize, Exclude, Weights and Method; SmoothingSpline adds SmoothingParam ([] = the data-dependent default); least-squares methods add Robust, Lower and Upper; NonlinearLeastSquares adds StartPoint, Algorithm, DiffMinChange, DiffMaxChange, Display, MaxFunEvals, MaxIter, TolFun and TolX. Library models fill in their default bounds (Gaussian widths and sine frequencies are nonnegative). Pass the options to fit as fit(x, y, fitType, opts); opts.Lower = [...] changes a field.
Example: opts = fitoptions('gauss1'); opts.Lower
Example: opts = fitoptions('Method', 'NonlinearLeastSquares', 'StartPoint', [1 1]); opts.StartPoint
Differences from MATLAB: the options are a struct value (class struct) with the method's fields; option names in calls are matched case-insensitively, also by unique prefix.

## cfit
Create a curve fit object from a fittype and coefficient values.
Syntax: f = cfit(fittype, coefficient1, coefficient2, ..., problem1, ...)
fit returns cfit objects for models of one independent variable. Call f(x) or feval(f, x); f.a reads coefficient a; coeffvalues, confint, predint, differentiate, integrate and plot work on it. A cfit made by this constructor has no confidence information.
Example: f = cfit(fittype('exp1'), 2, 0.5); f(0)   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: coefficients are read-only; make a new object to change them.

## sfit
Create a surface fit object from a fittype and coefficient values.
Syntax: f = sfit(fittype, coefficient1, coefficient2, ..., problem1, ...)
fit returns sfit objects for models of two independent variables. Call f(x, y) or f([x y]); f.p00 reads a coefficient; coeffvalues, confint, predint, differentiate and plot work on it.
Example: f = sfit(fittype('poly11'), 1, 2, 3); f(1, 1)   % 6
Differences from MATLAB: coefficients are read-only; make a new object to change them.

## confint
Confidence bounds for the coefficients of a fit.
Syntax: ci = confint(fitobject)
Syntax: ci = confint(fitobject, level)
Returns a 2-by-n array: lower bounds in the first row and upper bounds in the second, b +- t*sqrt(diag(inv(J'*J))*sse/dfe) with the t quantile at (1+level)/2 and dfe error degrees of freedom (level defaults to 0.95). Bounds are NaN without error degrees of freedom and for interpolants.
Example: f = fit((1:6)', [1.1 1.9 3.2 3.9 5.1 6.0]', 'poly1'); confint(f)
Differences from MATLAB: coefficients held at a bound are treated like free ones.

## predint
Prediction bounds of a fit at new points.
Syntax: ci = predint(fitobject, x)
Syntax: [ci, y] = predint(fitobject, x, level, intopt, simopt)
Returns an n-by-2 array of lower and upper bounds and the predicted values y. intopt 'observation' (default) bounds a new observation, 'functional' the fitted curve; simopt 'off' (default) gives non-simultaneous bounds from the t quantile, 'on' simultaneous bounds sqrt(m*F(level; m, dfe)) with m the number of coefficients (plus one for observations). Surface fits take x as [x y].
Example: f = fit((1:6)', [1.1 1.9 3.2 3.9 5.1 6.0]', 'poly1'); [ci, y] = predint(f, [2.5; 7])

## coeffnames
Coefficient names of a fittype or fit.
Syntax: names = coeffnames(fitobject)
Returns a column cell array of the coefficient names in model order.
Example: coeffnames(fittype('gauss1'))

## coeffvalues
Coefficient values of a fit.
Syntax: values = coeffvalues(fitobject)
Returns a row vector in the order of coeffnames.
Example: coeffvalues(fit((1:4)', [3 5 7 9]', 'poly1'))   % [2 1]
Differences from MATLAB: interpolant fits have no coefficient values here.

## numcoeffs
Number of coefficients of a fittype or fit.
Syntax: n = numcoeffs(fitobject)
Example: numcoeffs(fittype('fourier2'))   % 6

## numargs
Number of inputs of a fittype or fit: coefficients, problem parameters and independent variables.
Syntax: n = numargs(fitobject)
Example: numargs(fittype('exp2'))   % 5

## dependnames
Dependent variable name of a fittype or fit.
Syntax: name = dependnames(fitobject)
Returns a 1-by-1 cell array: y for curves and z for surfaces unless named with 'dependent'.
Example: dependnames(fittype('poly22'))

## indepnames
Independent variable names of a fittype or fit.
Syntax: names = indepnames(fitobject)
Example: indepnames(fittype('poly11'))

## probnames
Problem parameter names of a fittype or fit.
Syntax: names = probnames(fitobject)
Returns a column cell array (empty when the model has none).
Example: probnames(fittype('a*x+c', 'problem', 'c'))

## probvalues
Problem parameter values of a fit.
Syntax: values = probvalues(fitobject)
Example: f = fit((1:4)', [3 5 7 9]', fittype('a*x+c', 'problem', 'c'), 'problem', 1, 'StartPoint', 1); probvalues(f)   % 1

## islinear
True for models that are linear in their coefficients.
Syntax: tf = islinear(fitobject)
Polynomial library models and cell-array (linear term) models are linear and are fitted by linear least squares.
Example: [islinear(fittype('poly3')) islinear(fittype('exp1'))]   % [1 0]

## category
Model category of a fittype or fit.
Syntax: c = category(fitobject)
Returns 'library', 'custom' or 'interpolant'.
Example: category(fittype('a*x^2'))

## differentiate
Derivatives of a fit at given points.
Syntax: [fx, fxx] = differentiate(cfit, x)
Syntax: [fx, fy, fxx, fxy, fyy] = differentiate(sfit, x, y)
Results have the shape of x. Derivatives are Richardson-extrapolated central differences of the fitted model in data units (normalization is accounted for).
Example: f = cfit(fittype('poly2'), 1, 0, 0); differentiate(f, 3)   % 6
Differences from MATLAB: derivatives are numerical (about 10 correct digits for first derivatives of smooth models); at interpolant breakpoints they average the neighbouring pieces.

## integrate
Integral of a curve fit from x0 to each point.
Syntax: F = integrate(cfit, x, x0)
F has the shape of x; F(i) is the integral of the fit from x0 to x(i), by adaptive Gauss-Kronrod quadrature with interpolant breakpoints as interval ends.
Example: f = cfit(fittype('poly1'), 2, 0); integrate(f, 3, 0)   % 9
Differences from MATLAB: surface fits cannot be integrated.

## fitcknn
Fit a nearest-neighbour classification model.
Syntax: mdl = fitcknn(X,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitcknn(tbl,'ResponseVarName')
Syntax: mdl = fitcknn(tbl,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitcknn(X,Y,'NumNeighbors',k,'Distance',metric,'Standardize',true)
Distances are euclidean (default), cityblock, chebychev and minkowski (exponent 2). Scores are neighbour class fractions in sorted ClassNames order; ties choose the first class. Labels preserve their numeric, logical, cellstr, string or categorical type. Common properties are ClassNames, ResponseName, PredictorNames, NumObservations, X and Y. Numeric table predictor columns are supported; prediction tables select training predictor names in training order.
Example: mdl=fitcknn([0;2],[1;2]); [label,score]=predict(mdl,1)
Differences from MATLAB: advanced distance weights and custom metrics are unsupported. Training is bounded to 20000 rows, 512 predictors, 2000000 elements and 256 classes; prediction comparison work is bounded, so large queries should be batched.

## fitctree
Fit a CART classification tree using Gini impurity.
Syntax: mdl = fitctree(X,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitctree(tbl,'ResponseVarName')
Syntax: mdl = fitctree(tbl,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitctree(X,Y,'MaxNumSplits',n,'MinLeafSize',m,'MinParentSize',p,'SplitCriterion','gdi')
Defaults are MinLeafSize 1, MinParentSize 10, and at most NumObservations-1 splits. MaxNumSplits bounds the total splits, choosing the largest impurity reduction among pending leaves. Scores are class fractions at the reached leaf. NumNodes and Children expose tree structure; Children uses one-based node indices and zero for a leaf.
Example: mdl=fitctree([0;2],[1;2],'MinParentSize',2); [label,score]=predict(mdl,[0;2])
Differences from MATLAB: only finite numeric predictors and Gini splits are supported; pruning, categorical predictors, surrogates and view are unsupported. The split search is bounded to 50000000 row-feature visits, in addition to common classifier training limits.

## fitcsvm
Fit a binary support-vector classification model using SMO.
Syntax: mdl = fitcsvm(X,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitcsvm(tbl,'ResponseVarName')
Syntax: mdl = fitcsvm(tbl,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitcsvm(X,Y,'KernelFunction','rbf','KernelScale',s,'BoxConstraint',C,'Standardize',true)
The default kernel is linear; rbf and gaussian use exp(-squaredDistance/KernelScale^2). BoxConstraint defaults to 1. Scores are [-f f], where f is the signed decision value. Alpha contains nonnegative support-vector coefficients; Bias and SupportVectors are available, and Beta gives the linear coefficient vector. With Standardize enabled, SupportVectors and Beta use standardized predictor coordinates.
Example: mdl=fitcsvm([-2;-1;1;2],[1;1;2;2]); [label,score]=predict(mdl,[-1;1])
Differences from MATLAB: only binary C-SVC with linear and RBF kernels is supported; use fitcecoc for multiclass classification. KernelScale affects both linear and RBF kernels. The serial solver is bounded to 2048 observations, 100000000 kernel element products and 200000 pair updates; nonconvergence errors explicitly.

## fitcnb
Fit a Gaussian naive-Bayes classification model.
Syntax: mdl = fitcnb(X,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitcnb(tbl,'ResponseVarName')
Syntax: mdl = fitcnb(tbl,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitcnb(X,Y,'DistributionNames','normal','Prior','empirical')
Scores are normalized posterior probabilities with empirical class priors. DistributionParameters is a class-by-predictor cell array; each cell contains [mean;sampleStandardDeviation]. Sample variances are unbiased and floored at 1e-12 for constant or singleton groups.
Example: mdl=fitcnb([0;1;4;5],[1;1;2;2]); [label,score]=predict(mdl,[.2;4.2]); p=mdl.DistributionParameters;
Differences from MATLAB: only Gaussian distributions and empirical priors are supported; kernel and multinomial distributions are rejected. Common classifier training limits apply.

## crossval
Refit a classifier on randomized training and validation partitions.
Syntax: cvmdl = crossval(mdl)
Syntax: cvmdl = crossval(mdl,'KFold',k)
Syntax: cvmdl = crossval(mdl,'Holdout',p)
Syntax: cvmdl = crossval(mdl,'Leaveout','on')
Syntax: cvmdl = crossval(mdl,'CVPartition',c)
Returns a ClassificationPartitionedModel. The default is 10 folds; KFold must be between 2 and the observation count. A Fisher-Yates shuffle consumes the session rng stream. Holdout reserves ceil(p*NumObservations) observations, leaving at least one for training. Each fold refits the original classifier options and standardization on training rows only. Use kfoldPredict and kfoldLoss to evaluate held-out observations.
Example: rng(0); m=fitcknn((1:10)',[ones(5,1);2*ones(5,1)]); cv=crossval(m); loss=kfoldLoss(cv)
Differences from MATLAB: class-stratified partitions and supplied CVPartition objects are supported. Only classifier-model input is supported; function input is unsupported. Folds lacking the two classes needed by SVM error explicitly. Retained folds are bounded to 1000 and 8000000 predictor elements in total.

## predict
Predict responses from a fitted regression model or labels and scores from a classifier.
Syntax: ypred = predict(mdl,Xnew); [ypred,yci] = predict(mdl,Xnew); ypred = predict(mdl,tbl)
Syntax: label = predict(mdl,Xnew); [label,score] = predict(mdl,Xnew); [label,score] = predict(mdl,tbl)
Regression (LinearModel, GeneralizedLinearModel): matrix columns match the original predictor order; table predictors are matched by name and unused variables may be omitted. The second output has lower and upper 95 percent confidence bounds for the mean response; linear and normal GLM models use Student's t, binomial and poisson models use normal bounds on the linear predictor transformed through the inverse link. Classifiers: score columns follow mdl.ClassNames; prediction tables select numeric columns by mdl.PredictorNames, in any order.
Example: mdl=fitlm([0;1;2;3;4],[1;3;4;8;9]); [ypred,yci]=predict(mdl,[1.5;2.5])
Differences from MATLAB: only the two positional arguments are supported; no Alpha, simultaneous bounds or observation prediction intervals. Rank deficient regression models return NaN confidence intervals. Partitioned classifiers use kfoldPredict; other model types raise a named unsupported-model error.
Identified models: yp = predict(sys, data, k) returns the k-step-ahead prediction (default k = 1, Inf = simulation) of an idpoly, idtf, idss or idproc model as an iddata object, with zero initial conditions (yhat = y - Hk(q) e, Hk the first k terms of the noise model).

## resubLoss
Compute classifier resubstitution misclassification loss.
Syntax: loss = resubLoss(mdl)
Supports every classifier response label type and evaluates the training rows.
Example: m=fitcknn([0;2],[1;2]); resubLoss(m)
Differences from MATLAB: LossFun supports classiferror (default), mincost, binodeviance, exponential and hinge; custom weights and loss functions are unsupported.

## kfoldPredict
Predict the held-out observations of a partitioned classifier.
Syntax: label = kfoldPredict(cvmdl)
Syntax: [label,score] = kfoldPredict(cvmdl)
Outputs follow original observation order and the original ClassNames columns. For Holdout, untested numeric labels and scores are NaN, strings are missing, cellstr labels are empty, categorical labels are undefined, integer labels are zero, and logical labels are false. Only held-out rows contribute to kfoldLoss.
Example: m=fitcknn([0;1;4;5],[1;1;2;2]); cv=crossval(m,'Leaveout','on'); [label,score]=kfoldPredict(cv)
Differences from MATLAB: only one prediction per held-out row is supported; repeated partitions and optional prediction settings are unsupported.

## kfoldLoss
Compute held-out classifier misclassification loss.
Syntax: loss = kfoldLoss(cvmdl)
Evaluates each validation observation using its fold's fitted model; Holdout excludes all untested observations.
Example: m=fitcknn([0;1;4;5],[1;1;2;2]); cv=crossval(m,'Leaveout','on'); kfoldLoss(cv)
Differences from MATLAB: LossFun supports classiferror (default), mincost, binodeviance, exponential and hinge; per-fold modes and custom weights are unsupported.


## timetable
Table whose rows have datetime or duration timestamps.
Syntax: TT = timetable(rowTimes,v1,v2,...)
Syntax: TT = timetable(v1,...,'RowTimes',t)
Syntax: TT = timetable(v1,...,'SampleRate',fs,'StartTime',start)
Syntax: TT = timetable(v1,...,'TimeStep',dt)
RowTimes is a datetime or duration vector with one value per row, stored as a column. VariableNames and DimensionNames set the column and dimension names. Defaults are Time and Variables. TT.Time and TT.Properties.RowTimes expose the timestamps. Variables, row selection, size, height, width and display use ordinary table behavior.
Example: t = seconds([0;1;2]); x = [4;5;6]; TT = timetable(t,x); TT(1:2,:)
Differences from MATLAB: Calendar TimeStep requires an explicit datetime StartTime. Only datetime/duration row times are supported; timerange, preallocation, numeric row times, per-variable continuity and timetable persistence are not implemented.


## table2timetable
Convert a table to a timetable.
Syntax: TT = table2timetable(T)
Syntax: TT = table2timetable(T,'RowTimes',t)
With one argument, the first datetime or duration variable supplies row times and is removed from the variables. Its name becomes the first dimension name. An explicit RowTimes vector preserves the input variables and names the dimension Time.
Example: t = datetime(2024,1,[1;2]); x = [3;4]; T = table(t,x); TT = table2timetable(T)
Differences from MATLAB: RowTimes variable-name selection and sampling name-value options are not supported.


## timetable2table
Convert a timetable to an ordinary table.
Syntax: T = timetable2table(TT)
The row times become the first table variable, using the timetable's time dimension name. Other variables and their metadata are preserved.
Example: TT = timetable(seconds([0;1]),[3;4]); T = timetable2table(TT)
Differences from MATLAB: ConvertRowTimes options are not supported; row times are always included.


## istimetable
True for a timetable value.
Syntax: tf = istimetable(A)
Returns a logical scalar. Ordinary tables return false.
Example: istimetable(timetable(seconds([0;1]),[3;4]))
Differences from MATLAB: Supports the engine's shared table representation.


## retime
Resample or aggregate timetable rows at new times.
Syntax: R = retime(TT,newTimes,method)
Syntax: R = retime(TT,'daily',method)
Syntax: R = retime(TT,'regular',method,'TimeStep',dt)
Syntax: R = retime(TT,'regular',method,'SampleRate',fs)
Syntax: R = retime(TT,newTimes)
Supported regular grids are secondly, minutely, hourly, daily, monthly, yearly (the latter two require datetime row times), and 'regular' with 'TimeStep' or 'SampleRate'. Supported methods are fillwithmissing (default), previous, next, nearest, linear, spline, mean, sum, min, max, count, firstvalue and lastvalue. Aggregation uses left-closed time bins and omits missing numeric values. Explicit newTimes must be a sorted unique vector of the same time type and zone.
Example: TT = timetable(hours([0;12;24]),[1;3;5]); R = retime(TT,'daily','mean')
Differences from MATLAB: Other name-value options, function handles and per-variable methods are not supported. Aggregation and interpolation require real numeric variables. Row times must be sorted; linear and spline require unique input times. Bounded to 16777216 output elements and a conservative 256 MiB resampling workspace.


## synchronize
Combine two timetables on a common time vector.
Syntax: TT = synchronize(TT1,TT2)
Syntax: TT = synchronize(TT1,TT2,basis,method)
Syntax: TT = synchronize(TT1,TT2,'regular',method,'TimeStep',dt)
The default basis is union and the default method is fillwithmissing. Other bases are intersection, first, commonrange, and 'regular' with 'TimeStep' or 'SampleRate'. commonrange uses the union within the overlapping interval. Resampling methods are those of retime. Duplicate variable names receive _TT1 and _TT2 suffixes.
Example: A = timetable(seconds([0;2]),[1;3],'VariableNames',{'a'}); B = timetable(seconds([1;2]),[8;9],'VariableNames',{'b'}); C = synchronize(A,B)
Differences from MATLAB: Exactly two timetables and text time bases are supported. Explicit time vectors and other name-value options are not supported. Collisions remaining after suffixing produce a clear duplicate-name error.


## summary
Print or return a summary of a table or timetable.
Syntax: summary(T)
Syntax: s = summary(T)
Prints per-variable size, class, Description, and statistics (Min, Median, Max, NumMissing for numeric, datetime, and duration; True/False counts for logical; category counts for categorical; size and class only for text and other types). For timetables, RowTimes are also summarized. With an output argument, returns a scalar struct with one field per variable (and the time dimension for timetables).
Example: T = table([1;2;3],[true;false;true],'VariableNames',{'x','flag'}); s = summary(T)
Differences from MATLAB: Only table and timetable inputs are supported; 'Statistics' and 'Detail' name-value options are not supported.


## calendarDuration
Lengths of time in calendar years, months and days.
Syntax: cd = calendarDuration(y,m,d)
Syntax: cd = calendarDuration(y,m,d,h,mi,s)
Calendar components are immutable shared arrays. Year, month and day inputs are integers with scalar expansion; hours, minutes and seconds supply elapsed time. Months normalize into years. Addition to a datetime clamps the day to the last valid day of the destination month, then adds calendar days and elapsed time. Calendar durations support addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication. split returns separate calendar units.
Example: cd = calendarDuration(1,2,3); datetime(2024,1,31) + calmonths(1)
Differences from MATLAB: Calendar storage is capped at 128 MiB. Only these numeric constructor forms are supported. Format options, indexed assignment, ordering comparisons and persistence are not implemented. Only unzoned and UTC datetimes exist in this engine, so there are no daylight saving transitions.


## calyears
Create calendar years or extract whole calendar years.
Syntax: cd = calyears(n)
Syntax: n = calyears(cd)
Integer numeric input creates calendar durations. Calendar duration input extracts the normalized whole years.
Example: datetime(2024,2,29) + calyears(1)
Differences from MATLAB: Bounded two-dimensional arrays; constructor input must contain integers.


## calmonths
Create calendar months or extract calendar months.
Syntax: cd = calmonths(n)
Syntax: n = calmonths(cd)
Integer numeric input creates calendar durations. Calendar duration input extracts total whole months from the year and month components. Days and elapsed time are excluded.
Example: datetime(2023,1,31) + calmonths(1)
Differences from MATLAB: Bounded two-dimensional arrays; constructor input must contain integers.


## calweeks
Create calendar weeks or extract whole calendar weeks.
Syntax: cd = calweeks(n)
Syntax: n = calweeks(cd)
Each calendar week is seven calendar days. Extraction truncates the day component toward zero after division by seven; months and years are excluded.
Example: datetime(2024,1,1) + calweeks(2)
Differences from MATLAB: Bounded two-dimensional arrays; constructor input must contain integers.


## caldays
Create calendar days or extract calendar days.
Syntax: cd = caldays(n)
Syntax: n = caldays(cd)
Integer numeric input creates calendar durations in days. Calendar duration input extracts its day component. Calendar months are never converted to an assumed number of days.
Example: datetime(2024,2,28) + caldays(2)
Differences from MATLAB: Bounded two-dimensional arrays; constructor input must contain integers. Only unzoned and UTC datetimes are supported, without daylight saving transitions.


## iscalendarduration
True for a calendar duration value.
Syntax: tf = iscalendarduration(A)
Returns a logical scalar; fixed elapsed durations and other arrays return false.
Example: iscalendarduration(calmonths(2))
Differences from MATLAB: Supports the engine's calendar duration representation.


## between
Calendar duration separating two datetimes.
Syntax: cd = between(t1,t2)
Returns whole years and months, followed by remaining calendar days and elapsed time. Scalar expansion is supported. Adding the result to t1 reconstructs t2.
Example: a = datetime(2023,1,31); b = datetime(2024,3,3); cd = between(a,b); a + cd
Differences from MATLAB: Unit-selection options are not supported. Both datetimes must use the same time zone.

## pdepe
Solve one-dimensional parabolic and elliptic PDE systems.
Syntax: sol = pdepe(m,pdefun,icfun,bcfun,xmesh,tspan); sol = pdepe(m,pdefun,icfun,bcfun,xmesh,tspan,options)
Solves c*u_t = x^(-m)*(x^m*f)_x+s for slab (m=0), cylindrical (m=1), or spherical (m=2) geometry. Callbacks return [c,f,s]=pdefun(x,t,u,dudx), u0=icfun(x), and [pl,ql,pr,qr]=bcfun(xl,ul,xr,ur,t). Each output is an npde-by-1 column; c is nonnegative. Boundary conditions are p+q*f=0. At x=0 with m>0 the left condition is ignored and symmetry is enforced. Use strictly increasing finite xmesh (at least 3 points) and tspan (at least 2). The result has dimensions length(tspan)-by-length(xmesh)-by-npde, with a 2-D result for one equation. Zero c components and Dirichlet boundaries use the NDF differential-algebraic solve, including consistent initialization. At least one equation must be parabolic. RelTol and scalar or npde-vector AbsTol can be set with odeset; they control time error, so refine xmesh separately for spatial accuracy.
Example: p=@(x,t,u,d) deal(1,d,0); ic=@(x) sin(pi*x); bc=@(xl,ul,xr,ur,t) deal(ul,0,ur,0); sol=pdepe(0,p,ic,bc,linspace(0,1,11),[0 .05 .1]); size(sol)
Differences from MATLAB: real values only; supports RelTol and AbsTol options and one solution output. Events and other odeset settings are rejected explicitly. The parabolic/elliptic and zero/nonzero q patterns must stay fixed. Work limits are 512 mesh points and total mesh states, 16 equations, 10000 time points, 4194304 output values, 50000 residual evaluations (also bounding steps), and 2000000 callback calls. Uses dense serial NDF solves; no automatic mesh refinement. Also accepts two requested times.

## pdeval
Interpolate a PDE solution component and its spatial derivative.
Syntax: uout = pdeval(m,xmesh,ui,xout); [uout,duoutdx] = pdeval(m,xmesh,ui,xout)
Pass the geometry and spatial mesh used by pdepe and one solution row, such as sol(i,:,k). Query points must lie within the mesh. Both outputs have the shape of xout. Uses the solver's element interpolation: linear for m=0, quadratic in x for polar domains starting at zero, logarithmic for regular cylindrical domains, and reciprocal for regular spherical domains. At interior mesh points the derivative is taken from the interval to the right; at the last point it is taken from the left.
Example: [u,dudx]=pdeval(0,[0 .5 1],[0 1 2],[.25 .75])
Differences from MATLAB: finite real inputs and a single solution component only. Uses the same fixed-mesh limits as pdepe; returns an empty result for empty xout.

## decsg
Decompose constructive solid geometry into minimal regions.
Syntax: dl = decsg(gd,sf,ns); [dl,bt] = decsg(gd,sf,ns); [dl,bt] = decsg(gd)
Each column of gd is one shape, zero padded: circle [1;xc;yc;r], polygon [2;n;x1..xn;y1..yn], rectangle [3;4;x1..x4;y1..y4], ellipse [4;xc;yc;a;b;phi] with phi in radians. ns is a char matrix with one name per column, for example ['R1';'C1']'. The set formula sf combines the names with + (union), * (intersection), - (difference) and parentheses. Precedence, highest first: - (difference), * (intersection), + (union); equal operators associate left to right; parentheses override. Without sf every region inside any shape is kept. Each column of dl is one boundary segment: row 1 type (1 circle arc, 2 line, 4 ellipse arc), rows 2-3 start and end x, rows 4-5 start and end y, rows 6-7 the region to the left and right (0 outside), rows 8-10 centre and radius of circle arcs, rows 8-12 centre, semi-axes and angle of ellipse arcs. Arcs run counter-clockwise; every circle and ellipse is first split into four quarter arcs. bt(i,j) is true when region i lies inside shape j. Borders between two kept regions stay; csgdel removes them.
Example: R1=[3;4;-1;1;1;-1;-1;-1;1;1]; C1=[1;0;0;0.5;0;0;0;0;0;0]; gd=[R1 C1]; ns=['R1';'C1']'; [dl,bt]=decsg(gd,'R1-C1',ns); size(dl)
Differences from MATLAB: region numbering and segment order may differ. Tangent curves meet at one touch point. Up to 512 shapes and 4096 boundary pieces. The third to fifth outputs are not supported.

## csgdel
Delete borders between minimal regions of a decomposed geometry.
Syntax: [dl2,bt2] = csgdel(dl,bt); [dl2,bt2] = csgdel(dl,bt,bl)
Without bl every border with a region on both sides is removed; regions joined by removed borders become one region and are renumbered. bl lists dl columns to remove; a listed column that borders the outside is an error, and borders that end up with the same region on both sides are removed too. bt2(i,j) is true when any part of region i was inside shape j.
Example: gd=[3 3;4 4;0 1;2 3;2 3;0 1;0 0.5;0 0.5;1 1.5;1 1.5]; [dl,bt]=decsg(gd,'R1+R2',['R1';'R2']'); [dl2,bt2]=csgdel(dl,bt); size(dl2)
Differences from MATLAB: line pieces and arc pieces that become consecutive on one boundary stay split at their old junction points.

## createpde
Create a 2-D PDE model handle object.
Syntax: model = createpde; model = createpde(N)
Creates a pde.PDEModel handle object for a scalar PDE (N = 1) or a system of N coupled PDEs. Copying the handle aliases the same underlying model. Properties include PDESystemSize, IsTimeDependent, Geometry, Mesh, EquationCoefficients, BoundaryConditions, and InitialConditions.
Example: m = createpde(2); m.PDESystemSize
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D general PDE models only; specialised structural, thermal, and electromagnetic models (createpde('thermal', ...), femodel) and 3-D geometries are not supported.

## geometryFromEdges
Attach a 2-D decomposed geometry matrix to a PDE model.
Syntax: g = geometryFromEdges(model, dl)
Validates the decomposed geometry matrix dl (as produced by decsg or csgdel), stores the resulting pde.AnalyticGeometry object in model.Geometry, and returns it. The geometry exposes NumFaces, NumEdges, NumVertices, and Vertices (distinct edge endpoints in first-appearance order along dl columns). Raises an error if dl has an invalid row count, an open region boundary, or if model already has a mesh.
Example: R1=[3;4;-1;1;1;-1;-1;-1;1;1]; C1=[1;0;0;0.5;0;0;0;0;0;0]; dl=decsg([R1 C1],'R1-C1',['R1';'C1']'); m=createpde(); g=geometryFromEdges(m,dl); g.NumEdges
Differences from MATLAB: accepts decomposed geometry matrices dl only; function-handle geometry descriptions and 3-D geometries are not supported.

## pdegplot
Plot a 2-D PDE geometry with optional edge, face, and vertex labels.
Syntax: pdegplot(g); pdegplot(g, 'EdgeLabels', 'on', 'FaceLabels', 'on', 'VertexLabels', 'on'); h = pdegplot(...)
Plots every boundary edge of a pde.PDEModel, pde.AnalyticGeometry, or decomposed geometry matrix dl as a line object in the current axes with equal axis scaling. Circular and elliptical arcs are sampled smoothly. EdgeLabels ('E1'..), FaceLabels ('F1'.. at an interior point of each face), and VertexLabels ('V1'..) default to 'off' and accept 'on'/'off' or true/false. Returns the line handle array when an output argument is requested. If the geometry has more edges than available series slots on the axes (at most 64 series), all edges are combined into a single NaN-separated line object and a single handle is returned.
Example: R1=[3;4;-1;1;1;-1;-1;-1;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); h=pdegplot(dl,'EdgeLabels','on','FaceLabels','on'); numel(h)
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D geometries only; SubdomainLabels, FaceAlpha, and 3-D cell labels are not supported.

## generateMesh
Generate a 2-D triangular finite-element mesh for a PDE model.
Syntax: mesh = generateMesh(model); mesh = generateMesh(model, 'Hmax', hmax, 'Hmin', hmin, 'Hgrad', hgrad, 'GeometricOrder', 'quadratic'|'linear')
Meshes model.Geometry using constrained Delaunay triangulation and quality refinement, stores the resulting pde.FEMesh value object in model.Mesh, and returns it. GeometricOrder defaults to 'quadratic' (6-node triangles with midside nodes for edges (1,2), (2,3), (3,1) projected onto curved boundaries); 'linear' produces 3-node counter-clockwise triangles. Hgrad defaults to 1.5 (must satisfy 1 < Hgrad < 2). When omitted, Hmax defaults to the geometry bounding-box diagonal divided by 10, and Hmin defaults to Hmax / 4 (both must be positive with Hmin <= Hmax). Raises an error if model has no geometry.
Example: R1=[3;4;-1;1;1;-1;-1;-1;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); mesh=generateMesh(m,'Hmax',0.5,'GeometricOrder','linear'); size(mesh.Elements,1)
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D triangular meshes only; default Hmax is bounding-box diagonal / 10 and default Hmin is Hmax / 4; Hedge, Hface, Hvertex, and 3-D tetrahedral meshes are not supported.

## findNodes
Find node IDs in a 2-D PDE mesh by region, box, radius, or nearest point.
Syntax: ids = findNodes(mesh, 'region', 'Edge'|'Face', regionIDs); ids = findNodes(mesh, 'box', xlim, ylim); ids = findNodes(mesh, 'radius', center, r); ids = findNodes(mesh, 'nearest', points)
Returns a row vector of 1-based node IDs in a pde.FEMesh object. 'region', 'box', and 'radius' return sorted, unique IDs. 'nearest' accepts a 2-by-P matrix of query coordinates and returns a 1-by-P vector of nearest node IDs preserving query order.
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); mesh=generateMesh(m,'Hmax',0.5,'GeometricOrder','linear'); numel(findNodes(mesh,'box',[0 1],[0 1])) == size(mesh.Nodes,2)
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D meshes only; 'Vertex' and 3-D 'Cell' region types are not supported.

## findElements
Find element IDs in a 2-D PDE mesh by face, box, radius, or attached nodes.
Syntax: ids = findElements(mesh, 'region', 'Face', faceIDs); ids = findElements(mesh, 'box', xlim, ylim); ids = findElements(mesh, 'radius', center, r); ids = findElements(mesh, 'attached', nodeIDs)
Returns a sorted row vector of 1-based element IDs in a pde.FEMesh object. For 'box' and 'radius', an element is selected when all of its nodes (3 for linear, 6 for quadratic) lie inside the box or closed disk. 'attached' selects every element containing at least one of the specified node IDs.
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); mesh=generateMesh(m,'Hmax',0.5,'GeometricOrder','linear'); numel(findElements(mesh,'region','Face',1)) == size(mesh.Elements,2)
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D meshes only; 'box' and 'radius' always require all nodes of an element to lie inside the region (no 'completely'/'partially' flag).

## pdemesh
Plot a 2-D PDE mesh with optional node and element labels.
Syntax: pdemesh(model); pdemesh(mesh); pdemesh(nodes, elements); h = pdemesh(..., 'NodeLabels', 'on'|'off', 'ElementLabels', 'on'|'off')
Draws all unique triangle edges into the current axes with equal axis scaling. Quadratic elements draw curved edges smoothly through their midside nodes. Setting 'NodeLabels' or 'ElementLabels' to 'on' adds text objects at node coordinates or element centroids. Returns the line handle when an output argument is requested.
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); generateMesh(m,'Hmax',0.5,'GeometricOrder','linear'); h=pdemesh(m); strcmp(get(h,'Type'),'line')
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D meshes only; 3-D meshes, z-height plots (pdemesh(p,e,t,u)), and FaceAlpha are not supported.

## pdeplot
Plot 2-D PDE mesh data as colour maps, 3-D surfaces, iso-contours, and vector fields.
Syntax: h = pdeplot(model, Name, Value); h = pdeplot(mesh, Name, Value); h = pdeplot(nodes, elements, Name, Value)
Visualizes nodal data on a 2-D triangular mesh from a pde.PDEModel, a pde.FEMesh (such as results.Mesh), or raw (nodes, elements) matrices. Quadratic 6-node triangles are split into 4 linear triangles for drawing. Supported name-value options: 'XYData' (nodal colour vector, colorbar on by default), 'ZData' (nodal height vector with 3-D view), 'ColorBar' ('on'|'off'), 'Contour' ('on'|'off', iso-lines on the P1 triangle split), 'Levels' (positive integer count, default 10, or a level vector), 'Mesh' ('on'|'off'), 'FlowData' (2-by-N or N-by-2 nodal arrows via quiver), 'ColorMap' (name or RGB matrix), 'XYStyle' ('interp'|'flat'|'off'; 'off' draws only the mesh), 'ZStyle' ('continuous'|'discontinuous'|'off'), and 'Title'. Returns a column vector of graphics handles.
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); mesh=generateMesh(m,'Hmax',0.5,'GeometricOrder','linear'); u=mesh.Nodes(1,:)'; h=pdeplot(mesh,'XYData',u,'ColorBar','off'); strcmp(get(h(1),'Type'),'patch')
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D meshes only; legacy (p,e,t) 3-matrix signature, element-wise triangle data, FlowStyle 'arrow'|'cone', and 3-D pdeplot3D are not supported.

## specifyCoefficients
Specify equation coefficients for a 2-D PDE model (scalar or N-equation system).
Syntax: ca = specifyCoefficients(model, 'm', m, 'd', d, 'c', c, 'a', a, 'f', f); ca = specifyCoefficients(..., 'Face', faceIDs)
Sets the coefficients of the 2-D PDE m*d2u/dt2 + d*du/dt - div(c*grad(u)) + a*u = f on all faces or on the specified Face IDs. All five coefficient names 'm', 'd', 'c', 'a', and 'f' are required. Each value may be numeric or a function handle @(location,state) where location has fields x, y, subdomain and state has u, ux, uy, time. For scalar PDEs (N = 1), c may be a scalar, 2x1 [c11;c22], 3x1 [c11;c12;c22], or 4x1 [c11;c21;c12;c22]. For N-equation systems, c accepts 1, 2, 3, 4, N, 2N, 3N, 4N, N(2N+1), or 4N^2 rows in the MATLAB system layout (the 2-, 3-, and 4-element forms put the same 2x2 block on every equation and take precedence over the N-element form for N = 2, 3, 4 and over the 2N-element form for N = 2), or N^2 rows (isotropic N-by-N blocks, N >= 5); m, d, and a accept 1, N, N(N+1)/2, or N^2 rows (or an N-by-N matrix); f accepts a scalar or N-by-1 vector. Later calls override earlier assignments on the same faces. Returns the coefficient assignment record and updates model.EquationCoefficients.
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); ca=specifyCoefficients(m,'m',0,'d',0,'c',1,'a',0,'f',1); ca.f
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(2); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); ca=specifyCoefficients(m,'m',0,'d',0,'c',[1;0;1;2;0;2],'a',[1;0;1],'f',[1;2]); numel(ca.c)
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D PDE models only; 3-D 'Cell' regions are not supported yet.

## applyBoundaryCondition
Apply Dirichlet, generalized Neumann, or mixed boundary conditions to edges of a 2-D PDE model.
Syntax: bc = applyBoundaryCondition(model, 'dirichlet', 'Edge', edgeIDs, 'u', val); bc = applyBoundaryCondition(model, 'dirichlet', 'Edge', edgeIDs, 'u', val, 'EquationIndex', eqIDs); bc = applyBoundaryCondition(model, 'dirichlet', 'Edge', edgeIDs, 'h', h, 'r', r); bc = applyBoundaryCondition(model, 'neumann', 'Edge', edgeIDs, 'g', g, 'q', q); bc = applyBoundaryCondition(model, 'mixed', 'Edge', edgeIDs, ...)
Assigns boundary conditions on the specified geometry Edge IDs. Dirichlet conditions enforce u = val or h*u = r (optionally restricted to chosen components via 'EquationIndex' or 'Equation'). Generalized Neumann conditions enforce n.(c*grad(u)) + q*u = g, where g and q default to 0. Mixed conditions combine Dirichlet constraints ('u' with 'EquationIndex', or 'h'/'r') with Neumann ('g'/'q') on the remaining components. Edges without an explicit boundary condition default to zero-flux Neumann (g = 0, q = 0). Values may be numeric or function handles @(location,state) where location includes x, y, nx, ny, subdomain. The last assignment to an edge wins: it replaces every earlier condition on that edge, and with 'EquationIndex' the components not listed revert to the default zero Neumann condition.
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); bc=applyBoundaryCondition(m,'dirichlet','Edge',1:4,'u',0); bc.u
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(2); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); bc=applyBoundaryCondition(m,'mixed','Edge',1:4,'u',0,'EquationIndex',1,'g',[0;1]); numel(bc.EquationIndex)
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D 'Edge' regions only; 'Vertex' regions, coupled off-diagonal mixed 'h' constraints, and 3-D 'Face' boundary conditions are not supported yet.

## setInitialConditions
Set initial value and optional initial time derivative for a time-dependent 2-D PDE model.
Syntax: ic = setInitialConditions(model, u0); ic = setInitialConditions(model, u0, 'Face', faceIDs); ic = setInitialConditions(model, u0, ut0); ic = setInitialConditions(model, u0, ut0, 'Face', faceIDs); ic = setInitialConditions(model, results)
Assigns initial conditions u(x,y,t0) = u0 and, for second-order-in-time (hyperbolic, m ~= 0) equations, du/dt(x,y,t0) = ut0. Values u0 and ut0 may be real finite scalars, length-N vectors for N-equation systems, function handles @(location) where location has fields x, y, and subdomain, or a pde.StationaryResults object whose NodalSolution is used as u0. Optional 'Face', faceIDs restricts the assignment to specific faces. Stored in model.InitialConditions.
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); ic=setInitialConditions(m, @(loc) sin(pi*loc.x).*sin(pi*loc.y)); isa(ic.InitialValue, 'function_handle')
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D geometries only; 'Edge' and 'Vertex' region overrides and 3-D geometries are not supported yet.

## solvepde
Solve a stationary (linear or nonlinear) or time-dependent 2-D PDE model (scalar or N-equation system).
Syntax: results = solvepde(model); results = solvepde(model, tlist)
For stationary problems (m = 0, d = 0), solvepde(model) assembles the finite-element stiffness, reaction, and load terms on model.Mesh (linear 3-node or isoparametric quadratic 6-node triangles), applies generalized Neumann, mixed, and strong Dirichlet boundary conditions, and returns a pde.StationaryResults object with NodalSolution (N_nodes-by-N_comp), XGradients, YGradients, and Mesh. When coefficients depend on state (u, ux, uy), a damped Newton solver controlled by model.SolverOptions (ResidualTolerance default 1e-4, MaxIterations default 25, MinStep default 2^-16, ReportStatistics default 'off') is used. For time-dependent problems (d ~= 0 or m ~= 0), solvepde(model, tlist) integrates the semi-discrete system with ode15s using model.SolverOptions (RelativeTolerance 1e-3, AbsoluteTolerance 1e-6) and returns a pde.TimeDependentResults object with NodalSolution (N_nodes-by-Nt for scalar, N_nodes-by-N_comp-by-Nt for systems), SolutionTimes, XGradients, YGradients, and Mesh.
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); generateMesh(m,'Hmax',0.25,'GeometricOrder','linear'); specifyCoefficients(m,'m',0,'d',0,'c',1,'a',0,'f',1); applyBoundaryCondition(m,'dirichlet','Edge',1:4,'u',0); res=solvepde(m); max(res.NodalSolution) > 0
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); generateMesh(m,'Hmax',0.25,'GeometricOrder','linear'); specifyCoefficients(m,'m',0,'d',1,'c',1,'a',0,'f',0); applyBoundaryCondition(m,'dirichlet','Edge',1:4,'u',0); setInitialConditions(m,@(loc) sin(pi*loc.x).*sin(pi*loc.y)); res=solvepde(m,[0 0.05 0.1]); size(res.NodalSolution, 2) == 3
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D geometries only; nonlinear time-dependent solves and 3-D geometries are not supported yet. Time-dependent solves use the dense ode15s path and are limited to 4096 state DOFs. Time-dependent m, d, a, c and Neumann q are rejected. m and d must be nonzero on every face.

## solvepdeeig
Solve a 2-D PDE eigenvalue problem (scalar or N-equation system) in a given range.
Syntax: results = solvepdeeig(model, evr)
Solves the generalized symmetric eigenvalue problem -div(c*grad(u)) + a*u = lambda*d*u on model.Mesh for all eigenvalues lambda in evr = [lo hi] (lo may be -Inf, hi must be finite), returning a pde.EigenResults value object with Eigenvalues (k-by-1, ascending), Eigenvectors (N_nodes-by-k for scalar, N_nodes-by-N_comp-by-k for systems, M-normalized and zero at Dirichlet DOFs), and Mesh. Requires m = 0, positive definite d, symmetric c, and homogeneous boundary conditions (f, g, and Dirichlet r/u values are ignored; generalized Neumann q is included in K).
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); generateMesh(m,'Hmax',0.2,'GeometricOrder','quadratic'); specifyCoefficients(m,'m',0,'d',1,'c',1,'a',0,'f',0); applyBoundaryCondition(m,'dirichlet','Edge',1:4,'u',0); res=solvepdeeig(m,[0 60]); numel(res.Eigenvalues) >= 3
Differences from MATLAB: linear 2-D symmetric eigenvalue problems with m = 0 and positive definite d only; quadratic eigenvalue problems (nonzero m), nonsymmetric c, and 3-D geometries are not supported yet.

## interpolateSolution
Interpolate a 2-D PDE solution at arbitrary query points.
Syntax: uintrp = interpolateSolution(results, xq, yq); uintrp = interpolateSolution(results, xq, yq, iU); uintrp = interpolateSolution(results, xq, yq, iT); uintrp = interpolateSolution(results, xq, yq, iU, iT); uintrp = interpolateSolution(results, querypoints, ...)
Evaluates the finite-element solution of a pde.StationaryResults, pde.TimeDependentResults, or pde.EigenResults object at query coordinates (xq, yq) (or a 2-by-M matrix querypoints) using the mesh's linear (P1) or isoparametric quadratic (P2) shape functions. For pde.StationaryResults the optional 4th argument iU is the equation index. For scalar pde.TimeDependentResults and pde.EigenResults the optional 4th argument iT is the time-step or eigenmode index. For an N-equation time-dependent or eigenvalue result, the 4th argument iU is the equation index and the 5th argument iT is the time-step or eigenmode index. Query points outside the mesh return NaN.
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); generateMesh(m,'Hmax',0.3,'GeometricOrder','quadratic'); specifyCoefficients(m,'m',0,'d',0,'c',1,'a',0,'f',0); applyBoundaryCondition(m,'dirichlet','Edge',1:4,'u',@(l,s) 2*l.x+3*l.y); res=solvepde(m); abs(interpolateSolution(res, 0.5, 0.25) - 1.75) < 1e-12
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D meshes only; 3-D tetrahedral meshes are not supported yet.

## evaluateGradient
Evaluate the spatial gradient of a 2-D PDE solution at arbitrary query points.
Syntax: [gx, gy] = evaluateGradient(results, xq, yq); [gx, gy] = evaluateGradient(results, xq, yq, iU); [gx, gy] = evaluateGradient(results, xq, yq, iT); [gx, gy] = evaluateGradient(results, xq, yq, iU, iT); [gx, gy] = evaluateGradient(results, querypoints, ...)
Evaluates the finite-element gradient [du/dx, du/dy] of a pde.StationaryResults, pde.TimeDependentResults, or pde.EigenResults object at query coordinates (xq, yq) (or a 2-by-M matrix querypoints) using the mesh's linear (P1) or isoparametric quadratic (P2) shape function derivatives. For pde.StationaryResults the optional 4th argument iU is the equation index. For scalar pde.TimeDependentResults and pde.EigenResults the optional 4th argument iT is the time-step or eigenmode index. For an N-equation time-dependent or eigenvalue result, the 4th argument iU is the equation index and the 5th argument iT is the time-step or eigenmode index. Query points outside the mesh return NaN.
Example: R1=[3;4;0;1;1;0;0;0;1;1]; dl=decsg(R1); m=createpde(); geometryFromEdges(m,dl); generateMesh(m,'Hmax',0.3,'GeometricOrder','linear'); specifyCoefficients(m,'m',0,'d',0,'c',1,'a',0,'f',0); applyBoundaryCondition(m,'dirichlet','Edge',1:4,'u',@(l,s) 2*l.x+3*l.y); res=solvepde(m); [gx, gy] = evaluateGradient(res, 0.5, 0.25); abs(gx - 2) < 1e-12 && abs(gy - 3) < 1e-12
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D meshes only; 3-D tetrahedral meshes are not supported yet.

## firls
Design a linear-phase FIR filter by least squares.
Syntax: b = firls(n, f, a)
Syntax: b = firls(n, f, a, w)
Syntax: b = firls(n, f, a, ftype)
Syntax: b = firls(n, f, a, w, ftype)
f lists band edges in pairs on [0,1] (1 = Nyquist) and a the desired amplitude at each edge; the response is linear across each band and unconstrained between bands. w gives one weight per band. ftype 'hilbert' or 'differentiator' designs the antisymmetric types.
Example: b = firls(30, [0 0.3 0.4 1], [1 1 0 0]);
Example: b = firls(30, [0 0.3 0.4 1], [1 1 0 0], [1 10]);
Differences from MATLAB: none known for these forms.

## kaiserord
Estimate the Kaiser-window FIR order for given band edges and ripples.
Syntax: [n, Wn, beta, ftype] = kaiserord(f, a, dev)
Syntax: [n, Wn, beta, ftype] = kaiserord(f, a, dev, fs)
Syntax: c = kaiserord(f, a, dev, fs, 'cell')
Uses Kaiser's formulas from the smallest deviation and the narrowest transition. Wn is the middle of each transition (normalized), ftype the fir1 band type. Pass the results to fir1(n, Wn, ftype, kaiser(n+1, beta), 'noscale').
Example: [n, Wn, beta, ftype] = kaiserord([1000 1500], [1 0], [0.05 0.01], 8000);
Differences from MATLAB: none known. For highpass and bandstop an odd n needs n = n + rem(n, 2) before fir1.

## firpmord
Estimate the equiripple (firpm) FIR order for given band edges and ripples.
Syntax: [n, fo, ao, w] = firpmord(f, a, dev)
Syntax: [n, fo, ao, w] = firpmord(f, a, dev, fs)
Syntax: c = firpmord(f, a, dev, fs, 'cell')
Herrmann-Lam-Rabiner estimate; multiband specifications take the largest order over adjacent band pairs. fo and ao are firpm band edges and amplitudes, w the weights max(dev)./dev. Use firpm(n, fo, ao, w).
Example: [n, fo, ao, w] = firpmord([500 600], [1 0], [0.171 0.01], 2000);   % n = 22
Differences from MATLAB: the estimate can miss the specification by a dB or two; raise n if the response does not meet it.

## phasedelay
Phase delay of a digital filter, in samples.
Syntax: [phi, w] = phasedelay(b, a)
Syntax: [phi, w] = phasedelay(b, a, n)
Syntax: [phi, f] = phasedelay(b, a, n, fs)
Syntax: [phi, w] = phasedelay(sos, n)
Phase delay is -phase(w)/w at n points (default 512) on [0, pi); the value at w = 0 is the group delay there. A bare call plots it.
Example: [phi, w] = phasedelay([1 2 3 4 5], 1, 8);   % linear phase: phi = 2 everywhere
Differences from MATLAB: the digitalFilter form is not supported.

## iirnotch
Second-order IIR notch filter.
Syntax: [b, a] = iirnotch(w0, bw)
Syntax: [b, a] = iirnotch(w0, bw, ab)
w0 is the notch frequency and bw the bandwidth at level ab dB (default -3.0103), both normalized (1 = Nyquist). The gain is 1 at 0 and Nyquist and 0 at w0.
Example: [b, a] = iirnotch(50/500, 5/500);   % 50 Hz notch for Fs = 1 kHz
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## iirpeak
Second-order IIR peak (resonator) filter.
Syntax: [b, a] = iirpeak(w0, bw)
Syntax: [b, a] = iirpeak(w0, bw, ab)
w0 is the peak frequency and bw the bandwidth at level ab dB (default -3.0103), both normalized (1 = Nyquist). The gain is 1 at w0 and 0 at 0 and Nyquist.
Example: [b, a] = iirpeak(0.25, 0.05);
Differences from MATLAB: none known.

## findobj
Find graphics and UI component handles by properties.
Syntax: h = findobj(scope, 'Type', kind, property, value, ...)
Syntax: h = findobj(scope, '-depth', d, 'Type', kind, property, value, ...)
Syntax: h = findobj(scope, 'Tag', tag, ...)
The scope is groot or 0, a figure number, or one live figure, uifigure, UI container, axes, uiaxes, line, volume or UI component handle. Omit scope to search from root. A depth of 0 searches the scope itself, and Inf searches all descendants. Walks both classic figures and UI component trees including uiaxes graphics children (lines, patches, text, volumes, scatter, bar, stair, stem, images, constant lines and rectangles). Supported filters are Type, Number, DisplayName, Tag, Style and HandleVisibility, combined with AND.
HandleVisibility rule: classic figures and UI children default to 'on'; uifigure defaults to 'off'. Searching from root (groot, 0, or omitted scope) skips figures and subtrees whose HandleVisibility is 'off' (or 'callback' outside a callback) unless groot ShowHiddenHandles is 'on'. Passing a uifigure directly as scope searches its visible descendants.
Results use figure number, axes position and stored line order for classic figures, and tree order for UI hierarchies. Within an axes, volumes are returned in stacking order, front to back.
Example: f = uifigure('Visible', 'off'); ax = uiaxes(f); plot(ax, 1:4, (1:4).^2); h = findobj(f, 'Type', 'line'); close(f);
Differences from MATLAB: handle-array scopes, unfiltered lookup, logical operators (-not/-and/-or), -property, regular expressions and the 'flat' option are rejected.

## findall
Find all graphics and UI handles by properties, including hidden handles.
Syntax: h = findall(scope, 'Type', kind, property, value, ...)
Syntax: h = findall(scope, '-depth', d, property, value, ...)
Syntax: h = findall(property, value, ...)
Equivalent to findobj while ignoring HandleVisibility ('off' and 'callback') so default uifigure windows, hidden UI components and dialog figures are included in root and subtree searches.
Example: f = uifigure('Visible', 'off', 'Tag', 'app1'); h = findall(0, 'Type', 'figure', 'Tag', 'app1'); close(f);
Differences from MATLAB: handle-array scopes, unfiltered lookup, logical operators (-not/-and/-or), -property, regular expressions and the 'flat' option are rejected.

## allchild
Return the immediate children of a graphics handle, including hidden handles.
Syntax: h = allchild(parent)
Axes results include plotted series, text and volume objects in stacking order, front to back.
Example: V = reshape(1:27, 3, 3, 3); v = volshow(V); h = allchild(gca);
Differences from MATLAB: the parent must be a scalar handle.

## fitcdiscr
Fit a Gaussian discriminant classifier.
Syntax: mdl = fitcdiscr(X,Y,'DiscrimType','linear','Gamma',0,'Prior','empirical')
Supports matrix and numeric-predictor table inputs with response name, ResponseVarName pair, external Y or additive formula. Types are linear, quadratic, diagLinear, diagQuadratic, pseudoLinear and pseudoQuadratic. Mu gives class means; Sigma gives pooled or per-class sample covariances; Coeffs contains pairwise Const/Linear and Quadratic boundaries. Prior accepts empirical, uniform or a positive class vector. predict returns labels, posterior scores and expected costs. Numeric NaN responses are removed.
Example: m=fitcdiscr([0;1;4;5],[1;1;2;2]); [y,s,c]=predict(m,[1;4])
Differences from MATLAB: Gamma shrinkage is supported for linear discriminants. Finite numeric predictors are required; covariance work is bounded to 100000000 products and 4000000 class covariance entries. Constant predictors require pseudo types.


## fitclinear
Fit a regularized binary linear classifier.
Syntax: mdl = fitclinear(X,Y,'Learner','svm','Regularization','ridge','Lambda',lambda,'Solver','lbfgs')
Learner is svm (hinge, default) or logistic; Regularization is ridge (default) or lasso. Lambda defaults to 1/NumObservations. The objective is mean loss plus Lambda/2 times squared coefficient norm (ridge), or Lambda times coefficient L1 norm (lasso). Bias is unpenalized. Beta and Bias expose decision coefficients. Logistic scores are posterior probabilities; SVM scores are [-f f]. Table response-name and additive formula forms are supported.
Example: m=fitclinear([-2;-1;1;2],[1;1;2;2],'Learner','logistic'); [y,s]=predict(m,[-1;1])
Differences from MATLAB: Solver names lbfgs and sparsa select deterministic built-in solvers: SMO for hinge ridge, ADMM for hinge lasso and accelerated proximal gradient for logistic. Nonconvergence and work limits return errors. Lambda is a positive scalar; paths and sparse predictors are unsupported.


## fitcecoc
Fit a multiclass error-correcting output code classifier.
Syntax: mdl = fitcecoc(X,Y,'Coding','onevsone','Learners','svm')
Coding supports onevsone (default) and onevsall. Learners supports svm (linear kernel default), linear, tree, knn, discriminant, naivebayes or templateSVM/templateTree/templateLinear/templateDiscriminant. CodingMatrix contains class codes. predict returns labels and negated average binary losses, ignoring zero-coded learners for each class. Hinge loss is used for SVM scores and quadratic loss for posterior scores.
Example: m=fitcecoc([0;1;4;5;8;9],[1;1;2;2;3;3]); [y,negLoss]=predict(m,[0;4;9])
Differences from MATLAB: Only homogeneous OVO/OVA coding is supported, with at most 512 binary learners and 128 MiB retained model storage. Posterior calibration, custom decoding and custom codes are unsupported.


## fitcensemble
Fit an ensemble of classification trees.
Syntax: mdl = fitcensemble(X,Y,'Method','Bag','NumLearningCycles',100,'Learners','tree','LearnRate',1)
Methods are Bag, AdaBoostM1 (binary), AdaBoostM2 (multiclass), GentleBoost (binary), LogitBoost (binary) and RUSBoost. This build defaults to Bag for multiclass data and LogitBoost for binary data. Bag bootstraps all predictors; boosting defaults to stumps. templateTree configures MaxNumSplits and MinLeafSize. TrainedWeights exposes learner weights. predict returns labels and ensemble scores; loss/resubLoss/margin/edge and predictorImportance are available. oobLoss evaluates Bag rows excluded from bootstrap samples. rng controls bagging and undersampling.
