Example: rng(2); m=fitcensemble([0;1;4;5],[1;1;2;2],'NumLearningCycles',8); [y,s]=predict(m,[0;5])
Differences from MATLAB: Bag uses all predictors, without random feature selection; the default differs from MATLAB. At most 1000 cycles, 50000000 split-search units, and 128 MiB retained trees are supported. LearnRate is in (0,1]; sampling options and pruning are unsupported.


## cvpartition
Create reusable training and test partitions.
Syntax: c = cvpartition(n,'KFold',k); c = cvpartition(group,'Holdout',p); c = cvpartition(n,'Leaveout'); c = cvpartition(n,'Resubstitution')
A group vector creates stratified partitions. Properties are NumObservations, NumTestSets, TrainSize and TestSize. training and test return logical observation masks. repartition creates another partition of the same type; rng controls the random stream. Classification and regression crossval accept the same CVPartition objects, including stratified group partitions.
Example: rng(3); c=cvpartition([1;1;2;2],'KFold',2); mask=test(c,1)
Differences from MATLAB: Bounded to 20000 observations. Holdout is a fraction strictly between zero and one. Missing group labels, grouping-variable and custom partition options are unsupported.


## loss
Compute validation loss for classification or regression models.
Syntax: L = loss(mdl,X,Y,'LossFun','classiferror')
Regression learners support unweighted MSE (default or LossFun='mse'), omitting missing numeric test rows. Classification losses are available for every classifier. LossFun supports classiferror (default), mincost with the default zero-one cost matrix, binodeviance, exponential and hinge. The latter losses use signed positive-class score for binary problems and true-class score for multiclass problems, following the public classification loss formulas. Table predictors are selected by model predictor names.
Example: m=fitcknn([0;2],[1;2]); loss(m,[0;2],[1;2])
Example: m=fitrlinear([0;1;2],[1;2;4],'Lambda',0.1); loss(m,[0;2],[1;4])
Differences from MATLAB: Only the built-in zero-one cost matrix is supported. Observations are weighted by the model class priors; custom observation weights are unsupported.


## oobLoss
Compute out-of-bag loss for bagged classification or regression trees.
Syntax: L = oobLoss(mdl,'LossFun','classiferror')
Aggregates scores only from trees whose bootstrap samples excluded an observation. Rows without any out-of-bag prediction are omitted.
Example: rng(1); m=fitcensemble([0;1;4;5],[1;1;2;2],'Method','Bag','NumLearningCycles',20); oobLoss(m)
Regression ensembles return cumulative MSE by default; Mode='ensemble' returns the final scalar. Rows without an out-of-bag prediction are omitted; regression loss is NaN if none exist.
Example: rng(2); m=fitrensemble((0:9)',(0:9)','Method','Bag','NumLearningCycles',5); oobLoss(m,'Mode','ensemble')
Differences from MATLAB: Only Bag ensembles are supported. Classification returns scalar average loss with built-in LossFun names; regression supports unweighted MSE.


## predictorImportance
Estimate predictor importance from tree impurity reductions.
Syntax: importance = predictorImportance(mdl)
Supports fitctree, fitrtree and classification or regression tree ensembles. Returns mean Gini reduction per branch node, averaged over ensemble trees with learner weights. Regression booster trees use squared-error reduction.
Example: m=fitctree([0;1;4;5],[1;1;2;2],'MinParentSize',2); predictorImportance(m)
Example: m=fitrtree((0:7)',[0;0;1;1;4;4;5;5],'MinParentSize',2); predictorImportance(m)
Differences from MATLAB: Surrogate and permutation importance are unsupported.


## templateSVM
Create a svm learner template.
Syntax: t = templateSVM(Name,Value)
Pass the template as Learners to fitcecoc. Supported options match the corresponding learner subset.
Example: t=templateSVM()
Differences from MATLAB: Templates are immutable value structs; heterogeneous learner arrays are unsupported.


## templateTree
Create a tree learner template.
Syntax: t = templateTree(Name,Value)
Pass the template as Learners to fitcecoc, fitcensemble or fitrensemble. Supported options are MaxNumSplits, MinLeafSize, MinParentSize and PredictorSelection='allsplits'.
Example: t=templateTree()
Example: t=templateTree('MaxNumSplits',1); m=fitrensemble((0:9)',(0:9)','Learners',t,'NumLearningCycles',3); predict(m,[1;8])
Differences from MATLAB: Templates are immutable value structs; heterogeneous learner arrays are unsupported.


## templateLinear
Create a linear learner template.
Syntax: t = templateLinear(Name,Value)
Pass the template as Learners to fitcecoc. Supported options match the corresponding learner subset.
Example: t=templateLinear()
Differences from MATLAB: Templates are immutable value structs; heterogeneous learner arrays are unsupported.


## templateDiscriminant
Create a discriminant learner template.
Syntax: t = templateDiscriminant(Name,Value)
Pass the template as Learners to fitcecoc. Supported options match the corresponding learner subset.
Example: t=templateDiscriminant()
Differences from MATLAB: Templates are immutable value structs; heterogeneous learner arrays are unsupported.


## training
Return training observation indices.
Syntax: r = training(c); r = training(c,i)
Returns a logical column mask. A fold index is required when NumTestSets exceeds one.
Example: c=cvpartition(4,'KFold',2); r=training(c,1)
Differences from MATLAB: Only cvpartition objects are supported.


## test
Return test observation indices.
Syntax: r = test(c); r = test(c,i)
Returns a logical column mask. A fold index is required when NumTestSets exceeds one.
Example: c=cvpartition(4,'KFold',2); r=test(c,1)
Differences from MATLAB: Only cvpartition objects are supported.


## repartition
Create a fresh random partition.
Syntax: r = repartition(c)
Preserves the partition type and stratification; consumes the session rng stream.
Example: c=cvpartition(4,'KFold',2); r=repartition(c)
Differences from MATLAB: Only cvpartition objects are supported.

## fitrtree
Fit a CART regression tree using squared-error split improvements.
Syntax: mdl = fitrtree(X,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitrtree(tbl,'ResponseVarName'); mdl = fitrtree(tbl,'response~a+b'); mdl = fitrtree(tbl,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitrtree(X,Y,'MinLeafSize',1,'MinParentSize',10,'MaxNumSplits',20,'PredictorSelection','allsplits')
Predict with predict; inspect Children, CutPoint, CutPredictor, NodeMean and NumNodes. Trees grow by the largest available squared-error improvement. Defaults are MinLeafSize=1 and MinParentSize=10. MaxNumSplits also permits zero for a constant tree. Rows containing missing numeric predictors or responses are omitted during training.
Example: m=fitrtree((0:7)',[0;0;1;1;4;4;5;5],'MinParentSize',2); predict(m,[1;6])
Differences from MATLAB: numeric predictors only; categorical predictors, weights and surrogate splits are unsupported. All regression learners accept at most 20000 rows, 512 predictors and 2000000 elements; tree split searches also have a 100000000 element-visit budget. Unsupported options error explicitly.


## fitrsvm
Fit epsilon-insensitive support vector regression with a converged dual SMO solve.
Syntax: mdl = fitrsvm(X,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitrsvm(tbl,'response~a+b'); mdl = fitrsvm(tbl,'ResponseVarName')
Syntax: mdl = fitrsvm(X,Y,'KernelFunction','gaussian','KernelScale',1,'BoxConstraint',2,'Epsilon',0.1,'Standardize',true)
KernelFunction accepts linear, gaussian/rbf and polynomial; PolynomialOrder defaults to 3. KernelScale divides predictor coordinates; the RBF kernel is exp(-squaredDistance/KernelScale^2). Standardize uses sample standard deviations. Alpha contains signed nonzero dual coefficients in SupportVectors order; IsSupportVector indexes the retained training rows. Bias is unpenalized. Default BoxConstraint is iqr(Y)/1.349 for gaussian/rbf and 1 for linear/polynomial. Default Epsilon is iqr(Y)/13.49 (0.1 for zero IQR). A zero-IQR gaussian/rbf response uses C=1.
Example: m=fitrsvm([0;1;2;3],[0;1;2;3],'BoxConstraint',2,'Epsilon',0.1); predict(m,[0.5;2.5])
Differences from MATLAB: KernelScale='auto' uses a seeded sampled median-distance heuristic. The solver supports 2048 rows and 100000000 kernel element products, checks a 1e-9 dual KKT gap and errors on work or convergence limits.


## fitrgp
Fit exact Gaussian process regression by maximizing the profiled marginal likelihood.
Syntax: mdl = fitrgp(X,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitrgp(tbl,'response~a+b'); mdl = fitrgp(tbl,'ResponseVarName')
Syntax: mdl = fitrgp(X,Y,'Basis','constant','KernelFunction','squaredexponential','FitMethod','exact','Sigma',0.2)
Basis (also BasisFunction) accepts constant, none and linear. Kernels are squaredexponential, exponential, matern32, matern52 and rationalquadratic. KernelInformation exposes learned positive parameters. Beta is the generalized least-squares basis coefficient vector; Sigma is learned noise deviation and LogLikelihood is the fitted exact log likelihood. Initial length scale is mean(std(X)), initial signal and noise deviations are std(Y)/sqrt(2), and the rational-quadratic shape starts at 1. KernelParameters may override the kernel initial values. SigmaLowerBound is fixed at max(0.01*std(Y),1e-12).
Example: m=fitrgp([0;1;2;3;4;5],[0;0.8;1;0.2;-0.7;-1]); [p,sd,ci]=predict(m,[0.5;2.5])
Differences from MATLAB: only exact numeric GP models, up to 512 rows and a bounded likelihood work budget. Deterministic BFGS uses analytic gradients and Cholesky solves. Prediction sd includes observation noise and basis uncertainty; ci contains 95 percent normal prediction bounds. Extreme or unidentifiable parameters can vary across optimizers.


## fitrensemble
Fit least-squares boosted trees or bootstrap-aggregated regression trees.
Syntax: mdl = fitrensemble(X,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitrensemble(tbl,'response~a+b'); mdl = fitrensemble(tbl,'ResponseVarName')
Syntax: mdl = fitrensemble(X,Y,'Method','LSBoost','NumLearningCycles',100,'LearnRate',1,'Learners',templateTree('MaxNumSplits',1))
Method is LSBoost (default) or Bag. LSBoost starts at mean(Y) and fits residual trees; LearnRate is in (0,1]. Default trees use MinLeafSize=5, MinParentSize=10, and ten splits for boosting or unrestricted splits for Bag. Bag samples n rows with replacement per tree from the session rng stream and averages predictions. NumTrained and Method describe the ensemble; predictorImportance averages tree importance.
Example: rng(4); t=templateTree('MaxNumSplits',1,'MinLeafSize',1,'MinParentSize',2); m=fitrensemble((0:7)',[0;0;1;1;4;4;5;5],'Learners',t,'NumLearningCycles',3); predict(m,[1;6])
Differences from MATLAB: only numeric tree learners, no random predictor subspaces or observation weights. NumLearningCycles is capped at 1000 and cycles times predictor elements at 20000000. Bag stores in-bag membership for oobLoss.


## fitrlinear
Fit a regularized linear predictor with an unpenalized bias.
Syntax: mdl = fitrlinear(X,Y)
Syntax: mdl = fitrlinear(tbl,'response~a+b'); mdl = fitrlinear(tbl,'ResponseVarName')
Syntax: mdl = fitrlinear(X,Y,'Learner','leastsquares','Regularization','ridge','Lambda',0.1)
Learner accepts svm (default) and leastsquares; Regularization accepts ridge (default) and lasso. Lambda defaults to 1/n and accepts a nonnegative scalar or 'auto'. Least-squares loss is half MSE; svm uses epsilon-insensitive loss with optional Epsilon, default iqr(Y)/13.49 (0.1 for zero IQR). Ridge adds Lambda*sum(Beta.^2)/2; lasso adds Lambda*sum(abs(Beta)). Beta and Bias expose the fitted coefficients.
Example: m=fitrlinear([0;1;2;3],[1;3;4;7],'Lambda',0.1); b=m.Beta; predict(m,[0.5;2.5])
Differences from MATLAB: Only scalar Lambda and numeric predictors are supported. Ridge uses augmented pivoted QR; lasso least squares uses coordinate descent. Ridge svm uses linear dual SMO; lasso svm and unregularized svm use a bounded primal-dual solve with explicit convergence failures.


## prune
Return a regression tree with selected branches collapsed to their node means.
Syntax: p = prune(tree); p = prune(tree,'Level',k); p = prune(tree,'Nodes',indices)
Level=0 preserves the tree; higher levels remove successive weakest links according to squared-error cost complexity. Nodes uses one-based node indices. The original tree remains immutable.
Example: m=fitrtree((0:7)',[0;0;1;1;4;4;5;5],'MinParentSize',2); p=prune(m,'Nodes',1); predict(p,[0;7])
Differences from MATLAB: Level and Nodes are supported; Alpha is not. prune(tree) returns an unchanged copy; pruning levels are computed on request.

## rgb2lab
Convert sRGB colors to CIE 1976 L*a*b*.
Syntax: L = rgb2lab(RGB, 'WhitePoint', white, 'ColorSpace', space)

Accepts P-by-3 colormaps or M-by-N-by-3 images of class double, single, uint8 or uint16; returns double with the same shape. WhitePoint is d65 (default), d50, a, c, e, icc, or a positive 1-by-3 vector. ColorSpace is srgb (default), adobe-rgb-1998 or linear-rgb. Uses published RGB/XYZ matrices, Bradford adaptation and the CIE Lab formula.

Example: rgb2lab([1 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 1])

Differences from MATLAB: Single input returns double as specified by this app-engine contract. Four-dimensional image stacks and other RGB spaces are not supported.

## lab2rgb
Convert CIE 1976 L*a*b* colors to RGB.
Syntax: RGB = lab2rgb(L, 'WhitePoint', white, 'ColorSpace', space, 'OutputType', type)

Input is a double or single P-by-3 colormap or M-by-N-by-3 image. WhitePoint and ColorSpace match rgb2lab. OutputType is double, single, uint8 or uint16; default is the input class. Floating results preserve out-of-gamut values. Integer results are rounded and saturated.

Example: lab2rgb([50 0 0], 'OutputType', 'uint8')

Differences from MATLAB: Four-dimensional stacks and other RGB spaces are not supported.

## rgb2ycbcr
Convert RGB to BT.601 studio-range YCbCr.
Syntax: Y = rgb2ycbcr(RGB)

Accepts P-by-3 colormaps or M-by-N-by-3 images. Preserves double, single, uint8 or uint16 class and shape. For uint8, luma ranges from 16 to 235 and chroma from 16 to 240; floating results divide these values by 255, and uint16 multiplies them by 257.

Example: rgb2ycbcr(uint8([0 0 0;255 255 255]))

Differences from MATLAB: None for supported forms.

## ycbcr2rgb
Convert BT.601 studio-range YCbCr to RGB.
Syntax: RGB = ycbcr2rgb(Y)

Accepts P-by-3 colormaps or M-by-N-by-3 images of class double, single, uint8 or uint16. Preserves shape and class; RGB is saturated to its class range.

Example: ycbcr2rgb([16 128 128;235 128 128]/255)

Differences from MATLAB: None for supported forms.

## multithresh
Compute multilevel Otsu image thresholds.
Syntax: [levels, metric] = multithresh(A, N)

N defaults to 1 and must be an integer from 1 to 20. Returns a 1-by-N vector in the input class and range, plus a double effectiveness metric in [0,1]. N=1 uses graythresh scaled to the class range and cast to the input class. Other N use 256 bins across the observed finite range and exact dynamic programming. NaNs are ignored; infinities occupy end bins. Degenerate inputs return zero metric.

Example: [levels, metric] = multithresh(uint8([0 20 90 120 220 255]), 2)

Differences from MATLAB: N=1 follows the task-required graythresh class-range histogram instead of an observed-range histogram. For N>1, optimization is globally optimal on the histogram; tied optima choose the earliest boundaries. Degenerate extra thresholds repeat the maximum.

## imquantize
Quantize image values at ordered thresholds.
Syntax: [Q, index] = imquantize(A, levels, values)

levels is a nonempty, finite, strictly increasing vector. A value equal to a threshold belongs to the lower interval. Without values, Q and index are double labels from 1 to numel(levels)+1. With values, Q preserves the class of that vector. Outputs preserve the image dimensions.

Example: [Q, index] = imquantize([0 1 2 3], [1 2], uint8([10 20 30]))

Differences from MATLAB: None for supported finite inputs.

## adaptthresh
Compute locally adaptive image thresholds.
Syntax: T = adaptthresh(I, sensitivity, 'NeighborhoodSize', size, 'ForegroundPolarity', polarity, 'Statistic', statistic)

Returns a double threshold image in [0,1]. Defaults: sensitivity .5, NeighborhoodSize 2*floor(size(I)/16)+1, bright polarity and mean statistic. mean, median and gaussian use replicated borders. Accepts 2-D images and 3-D grayscale volumes. Neighborhood dimensions must be positive odd integers. imbinarize(I,T) compares intensities with this image; imbinarize(I,'adaptive',...) also accepts Sensitivity and the same options, and selects the specified foreground polarity.

Example: adaptthresh(reshape(0:24,5,5)/24, .5, 'NeighborhoodSize', 3)

Differences from MATLAB: The public reference does not specify a numeric sensitivity mapping, Gaussian sigma or border rule. This implementation uses 2*(1-sensitivity) times the local statistic for bright foreground, 2*sensitivity for dark, and Gaussian sigma=(windowSize-1)/6. This numerical compatibility choice is not verified against MATLAB. Median and Gaussian work is capped at 100 million taps; windows at 1000001 per axis.

## label2rgb
Convert nonnegative region labels to RGB colors.
Syntax: RGB = label2rgb(L, cmap, zerocolor, 'shuffle')

Returns an M-by-N-by-3 uint8 image. Default colormap is jet and background color is white. A numeric colormap must have at least max(L(:)) rows. Colormaps may also be named. zerocolor accepts a color name, RGB triplet or hex code. shuffle permutes colors using the engine RNG stream; default is noshuffle.

Example: label2rgb([0 1;2 0], [1 0 0;0 1 0], 'white')

Differences from MATLAB: Function-handle colormaps and categorical labels are not supported. Labels are bounded at 1000000; named engine colormaps have their existing 4096-row limit. Named palettes use the engine color ramps.

## labeloverlay
Blend labeled regions onto an image.
Syntax: B = labeloverlay(A, L, 'Transparency', alpha, 'Colormap', cmap, 'IncludedLabels', labels)

Returns uint8 RGB. A is grayscale or RGB; L has matching height and width. Transparency defaults to .5 (0 is opaque, 1 is transparent). Default jet colors are shuffled using the engine RNG; numeric colormaps retain their order. Background and excluded labels retain the input image.

Example: labeloverlay(uint8([100 100;100 100]), [0 1;1 0], 'Colormap', [1 0 0])

Differences from MATLAB: Categorical labels, ColorAssignment options and the recently added second colormap output are not supported. Named palettes use the engine color ramps.

## imoverlay
Burn a binary mask into an image.
Syntax: B = imoverlay(A, BW, color)

Returns uint8 RGB. Any nonzero mask value selects a pixel. Mask dimensions must match the grayscale or RGB image. color defaults to yellow and accepts RGB triplets, color names, short names and hex codes.

Example: imoverlay(uint8([100 100;100 100]), [0 1;1 0], 'red')

Differences from MATLAB: None for supported forms.

## boundarymask
Find pixels adjacent to a different region label.
Syntax: BW = boundarymask(L, conn)

Returns a logical matrix with the same shape. conn is 4 or 8 (default). A boundary pixel has an in-image neighbor with a different label. Logical images are also accepted; a constant image has no boundaries.

Example: boundarymask([0 0 0;0 1 0;0 0 0], 4)

Differences from MATLAB: None for supported forms.

## impixel
Sample image pixels at specified columns and rows.
Syntax: P = impixel(I, c, r)

Also accepts impixel(X,map,c,r) for indexed images and [c,r,P] outputs. P is a P-by-3 matrix: actual RGB values, repeated grayscale intensities, or indexed colormap rows. Coordinates round to the nearest pixel; outside samples are NaN. Numeric images return double; indexed samples preserve the colormap class. Integer indexed images use zero-based indices, floating indexed images use one-based indices.

Example: impixel(uint8([10 20;30 40]), [1 2], [1 2])

Differences from MATLAB: Interactive and world-coordinate forms are not supported; interactive forms return a clear error.

## bwdist
Distance to the nearest nonzero image pixel.
Syntax: [D, idx] = bwdist(BW, method)
BW is a real numeric or logical 2-D image. method defaults to 'euclidean'; 'cityblock', 'chessboard' and 'quasi-euclidean' are also supported. D is single and idx is uint32, with one-based column-major nearest-pixel indices. Any nearest pixel may resolve a tie. Without foreground, distances are Inf and indices are zero. Euclidean distance is exact before conversion to single and takes linear time.
Example: [D, idx] = bwdist(logical([0 0 0; 0 1 0; 0 0 0]))
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D only; segmentation workspace is limited to 2097152 samples.

## watershed
Label catchment basins and watershed ridge lines.
Syntax: L = watershed(A, conn)
Meyer priority flooding labels regional minima and expands them in increasing height order. Ridge pixels have label zero. conn is 4 or 8, default 8. L is double. Equal-height queue entries use deterministic insertion order. NaN is rejected; infinite heights are accepted.
Example: watershed(repmat([1 0 1 2 1 0 1], 5, 1), 4)
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D only; plateau tie choices can differ.

## activecontour
Evolve a mask towards image region boundaries.
Syntax: BW = activecontour(A, mask)
Syntax: BW = activecontour(A, mask, n, method, 'SmoothFactor', smooth, 'ContractionBias', bias)
mask is a binary image matching the first two image dimensions; multichannel images require a logical mask. Numeric zero/one masks are accepted for grayscale images, as in the public examples. n defaults to 100. method is 'Chan-Vese' (default) or 'edge'. The Chan-Vese method accepts multichannel images and minimises two-region intensity energy. The grayscale edge method uses a geodesic level set. SmoothFactor is nonnegative (defaults 0 and 1 respectively); positive ContractionBias encourages shrinking (defaults 0 and 0.3). Output BW is logical. Evolution is cancellable and the initial image-border layer is removed.
Example: I=zeros(9); I(3:7,3:7)=1; M=zeros(9); M(2:8,2:8)=1; activecontour(I,M,20)
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D spatial images only; discrete evolution and stopping can differ from MATLAB's numerical solver.

## imsegkmeans
Segment image channels using k-means clustering.
Syntax: [L, centers] = imsegkmeans(I, k)
Syntax: [L, centers] = imsegkmeans(I, k, 'NumAttempts', n, 'MaxIterations', m, 'Threshold', t, 'NormalizeInput', flag)
I is single, uint8, uint16, int8 or int16; use im2single for double images. Pixels are observations and image planes are features. Defaults: 3 attempts, 100 iterations, threshold 1e-4, per-channel zero-mean/unit-variance normalization enabled. Each center must move less than Threshold to stop. Centers are restored to input units and class, in a k-by-channels matrix. L matches the first two input dimensions and is uint8 for k<=255, uint16 for k<=65535, then uint32. Uses the engine rng stream and k-means++ core.
Example: rng(1); [L,C]=imsegkmeans(uint8([10 10 200; 10 200 200]),2)
Differences from MATLAB: rng controls reproducibility as required by MatRust; repeated calls advance the stream. Pixel-by-cluster workspace is limited to 2097152 elements.

## grayconnected
Flood-fill pixels with intensity close to a seed.
Syntax: BW = grayconnected(I, row, column, tolerance)
Selects the 8-connected region within the inclusive seed intensity plus/minus tolerance. Default tolerance is 32 for integer images and 0.1 for floating images. Output is logical and has the input shape.
Example: grayconnected([0 .05 .8; .05 .1 .9],1,1)
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D only; the newer Connectivity name-value argument is not supported.

## bwboundaries
Trace closed object and hole boundaries.
Syntax: [B, L, N, A] = bwboundaries(BW, conn, options)
conn is 4 or 8 (default 8). options is 'holes' (default) or 'noholes' and may follow BW directly. B is a column cell array of row-column coordinate matrices, with the starting pixel repeated at the end. Objects precede holes. N counts objects; L is a double label matrix including holes when requested. A is sparse logical with A(child,parent)=true. Labels follow column-major component discovery. Uses Moore-neighbour tracing with the directed-edge stopping criterion.
Example: [B,L,N,A]=bwboundaries(logical([1 1 1; 1 0 1; 1 1 1]))
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D only; newer TraceStyle and CoordinateOrder options are not supported. Singleton boundaries repeat their sole pixel. Boundary workspace is limited to 524288 pixels.

## bwperim
Find foreground pixels adjacent to background.
Syntax: BW2 = bwperim(BW, conn)
conn defaults to 4, or may be 8. Outside the image is background. Numeric nonzero pixels are foreground. Returns logical with the input dimensions.
Example: bwperim(true(3))
Differences from MATLAB: 2-D only; no interactive display form.

## bwarea
Estimate binary area with 2-by-2 neighbourhood weights.
Syntax: total = bwarea(BW)
Zero-padded windows contribute 0, 1/4, 1/2 (two adjacent), 3/4 (two diagonal), 7/8 or 1 for zero through four foreground pixels. Each pixel participates in four windows. Nonzero is foreground; total is a double scalar.
Example: bwarea([1 0; 0 1])   % 2.25
Differences from MATLAB: none known within the segmentation workspace limit.

## bwareafilt
Keep binary objects by pixel count.
Syntax: BW2 = bwareafilt(BW, range, conn)
Syntax: BW2 = bwareafilt(BW, n, keep, conn)
BW must be logical. range is inclusive [low high]; n is a positive integer. keep is 'largest' (default) or 'smallest'. conn defaults to 8, or may be 4. Optional arguments may be omitted. Ties retain the first n objects, using column-major component discovery order.
Example: bwareafilt(logical([1 0 1 1; 0 0 1 1]),1)
Differences from MATLAB: scalar 4/8 connectivity only.

## bwpropfilt
Keep binary objects by a scalar region property.
Syntax: BW2 = bwpropfilt(BW, attrib, range, conn)
Syntax: BW2 = bwpropfilt(BW, attrib, n, keep, conn)
Syntax: BW2 = bwpropfilt(BW, I, attrib, range, conn)
Uses existing scalar regionprops properties: Area, Extent, EquivDiameter, FilledArea, MajorAxisLength, MinorAxisLength, Eccentricity, Orientation, Perimeter, MeanIntensity, MinIntensity and MaxIntensity. I is required for intensity properties. range is inclusive; n keeps the largest objects by default. Optional keep ('largest' or 'smallest') and conn (4 or 8, default 8) follow the selection. Ties retain the first n in column-major component order. BW and output are logical.
Example: bwpropfilt(logical([1 0 1 1; 0 0 1 1]),'Area',[2 5])
Differences from MATLAB: only scalar properties implemented by regionprops; no connected-component struct input or custom connectivity.

## bwselect
Select connected components containing seed pixels.
Syntax: [BW2, idx] = bwselect(BW, c, r, n)
Column and row vectors c and r identify seed pixels; coordinates are rounded to pixel centres. n is connectivity 4 or 8 (default 8). Outside-image seeds are ignored. BW2 is logical; idx is a double column vector of selected one-based linear indices.
Example: bwselect(logical([1 0 1; 1 0 1]),3,1,8)
Differences from MATLAB: only noninteractive 2-D pixel-coordinate forms.

## iddata
Time-domain input-output data for system identification.
Syntax: data = iddata(y, u, Ts)
Syntax: data = iddata(y, [], Ts)
Syntax: data = iddata(y, u, Ts, Name, Value)
y is N-by-ny output data and u N-by-nu input data (row vectors are taken as one channel; [] makes a time series); Ts defaults to 1. Properties: OutputData, InputData, Ts, Tstart, OutputName, InputName, OutputUnit, InputUnit, TimeUnit, Name, Domain, InterSample. Options: Ts, Tstart, OutputName, InputName, OutputUnit, InputUnit, TimeUnit, Name. data(samples), data(samples, outputs, inputs) select samples (Tstart follows the first one) and channels; size(data) is [N ny nu]; detrend(data) removes means.
Example: d = iddata([1;2;3;4],[1;0;0;0],0.1); d(2:3).OutputData
Differences from MATLAB: one experiment only (no merge or getexp), no frequency-domain data, no plot; data must be finite.

## idpoly
Polynomial input-output model A y = B/F u + C/D e.
Syntax: m = idpoly(A, B, C, D, F, NoiseVariance, Ts)
Syntax: m = idpoly(sys)
Coefficients are rows in powers of q^-1; A, C, D and F are monic and [] means 1; B carries the input delay as leading zeros. Ts defaults to 1. sys is a discrete tf. tf(m) and ss(m) give the measured dynamics B/(A F), so step, bode, lsim, pole and the other LTI functions accept m.
Example: m = idpoly([1 -0.8],[0 0.5],[],[],[],1,0.1); dcgain(m)   % 2.5
Differences from MATLAB: discrete-time single-input single-output models only.

## idtf
Identified transfer-function model.
Syntax: m = idtf(num, den)
Syntax: m = idtf(num, den, Ts)
Syntax: m = idtf(sys)
num and den are in descending powers of s (Ts = 0, the default) or z. IODelay and InputDelay are seconds (continuous) or samples (discrete). tf(m) converts to the LTI tf value (continuous models with a delay cannot be converted).
Example: m = idtf(2,[1 3 2]); dcgain(m)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: single-input single-output only; no parameter covariance.

## idss
Identified state-space model in innovations form.
Syntax: m = idss(A, B, C, D)
Syntax: m = idss(A, B, C, D, K, x0, Ts)
Syntax: m = idss(sys)
x(t+1) (or dx/dt) = A x + B u + K e, y = C x + D u + e. K defaults to zero, Ts to 0 (continuous); x0 is accepted and not stored. ss(m) gives the LTI ss value.
Example: m = idss(-1,1,1,0); dcgain(m)   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: simulation, compare and predict support one input and one output.

## idproc
Low-order continuous process model.
Syntax: m = idproc(Type)
Syntax: m = idproc(Type, Name, Value)
Type is 'P' with 0 to 3 poles and optional letters D (delay Td), Z (zero Tz) and U (underdamped pair Tw, Zeta), e.g. 'P1', 'P1D', 'P2', 'P2DZ', 'P2U'. G(s) = Kp (1 + Tz s) e^(-Td s) / ((1 + Tp1 s)(1 + Tp2 s)(1 + Tp3 s)). Unset parameters are NaN.
Example: m = idproc('P1','Kp',2,'Tp1',4); dcgain(m)   % 2
Differences from MATLAB: integrating (I) types are not supported yet; no parameter bounds.

## arx
Estimate an ARX model by least squares.
Syntax: m = arx(data, [na nb nk])
Syntax: m = arx(data, na)
Syntax: m = arx(data, orders, 'InputDelay', d)
A(q) y = B(q) u(t - nk) + e by linear least squares over the samples t > max(na, nb + nk - 1) (no unmeasured past). The second form fits an AR model to time-series data. Report.Fit holds FitPercent, LossFcn, MSE, FPE, AIC, AICc, nAIC and BIC.
Example: u = sin((1:50)'); y = filter([0 1],[1 -0.5],u); m = arx(iddata(y,u,1),[1 1 1]); m.A   % [1 -0.5]
Differences from MATLAB: single-output single-input data; no option set, regularisation or multi-experiment data.

## armax
Estimate an ARMAX model by prediction-error minimisation.
Syntax: m = armax(data, [na nb nc nk])
A(q) y = B(q) u(t - nk) + C(q) e. Started from a Hannan-Rissanen regression (high-order ARX residuals as noise regressors) and refined by Levenberg-Marquardt on the one-step prediction errors with zero initial conditions; deterministic.
Example: u = sin((1:60)'); y = filter([0 1],[1 -0.5],u); m = armax(iddata(y,u,1),[1 1 1 1]); m.A(2)   % -0.5
Differences from MATLAB: single-output single-input data; no option set; initial conditions are zero.

## oe
Estimate an output-error model.
Syntax: m = oe(data, [nb nf nk])
y = B(q)/F(q) u(t - nk) + e by prediction-error minimisation (Levenberg-Marquardt), started from ARX and two instrumental-variable steps.
Example: u = sin((1:60)'); y = filter([0 1],[1 -0.5],u); m = oe(iddata(y,u,1),[1 1 1]); m.F(2)   % -0.5
Differences from MATLAB: single-output single-input data; no option set; initial conditions are zero.

## bj
Estimate a Box-Jenkins model.
Syntax: m = bj(data, [nb nc nd nf nk])
y = B/F u(t - nk) + C/D e by prediction-error minimisation, started from an output-error fit of B/F and a Hannan-Rissanen ARMA fit of C/D to its residuals.
Example: u = sin((1:60)'); y = filter([0 1],[1 -0.5],u); m = bj(iddata(y,u,1),[1 1 1 1 1]); m.F(2)   % -0.5
Differences from MATLAB: single-output single-input data; no option set; initial conditions are zero.

## tfest
Estimate a transfer function.
Syntax: m = tfest(data, np)
Syntax: m = tfest(data, np, nz)
Syntax: m = tfest(data, np, nz, iodelay)
Syntax: m = tfest(data, np, nz, iodelay, 'Ts', Ts)
Continuous model (default) with np poles and nz zeros (default np - 1), fitted to the zero-order-hold simulation error by Levenberg-Marquardt from a discrete output-error model mapped by s = log(z)/Ts. With 'Ts' equal to the data sample time the model is discrete. iodelay is fixed, in seconds (samples when discrete).
Example: u = ones(60,1); y = filter([0 1-exp(-0.1)],[1 -exp(-0.1)],u); m = tfest(iddata(y,u,0.1),1,0); m.Denominator   % [1 1]
Differences from MATLAB: single-output single-input data; the delay is not estimated; no noise model.

## ssest
Estimate a state-space model by prediction-error minimisation.
Syntax: m = ssest(data, nx)
Syntax: m = ssest(data, nx, 'Ts', Ts, 'Feedthrough', tf)
Continuous (default) or discrete idss model of order nx, fitted as an output-error model (K = 0) and returned in controller canonical form.
Example: u = sin((1:80)'/3); y = filter([0 1],[1 -0.5],u); m = ssest(iddata(y,u,1),1,'Ts',1); m.A   % 0.5
Differences from MATLAB: single-output single-input data; no disturbance model (K = 0); canonical rather than free parameterisation.

## n4sid
Estimate a state-space model by subspace identification.
Syntax: m = n4sid(data, nx)
Syntax: m = n4sid(data, 1:10)
Syntax: m = n4sid(data, nx, 'Feedthrough', tf)
Discrete idss model by PO-MOESP: RQ factorisation of the block Hankel matrices of past and future data, SVD for the observability matrix, A and C from its shift structure, then B, D and the initial state by least squares. A range picks the order at the largest singular-value gap; deterministic.
Example: u = sin((1:80)'/3); y = filter([0 1],[1 -0.5],u); m = n4sid(iddata(y,u,1),1); m.A   % 0.5
Differences from MATLAB: single-output single-input data; no disturbance model (K = 0); no weighting options.

## procest
Estimate a low-order continuous process model.
Syntax: m = procest(data, Type)
Type as in idproc, e.g. 'P1', 'P1D', 'P2', 'P2DZ', 'P2U'. The delay is started from an integer scan of ARX fits and estimated as a continuous parameter; the fit is the zero-order-hold simulation error minimised by Levenberg-Marquardt.
Example: t = (0:0.1:8)'; m = procest(iddata(2*(1-exp(-t/2)),ones(81,1),0.1),'P1'); [m.Kp m.Tp1]
Differences from MATLAB: integrating (I) types are not supported yet; no parameter bounds or initial guesses.

## compare
Compare model output with measured data.
Syntax: [y, fit, x0] = compare(data, sys)
Syntax: [y, fit, x0] = compare(data, sys, k)
Syntax: [y, fit, x0] = compare(data, sys, 'InitialCondition', ic)
y is an iddata object with the simulated (k = Inf, default) or k-step-predicted output; fit = 100 (1 - norm(y - yhat)/norm(y - mean(y))). ic is 'e' (estimate the initial state by least squares, default), 'z' (zero) or a state vector of the sampled realisation; x0 is that state.
Example: d = iddata(filter([0 1],[1 -0.5],ones(20,1)),ones(20,1),1); [~,fit] = compare(d, idpoly([1 -0.5],[0 1]))   % 100
Differences from MATLAB: one model per call; no plot (called without outputs it returns y).

## resid
Residuals and their correlation tests.
Syntax: [E, R, S] = resid(data, sys)
Syntax: [E, R, S] = resid(data, sys, M)
E is an iddata object of one-step prediction errors (zero initial conditions). R is the (M+1)-by-2-by-2 covariance array R(tau+1,i,j) = 1/N sum z_i(t+tau) z_j(t) of z = [e u] (M = 25 by default). S has Lags, AutoCorr (normalised), AutoBound = 2.5758/sqrt(N), CrossLags (-M..M), CrossCorr (e(t) with u(t-tau), normalised), CrossBound = 2.5758 sqrt(P/N) with P = sum rho_e(k) rho_u(k), and Confidence (99).
Example: d = iddata(randn(50,1),randn(50,1),1); [E,R,S] = resid(d, idpoly(1,[0 0])); S.AutoBound
Differences from MATLAB: S is a MatRust addition replacing the plot; frequency-domain residual tests are not supported.

## sim
Simulate an identified model.
Syntax: y = sim(sys, data)
Syntax: y = sim(sys, u)
Zero-initial-state response of the measured dynamics. With iddata input the result is an iddata object with the simulated OutputData; with a numeric input vector (discrete models) a column vector.
Example: sim(idpoly([1 -0.5],[0 1]), [1;0;0])   % [0; 1; 0.5]
Differences from MATLAB: no noise, initial-condition or option arguments; single input and output.

Neural network form: y = sim(net,x), equivalent to net(x). Configure the network first. Matrix columns are samples; cell sequences return cell sequences.
Example: n = configure(fitnet(2),[0 1],[0 1]); y = sim(n,[0 1]);


MPC form: simulate an mpc object using the existing mpcmove controller and the discretized simulation plant.
Syntax: [y,t,u,xp,xmpc,options] = sim(c,T,r[,v][,options])
T is a positive integer count of stored samples, at most 65536; t=(0:T-1)'*c.Ts. There are T-1 plant transitions. y is T-by-Ny (physical output order), u is T-by-Nmv (requested MVs, excluding input noise), and xp is T-by-Nxp (physical states before each transition). y excludes OutputNoise. No-output calls draw outputs and MVs in two subplots; requesting any output suppresses plotting. At most six outputs.
r has physical output columns; v has measured disturbance columns. Signals hold their last row. Empty r/v use controller nominal Y/MD input offsets. With lookahead off, the current row is held over the horizon; RefLookAhead='on' passes p reference rows starting at the current sample and MDLookAhead='on' passes p+1 disturbance rows, holding the final available row.
xmpc is a T-by-1 struct array with Plant, Disturbance, Noise, LastMove and Covariance. Each snapshot is taken after mpcmove: Plant is the observer's next prior, LastMove is the current requested MV. Snapshots are independent values; open-loop xmpc is an empty 0-by-1 struct array.
Example: c=mpc(ss(.8,.2,1,0,.1)); [y,t,u,xp,xc,o]=sim(c,3,1); size(y)
Differences from MATLAB: MPC supports the mpc object only, fixed controller weights/constraints, and matching physical signal groups for mismatch plants. Discrete mismatches must already use c.Ts. Controller histories are limited to 13107 samples by struct storage; workspace limits also apply.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/mpc/ref/mpc.sim.html

## profile
Collect function calls, elapsed time, source-line counts and optional call history.
Syntax: profile on
Syntax: profile on -history -historysize 1000 -timer real
Syntax: profile off
Syntax: profile resume
Syntax: profile clear
Syntax: profile viewer
Syntax: p = profile('info')
Syntax: s = profile('status')
'on' clears statistics; 'resume' retains them. 'off', 'clear', 'info' and 'viewer' stop collection. Settings persist across clear. Options also work alone while off; -nohistory disables history. The viewer prints function, calls, total time and self time, sorted by total time. FunctionTable is an N-by-1 struct array (empty 0-by-1); builtin ExecutedLines is 0-by-3. FunctionHistory is 2-by-N, with entry/exit in row 1 and 1-based function index in row 2. Children and Parents provide FunctionTableIndex and the documented Index alias.
Example: profile on; x=sum([1 2]); profile off; p=profile('info'); p.FunctionTable.NumCalls   % 1
Differences from MATLAB: History defaults off with 1000000 events maximum; timestamp history is unsupported. All timers use the monotonic elapsed clock, retaining the selected real/cpu/performance name. ClockSpeed is 0 (unknown); ClockPrecision reports nominal nanosecond representation. TotalRecursiveTime is 0. The engine bounds retained functions to 1024, call graph edges to 4096, executed lines to 65536 and retained source to 16 MiB. No desktop viewer is opened. Profiling overhead affects measured times.

## profsave
Save a profiler snapshot as plain HTML files.
Syntax: profsave
Syntax: profsave(p)
Syntax: profsave(p, folder)
Without p, stops collection and reads profile('info'). The default destination is profile_results in Current Folder. Creates file0.html with the summary and file1.html, file2.html, etc. with escaped source-line listings. A missing destination folder is created. Pass the structure returned by profile('info').
Example: p=profile('info'); isempty(p.FunctionTable)   % true in a fresh session
Differences from MATLAB: Plain HTML without scripts or interactive navigation; source listing uses retained source when available, otherwise reads FileName. Output is limited to 64 MiB. Clock values and timers follow profile's documented MatRust limits.

## confusion

Classification confusion value, counts, sample indices and class rates.
Syntax: [c,cm,ind,per] = confusion(targets,outputs)
Targets are S-by-Q one-hot columns; outputs in [0,1] select the first maximum. A binary row uses outputs >= 0.5. Counts and index cells have target rows and output columns. per columns are FN/output-negatives, FP/output-positives, TP/output-positives and TN/output-negatives; zero denominators give NaN.
Example: [c,cm,ind,per] = confusion([0 1 1],[.1 .9 .2]);
Differences from MATLAB: finite matrices only; at most 256 classes.

## plotconfusion

Plot classification counts, percentages, precision, recall and accuracy.
Syntax: h = plotconfusion(targets,outputs)
Syntax: h = plotconfusion(t1,y1,name1,t2,y2,name2,...)
Creates a new figure with output rows, target columns, green diagonal and red off-diagonal cells. Categorical vectors include unused categories. Named datasets occupy separate subplots.
Example: h = plotconfusion([0 1 1],[.1 .9 .2]);
Differences from MATLAB: the 256-text-per-axes graphics limit bounds class count; undefined categorical labels and cell input sequences are unsupported.

## ploterrhist

Plot stacked error histograms with a zero-error reference.
Syntax: h = ploterrhist(errors)
Syntax: h = ploterrhist(e1,name1,e2,name2,...,'bins',20)
Creates a new figure with shared equal-width bins for all datasets; the default is 20 bins.
Example: h = ploterrhist([-1 0 .5 1],'Training',[0 .2],'Test','bins',10);
Differences from MATLAB: finite nonempty matrices only; at most 16 datasets and 10000 bins. Stacks are ordinary patch objects.

## plotperform

Plot training-record performance curves on logarithmic axes.
Syntax: h = plotperform(tr)
Creates a new figure from epoch and perf with optional vperf and tperf. The best marker reads best_epoch and best_vperf, or best_perf when validation is absent.
Example: tr=struct('epoch',[0 1 2],'perf',[1 .5 .25],'vperf',[1.2 .4 .6],'best_epoch',1,'best_vperf',.4); h=plotperform(tr);
Differences from MATLAB: scalar records only, one value per epoch; the performance label is Mean Squared Error (mse).

## plotregression

Plot targets and outputs, a least-squares fit and the identity line.
Syntax: h = plotregression(targets,outputs)
Syntax: h = plotregression(t1,y1,name1,t2,y2,name2,...)
Creates a new figure; titles show correlation R and the output label shows slope and intercept. Named datasets occupy separate subplots.
Example: h = plotregression([1 2 3 4],[2 3 5 4],'Training');
Differences from MATLAB: finite matrices of equal size, at least two observations and nonconstant targets are required; at most 16 datasets.

## plotroc

Plot receiver operating characteristics and a diagonal reference.
Syntax: h = plotroc(targets,outputs)
Syntax: h = plotroc(t1,y1,name1,t2,y2,name2,...)
Creates a new figure with class legends; named datasets occupy separate subplots. Numeric inputs follow roc.
Example: h = plotroc([0 1 1],[.1 .9 .2]);
Differences from MATLAB: finite numeric matrices only; at most 16 datasets and 63 class curves per axes.

## plottrainstate

Plot training-record gradient, mu and validation checks.
Syntax: h = plottrainstate(tr)
Creates a new figure of stacked axes using epoch, gradient, optional mu and val_fail; titles show final values. Gradient and mu use logarithmic scales.
Example: tr=struct('epoch',[0 1 2],'gradient',[1 .1 .01],'mu',[.01 .001 .0001],'val_fail',[0 0 1]); h=plottrainstate(tr);
Differences from MATLAB: scalar records with these state fields only; arbitrary additional training states are unsupported.

## roc

Receiver operating characteristic for each network output row.
Syntax: [tpr,fpr,thresholds] = roc(targets,outputs)
Use one-hot targets or a binary row and outputs in [0,1]. Thresholds descend through distinct observed scores and endpoints 1 and 0; a score >= threshold is positive. Rates divide by actual positives and actual negatives; absent classes give NaN. Multiple rows return 1-by-S cell arrays; one row returns vectors.
Example: [tpr,fpr,thresholds] = roc([0 1 1],[.1 .9 .2]);
Differences from MATLAB: finite matrices only; categorical inputs and cell input sequences are unsupported.

## train
Train a shallow supervised neural network.
Syntax: [net,tr] = train(net,x,t[,xi,ai,ew][,Name,Value])
net.trainFcn selects the training function: trainlm, trainscg, trainbr, traingd, traingdm, traingdx, trainrp or trainbfg. trainlm and trainbr require squared-error performance ('mse' or 'sse').
Static cell sequences are concatenated by sample. Xi and Ai must be empty.
EW accepts a nonnegative scalar, sample row, output column or target-sized matrix.
useParallel, useGPU and showResources are accepted execution hints and ignored.
showWindow is ignored; showCommandLine prints every trainParam.show epochs.
The record contains epoch 0, performance, validation/test performance, gradient,
validation failures, algorithm states and the stopping reason. With validation
active the returned network uses the best validation weights. Empty validation/test
divisions have empty vperf/tperf series and NaN best_vperf/best_tperf.
Example: rng(1); n=fitnet(3); n.divideFcn='dividetrain'; n.trainParam.epochs=5; [n,tr]=train(n,[-1 0 1],[1 0 1]);

## dividerand
Divide samples randomly using the global rng stream (default 70/15/15).
Syntax: [trainInd,valInd,testInd] = dividerand(Q[,trainRatio,valRatio,testRatio])
Ratios are normalized; training/validation counts are rounded and test gets the remainder.
Example: rng(0); [a,b,c]=dividerand(20,0.7,0.15,0.15);

## divideblock
Divide samples into consecutive training, validation and test blocks.
Syntax: [trainInd,valInd,testInd] = divideblock(Q[,trainRatio,valRatio,testRatio])
Example: [a,b,c]=divideblock(20,0.7,0.15,0.15);

## divideint
Divide samples using deterministic weighted interleaved indices.
Syntax: [trainInd,valInd,testInd] = divideint(Q[,trainRatio,valRatio,testRatio])
Example: [a,b,c]=divideint(12,1,1,1);

## divideind
Use explicit disjoint sample indices, discarding indices greater than Q.
Syntax: [trainInd,valInd,testInd] = divideind(Q,trainInd,valInd,testInd)
Example: [a,b,c]=divideind(10,1:6,7:8,9:12);

## dividetrain
Use every sample for training, leaving validation and test empty.
Syntax: [trainInd,valInd,testInd] = dividetrain(Q)
Example: [a,b,c]=dividetrain(10);

## selforgmap
Create a batch self-organizing map.
Syntax: net = selforgmap(dimensions,coverSteps,initNeighbor,topologyFcn,distanceFcn)
Defaults: [8 8], 100, 3, hextop, linkdist. Full one-hot output. Up to 2048 neurons; PCA initialization centered at the data-range midpoint.
Example: n=configure(selforgmap([2 2]),[0 1 0 1;0 0 1 1]); vec2ind(n([0;0]))

## gridtop
Rectangular neuron positions.
Syntax: p = gridtop(dimensions)
Coordinates start at zero; the first dimension varies fastest.
Example: gridtop([2 2])

## hextop
Hexagonal neuron positions.
Syntax: p = hextop(dimensions)
Alternating rows are shifted by one half; vertical spacing is sqrt(3)/2.
Example: hextop([2 2])

## randtop
Random neuron positions using the global random stream.
Syntax: p = randtop(dimensions)
Coordinates lie in the dimension ranges.
Example: rng(1); randtop([2 2])

## dist
Euclidean distance between neuron positions.
Syntax: d = dist(positions)
Returns a square matrix of pairwise column distances.
Example: dist([0 1 0;0 0 1])

## linkdist
Graph link distance between neuron positions.
Syntax: d = linkdist(positions)
Positions within unit Euclidean distance are neighbors. Disconnected distance equals the neuron count.
Example: linkdist(gridtop([2 2]))

## boxdist
Maximum coordinate distance between neuron positions.
Syntax: d = boxdist(positions)
Returns a square distance matrix.
Example: boxdist(gridtop([2 2]))

## mandist
Manhattan distance between neuron positions.
Syntax: d = mandist(positions)
Sums absolute coordinate differences.
Example: mandist(gridtop([2 2]))

## narxnet
Create a nonlinear autoregressive network with external input.
Syntax: net = narxnet(inputDelays,feedbackDelays,hiddenSizes,feedbackMode,trainFcn)
Defaults: 1:2, 1:2, 10, open, trainlm. Prepare cell sequences with preparets. Input processing settings apply to the common expanded tap matrix. Open-loop training uses static backpropagation on ascending delay taps; closed-loop simulation is supported. Closed-loop training is unsupported.
Example: n=narxnet(1:2,1:2,3); n.numInputs

## narnet
Create a nonlinear autoregressive network.
Syntax: net = narnet(feedbackDelays,hiddenSizes,feedbackMode,trainFcn)
The open feedback input receives observed target values. Close the loop to predict future values.
Example: n=narnet(1:3,4); n.numInputDelays

## timedelaynet
Create a tapped-delay feedforward network.
Syntax: net = timedelaynet(inputDelays,hiddenSizes,trainFcn)
Delays must be increasing nonnegative integers. Default division is block division by time.
Example: n=timedelaynet(0:2,4); n.numInputDelays

## preparets
Prepare time-series inputs, initial states and targets.
Syntax: [Xs,Xi,Ai,Ts,EWs,shift] = preparets(net,Xnf,Tnf,Tf,EW)
For TDNN use preparets(net,X,T). For NAR use preparets(net,{},{},T). State cells are chronological, oldest first. Xi is inputs by maximum input delay; Ai is layers by maximum feedback layer delay.
Example: [xs,xi,ai,ts,ew,shift]=preparets(narxnet(1:2,1:2),con2seq(1:6),{},con2seq(2:7)); shift

## closeloop
Convert observed feedback to internal predicted feedback.
Syntax: [netc,Xic,Aic] = closeloop(net,Xf,Af)
States are optional. Zero-delay closed feedback is rejected as an algebraic loop.
Example: n=closeloop(narxnet(1:2,1:2)); n.outputs{2}.feedbackMode

## openloop
Convert internal feedback to observed target input.
Syntax: [neto,Xio,Aio] = openloop(net,Xf,Af)
States are optional. Learned weights and processing settings are preserved.
Example: n=openloop(closeloop(narnet(1:2))); n.outputs{2}.feedbackMode

## removedelay
Produce a dynamic network response earlier.
Syntax: net = removedelay(net,n)
Defaults to one: decrease external input delays and increase feedback delays. Reject removal exceeding the minimum input delay.
Example: n=removedelay(narxnet(1:2,1:2)); n.inputWeights{1,1}.delays

## con2seq
Convert matrix columns into cell timesteps.
Syntax: X = con2seq(x)
Syntax: X = con2seq(b,TS)
With a matrix input, each cell contains one column vector. The two-input form splits each N-by-1 batch cell into TS blocks.
Example: con2seq([1 2 3;4 5 6])

## seq2con
Join cell timesteps into matrix columns.
Syntax: x = seq2con(X)
Returns an N-by-1 cell column, including the single-signal case. Each cell contains all timesteps as concurrent columns.
Example: seq2con({[1;4],[2;5]})

## tonndata
Convert data into neural-network cell time-series form.
Syntax: [y,wasMatrix] = tonndata(x,columnSamples,cellTime)
Transpose samples when columnSamples is false. Split matrix columns into cell timesteps when cellTime is false.
Example: [y,m]=tonndata([1 2 3],true,false)

## fromnndata
Reverse a neural-network data conversion.
Syntax: x = fromnndata(y,wasMatrix,columnSamples,cellTime)
Use wasMatrix returned by tonndata.
Example: fromnndata({1,2,3},true,true,false)

## plotsomtop
Plot an editable self-organizing map view.
Syntax: f = plotsomtop(net)
Uses ordinary patch, line and text objects. Geometry follows the neuron positions. One or two topology dimensions are supported. Faces are triangulated and batched; weight/distance colors use 31/32 levels. At most 16 weight planes and 10000 faces are supported; hit labels are shown for up to 256 neurons.
Example: x=[0 1 0 1;0 0 1 1]; n=configure(selforgmap([2 2]),x); f=plotsomtop(n)

## plotsomnc
Plot an editable self-organizing map view.
Syntax: f = plotsomnc(net)
Uses ordinary patch, line and text objects. Geometry follows the neuron positions. One or two topology dimensions are supported. Faces are triangulated and batched; weight/distance colors use 31/32 levels. At most 16 weight planes and 10000 faces are supported; hit labels are shown for up to 256 neurons.
Example: x=[0 1 0 1;0 0 1 1]; n=configure(selforgmap([2 2]),x); f=plotsomnc(n)

## plotsomnd
Plot an editable self-organizing map view.
Syntax: f = plotsomnd(net)
Uses ordinary patch, line and text objects. Geometry follows the neuron positions. One or two topology dimensions are supported. Faces are triangulated and batched; weight/distance colors use 31/32 levels. At most 16 weight planes and 10000 faces are supported; hit labels are shown for up to 256 neurons.
Example: x=[0 1 0 1;0 0 1 1]; n=configure(selforgmap([2 2]),x); f=plotsomnd(n)

## plotsomplanes
Plot an editable self-organizing map view.
Syntax: f = plotsomplanes(net)
Uses ordinary patch, line and text objects. Geometry follows the neuron positions. One or two topology dimensions are supported. Faces are triangulated and batched; weight colors use up to 31 levels (fewer with several planes, which share the 64-series plot limit); distance colors use 32. At most 16 weight planes and 10000 faces are supported; hit labels are shown for up to 256 neurons.
Example: x=[0 1 0 1;0 0 1 1]; n=configure(selforgmap([2 2]),x); f=plotsomplanes(n)

## plotsomhits
Plot an editable self-organizing map view.
Syntax: f = plotsomhits(net,x)
Uses ordinary patch, line and text objects. Geometry follows the neuron positions. One or two topology dimensions are supported. Faces are triangulated and batched; weight/distance colors use 31/32 levels. At most 16 weight planes and 10000 faces are supported; hit labels are shown for up to 256 neurons.
Example: x=[0 1 0 1;0 0 1 1]; n=configure(selforgmap([2 2]),x); f=plotsomhits(n,x)

## plotsompos
Plot an editable self-organizing map view.
Syntax: f = plotsompos(net[,x])
Uses ordinary patch, line and text objects. Geometry follows the neuron positions. One or two topology dimensions are supported. Faces are triangulated and batched; weight/distance colors use 31/32 levels. At most 16 weight planes and 10000 faces are supported; hit labels are shown for up to 256 neurons.
Example: x=[0 1 0 1;0 0 1 1]; n=configure(selforgmap([2 2]),x); f=plotsompos(n,x)

## nnstart
Open the desktop app picker for neural-network work.
Syntax: nnstart
The picker includes Neural Net Fitting, Neural Net Pattern Recognition, Neural Net Clustering and Neural Net Time Series.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the desktop; no arguments or outputs. The command-line engine reports "nnstart requires the desktop".

## nftool
Open Neural Net Fitting in the desktop.
Syntax: nftool
Choose workspace predictors and responses or the synthetic sine example. Split samples, configure the network and select Train. Stop retains the current trained network and records "User stop.". Export writes the network, training record, outputs and errors; Generate script saves the reproducible training recipe.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the desktop; no arguments or outputs. Data is bounded to 50000 samples, 256 rows per array and 2000000 combined elements. Generated scripts are limited to 1 MiB, including checkpoints. Model MAT-file save is not provided.

## nprtool
Open Neural Net Pattern Recognition in the desktop.
Syntax: nprtool
Choose one-hot targets or categorical/integer class labels. Class labels are converted to category codes and then indicator columns with ind2vec; their order follows categorical. The synthetic example contains two generated Gaussian classes. Training progress, Stop, confusion counts and ROC curves stay inside the app.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the desktop; no arguments or outputs. The data and script limits are the same as nftool, with additional class limits from the neural plotting functions. Only registered training algorithms are offered.

## nctool
Open Neural Net Clustering in the desktop.
Syntax: nctool
Choose a workspace matrix or seeded Gaussian example, map dimensions, hexagonal or rectangular topology and epochs. Train a batch SOM with live progress and Stop; inspect neighbour distances, hits, two-channel weight positions, weight planes and topology. Export the network, training record, cluster indices and hits, or generate a reproducible script.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the desktop; no arguments or outputs. The app supports at most 1024 neurons, 16 input channels, 10000 weight-plane faces, 8000000 neuron-samples, 50000 samples and 1000000 input elements. Generated scripts including checkpoints are limited to 1 MiB.

## ntstool
Open Neural Net Time Series in the desktop.
Syntax: ntstool
Choose NARX, NAR or an input-output delay network. Import matrices or a cell sequence of column vectors, or use a damped oscillator example. Train with chronological training/validation/test blocks after delay removal. Inspect subset MSE and correlation, responses, error correlations and multi-step predictions. Export the open and closed networks, record and outputs, or generate a reproducible script.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the desktop; no arguments or outputs. Delays are contiguous from 1 to the selected maximum (at most 128); prediction horizon is 1–1000. Predictions continue from final observed states, holding external inputs at their last value. Series plots show the first eight channels; metrics and exports retain all channels. Correlation plots use biased xcorr over at most 20 lags. Sources are bounded to 50000 time steps, 256 channels and 1000000 elements each; delayed data to 2000000 elements, with the engine's 65536-slot cell bound also applying. Concurrent sequences are not supported. Generated scripts including checkpoints are limited to 1 MiB.

## trimf
Evaluate a fuzzy membership function.
Syntax: y = trimf(x,parameters)
Output preserves input shape and NaNs. Parameters use MathWorks order. Crisp shoulders are supported; Gaussian sigma zero uses the pointwise limit.
Example: trimf([0 0.5 1],[0 0.5 1])
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## trapmf
Evaluate a fuzzy membership function.
Syntax: y = trapmf(x,parameters)
Output preserves input shape and NaNs. Parameters use MathWorks order. Crisp shoulders are supported; Gaussian sigma zero uses the pointwise limit.
Example: trapmf([0 0.5 1],[0 0.2 0.8 1])
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

Syntax: y = linsmf(x,parameters)
Output preserves input shape and NaNs. Parameters use MathWorks order. Crisp shoulders are supported; Gaussian sigma zero uses the pointwise limit.
Example: linsmf([0 0.5 1],[0 1])

Evaluate a fuzzy membership function.
Syntax: y = linzmf(x,parameters)
Output preserves input shape and NaNs. Parameters use MathWorks order. Crisp shoulders are supported; Gaussian sigma zero uses the pointwise limit.
