## evalmf
Evaluate fuzzy membership objects.
Syntax: y = evalmf(mf,x); y = evalmf(x,parameters,type)
A scalar MF preserves x shape; a vector of MFs returns one column per MF for scalar or vector x. Custom functions must preserve input shape.
Example: evalmf(fismf("trimf",[0 0.5 1]),[0 0.5 1])
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## defuzz
Defuzzify a sampled fuzzy set.
Syntax: y = defuzz(x,mf,method)
Methods: centroid, bisector, mom, lom, som. x must be finite and strictly increasing, and mf finite and nonnegative. centroid uses the sampled weighted mean; bisector divides the piecewise-linear area between adjacent samples into two equal halves (matching scikit-fuzzy); zero-area sets error. For all-zero sets, maxima methods use all samples.
Example: defuzz([0 1 2],[0 1 0],"centroid")
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable. bisector uses piecewise-linear area integration between samples, which may differ slightly from MATLAB on coarse grids.

## mamfis
Create a Mamdani fuzzy inference system.
Syntax: fis = mamfis(Name=Value,...)
Defaults: min AND, max OR, min implication, max aggregation, centroid defuzzification. Three uniformly spaced MFs per configured variable; default rules cover all input combinations. AddRules="none" omits rules.
Example: mamfis(NumInputs=2,NumOutputs=1)
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## sugfis
Create a Sugeno fuzzy inference system.
Syntax: fis = sugfis(Name=Value,...)
Defaults: prod AND, probor OR, prod implication, sum aggregation, wtaver defuzzification. Output MFs are constant. Objects have value semantics.
Example: sugfis(NumInputs=1,NumOutputs=1)
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## fisvar
Create a fuzzy variable.
Syntax: var = fisvar(range,Name=name)
Defaults: Name="var", Range=[0 1], no membership functions.
Example: fisvar([0 10],Name="speed")
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## fismf
Create a fuzzy membership function object.
Syntax: mf = fismf(type,parameters,Name=name)
Defaults: Name="mf", Type="trimf", Parameters=[0 0.5 1]. Custom function names and handles are stored; evalmf calls them with x and parameters.
Example: fismf("gaussmf",[0.2 0.5],Name="medium")
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable. Changing Type converts parameters using the existing support interval; exact shape equivalence is not guaranteed.

## fisrule
Create fuzzy rule objects.
Syntax: rules = fisrule(text); rules = fisrule(numericRows,numInputs)
Text descriptions use symbolic or verbose syntax. Text-only constructors leave Antecedent and Consequent empty; addRule resolves variable and membership names.
Example: fisrule([1 -2 1 0.5 2],2)
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## addInput
Add an input to a fuzzy system.
Syntax: fis = addInput(fis,range,Name=Value,...)
Default range [0 1], NumMFs=0; MFType supports trimf and gaussmf.
Example: addInput(mamfis,[0 10],Name="speed",NumMFs=3)
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## addOutput
Add an output to a fuzzy system.
Syntax: fis = addOutput(fis,range,Name=Value,...)
Sugeno outputs support constant and linear MFs; linear parameters have one coefficient per input followed by a constant.
Example: addOutput(sugfis,[0 10],Name="tip",NumMFs=3)
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## addMF
Add a membership function.
Syntax: fis = addMF(fis,varName,type,parameters,Name=name); var = addMF(var,type,parameters)
Specify VariableType="input" or "output" to disambiguate shared variable names. Membership function names must be unique per variable.
Example: addMF(fisvar,"trimf",[0 0.5 1],Name="medium")
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## removeInput
Remove a fuzzy input and update rules.
Syntax: fis = removeInput(fis,inputName)
Removes the antecedent column; rules using no remaining inputs are removed. Linear Sugeno output coefficients are adjusted.
Example: removeInput(mamfis(NumInputs=1),"input1")
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## removeOutput
Remove a fuzzy output and update rules.
Syntax: fis = removeOutput(fis,outputName)
Removes the consequent column; rules using no remaining outputs are removed.
Example: removeOutput(sugfis(NumOutputs=1),"output1")
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## removeMF
Remove a membership function and update rules.
Syntax: fis = removeMF(fis,varName,mfName); var = removeMF(var,mfName)
References to the removed MF become zero; higher indices shift down with NOT signs preserved. Rules with empty antecedents or consequents are removed.
Example: removeMF(addMF(fisvar,"trimf",[0 0.5 1],Name="medium"),"medium")
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## addRule
Add numeric, symbolic, or verbose fuzzy rules.
Syntax: fis = addRule(fis,rules)
Numeric rows contain input indices, output indices, weight, and connection (1 AND or 2 OR). Negative indices mean NOT; zero means do not care. showrule text can be added back.
Example: addRule(mamfis(NumInputs=1,NumOutputs=1,AddRules="none"),[1 1 1 1])
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## showrule
Display fuzzy system rules.
Syntax: text = showrule(fis,Format=format)
Formats: verbose (default), symbolic, indexed. Returns a character matrix; RuleIndex selects rules. Names are resolved from current FIS variables and MFs.
Example: showrule(mamfis(NumInputs=1,NumOutputs=1),Format="symbolic")
Differences from MATLAB: Type-1 fuzzy systems only. Saving fuzzy objects to MAT files is not supported yet. Object arrays are bounded to 65536 rules, 64 variables per direction and 256 MFs per variable.

## evalfis
Evaluate a type-1 Mamdani or Sugeno fuzzy inference system.
Syntax: [y,fuzzifiedIn,ruleOut,aggregatedOut,ruleFiring] = evalfis(fis,input,options)
Input rows are samples and columns are inputs. A vector with one element per input is one sample. Intermediate outputs describe the last sample. Options are optional. Out-of-range inputs are clipped. Empty outputs default to the midpoint of the output range.
Example: f=mamfis(NumInputs=2,NumOutputs=1); y=evalfis(f,[.2 .7]);
Differences from MATLAB: type-1 objects only; inputs must be finite. Uses the existing piecewise linear defuzzification kernel.

## evalfisOptions
Create evaluation options for a fuzzy inference system.
Syntax: options = evalfisOptions(Name=Value)
NumSamplePoints defaults to 101. OutOfRangeInputValueMessage, NoRuleFiredMessage and EmptyOutputFuzzySetMessage accept 'warning' (default), 'error' or 'none'. Options have value semantics and editable properties.
Example: options=evalfisOptions(NumSamplePoints=51,NoRuleFiredMessage='error');
Differences from MATLAB: NumSamplePoints is limited to 65536; no type-2 inference options.

## readfis
Read a type-1 fuzzy inference system from a text file.
Syntax: fis = readfis(filename)
Reads [System], [InputN], [OutputN] and [Rules] sections. Adds .fis when no extension is specified. Errors name the offending line. Custom function names are preserved without executing file contents.
Example: f=mamfis(NumInputs=1,NumOutputs=1); writefis(f,'help-readfis.fis'); g=readfis('help-readfis.fis'); assert(isequal(f,g)); delete('help-readfis.fis');
Differences from MATLAB: text FIS version 2.0 only; no MAT files or file-selection dialog. File size is limited to 16 MiB.

## writefis
Write a fuzzy inference system to a text file.
Syntax: writefis(fis,filename)
Writes the version 2.0 .fis text format. Adds .fis if no extension is specified. Single quotes in names are doubled. Named custom membership and inference functions are preserved.
Example: f=sugfis(NumInputs=1,NumOutputs=1); writefis(f,'help-writefis.fis'); g=readfis('help-writefis.fis'); assert(isequal(f,g)); delete('help-writefis.fis');
Differences from MATLAB: preserves the FIS Name for exact round trips. No dialogs or MAT files. Anonymous function handles cannot be written. DisableStructuralChecks is retained as an optional system field.

## gensurf
Generate a fuzzy inference output surface or its data.
Syntax: [X,Y,Z] = gensurf(fis,options)
Defaults to output 1, inputs 1 and 2, and a 15-by-15 grid. A one-input system returns column vectors X and Z and empty Y. With no outputs, creates an editable surface or line plot. Extra inputs use their range midpoints unless ReferenceInputs is specified.
Example: f=mamfis(NumInputs=2,NumOutputs=1); [X,Y,Z]=gensurf(f,gensurfOptions(NumGridPoints=5));
Differences from MATLAB: type-1 systems only; no axes-target argument.

## gensurfOptions
Create fuzzy surface generation options.
Syntax: options = gensurfOptions(Name=Value)
InputIndex selects one or two distinct inputs (default [1 2]). OutputIndex defaults to 1. NumGridPoints defaults to 15 and can contain one or two counts. ReferenceInputs defaults to 'auto'; numeric vectors must provide a finite value for each unused input. NumSamplePoints defaults to 101.
Example: options=gensurfOptions(InputIndex=[1 3],OutputIndex=2,NumGridPoints=[5 7],ReferenceInputs=[NaN .3 NaN]);
Differences from MATLAB: grid counts and output sample counts are limited to 65536 and the workspace memory budget.

## plotmf
Plot the membership functions of a fuzzy input or output variable.
Syntax: [x,mf] = plotmf(fis,'input',index,numPoints)
The type is 'input' or 'output'; numPoints defaults to 181. Data outputs are numPoints-by-numMFs matrices. With no outputs, creates editable lines and MF text labels, with variable name on the x axis and Degree of membership on the y axis.
Example: f=mamfis(NumInputs=1,NumOutputs=1); [x,m]=plotmf(f,'input',1); assert(isequal(size(m),[181 3]));
Differences from MATLAB: type-1 only; Sugeno output MFs cannot be plotted. No axes-target argument.

## plotfis
Display a block diagram of a fuzzy inference system.
Syntax: plotfis(fis)
Creates ordinary editable rectangles, lines and text for the system, its inputs and outputs. Labels show names, membership function counts, system type and rule count.
Example: f=mamfis(NumInputs=2,NumOutputs=1); plotfis(f);
Differences from MATLAB: uses a simple block diagram in one axes; FIS trees and display name-value options are unsupported.

## fuzzyLogicDesigner
Build and inspect a type-1 fuzzy inference system in the desktop.
Syntax: fuzzyLogicDesigner; fuzzyLogicDesigner(fis); fuzzyLogicDesigner('file.fis')
Open a new Mamdani system, an existing scalar mamfis or sugfis, or a FIS file. Edit variables, membership functions and rules; inspect memberships, inference, surfaces and the system diagram. Export the accepted FIS to the workspace, save a FIS file, or generate a script that rebuilds it.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the desktop. Supports the engine's built-in type-1 membership and inference methods; custom functions and type-2 systems are rejected. Surface grids use 2 to 201 points per axis; scripts are limited to 900 KiB. Stop cancels background work and retains the last good views. The command-line engine reports "fuzzyLogicDesigner requires the desktop".

## appdesigner
Build, edit, save and run graphical MATLAB apps in the desktop.
Syntax: appdesigner; appdesigner('MyApp.m'); appdesigner('MyApp.mlapp')
Open App Designer with a new app named app1, or open an existing app file. Files saved by MatRust App Designer open for editing in Design View and Code View; hand-written classdef .m files and simple-layout .mlapp files open read-only as code. Place UI components from the palette into uigridlayout cells, inspect and edit properties, add and edit callbacks in Code View, save as a plain classdef .m file (< matlab.apps.AppBase), and run the app as a live uifigure window.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the desktop; the command-line engine reports "appdesigner requires the desktop". Saves plain classdef .m files only and opens .mlapp files read-only. GUIDE .fig files, uihtml, App Testing Framework (matlab.uitest), web apps, compiler deployment, Live Editor tasks and custom UI component authoring (ComponentContainer) are not supported.

## int2bit
Convert integers to column-wise bits.
Syntax: y = int2bit(x,n,msbfirst)
Default MSB first; false selects LSB first. Stacks n low bits per value down each column, preserving other dimensions. Signed inputs use two's complement. Floating input retains class (n <= 53 double, 24 single); signed integers produce int8, unsigned integers uint8 (n <= 64).
Example: int2bit([12 5],4)
Differences from MATLAB: logical input is rejected, as in the public input type list. Arrays use engine memory limits.

## bit2int
Convert column-wise groups of bits to integers.
Syntax: y = bit2int(x,n,msbfirst,IsSigned=false)
The number of rows must be a multiple of n. Default MSB first. IsSigned interprets the high bit as two's complement. Double/logical inputs produce double; single produces single; integer output widens as required.
Example: bit2int([1;0;1;0],4)
Differences from MATLAB: conversion is limited to 53 bits for double, 24 for single, 64 for integer inputs; unrepresentable signed integer output errors.

## de2bi
Convert decimal integers to rows of base-p digits.
Syntax: b = de2bi(d,n,p,flg)
Defaults: minimum digit count, base 2, 'right-msb'. Specify [] to infer n, or 'left-msb' for descending significance. Input is flattened column-wise; output has one row per input element. Too few columns is an error.
Example: de2bi([2 5 7],3,2,'left-msb')
Differences from MATLAB: base is limited to 2..65536, digit count to 4096; integer outputs are double.

## bi2de
Convert rows of base-p digits to decimal integers.
Syntax: d = bi2de(b,p,flg)
Defaults: base 2, 'right-msb'. Supports 'left-msb'. Each input row becomes one output integer; every digit must be a nonnegative integer less than p.
Example: bi2de([1 0 1;1 1 0],2,'left-msb')
Differences from MATLAB: results above flintmax are rejected; integer inputs produce double.

## pskmod
Modulate symbols using phase shift keying.
Syntax: y = pskmod(x,M,phaseoffset,symorder,InputType='integer')
Default phase 0 and Gray order. 'bin' and custom permutations label points counterclockwise starting at phaseoffset. InputType='bit' groups log2(M) rows MSB first. PlotConstellation=true draws points and integer labels.
Example: pskmod((0:7)',8,pi/8,'gray')
Differences from MATLAB: M <= 65536. Gray/bit modes require powers of two; binary/custom integer mode supports other M. Complex single storage is unavailable; single inputs require OutputDataType='double'.

## pskdemod
Demodulate phase shift keyed symbols.
Syntax: z = pskdemod(y,M,phaseoffset,symorder,OutputType='integer',NoiseVariance=1)
Same constellation ordering as pskmod. OutputType supports integer, bit, llr and approxllr. Exact LLR uses LogSumExp; approxllr uses max-log distances. Bit/LLR output stacks log2(M) rows per symbol, MSB first. NoiseVariance is a positive scalar or vector matching the last input dimension. OutputDataType supports double/single and 8/16/32-bit integer classes; bit output also supports logical. Soft output retains input floating class.
Example: pskdemod(pskmod((0:3)',4),4,OutputType='bit')
Differences from MATLAB: complex input is double; distance work is bounded. PlotConstellation uses ordinary plot/text objects.

## qammod
Modulate symbols using quadrature amplitude modulation.
Syntax: y = qammod(x,M,symOrder,UnitAveragePower=false,InputType='integer')
Default Gray order. Binary/custom order is supported. Square QAM for even log2(M), rectangular 2/8-QAM, cross QAM for odd log2(M)>3. Minimum distance is 2 unless UnitAveragePower=true. InputType='bit' groups log2(M) rows MSB first. PlotConstellation=true draws labeled points.
Example: qammod((0:15)',16,UnitAveragePower=true)
Differences from MATLAB: M is a power of two <= 65536. OutputDataType='single' is rejected because engine complex storage is double; single input can specify OutputDataType='double'. Fixed-point objects are unsupported.

## qamdemod
Demodulate QAM symbols using hard or soft decisions.
Syntax: z = qamdemod(y,M,symOrder,UnitAveragePower=false,OutputType='integer',NoiseVariance=1)
Uses qammod constellations. OutputType supports integer, bit, llr (LogSumExp) and approxllr (max-log). Bit/LLR output expands the first dimension by log2(M). NoiseVariance is a positive scalar or vector matching the last input dimension. Hard output supports OutputDataType double/single and 8/16/32-bit integers, plus logical for bits. Soft output retains input floating class; its OutputDataType option is ignored.
Example: qamdemod(qammod((0:15)',16),16)
Differences from MATLAB: fixed-point and complex single storage are unavailable. Soft/general decisions are bounded to 200 million distance operations per call. PlotConstellation uses plot/text.

## pammod
Modulate symbols using pulse amplitude modulation.
Syntax: y = pammod(x,M,initphase,symorder)
Default phase 0 and binary order. Gray order is available. Levels range from -(M-1) to M-1 with minimum distance 2, rotated by initphase. [] selects the default phase.
Example: pammod(0:3,4,pi/4,'gray')
Differences from MATLAB: M is a power of two <= 65536; complex single output is unavailable.

## pamdemod
Demodulate pulse amplitude modulation.
Syntax: z = pamdemod(y,M,initphase,symorder)
Default phase 0 and binary order. Projects onto the rotated amplitude axis and returns the nearest symbol. Gray order is available.
Example: pamdemod(pammod(0:3,4,pi/4,'gray'),4,pi/4,'gray')
Differences from MATLAB: modulation order is bounded to 65536.

## genqammod
Modulate using an arbitrary constellation.
Syntax: y = genqammod(x,const,InputType='integer')
Symbol 0 selects the first constellation element. Output has the input shape. Bit input groups log2(length(const)) rows MSB first and requires a power of two constellation size.
Example: genqammod([0 1 2],[-1 1 1i])
Differences from MATLAB: constellation size is 2..65536; complex single output is unavailable.

## genqamdemod
Demodulate using an arbitrary constellation.
Syntax: z = genqamdemod(y,const,OutputType='integer',NoiseVariance=1)
Returns zero-based indices of minimum-distance constellation points. Bit, exact llr and approxllr output require a power of two constellation size and stack MSB-first rows. Exact soft decisions use LogSumExp.
Example: genqamdemod([-0.9 0.8 0.9i],[-1 1 1i])
Differences from MATLAB: 2..65536 points and at most 200 million distance operations per call; complex single storage is unavailable.

## awgn
Add white Gaussian noise using the session random stream.
Syntax: [y,variance] = awgn(x,snr,signalpower,seed,powertype)
Default signal power is 0 dBW, powertype 'db'. 'measured' uses mean(abs(x(:)).^2) across all channels. 'linear' means SNR ratio and signal power in watts. Optional integer seed creates an independent temporary stream and leaves rng state unchanged. Real input gets real noise; complex input gets circular complex noise of the specified total variance. Output preserves input dimensions.
Example: rng(5); [y,v]=awgn(ones(8,1),10,'measured'); v
Differences from MATLAB: no built-in RandStream exists; numeric seeds only. SNR must be scalar. Normal draws follow the existing session generator, which does not promise bit identity with MATLAB randn.

## wgn
Generate white Gaussian noise samples in volts.
Syntax: y = wgn(m,n,power,imp,seed,powertype,outputtype)
Defaults: impedance 1 ohm, dBW power, real output. Power types: 'dBW', 'dBm', 'linear'; output types: 'real', 'complex'. Complex noise splits power equally between real and imaginary components. Optional integer seed uses an independent temporary stream; otherwise draws from rng.
Example: rng(5); y=wgn(4,2,0,1,45,'dBW','complex')
Differences from MATLAB: numeric seeds only; no built-in RandStream object. Normal draws follow the existing session generator.

## biterr
Count differing bits and compute bit error ratios.
Syntax: [number,ratio,individual] = biterr(x,y,k,flg)
Nonnegative integer inputs. Default k is the width of the largest value (at least 1). Same-size arrays default to overall comparison. Matrix/row-vector inputs default to row-wise comparison; matrix/column-vector inputs default to column-wise. Explicit 'overall', 'row-wise', 'column-wise' follow the public comparison table. individual contains per-pair bit counts with the larger input shape. Ratios divide each count by the bits compared for that count: k times the full expanded size for overall, k times the column count for row-wise, and k times the row count for column-wise. [] selects the default k.
Example: [n,r,i]=biterr([1 2;3 4],[1 3;0 4],3)
Differences from MATLAB: at most 64 bits per integer; empty input is rejected.

## symerr
Count differing symbols and compute symbol error ratios.
Syntax: [number,ratio,individual] = symerr(x,y,flg)
Same-size arrays default to overall comparison. Matrix/row or column vectors compare each row or column. Flags: 'overall', 'row-wise', 'column-wise'. Ratios divide each count by its comparison size; overall broadcasting divides by the full expanded size, matching the public worked example (3/4). Row-wise and column-wise divide by the column and row counts respectively. individual is logical with the larger input shape.
Example: [n,r,i]=symerr([1 2;3 4],[1 3],'overall')
Differences from MATLAB: empty input is rejected. Real and complex numeric symbols are accepted.

## berawgn
Compute analytical BER and SER for uncoded AWGN channels.
Syntax: [ber,ser] = berawgn(EbNo,modtype,modulationArguments)
EbNo is in dB. Families: 'psk',M,'diff'|'nondiff'; 'oqpsk','diff'|'nondiff'; 'dpsk',M; 'fsk',M,'coherent'|'noncoherent'; 'msk','on'|'off','coherent'|'noncoherent'; 'pam',M; 'qam',M. PSK defaults to nondiff; MSK defaults to coherent. Implements the public analytical expressions with Gray labeling, exact PAM/QAM bit sums, integrated PSK/DPSK probabilities, orthogonal FSK and differential BPSK/QPSK. Odd-order QAM theory uses the documented rectangular constellation, even though qammod uses cross QAM for M>8. Noncoherent MSK returns the documented optimum-block upper bound (an approximation to error performance); it is independent of precoding. Other implemented families use exact expressions with numerical quadrature rather than SER/log2(M) approximations.
Example: [ber,ser]=berawgn(0:2:12,'qam',16)
Differences from MATLAB: M <= 1024, noncoherent FSK M <= 64; integration work and vector size are bounded. Nonorthogonal FSK rho and CPFSK are not supported. Uses direct formula evaluation and adaptive numerical quadrature.

## qfunc
Evaluate the Gaussian upper-tail Q function.
Syntax: y = qfunc(x)
Elementwise 0.5*erfc(x/sqrt(2)), retaining input shape and floating precision.
Example: qfunc([0 1 2])
Differences from MATLAB: real numeric input only; uses the existing libm erfc kernel.

## qfuncinv
Evaluate the inverse Gaussian upper-tail Q function.
Syntax: x = qfuncinv(y)
Elementwise sqrt(2)*erfcinv(2*y), for probabilities in [0,1]. Endpoints return +Inf and -Inf; NaN propagates. Retains input shape and floating precision.
Example: qfuncinv(qfunc([0 1 2]))
Differences from MATLAB: uses the existing erfcinv kernel; out-of-range probabilities produce an error.

## rcosdesign
Design a unit-energy raised-cosine pulse-shaping FIR filter.
Syntax: b = rcosdesign(beta,span,sps,shape)
beta is in [0,1]; span and sps are positive integers with even span*sps. The row output has span*sps+1 taps. shape is 'sqrt' (default) or 'normal'; analytic limits handle zero rolloff and singular points.
Example: b=rcosdesign(.25,6,4); assert(abs(sum(b.^2)-1)<1e-14);
Differences from MATLAB: Finite filters are limited to 8388608 samples and the workspace memory budget.

## fskmod
Modulate integer symbols using frequency-shift keying.
Syntax: y = fskmod(x,M,freqsep,nsamp,Fs,phasecont,symorder)
M is a power of two, x contains integers 0 through M-1, and columns are independent channels. nsamp is an integer greater than 1. Fs defaults to 1; (M-1)*freqsep must not exceed Fs. phasecont is 'cont' (default) or 'discont'; symorder is 'bin' (default) or 'gray'. Vectors retain their orientation.
Example: x=[0 1 3 2]; y=fskmod(x,4,1,8,8); assert(isequal(fskdemod(y,4,1,8,8),x));
Differences from MATLAB: Output is limited to 8388608 samples. Modulation orders are limited to 65536. Work is cancellable and bounded.

## fskdemod
Demodulate FSK signals using noncoherent correlation.
Syntax: z = fskdemod(y,M,freqsep,nsamp,Fs,symorder)
Fs defaults to 1. symorder is 'bin' (default) or 'gray'. Input length per channel must be a multiple of nsamp. Each output is the symbol whose tone has the largest squared correlation magnitude; columns are independent channels.
Example: z=fskdemod(fskmod([0 1 2 3],4,1,16,16),4,1,16,16); assert(isequal(z,[0 1 2 3]));
Differences from MATLAB: Correlation work is capped at 100000000 sample-tone products as well as the evaluation and memory budgets.

## dpskmod
Differentially modulate integer phase symbols.
Syntax: y = dpskmod(x,M,phaserot,symorder)
M is a power of two. phaserot defaults to 0 and [] selects the default. symorder is 'bin' (default) or 'gray'. Each column starts with reference phase zero, then accumulates the symbol phase increment and phaserot. Vector orientation is preserved.
Example: x=[0 1 3 2]; y=dpskmod(x,4,pi/4,'gray'); assert(isequal(dpskdemod(y,4,pi/4,'gray'),x));
Differences from MATLAB: Orders are limited to 65536 and work obeys evaluation and memory budgets.

## dpskdemod
Recover differentially encoded phase symbols.
Syntax: z = dpskdemod(y,M,phaserot,symorder)
Defaults and shapes match dpskmod. The first reference is 1+0i; an unknown channel phase can corrupt the first recovered symbol, which should then be discarded. Later symbols use successive-sample phase differences.
Example: z=dpskdemod(dpskmod([0 1 2 3],4),4); assert(isequal(z,[0 1 2 3]));
Differences from MATLAB: Orders are limited to 65536 and finite numeric input is required.

## mskmod
Generate minimum-shift-keyed baseband samples.
Syntax: [y,phaseout] = mskmod(x,nsamp,dataenc,initphase)
Binary x is a vector or a matrix of independent channels. nsamp is a positive integer. dataenc is 'diff' (default) or 'nondiff'; [] selects defaults. Initial phases are integer multiples of pi/2, one per channel. Output is a column vector or a matrix with nsamp samples per input bit. phaseout permits block continuation.
Example: b=[0;1;1;0]; [y,p]=mskmod(b,8); assert(isequal(mskdemod(y,8),b));
Differences from MATLAB: Uses CPFSK with h=1/2 for diff and staggered half-sine I/Q precoding for nondiff. Output is limited to 8388608 samples.

## mskdemod
Demodulate MSK samples and retain streaming state.
Syntax: [z,phaseout,stateout] = mskdemod(y,nsamp,dataenc,initphase,initstate)
Arguments match mskmod. Input rows per channel must be a multiple of nsamp. initstate is nsamp-by-channels containing the preceding received symbol; stateout returns the final received symbol. Pass phaseout and stateout into the next block. Output bits are columns.
Example: b=[0;1;1;0]; [z,p,s]=mskdemod(mskmod(b,8),8); assert(isequal(z,b));
Differences from MATLAB: Uses a two-template symbol correlator referenced to the preceding symbol boundary; exact noisy decisions can differ from other receiver implementations.

## ofdmmod
Modulate already-mapped complex subcarriers using OFDM.
Syntax: y = ofdmmod(x,nfft,cplen,nullidx,pilotidx,pilots, OversamplingFactor=value)
x is data-subcarriers by symbols by streams, optionally by batches. nfft is an integer at least 8. Centered one-based null and pilot indices must be unique and disjoint; DC is floor(nfft/2)+1. Pilots have pilot-subcarriers by symbols by streams by batches shape. cplen is a nonnegative integer scalar <=nfft or a row vector per symbol (vector entries can exceed nfft). OversamplingFactor defaults to 1 and its products with nfft and every cplen must be integers.
Example: x=reshape(1:16,8,2)+1i; y=ofdmmod(x,8,2); z=ofdmdemod(y,8,2); assert(max(abs(z(:)-x(:)))<1e-12);
Differences from MATLAB: Oversampling factors below 1 and dlarray/gpuArray are unsupported. FFTs are capped at 1048576 points; output and scratch obey memory and work limits.

## ofdmdemod
Recover data and pilots from OFDM samples.
Syntax: [x,pilots] = ofdmdemod(y,nfft,cplen,symOffset,nullidx,pilotidx, OversamplingFactor=value)
y is time samples by streams, optionally by batches. symOffset defaults to cplen; [] selects the default. A scalar or per-symbol row vector must lie in [0,cplen] and produce integer oversampled offsets. Phase correction recovers the same subcarriers for every valid FFT-window offset. Output data and pilots retain symbols, streams and batches dimensions.
Example: x=reshape(1:12,6,2)+1i; y=ofdmmod(x,8,[2 4],[1;5]); z=ofdmdemod(y,8,[2 4],0,[1;5]); assert(max(abs(z(:)-x(:)))<1e-12);
Differences from MATLAB: Same FFT, oversampling, sample and memory bounds as ofdmmod.

## scatterplot
Display signal samples in the in-phase/quadrature plane.
Syntax: h = scatterplot(x,n,offset,plotstring,h)
n defaults to 1, offset to 0, and plotstring to 'b.'. Plots samples offset+1, offset+1+n and so on. Complex vectors supply I/Q components; a real two-column matrix supplies I and Q columns; real vectors use Q=0. Without a target creates a new figure; an existing figure target respects hold. The return value is the figure handle.
Example: f=scatterplot([1+1i -1+1i -1-1i 1-1i]);
Differences from MATLAB: Creates ordinary editable line objects with markers; no separate communications graphics object.

## eyediagram
Overlay signal traces in an eye diagram.
Syntax: h = eyediagram(x,n,period,offset,plotstring,h)
n>1 is the samples per trace (usually twice the samples per symbol). period defaults to 1, offset to 0 in [0,n-1], and plotstring to 'b-'. Traces are centered on samples offset+1+k*n with horizontal limits +/-period/2. Complex vectors or real two-column I/Q data create two axes; real vectors create one. Partial edge traces use NaN padding; neighboring even-length traces share their boundary sample.
Example: f=eyediagram(mskmod([0;1;1;0;1;0],8),16);
Differences from MATLAB: Uses ordinary editable lines and axes. Odd n uses symmetric sample positions inside the period.

## berfit
Fit smooth closed-form curves to empirical BER measurements.
Syntax: [fitber,fitprops] = berfit(empEbNo,empBER,fitEbNo,options,fittype)
Empirical vectors have at least four samples; EbNo is strictly ascending in dB and BER is in (0,1]. fitEbNo defaults to empEbNo and must have at least as many points. fittype is 'exp', 'exp+const', 'polyRatio' or 'doubleExp+const'; omission chooses the valid fit with smallest squared log-BER error. options is [] or a scalar struct with Display, MaxFunEvals, MaxIter, TolFun and TolX (also optimset canonical aliases). Fits use linear EbNo internally. fitprops includes fitType, coeffs, sumSqErr, exitState, funcCount and iterations. Without outputs, plots empirical and fitted BER on semilogy; fittype 'all' plots every valid fit.
Example: x=0:.25:2; y=.5*erfc(sqrt(10.^(x/10))); z=berfit(x,y); assert(max(abs(z./y-1))<1e-3);
Differences from MATLAB: Uses bounded local Nelder-Mead with scaled coefficients and independent starting estimates, so selected fits and coefficients can differ from MATLAB. Zero BER observations and unsupported optimizer fields are rejected. Empirical data are limited to 65536 points; invalid/nonmonotone fits return [].

## bertool
Compare theoretical and simulated bit error rates in the desktop.
Syntax: bertool; bertool()
Keep, rename, show and export seeded BER datasets. Theory uses berawgn; Monte Carlo uses engine modems, awgn and biterr. Stop preserves completed points. Generate script rebuilds the selected datasets.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the desktop; no Simulink or user simulation functions. Eb/N0 has at most 128 increasing values in -30 to 60 dB; simulations have at most 2000000 bits per point and 32 kept datasets. The headless engine reports "bertool requires the desktop".

## econometricModeler
Open the desktop app for series preparation and econometric diagnostics.
Syntax: econometricModeler
Load workspace vectors, matrix columns or numeric table/timetable variables; retain transformed series and ADF, KPSS, PP, Ljung-Box and ARCH tests. ACF and PACF views use the engine's correlogram functions. Export writes a results struct; generated scripts reproduce the retained transforms, options and results from the source variables.
The desktop host must install the app launch hook. No inputs or outputs are accepted.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the MatRust desktop; model fitting and forecasting are not available yet.

## wirelessWaveformGenerator
Generate and inspect reproducible wireless waveforms in the desktop.
Syntax: wirelessWaveformGenerator; wirelessWaveformGenerator()
Configure PSK, QAM, PAM, FSK, MSK or custom OFDM, pulse shaping, sample rate and impairments. Export a complex waveform and its settings, or save the script that reproduces them and their plots. Workspace bit inputs are captured for reproducibility.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the desktop; no radio hardware or standards-specific waveform generators. Waveforms are bounded to 1048576 samples; OFDM FFT sizes are powers of two from 8 to 256, pilots have unit amplitude, and workspace bit sources have at most 131072 bits. The headless engine reports "wirelessWaveformGenerator requires the desktop".

## autocorr
Sample autocorrelation of a univariate time series.
Syntax: [acf,lags,bounds,h] = autocorr(y,NumLags=L,NumMA=q,NumSTD=s)
Defaults: L=min(20,T-1), q=0, s=2. Biased sample ACF; bounds are [upper;lower] using Bartlett's MA(q) formula. NaNs retain time positions and each lag averages available pairs. With no outputs or four outputs, draws a stem plot and confidence bounds. Historical positional (y,L,q,s) syntax is accepted.
Example: [a,l,b]=autocorr([1 3 2 5 4 7 6 2],NumLags=3)
Differences from MATLAB: numeric vectors only; table/timetable inputs, explicit axes input are unsupported. At most 1000000 observations, 2048 lags and 100000000 work units. Uses direct sums for short bounded lag sequences.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/autocorr.html

## parcorr
Sample partial autocorrelation of a univariate time series.
Syntax: [pacf,lags,bounds,h] = parcorr(y,NumLags=L,NumAR=p,NumSTD=s,Method='ols')
Defaults: L=min(20,T-1), p=0, s=2. Method is 'ols' for complete data and 'yule-walker' with missing data. OLS fits successive AR models with an intercept; Yule-Walker uses sample autocorrelations. Bounds are [s/sqrt(T);-s/sqrt(T)] beyond NumAR. NaNs retain time positions; explicit OLS rejects NaNs. No outputs or four outputs draws stems and bounds. Historical positional (y,L,p,s) is accepted.
Example: [p,l,b]=parcorr([1 3 2 5 4 7 6 2],NumLags=2,Method='yule-walker')
Differences from MATLAB: numeric vectors only; table/timetable and explicit axes input unsupported. Rank-deficient or underdetermined OLS fits are rejected. At most 2048 lags, 2000000 design elements and 100000000 work units.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/parcorr.html

## crosscorr
Sample cross-correlation between two univariate time series.
Syntax: [xcf,lags,bounds,h] = crosscorr(y1,y2,NumLags=L,NumSTD=s)
Defaults: L=min(20,min(T1,T2)-1), s=2. Positive k correlates y1(t) with y2(t+k). Each series is centered before zero padding the shorter sequence; missing cross products are omitted. Output orientation follows y1; bounds are [s/sqrt(min(T1,T2));-s/sqrt(min(T1,T2))]. No outputs or four outputs draws stems and bounds. Historical positional (y1,y2,L,s) is accepted.
Example: [x,l,b]=crosscorr([1 3 2 5 4 7],[2 1 4 3 6 5],NumLags=2)
Differences from MATLAB: numeric vectors only; tables/timetables and explicit axes unsupported. Uses bounded direct sums. Missing-pair normalization and unequal-length centering can differ from MATLAB releases.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/crosscorr.html

## lbqtest
Ljung-Box test for residual autocorrelation.
Syntax: [h,pValue,stat,cValue] = lbqtest(res,Lags=L,Alpha=a,DoF=d)
Defaults: L=min(20,T-1), a=.05, d=L. Computes T*(T+2)*sum(acf(1:L).^2./(T-(1:L))) and a chi-square right-tail probability. Lags, Alpha and DoF can be equal-length vectors; scalars expand, and any row vector produces row outputs. DoF is positive and no larger than Lags. NaNs retain their time positions as in autocorr.
Example: [h,p,s,c]=lbqtest([1 -2 3 -1 2 -3 1 2],Lags=[1 2],DoF=[1 1])
Differences from MATLAB: numeric vectors only; tables/timetables unsupported. Bounded to 2048 lags and 1024 tests.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/lbqtest.html

## archtest
Engle LM test for residual conditional heteroscedasticity.
Syntax: [h,pValue,stat,cValue] = archtest(res,Lags=L,Alpha=a)
Defaults: L=1 and a=.05. Regresses squared residuals on an intercept and L lagged squares; stat=(T-L)*R^2, with a chi-square distribution on L degrees of freedom. Equal-length vector options perform separate tests; scalars expand and any row vector yields row outputs. Missing observations are rejected.
Example: [h,p,s,c]=archtest([1 -2 3 -1 2 -3 1 2 4 -2 1 -3],Lags=2)
Differences from MATLAB: numeric vectors only; tables/timetables unsupported. Singular or underdetermined regressions are rejected. At most 2048 lags, 1024 tests and 2000000 design elements.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/archtest.html

## adftest
Augmented Dickey-Fuller unit-root test.
Syntax: [h,pValue,stat,cValue,reg] = adftest(y,Model='AR',Lags=0,Test='t1',Alpha=.05)
Models: AR has no deterministic terms; ARD adds an intercept; TS adds intercept and trend. Lags counts lagged differences. Test t1 is the studentized phi-1, t2 is T*(phi-1)/(1-sum(b)), and F tests joint restrictions (phi=1,c=0) for ARD or (phi=1,trend=0) for TS. AR has no F test. NaNs are removed before lagging. Vector Lags, Alpha, Model and Test expand scalars and must otherwise match in length. reg contains coefficient, covariance, residual, fitted-value and fit statistics.
Example: [h,p,s,c,r]=adftest([1 3 2 5 4 7 6 2 3 1 5 2],Model='ARD',Lags=1)
Differences from MATLAB: t1/t2 use published MacKinnon (1996) finite-sample response surfaces with linear quantile interpolation; p-values clamp to [.001,.999] with warnings. These differ from MATLAB's private simulation tables. F uses Dickey-Fuller (1981) phi1/phi3 tables, interpolated in 1/T and probability; its published range is [.01,.99], also the supported F Alpha and p-value range. Samples below 20 (F:25) use the minimum table size with a warning. Numeric vectors only; tables/timetables unsupported. Bounds: 2048 lags, 1024 tests, 2000000 design elements and 100000000 work units. reg.names is a string vector.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/adftest.html

## pptest
Phillips-Perron unit-root test with Bartlett long-run variance correction.
Syntax: [h,pValue,stat,cValue,reg] = pptest(y,Model='AR',Lags=0,Test='t1',Alpha=.05)
Models AR, ARD and TS match adftest. Lags controls the Newey-West covariance bandwidth; the regression always contains only one lagged level. Test t1 is the corrected tau statistic; t2 is the corrected rho statistic. Missing observations are removed. Vector options expand as in adftest. reg additionally contains residual autoCov and the scalar long-run variance NWEst.
Example: [h,p,s,c,r]=pptest([1 3 2 5 4 7 6 2 3 1 5 2],Model='ARD',Lags=2)
Differences from MATLAB: numeric vectors only; tables/timetables unsupported. Published MacKinnon (1996) tau/rho response surfaces and linear quantile interpolation differ from MATLAB simulation tables. P-values clamp to [.001,.999] with warnings; fewer than 20 regression observations use the T=20 surface with a warning. Same limits as adftest; reg.names is a string vector.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/pptest.html

## kpsstest
KPSS test of level or trend stationarity against a unit root.
Syntax: [h,pValue,stat,cValue,reg] = kpsstest(y,Lags=0,Trend=true,Alpha=.05)
Regresses y on an intercept and, by default, a trend. The statistic is the sum of squared cumulative residuals divided by T^2 times the Bartlett Newey-West long-run variance. NaNs are removed. Vector Lags, Trend and Alpha expand scalars and must otherwise have equal lengths; any row option yields row outputs. Alpha is in [.01,.10]. Published Kwiatkowski et al. (1992) Table 1 critical values are interpolated linearly; p-values clamp to [.01,.10] with warnings. reg includes numeric regression statistics, autoCov and Bartlett HAC coefficient standard errors NWEst.
Example: [h,p,s,c,r]=kpsstest([1 3 2 5 4 7 6 2 3 1 5 2],Trend=false,Lags=1)
Differences from MATLAB: numeric vectors only; tables/timetables unsupported. Same resource bounds as adftest. reg.names is a string vector.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/kpsstest.html

## lagmatrix
Create lagged and led columns of time series data.
Syntax: [YLag,TLag] = lagmatrix(Y,lags)
Each row of Y is an observation and each column a series. Positive shifts are lags; negative shifts are leads. Output columns contain all input series shifted by lags(1), followed by all series shifted by lags(2), and so on. Unknown values are NaN. TLag is the original column time base (1:size(Y,1))'.
Example: [Y,t]=lagmatrix([1 -1;2 -2;3 -3],[1 0 -1])
Differences from MATLAB: numeric 2-D inputs and default Shape='same' only; table/timetable, Y0, YF, Shape and DataVariables options are explicitly unsupported. At most 2048 shifts and 2000000 output elements.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/lagmatrix.html

## arima
Create a scalar-variance ARIMA or ARIMAX model.
Syntax: arima(p,D,q) or arima(Name=Value)
Example: m = arima(1,1,1); m.P
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric series only; lag degrees up to 256 per component and 128 active parameters. Conditional variance objects are not supported yet.

## estimate
Estimate NaN parameters of ARIMA, ARIMAX (regARIMA), and GARCH, EGARCH or GJR models by conditional maximum likelihood, including ARIMA with a conditional Variance model.
Syntax: [m,cov,logL,info] = estimate(m,y,Name=Value)
Example: m = arima(0,0,0); o = optimoptions(@fmincon,Algorithm="sqp",ConstraintTolerance=1e-7); f = estimate(m,[1;2;1;3;2;4],Options=o,Display="off"); f.Constant
Options accepts optimoptions(@fmincon,...) or a scalar struct. Algorithm="sqp" (default), "interior-point", "active-set", and the legacy "quasi-newton" name all run the same native dense SQP with OPG covariance. Supported controls include ConstraintTolerance (default 1e-7), OptimalityTolerance, StepTolerance, MaxIterations, MaxFunctionEvaluations and Display ("off", "none", "iter", "final"). Options.Display only controls optimizer iteration output; estimate's Display ("params" default, "full", "iter", "diagnostics", "off") controls the parameter report and diagnostics (Display="off" suppresses all output).
Constraints: positive innovation variance or GARCH/GJR constant; Student t DoF > 2; stationary nonseasonal/seasonal AR and invertible MA polynomials. GARCH/GJR coefficients are nonnegative and sum(GARCH)+sum(ARCH)+0.5*sum(Leverage) <= 1-ConstraintTolerance (the leverage term applies to GJR). GJR also requires ARCH+Leverage >= 0 at every lag. EGARCH requires a stable GARCH polynomial; its ARCH and leverage coefficients are unrestricted. Polynomial constraints use a scaled Schur test to bound companion-root moduli by 1-ConstraintTolerance (lag-operator roots lie outside the reciprocal radius). Known parameters stay fixed. User-given starting values (Constant0, AR0, SAR0, MA0, SMA0, Beta0, Variance0, DoF0, GARCH0, ARCH0, Leverage0, Offset0) override automatic starts and must be feasible (infeasible user starts error).
Differences from MATLAB: numeric series only; up to 128 active parameters and lag degrees up to 256 per ARIMA component (128 for volatility). The accepted algorithm names share one SQP implementation. Conditional likelihood uses the supplied presamples or the documented model-specific defaults; it is not an exact stationary Kalman likelihood. With X and no Y0, the first P responses are the presample, so the effective sample is P observations shorter.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/arima.estimate.html and https://www.mathworks.com/help/econ/garch.estimate.html

## infer
Infer conditional ARIMA innovations and constant innovation variances.
Syntax: [E,V,logL] = infer(m,y,Name=Value)
Example: m = arima(Constant=0,AR=0.5,Variance=1); infer(m,[1;2;3],Y0=0)
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric series only; lag degrees up to 256 per component and 128 active parameters. Conditional variance objects are not supported yet.

## forecast
Forecast responses and integrated psi-weight mean square errors.
Syntax: [Y,YMSE,V] = forecast(m,n,Y0,Name=Value)
Example: m = arima(Constant=0,AR=0.5,Variance=1); [y,mse] = forecast(m,3,2)
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric series only; lag degrees up to 256 per component and 128 active parameters. Conditional variance objects are not supported yet. An ARIMAX forecast infers E0 from Y0 only when X0 is given; otherwise E0 = 0.

## simulate
Simulate ARIMA responses using the session random stream.
Syntax: [Y,E,V] = simulate(m,n,Name=Value)
Example: rng(1); m = arima(Constant=0,Variance=1); simulate(m,3)
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric series only; lag degrees up to 256 per component and 128 active parameters. Conditional variance objects are not supported yet.

## summarize
Display or return ARIMA estimation results and parameter tables.
Syntax: results = summarize(m)
Example: m = arima(1,0,0); summarize(m)
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric series only; lag degrees up to 256 per component and 128 active parameters. Conditional variance objects are not supported yet.

## aicbic
Compute AIC, BIC and corrected, consistent and Hannan-Quinn criteria.
Syntax: [aic,bic,ic] = aicbic(logL,numParam,numObs,Normalize=false)
Example: [a,b,ic] = aicbic([-10 -12],[2 3],100); a
Differences from MATLAB: Numeric logL and parameter counts only; no table or timetable input.

## garch
Create a GARCH conditional variance model.
Syntax: m = garch(P,Q)
GARCH degree P refers to variance lags; Q refers to innovation lags. NaN parameters are estimated, known values stay fixed. Gaussian and standardized Student t innovations are supported.
Example: garch(1,1)
Differences from MATLAB: numeric arrays only; degree limited to 128 and estimated parameters to 128. MLE uses the shared native constrained SQP with OPG covariance (see estimate for algorithms and constraints). EGARCH forecasts exponentiate expected log variance and have the documented Jensen bias.

## egarch
Create an EGARCH log conditional variance model.
Syntax: m = egarch(P,Q)
GARCH degree P refers to variance lags; Q refers to innovation lags. NaN parameters are estimated, known values stay fixed. Gaussian and standardized Student t innovations are supported.
Example: egarch(1,1)
Differences from MATLAB: numeric arrays only; degree limited to 128 and estimated parameters to 128. MLE uses the shared native constrained SQP with OPG covariance (see estimate for algorithms and constraints). EGARCH forecasts exponentiate expected log variance and have the documented Jensen bias.

## gjr
Create a GJR asymmetric conditional variance model.
Syntax: m = gjr(P,Q)
GARCH degree P refers to variance lags; Q refers to innovation lags. NaN parameters are estimated, known values stay fixed. Gaussian and standardized Student t innovations are supported.
Example: gjr(1,1)
Differences from MATLAB: numeric arrays only; degree limited to 128 and estimated parameters to 128. MLE uses the shared native constrained SQP with OPG covariance (see estimate for algorithms and constraints). EGARCH forecasts exponentiate expected log variance and have the documented Jensen bias.

## estimate
Estimate unknown conditional variance parameters by maximum likelihood.
Syntax: [m,cov,logL,info] = estimate(m,y,Name=Value)
GARCH degree P refers to variance lags; Q refers to innovation lags. NaN parameters are estimated, known values stay fixed. Gaussian and standardized Student t innovations are supported.
Example: estimate(garch(),[1;-1;2;-2],Display='off')
Differences from MATLAB: numeric arrays only; degree limited to 128 and estimated parameters to 128. MLE uses the shared native constrained SQP with OPG covariance (see estimate for algorithms and constraints). EGARCH forecasts exponentiate expected log variance and have the documented Jensen bias.

## infer
Infer conditional variances and log likelihood.
Syntax: [v,logL] = infer(m,y,E0=e0,V0=v0)
GARCH degree P refers to variance lags; Q refers to innovation lags. NaN parameters are estimated, known values stay fixed. Gaussian and standardized Student t innovations are supported.
Example: infer(garch(Constant=0.1,GARCH=0.7,ARCH=0.2),[1;-1;2])
Differences from MATLAB: numeric arrays only; degree limited to 128 and estimated parameters to 128. MLE uses the shared native constrained SQP with OPG covariance (see estimate for algorithms and constraints). EGARCH forecasts exponentiate expected log variance and have the documented Jensen bias.

## forecast
Forecast conditional variances from a volatility model.
Syntax: v = forecast(m,numPeriods,Y0,V0=v0)
GARCH degree P refers to variance lags; Q refers to innovation lags. NaN parameters are estimated, known values stay fixed. Gaussian and standardized Student t innovations are supported.
Example: forecast(garch(Constant=0.1,GARCH=0.7,ARCH=0.2),3,[1;-1;2])
Differences from MATLAB: numeric arrays only; degree limited to 128 and estimated parameters to 128. MLE uses the shared native constrained SQP with OPG covariance (see estimate for algorithms and constraints). EGARCH forecasts exponentiate expected log variance and have the documented Jensen bias.

## simulate
Simulate conditional variances and responses.
Syntax: [v,y] = simulate(m,numObs,NumPaths=numPaths)
GARCH degree P refers to variance lags; Q refers to innovation lags. NaN parameters are estimated, known values stay fixed. Gaussian and standardized Student t innovations are supported.
Example: rng(1);simulate(garch(Constant=0.1,GARCH=0.7,ARCH=0.2),3)
Differences from MATLAB: numeric arrays only; degree limited to 128 and estimated parameters to 128. MLE uses the shared native constrained SQP with OPG covariance (see estimate for algorithms and constraints). EGARCH forecasts exponentiate expected log variance and have the documented Jensen bias.

## summarize
Display or return volatility model estimation results.
Syntax: results = summarize(m)
GARCH degree P refers to variance lags; Q refers to innovation lags. NaN parameters are estimated, known values stay fixed. Gaussian and standardized Student t innovations are supported.
Example: summarize(garch(1,1))
Differences from MATLAB: numeric arrays only; degree limited to 128 and estimated parameters to 128. MLE uses the shared native constrained SQP with OPG covariance (see estimate for algorithms and constraints). EGARCH forecasts exponentiate expected log variance and have the documented Jensen bias.

## getEstimator
Obtain the MPC Kalman gains and augmented observer model.
Syntax: [L,M,A,Cm,Bu,Bv,Dvm] = getEstimator(c)
L is the predictor gain and M the measurement-update gain. State order is plant, input disturbance, output disturbance, noise. Bv and Dvm include a final constant-one input for nominal DX. Unit white noise acts on MV, MD and disturbance/noise model inputs, including cross covariance.
Example: c=mpc(ss(0.8,0.2,1,0,0.1)); [L,M,A,Cm,Bu,Bv,Dvm]=getEstimator(c)
Differences from MATLAB: the 'sys' form is not supported yet. At most 128 augmented states, plant inputs/outputs, and inputs per stochastic model; discrete sample-time resampling is not supported yet. Custom estimation returns empty gains.

## setEstimator
Set MPC observer gains or choose default or custom state estimation.
Syntax: setEstimator(c,L,M) | setEstimator(c,'default') | setEstimator(c,'custom')
Empty L defaults to A*M; omitted or empty M defaults to zero. Custom mode suppresses Kalman design. Actual controller model, scaling or weight changes restore default estimation. Reassigning unchanged settings, bounds or names preserves supplied/custom estimation.
Example: c=mpc(ss(0.8,0.2,1,0,0.1)); setEstimator(c,[0.1;0.2],[0.3;0.4]); [L,M]=getEstimator(c)
Differences from MATLAB: controllers have value semantics. A statement updates its named controller argument; c=setEstimator(c,...) also returns the updated controller. Model dimensions and finite gains are validated; observer stability of supplied gains is the caller's responsibility.

## getoutdist
Retrieve the discrete MPC output disturbance model.
Syntax: [model,channels] = getoutdist(c)
Default integrators are tried on measured outputs by decreasing total absolute output weight, ties in plant output order, preserving observability. Each default integrator is Ts/(z-1), the ZOH discretization of 1/s. Channels without an integrator have zero gain. Returned channels are one-based plant output indices; custom models return empty channels.
Example: c=mpc(ss(0.8,0.2,1,0,0.1)); [model,channels]=getoutdist(c)
Differences from MATLAB: an absent disturbance model returns [] because zero-port ss objects are not supported yet; discrete sample-time resampling and delay models are not supported yet.

## setoutdist
Set or reset the MPC output disturbance model.
Syntax: setoutdist(c,'model',model) | setoutdist(c,'integrators')
A model has one output per plant output and independent unit white-noise inputs. Static numeric gains and LTI models are accepted. [] or an omitted model restores the default integrators.
Example: c=mpc(ss(0.8,0.2,1,0,0.1)); setoutdist(c,'model',2); getoutdist(c)
Differences from MATLAB: value semantics; the statement updates its named controller argument. Discrete sample-time resampling is not supported yet. Observability is checked on estimator initialization.

## getindist
Retrieve the discrete MPC input disturbance model.
Syntax: [model,channels] = getindist(c)
Default integrators are added to unmeasured input disturbance channels before output integrators, preserving observability. Each default integrator is Ts/(z-1). Other UD channels use static unity gain. Channels are one-based indices within the UD vector; custom models return empty channels.
Example: p=ss(0.8,[0.2 0.4],1,[0 0],0.1); p=setmpcsignals(p,'MV',1,'UD',2); c=mpc(p); [model,channels]=getindist(c)
Differences from MATLAB: an absent disturbance model returns [] because zero-port ss objects are not supported yet; discrete sample-time resampling is not supported yet.

## setindist
Set or reset the MPC input disturbance model.
Syntax: setindist(c,'model',model) | setindist(c,'integrators')
A model has one output per UD and independent unit white-noise inputs. Static numeric gains and LTI models are accepted. [] or an omitted model restores default integrators.
Example: p=ss(0.8,[0.2 0.4],1,[0 0],0.1); p=setmpcsignals(p,'MV',1,'UD',2); c=mpc(p); setindist(c,'model',0.5); getindist(c)
Differences from MATLAB: value semantics; the statement updates its named controller argument. Discrete sample-time resampling is not supported yet.

## mpcstate
Create an MPC controller state handle with validated properties.
Syntax: s = mpcstate(c[,plant,disturbance,noise,lastMove,covariance])
Plant defaults to nominal X and LastMove to nominal MV values, in absolute engineering units. Disturbance (input then output) and Noise states start at zero. Covariance defaults to the steady-state a-priori covariance, or [] in custom mode. Optional [] arguments retain defaults. Copies of a state handle share property updates.
Example: c=mpc(ss(0.8,0.2,1,0,0.1)); s=mpcstate(c); s.Plant=2; s.LastMove=0.1; disp(s)
Differences from MATLAB: assign complete property vectors; indexed property edits are not supported yet. Covariance must have the total state dimension and be symmetric. Controllers use value semantics, state objects use handle semantics.

## setmpcsignals
Set MPC signal types on an LTI plant model.
Syntax: plant = setmpcsignals(plant,'MV',mv,'MD',md,'UD',ud,'MO',mo,'UO',uo)
Unspecified inputs default to MV and unspecified outputs to MO. Indices are one-based vectors without overlap. Full names ManipulatedVariables, MeasuredDisturbances, UnmeasuredDisturbances, MeasuredOutputs and UnmeasuredOutputs are also accepted.
Example: p=ss(0.8,[0.2 0.4],1,[0 0],0.1); p=setmpcsignals(p,'MV',1,'MD',2); c=mpc(p)
Differences from MATLAB: at most 128 plant inputs and outputs. Configure signal types before constructing the controller; later model transformations can discard MPC signal metadata.

## mpcDesigner
Open the native MPC Designer to tune and compare linear controllers.
Syntax: mpcDesigner; mpcDesigner(plant); mpcDesigner(mpcobj)
Choose a workspace ss, tf, zpk or mpc variable. Create, duplicate and rename controllers; edit physical signal roles, sample time, horizons, weights and MV/OV constraints, then Apply controller. Run scenario uses accepted controllers. Invalid edits, errors and cancellation retain the last completed results.
Scenarios support 1..10000 stored samples (default 30), finite literal reference and measured-disturbance rows or time-row matrices, optional plant initial state, and reference/MD lookahead. Physical reference columns include all outputs; disturbance columns follow physical MD order. Short signals hold their final row. Empty reference/MD inputs resolve from the selected controller nominal signals and are shared by both alternatives; empty plant state uses each plant nominal X. Duration is (samples-1)*Ts; returned time, physical outputs and MV channels come from sim. Unmeasured outputs are labeled and are not measured feedback.
Compare one other accepted controller with identical physical channel roles/counts and Ts; no resampling. Runs use fresh independent controller state. Outputs and Manipulated variables show one selected channel, controller identities with solid/dashed curves, neutral reference and finite scalar bounds; Data shows numeric time and both alternatives. Horizon-varying bounds remain controller settings, not simulation-time overlays.
Generate script and workspace export share one builder and reproduce the completed run snapshot, its accepted controllers, reference, disturbances, initial state and lookahead options, even after draft edits. Source workspace variables are explicit dependencies and must retain their accepted values. Choose a checked scenario prefix for r/v/x0/options/y/t/u (and y2/t2/u2 when comparing). Existing workspace names are replaced transactionally; invalid names, errors and cancellation publish no partial export. Controller only preserves construction-only export; All controllers includes the accepted list in that mode.
Differences from MATLAB: requires the MatRust desktop and named workspace sources. At most 16 controllers, 128 channels/states, 10000 prediction steps, literal fields of 32768 bytes/10000 entries and a 1 MiB generated script; engine memory and cancellation limits also apply. Session files, nonlinear, adaptive/gain-scheduled and explicit MPC, code generation, simulation plant mismatch, noise/UD scenario editors and custom controller initial states are not exposed in this app. Review diagnostics are independent of scenario execution.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/mpc/ref/mpcdesigner-app.html

## mpcmove
Compute an optimal linear MPC move and update the controller state handle.
Syntax: mv = mpcmove(c,s,ym,r[,v,options])
Syntax: [mv,Info] = mpcmove(c,s,ym,r[,v,options])
References have ny columns and 1..p rows; measured disturbances have nmd columns and 1..p+1 rows (current first). Repeat the last supplied row. Empty or omitted ym, r and v use nominal values. Default estimation corrects with M before optimization and advances the prior estimate with L afterward. Custom estimation leaves Plant, Disturbance and Noise for the caller to update. LastMove and handle aliases update in place.
The standard cost sums squared scaled weighted output errors, MV target errors and MV increments, plus Weights.ECR times Slack squared. Info.Cost includes constant terms, without a factor of 1/2. Public OV properties, weights, scales, bounds, reference columns and Yopt columns all use physical plant output order. Weights.ECR must be positive and finite. When any MVRate weight is zero and the move Hessian is singular or has condition above 1e12, add 20*sqrt(eps) to move-coordinate diagonals; Info.Cost excludes this numerical regularization. MV.Target defaults to the nominal MV. Scalar or vector blocking holds specified moves constant. Bounds use scaled ECR softening, with zero ECR meaning hard.
Info contains Uopt, Yopt, Xopt, Topt, Slack, Iterations, QPCode and Cost. Uopt/Yopt/Xopt have p+1 rows, the final Uopt row repeats, Xopt omits measurement-noise states, and trajectories use engineering units. Solver failure holds LastMove; Iterations is -1 for infeasibility, -2 for numerical failure, 0 for an iteration limit. QPCode is feasible, infeasible or unreliable; Cost is meaningful for feasible solutions.
Example: c=mpc(ss(.8,.2,1,0,.1)); s=mpcstate(c); [mv,Info]=mpcmove(c,s,0,1); Info.Cost
Differences from MATLAB: Dense active-set QPs only; at most 200 blocked moves including slack, 4000 inequalities and 128 augmented states, with host workspace limits. Other algorithms and custom constraints are not supported here.

## mpcmoveopt
Create runtime overrides for mpcmove as a scalar structure.
Syntax: options = mpcmoveopt
Supported fields (default []): OutputWeights, MVWeights, MVRateWeights, ECRWeight, OutputMin, OutputMax, MVMin, MVMax, MVUsed (also accepts the documented spelling MVused). Nonempty weight overrides must match the controller constant/time-varying format. Bound overrides require existing finite controller bounds; a row override translates a time-varying profile, and a matrix replaces it. Repeat the final row through the horizon. MVUsed supplies the actual previously applied MV in engineering units, correcting the prior state and rate baseline.
Example: c=mpc(ss(.8,.2,1,0,.1)); c.MV.Max=1; s=mpcstate(c); o=mpcmoveopt; o.MVMax=.5; o.MVRateWeights=.2; mv=mpcmove(c,s,0,1,[],o)
Differences from MATLAB: Options are a structure; other fields explicitly error as not supported, including MVTarget, OnlyComputeCost, CustomConstraint and horizon overrides. Plain scalar structures with supported fields are also accepted.


## mpcsimopt
Create MPC simulation options as a scalar structure.
Syntax: options = mpcsimopt; options = mpcsimopt(c)
Initial state/signal/Model/MVSignal fields default to []. OpenLoop, RefLookAhead, MDLookAhead and StatusBar default to 'off'; Constraints defaults to 'on'. These switches require 'on' or 'off'. StatusBar is accepted and ignored. Unknown fields raise errors naming the field.
PlantInitialState is an absolute physical state vector, defaulting to the simulation plant nominal X. ControllerInitialState is an mpcstate, defaulting to mpcstate(c). A supplied controller state is copied into a private handle for each run, including its warm-start data, so repeated simulations do not mutate the caller.
UnmeasuredDisturbance has Nud columns in physical UD order (default: simulation nominal UD inputs). InputNoise has Nmv columns and is added to the requested physical MVs at the plant. OutputNoise has Nmo columns in physical measured output order and is added only to controller measurements. All signals must be finite, have at most 65536 rows, and hold the final row.
Model accepts an LTI plant or a scalar struct with Plant and optional Nominal (X,U,Y,DX). It changes only the simulation plant. Input/output channel groups must match c.Model.Plant. U/Y inherit controller nominal offsets; X/DX inherit only between ss models with equal state dimension, otherwise zero. Continuous DX is integrated under ZOH once, using the simulation plant dynamics. Nominal offsets are applied once.
OpenLoop='on' bypasses mpcmove. MVSignal has Nmv columns and includes absolute MV offsets; its empty default means zero MVs. Reference is ignored in open loop. Constraints='off' uses a private controller copy with all MV, MV-rate and output bounds removed; the caller's controller remains intact.
Example: c=mpc(ss(.8,.2,1,0,.1)); o=mpcsimopt(c); o.OpenLoop='on'; o.MVSignal=[1;2]; [y,t,u]=sim(c,4,0,o)
Differences from MATLAB: Plain structure, no GUI status bar; ControllerInitialState is isolated per run. ShowOutputNoise and other unlisted options are unsupported. Signals use physical engineering units; noise is additive and UD is an absolute plant input.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/mpc/ref/mpcsimopt.html

## review
Review an MPC controller with bounded text and numerical diagnostics, without plots or changing the controller or estimator mode.
Syntax: review(c)
Syntax: report = review(c)
Zero outputs prints the report even with a semicolon. One output returns a scalar struct silently. No GUI is opened. The text is also report.Text (at most 32768 bytes, subject to host limits). Long vectors show their first eight column-major entries with an explicit ellipsis; report.Weights retains the complete shared weight matrices.
Example: c=mpc(ss(.8,.2,1,0,.1),.1,6,2); r=review(c); r.NominalStability.MaxAbsEigenvalue
Example: c=mpc(ss(.8,.2,1,0,.1)); review(c);
Fields: Plant (States, Inputs, Outputs, MV, MD, UD, MO, UO, Ts), PredictionHorizon, ControlHorizon, Weights, InternalStability, NominalStability, SteadyState, BaselineError, HessianMatrix, Regularization, HardConstraints and Text. Each check contains numeric Assessed and Pass (0/1), Reason and numeric results. Pass=0 with Assessed=0 means not assessed; an unavailable numeric result is NaN and its Matrix is empty. HardConstraints has IssueCount, FiniteBoundEntries and bounded Details. FiniteBoundEntries counts stored finite profile entries, not repeated horizon values.
InternalStability.MaxAbsEigenvalue and Matrix describe Ac, the unconstrained controller alone, with state z=[augmented observer prior; previous scaled MV]. Its pole test allows max |eig(Ac)| <= 1+1e-9, including the default integral controller's unit pole; this is not a claim of asymptotic stability. NominalStability.MaxAbsEigenvalue and Matrix describe Acl, the physical plant connected to that controller, with state [physical plant deviation; z]. Strict nominal stability requires max |eig(Acl)| < 1-1e-9. Neither matrix is the open-loop plant A.
Conventions: signals use scaled deviations internally; plant states stay in engineering units. Prediction rows are internally MO then UO; public OV properties, output weights/scales, bounds and references use physical plant output order. Report steady-state error rows/columns follow physical plant output/reference order. MD and UD stay at nominal, with zero stochastic inputs. References are constant physical values. Nominal U, Y, X, discretized DX, scale factors and MV targets enter the same move objective as mpcmove. Constraints are ignored for stability and offset analysis.
Exact realization: let the first-move law from the actual QP be u=Kx*x_corrected+Kl*u_previous+Kr*r_deviation+k0. Let A, B=Bu, Cm, M and L be the prediction/estimator matrices; x_corrected=(I-M*Cm)*prior+M*ym_deviation, apart from the nominal affine term. Define U=[Kx*(I-M*Cm), Kl], D=Kx*M, Ac=[A-L*Cm,0]+[B;I]*U (the first bracket has a zero bottom row), By=[L+B*D;D], Br=[B*Kr;Kr]. For physical plant Ap, scaled MV matrix Bp, and measured plant rows Cp divided by their output scales, Acl=[Ap+Bp*D*Cp, Bp*U; By*Cp, Ac], Bref=[Bp*Kr;Br]. Matrix dimensions and a bounded Schur iteration are checked before the eigensolve. Custom supplied L/M gains are used as supplied; custom external state estimation is not assessed.
SteadyState.Matrix is Error=I-Ccl*((I-Acl)\Bref), where Ccl=[physical plant C,0]. BaselineError=-Ccl*((I-Acl)\b) also includes the nominal affine term b. No inverse is formed. MaxAbsOffset is the maximum absolute baseline error and unit-step error over positive-output-weight rows/references; zero-weight outputs are excluded from the verdict. Pass requires <=1e-6 engineering units. This tests separate unit steps and the baseline, not all combined reference amplitudes. A non-strictly-stable nominal loop, a rank-deficient I-Acl (smallest singular value <=1e-12*max(1,largest)), a solve residual above 1e-10, or no controlled outputs produces an explicit not-assessed reason.
HessianMatrix.Matrix is the exact condensed solver H in 0.5*z'*H*z+f'*z, z=[scaled MV increments at block starts; ECR slack]. It includes the 2*Weights.ECR slack diagonal and any mpcmove regularization. ConditionNumber=max eig(H)/min eig(H) for SPD H, Inf otherwise. Healthy requires SPD, condition <=1e12 and zero added regularization. Regularization reports the diagonal actually added to move coordinates; a regularized singular objective is never advertised healthy. The Hessian is assembled by the same helper used by mpcmove; it is not the plant, estimator covariance or an uncondensed surrogate.
HardConstraints checks hard MV/rate interval reachability starting at nominal LastMove across the horizon, including held increments, and contradictory hard OV Min/Max. Soft bounds (positive ECR) do not restrict these hard intervals. Details identify the channel and first conflicting step. A pass means no contradiction found by these checks; it does not guarantee plant/output reachability or closed-loop feasibility. Ordinary finite bounds are listed without being declared invalid. Profiles hold their final row as in mpcmove.
Limits: numerical analysis supports up to 32 plant/augmented states, 16 physical inputs/outputs, prediction horizon 128 and 64 QP variables including slack, subject to existing prediction/QP and host memory limits. Blocking vectors and time-varying weight rows retain the actual Hessian check but give explicit not-assessed stability/offset results. Oversized models, construction failures and singular steady-state systems also carry explicit reasons. Cancellation is checked throughout; dense eigensolves have bounded iteration counts. These nominal unconstrained diagnostics are not a safety guarantee for arbitrary constrained trajectories.
Differences from MATLAB: documented numeric nested structs and text only; no GUI, memory-size test, mixed-constraint feasibility proof or soft-weight balance recommendation. The internal pole criterion and strict nominal criterion are stated above. Nonlinear, adaptive, explicit MPC and code generation remain unsupported.
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/mpc/ref/mpc.review.html
Reference: https://www.mathworks.com/help/mpc/ug/optimization-problem.html


## VideoReader
Create a shared handle for a local video stream.
Syntax: v = VideoReader(filename)
Syntax: v = VideoReader(filename, 'CurrentTime', t, 'Tag', tag, 'UserData', data)
Reads the first video stream of RIFF AVI and OpenDML AVI/AVIX. Supports baseline Motion JPEG (MJPG, mjpg, AVRn, dmb1), including standard-table AVI1 frames without DHT, and BI_RGB 24-bit BGR, 32-bit BGRX and 8-bit palettes. Read-only properties: Name, Path, Duration, FrameRate, NumFrames, Height, Width, BitsPerPixel, VideoFormat and Colormap. CurrentTime, Tag and UserData are writable. Copies share the same playback position. Native AVI files remain closed between reads. Other containers and AVI codecs use ffmpeg and ffprobe executables on PATH, or the absolute executable paths in MATRUST_FFMPEG and MATRUST_FFPROBE (also settable with setenv). Relative overrides are errors; empty overrides clear the override. Empty and relative PATH entries are skipped; the current folder is never searched implicitly. No executable is linked or bundled. Tool lookup is cached per engine; changing PATH or an override resets the lookup. VideoReader.getFileFormats() adds common ffmpeg formats when ffmpeg is found, with Extension, Description, ContainsVideo and ContainsAudio fields. Missing tools produce an explicit error.
Example: f=VideoReader.getFileFormats(); f(1).Extension   % avi
Differences from MATLAB: local files only, no audio decoding or remote files. The format list contains struct records rather than FileFormatInfo objects. ffmpeg output is uint8 RGB24 or Grayscale, including high-bit-depth inputs. Metadata capture is limited to 1 MiB; unknown frame counts require a full ffprobe -count_frames pass (potentially expensive). Pipe operations and tool exit time out after 10 seconds; stderr is capped at 32 KiB. Sequential readFrame reuses one streaming child; seeking and indexed reads restart it. This backend is unavailable in wasm builds. Indexed read preserves CurrentTime here; MATLAB R2026b updates it. Progressive JPEG and interlaced JPEG fields are not supported.

## hasFrame
Determine whether a VideoReader has another frame.
Syntax: available = hasFrame(v)
Syntax: available = v.hasFrame()
Returns a logical scalar. CurrentTime equal to Duration means no more frames. A zero-size AVI drop frame remains a frame and repeats its predecessor.
Example: f=VideoReader.getFileFormats(); f(1).ContainsVideo   % true
Differences from MATLAB: audio is ignored.

## readFrame
Read and advance a VideoReader by one frame.
Syntax: frame = readFrame(v)
Syntax: frame = v.readFrame('native')
Returns top-down H-by-W-by-3 uint8 RGB, or H-by-W uint8 for grayscale. Indexed frames are expanded to RGB unless 'native' is requested. Native grayscale and indexed output is a struct with uint8 cdata and colormap (empty for grayscale). Advances CurrentTime by 1/FrameRate, capped at Duration. Reading past the end raises an error. Seek with v.CurrentTime=t; timestamps select the containing frame interval.
Example: f=VideoReader.getFileFormats(); f(1).ContainsAudio   % false
Differences from MATLAB: see VideoReader for formats. Work is cancellable between frames, pipe chunks and native JPEG blocks.

## read
Read VideoReader frames by one-based index without changing CurrentTime.
Syntax: frames = read(v)
Syntax: frame = read(v, k)
Syntax: frames = read(v, [first last])
Syntax: frames = read(v, [first Inf], 'native')
Reads all frames by default; Inf selects the last frame. RGB results are H-by-W-by-3-by-F uint8 and grayscale results H-by-W-by-1-by-F uint8, with trailing singleton dimensions omitted. Native indexed or grayscale output is a 1-by-F struct array with cdata and colormap. Output and decoder scratch are checked against the evaluation memory limit before allocating; use ranges for larger files.
Example: f=VideoReader.getFileFormats(); f(1).Description
Differences from MATLAB: read preserves CurrentTime by this slice's explicit contract; MATLAB R2026b updates it to the frame after the last one read. See VideoReader for supported formats.

## implay

Open the desktop Video Viewer.

Syntax: implay, implay(filename), implay(V), implay(V,fps)

Example: try, implay; catch err, disp(err.message); end

Opens the desktop Video Viewer for AVI files or real uint8, uint16, double, single or logical workspace sequences. Gray sequences are H-by-W-by-F; RGB sequences are H-by-W-by-3-by-F. Workspace sequences default to 20 frames per second. The CLI reports "implay requires the desktop". Store array inputs in a workspace variable before opening them. Use sample data writes a short Motion JPEG AVI in the temporary folder and opens that file.

Differences from MATLAB: desktop only; AVI input and multidimensional workspace arrays are supported. Movie structs, audio, pixel-region tools and colormap editing are not supported.

## VideoWriter
Create a shared handle for a video writer.
Syntax: w = VideoWriter(filename)
Syntax: w = VideoWriter(filename, profile)
Default profile is 'Motion JPEG AVI'; also supports 'Uncompressed AVI', 'Grayscale AVI' and 'Indexed AVI'. With ffmpeg available, also supports 'MPEG-4' (.mp4), 'Motion JPEG 2000' (.mj2, lossy) and 'Archival' (.mj2, lossless). Missing extensions use the selected profile's extension. VideoWriter.getProfiles() adds these profiles only when ffmpeg is found. Read-only properties: Filename, Path, FileFormat, ColorChannels, VideoBitsPerPixel, VideoCompressionMethod, VideoFormat, Height, Width, FrameCount and Duration. Set FrameRate (default 30), Quality (integer 0 to 100, default 75, MJPEG or MPEG-4 only) and Colormap (indexed only) before open. Height and Width are fixed by the first frame. Copies share writing state. JPEG 2000 profiles expose LosslessCompression (Archival defaults true), CompressionRatio (integer >1, default 10, set only while lossy), and MJ2BitDepth (this slice supports 8 or 16 only). Set profile properties before open.
Example: w=VideoWriter('example.avi'); w.FrameRate   % 30
Example: p=VideoWriter.getProfiles(); p(1).Name   % Motion JPEG AVI
Differences from MATLAB: constant-rate output; MPEG-4 uses libx264/yuv420p when available and falls back to mpeg4. JPEG 2000 requires libopenjpeg or jpeg2000. MPEG-4 odd dimensions are padded on the right/bottom to even dimensions. Profiles are struct records rather than ProfileInfo objects; FileExtensions is a character vector. Dimensions are limited to 32767, FrameRate to [0.001,4294], movi data to 1 GiB, and frame count to 1000000. Indexed palettes are padded to 256 entries on disk. No audio or GUI. External encoders use bounded rawvideo pipes and temporary files beside the destination; successful close publishes the file. Errors/cancellation discard external output and preserve an existing destination. Executable discovery follows VideoReader.

## open
Open a VideoWriter for writing and lock its properties.
Syntax: open(w)
Syntax: w.open()
Creates a unique temporary file in the destination directory. Opening an already open writer has no effect. Reopening a closed writer resets frame counts and dimensions; the old destination remains intact until the replacement is finalized.
Example: w=VideoWriter(tempname); open(w); close(w)   % empty writer leaves no output
Differences from MATLAB: atomic replacement delays discarding an existing destination until close. An open writer with no frames leaves no output on close.
